Summer grew progressively fiercer. It was the terrible African summer—after nine in the morning, one could no longer go out in the sun. After eleven o'clock, it felt to Shankar as if every direction were blazing with fire. Yet he heard from the men on the train that compared to the heat of Central Africa and South Africa, this was supposedly nothing at all!

Soon an incident occurred that turned the course of Shankar's life down a completely different path. One morning Shankar had gone fishing. When he was returning, it was three in the afternoon. When the station was still about a mile away, Shankar heard someone in that sun-scorched plain uttering something in a faint, anguished voice. Noting the direction from which the voice was coming, he walked a short distance and saw someone sitting in the scanty patch of shade beneath a yucca tree.

Shankar walked quickly up to him. The man was a European—wearing a patched, tattered, and dirty coat and trousers. He had a face full of red beard, large eyes, and handsome features; one could tell his body had once been quite strong, though now it was emaciated, probably from illness, hardship, and starvation. The man lay slumped against the trunk of the tree in exhaustion. The dirty sola topee on his head had rolled to one side—and beside him lay a large khaki cloth haversack.

Shankar asked in English, "Where are you coming from?" Without answering the question, the man raised his hand to his mouth, made a gesture of drinking, and said, "A little water! Water!"

Shankar said, "There is no water here. Can you lean on me and walk as far as the station?"

With great difficulty, leaning on him part of the way and toward the end practically riding on Shankar's shoulders, the man reached the platform. Bringing him in had caused a delay; the afternoon train had already left in his absence. He made a bed for the man in the station room and laid him down, revived him with water, and brought him some food as well. He perked up a bit, to be sure, but Shankar saw that the man had a high fever. From many days of irregular living, exhaustion, and starvation, his body had broken down completely—he would not recover in just a few days.

A little later, the man introduced himself. His name was Diego Alvarez—Portuguese by birth, though the African sun had burned his complexion copper-brown.

Shankar kept him at the station for the night. But seeing his illness, he found himself in a predicament—there was no medicine here, no doctor; the morning train did not go toward Mombasa, though the guard on the afternoon train could take the patient along. But there was still a long way to go before the night was over. Had the afternoon train been caught at the station, there would have been no problem at all. Shankar stayed awake all night sitting beside the patient. There was no strength left in the man's body. Most likely hardship and starvation were the causes of his illness. In this distant foreign land, he had no one—if Shankar did not look after him, who would?... Ever since childhood, he had been unable to bear the suffering of others—the way Shankar nursed him all through the night, none of the man's own kin could have done any more than he did.

That night, when the moon was rising from behind the low range of hills in the northeast—the silent midnight throbbing with stillness—suddenly the terrifying roar of a lion was heard across the plain. The patient had been dozing; at the lion's roar, he started and sat bolt upright in bed. Shankar said, "Don't be afraid—lie down. A lion is roaring outside; the door is shut."

Input: It felt as though someone were gently stroking my body—ever so lightly. The inside of my head was burning and scorching to cinders then—who was tending to me, I neither could make out nor tried to understand. "So thirsty—a little water." Someone held a glass of water to my lips. After drinking the water, I lay still for a long time. In the darkness I could see nothing—yet someone was fanning me with a hand-fan. * * * * Suddenly, two drops of water fell upon my forehead. What water was this? Again—one, two, three drops! One drop fell upon my lips—and I realised it was tears! Who was sitting at the head of my bed weeping at this hour of the night? Just then, I thought of one person. Yes—one person! Yet, yet why would she weep? Illness, I suppose, makes the human heart fragile. Otherwise, why did a heart as hard as stone as mine get soaked and soften at just a few drops of tears? Softly I called out, "Benu?" I got no answer. "Benu?" The breeze of the fan stopped. "Benu, speak to me!" In an exceedingly faint, trembling voice came the reply, "What is it?" "Why are you crying?" "I'm not crying." "Don't tell a lie." In a fearful, halting voice, Benu said, "I won't—I won't cry anymore." I lay silent. What I was thinking at that moment, I no longer remember. After a long while, I asked, "Why are you awake so late into the night?" "Because you have a fever!" "If I have a fever, what is that to you?" I received no answer. Instead, two drops of water fell upon my forehead. Even eyes that have no sight hold tears of pain! O God! Can two drops of tears lay bare the feelings of a heart like this? Something came over my heart—I reached out both arms and drew Benu down upon my chest. Pressing my face to hers, I kissed her. Benu murmured something indistinctly. Her whole body trembled once from head to foot. Her head drooped onto my shoulder. Then, throwing both arms tight around my chest with all her might, she lay completely still. * * * When the silent funeral pyre of dawn blazed up in the eastern clouds, its light fell upon Benu's blind eyes and dark body. Blind Benu—dark Benu! Even then, she was lying motionless upon my chest just as before. In the half-light and half-shadow of daybreak, I looked once at Benu's blind eyes and dark body. Never before had I looked at her like that, and never afterwards did I get the time to look at her again. Slowly, gently, I ran my hand over her two eyelids. Just as raindrops trapped inside a lotus cup spill over when shaken, tears poured down again in a stream from Benu's eyes. "Benu!" "Oh no, please no, I won't do it again!" "What won't you do?" "I won't cry anymore!" Breaking through my choked throat, I cried out—"No—weep! Let me weep too." And after that? After that, my fever turned into smallpox. Smallpox did not take my life, but it gouged out both my eyes. Like Benu, I too am blind!

Rafi's throat went dry. "Sir, I thought I was going to get scolded in the meeting. Last month's delivery was late..."

"It was late because you caught the client's faulty requirements and rebuilt the whole thing from scratch. That's the mark of real work." Taking a bite of khichuri, Dulabhai said, "Now eat. You'll go to the meeting at four, and keep a look on your face as if your stomachache just cleared up a moment ago."

Rafi ate quietly. The khichuri was warm, and his head was slowly clearing too.

The meeting wrapped up in the evening. Back home, he opened his phone and saw messages still coming into the group. Chhoto Mama had given it a headline: "Rafi's Stomachache: An Investigation." Fupi had posted a recipe for ginger-lemon tea. Boro Chacha wanted to know whether he still needed the hajmola or if he should send it over.

And at the very end, another alarming message from Dadi—not a voice note this time, but text, full of spelling mistakes, surely typed out by someone else for her:

"Dadubhai, has the pain gone down? Come home tomorrow, I'll make bharta for you."

Rafi stared at the screen for a long time. Then he typed—in the right group this time, making sure there was no mistake:

"Dadi, the pain is gone. And I became a team lead today. I'm coming tomorrow—keep some rice ready with the bharta too."

Within five seconds of hitting send, 46 out of the 47 members started typing all at once. Only one person stayed quiet, and that was Chhoto Mama. Because he was already on the phone announcing to the whole group, "Didn't I tell you the boy wasn't running away, he was actually preparing for his meeting!"

Rafi placed his phone face down and smiled. Next time, before trying to run away anywhere, he would at least check the name of the group first—that much he had decided for sure.

Meanwhile, just as your anger kept growing, Bindu's age kept advancing too. Over that perfectly natural matter, all of you grew unnaturally agitated. There is one thing I wonder about when I think of it: why didn't you simply turn Bindu out of your house by force? I understand full well that deep down you are afraid of me. The intelligence that the Creator gave me is something you cannot help respecting inwardly.

In the end, unable to get rid of Bindu by your own power, you sought the refuge of Prajapati, the god of marriage. A groom was settled for Bindu. My elder sister-in-law said, "What a relief! Mother Kali has saved the honour of our family."

I did not know what sort of man the groom was; I heard from all of you that he was worthy in every respect. Bindu clung to my feet and began to weep, saying, "Didi, why must I get married at all?"

I tried hard to console her and said, "Bindu, don't be afraid—I've heard your groom is a good man."

Bindu said, "If the groom is a good man, what do I have that he could possibly like about me?"

The groom's party did not even mention coming to see Bindu before the wedding. Bordi was greatly relieved at that.

Yet day and night, Bindu's weeping would not stop. How terrible her anguish was, I alone knew. I had fought many battles in the household for Bindu's sake, but I did not have the courage to say that her marriage should be called off. On what strength could I even say it? If I were to die, what would become of her?

First of all, she was a girl, and on top of that, a dark-skinned girl; whose house she was going to, and what would become of her there, was better not thought about. Even to think of it made my heart tremble.

Bindu said, "Didi, there are still five days left before the wedding—couldn't death come to me before then?"

I scolded her sharply; yet the Knower of Hearts knows that if Bindu could have passed away in some painless manner, I would have felt relieved.

On the day before the wedding, Bindu went to her elder sister and said, "Didi, I'll happily lie in a corner of your cowshed, I'll do whatever you tell me to do—I beg at your feet, please don't cast me away like this."

For some time now, tears had been falling in secret from Didi's eyes, and they fell that day too. Yet it is not only a matter of the heart; there are the scriptures as well. She said, "You know, Bindi, a husband is a woman's destiny, her salvation, her everything. If suffering is written on your forehead, no one can undo it."

The real truth was that there was no way out in any direction—Bindu had to get married, and whatever happened after that would happen.

I had wanted the wedding to take place right here in our house. But you all insisted that it must take place at the groom's house—that was their family custom.

I understood that if you had to spend a single coin on Bindu's wedding, your family deity would never tolerate it. So I had to remain silent. Yet there is one thing none of you know. I had wanted to tell Didi, but I didn't—for she would have died of fright if she knew—that I secretly decked Bindu out with some of my own jewellery. I suspect it must have caught Didi's eye, but even seeing it, she pretended not to see. In the name of dharma, please forgive her for that.

How wonderful it felt! Where was he? Lying on the wooden cot beside the window of their village home? Would the branches and leaves of the hog-plum tree meet his eyes the moment he opened them? Truly? Would he see them when he opened his eyes?

Shankar slowly opened his eyes.

A dark plain. In the distance, that huge baobab tree stood like a giant in the dim darkness. Suddenly it seemed to him that something was moving on top of a low, round, umbrella-like thatched shed in front of him. The very next moment, he froze with fear and astonishment.

A huge lion was trying to dig a hole in the thatched roof by clawing at it with its paws, and every now and then it brought its nose close to the hole in the roof and sniffed at something!

The distance from him to the shed was twenty cubits at most.

Shankar realized he was in terrible danger. The lion was busy clawing at the thatch of the shed to make a hole; it would go in through there and take a man—it had not seen Shankar yet. There was no one outside the tents anywhere; out of fear of lions, no one stayed outside late at night. He himself was completely unarmed, without even a single stick in his hand.

Shankar began to retreat silently toward the engineer's tent, keeping his eyes on the lion. One minute... two minutes... Shankar had not known before this that he had such control over his own nervous system. Not a single sound of fear escaped his mouth
nor did he try to suddenly turn around and run.

Lifting the flap of the engineer's tent, he went inside and saw the sahib still sitting at the table working. Before the sahib, surprised by his manner, could ask anything, he said, "Sahib, a lion!..."

The sahib jumped up. "Where? Where?"

There was a .375 Mannlicher rifle on the gun rack—the sahib took it down. He gave another rifle to Shankar. The two of them lifted the tent flap and came out slowly. A short distance away was that round shed of the coolie lines. But where was the lion on the roof? Pointing with his finger, Shankar said, "I just saw it, sir. Right on top of that shed, the lion was clawing at the thatch with its paw."

The sahib said, "It has run off. Wake everyone up."

A little later, a great uproar broke out in the camp. Armed with sticks, spears, pickaxes, and clubs, the band of coolies came out shouting—searching everywhere; the thatched roof was indeed found torn open. The lion's paw prints were also found. But the lion had vanished. More wood and dry straw were thrown onto the fire pit and the fire was blazed up again. Many did not sleep well that night, nor did anyone really stay outside the tents. Toward the end of the night, Shankar had fallen asleep for a bit lying in his own tent—his sleep was broken by the sound of a great commotion. The Maasai coolies were shouting, "Simba! Simba!" Two gunshots rang out. Shankar came out of his tent, asked what had happened, and learned that the lion had come and mauled a pack mule in the stable—just moments ago! Everyone had dozed off a little toward the end of the night, and right at that time this happened.

The next day, as evening was falling, the lion carried off a young coolie from within a hundred cubits of the camp. Four days later, it took another coolie from beneath the baobab tree.

Input: The ship was sailing on blue waters. This ship was entirely their own. The entire sea route to Amrita-Dwip was drawn on their map. Just looking at that map made it clear that no merchant vessel or passenger liner ever called at that island; there was no mention of the island on any chart at all. Consequently, at Bimal and Kumar's proposal, an entire ship had been chartered. This was nothing new for them either. For it was by chartering an entire ship like this that they had once before rediscovered "Lost Atlantis." Jayanta, Manik, and Sundarbabu had had no desire to join this expedition. Bimal and Kumar had practically dragged them along by force. Naturally, their old servant and veritable guardian Ramhari, despite expressing plenty of irritation, had not failed to come along in the end this time either, just as on other occasions. And in such a case, it goes without saying that their ever-faithful four-legged warrior Bagha would not fail to come along wagging his tail either. Among their old group, only Binaybabu and Kamal could not be had as companions this time. Driven by malaria, Binaybabu was now busy making good use of quinine and slices of ginger, while Kamal was about to sit for his final examination at the Medical College this year. The name of the ship was the "Little Majestic." Though small in size, for the comfort and convenience of the passengers there was no lack of a splendidly furnished lounge, dining saloon, promenade deck, palm court, and the like aboard her. Chartering such a ship was certainly a very costly affair, but everyone knew that Bimal and Kumar were extremely wealthy. On top of that, Jayanta too had refused to be a non-paying guest, and he himself was a decidedly wealthy man. By then the ship had nearly crossed the Tung-Hai, or East Sea, and was advancing past the Ryukyu Islands toward the Pacific Ocean. Above, below, and on all four sides stretched only an endless expanse of blue—restless near at hand, tranquil in the distance. In this world of blue, only the garlands of white foam below and the flocks of white seabirds in the sky above were creating a new hue. On Nature's palette there was no other color now. Nor was there the chime of new melodies in Nature's music here. There was neither the rustle of exuberant greenery nor the melodic play of songbirds; only a wild wind blew with a rushing roar, and only the surging, murmuring chant of the primeval ocean rose—both of these sounds born in the very first age of the earth, when green trees and songbirds had not yet come into being. Pacing up and down the open promenade deck, Manik said, "How much longer until our sea voyage ends, Bimalbabu?" Bimal said, "Not much longer now. We have already covered three-fourths of the way. I know the map by heart. Going a little further ahead, we shall come near the Bonin Islands. Keeping them to our left, we shall have to head roughly southeast. Right after that lies Amrita-Dwip." Manik said, "The island is surely not large. For if it were, it would be mentioned on mariners' charts. I see countless such unknown tiny islands in the sea around here. How will you recognize Amrita-Dwip?"

Input: Through a gap in a cluster of palm trees, the face of the full moon was peeking out playfully. Over water, land, and sky—everywhere—the silvery outlines of moonlight lay scattered, and seeing that day and night had struck up a friendship, the darkness today seemed too afraid to take on its own form. One by one, everyone climbed into the lifeboat! Piercing the clear water of the lake, the moonlight reached down into the depths below. Yet their eyes could not spot what they were searching for down there. Even so, the possibility of something terrifyingly impossible kept the blue depths of the lake shrouded in mystery. * * * * Putting out the lamp of the moon, the crimson dawn arrived. Flooding the ocean with light, it painted the blood-red tilak of the young sun across the eastern sky. The ship was speeding toward Amrita-Dwip. While taking his morning walk on the deck, Sundarbabu paused for a moment, holding on to the ship's railing. And instantly, his eyes gave a violent start. In an excited voice he called out, "Jayanta! Manik! Bimalbabu! Kumarbabu!" Everyone had been strolling about here and there, and at Sundarbabu's urgent summons they came rushing over at once. Pale-faced, Sundarbabu pointed a finger toward the sea. Right beside the ship, floating in the blue water, was the bloodless, white corpse of a human being. Its expressionless, unblinking, wide-open eyes stared blankly toward the ship. There was not the slightest sign of life in its stiff body, it was true—yet how astonishing, against the current, it was rushing along with a whooshing sound right alongside the speeding ship! With a stunned face, Jayanta said, "Am I dreaming?" Bimal said nothing; leaning out over the railing, he began to examine the figure more closely. Sundarbabu said in a bitter voice, "Manik, is that your mermaid? Is that the corpse of an old Chinaman? That is the very thing that attacked me yesterday!" Manik said, "Surely he was a passenger on the pirate ship, and drowned in yesterday's typhoon." —"Hmph, drowned indeed! Which is why he's forging ahead against the current, racing neck and neck with a steamship!" Trembling all over, Ramhari said, "Chant the name of Ram, everyone—chant the name of Ram—chant the name of Ram. That's a ghoul, it wants to drink our blood!" Kumar said, "Bimal, remember the Taoist sages. Those who become 'Hsien' or immortals can move unhindered through water, land, and air! Perhaps today we are clearly seeing one of the 'Hsien' of Amrita-Dwip right before our eyes." Jayanta said, "In this day and age, how can we believe such preposterous tales?" Bimal said, "We have no choice but to believe it, Jayantababu! During the Dragon's Nightmare case, didn't I remind you that no one can say how many hundreds of years Trailanga Swami of Kashi lived? That from time to time his body, too, would float about on the waters of the Ganga for years on end? The story of Trailanga Swami isn't mythology—it belongs to the modern age!" —"Bimalbabu, I can't find any argument to counter you, nor do I have the power to dismiss what I am seeing plainly before my eyes. Still, I feel as though all of us have gone mad together! Is even this possible? A swift yet stiff, motionless corpse racing alongside a modern steamship! After this, what is left for me to disbelieve? Now I wouldn't even be surprised to see an immovable mountain get up and walk!"

Input: The frontier provinces that stood like the main gate to Northern India—and through which the Greeks first had to wield their swords with all their might as they advanced—had certain distinct characteristics in that age. Nowadays, the lands along India's northern frontier are inhabited chiefly by Muslims. However, Alexander came to India many hundreds of years before the birth of Muhammad. Consequently, there was not a single Muslim in the world at that time (nor was there a single Christian, for Alexander crossed the Hindu Kush mountains with his army three hundred and twenty-seven years before the birth of Jesus Christ). The religion prevailing in India then was mainly Vedic Hinduism. The European Greeks were idol-worshippers. Yet as I have hinted earlier, the Hindus in all likelihood did not fashion images or build temples for worship at that time, or even if they did, the practice had not become widespread. The opinion of many historians is that the custom of building temples and fashioning idols became prevalent in this country in imitation of the Greeks. Jainism and Buddhism had gained some footing in India by then, it is true, yet no images of the Jina or the Buddha had been made either. The very first image of the Buddha was also born as a result of Greek influence. The frontier lands were inhabited at that time not only by the people of India, but also by various foreign peoples. From one direction came the inhabitants of China, from another came nomadic tribes of Central Asia such as the Sakas and the Huns, and from yet another came Aryans such as the Persians and the Greeks. As a result of mingling with people of so many different religions and races, the outlook of many Indians living along the frontier had become largely cosmopolitan. Under such circumstances, it was only natural for feelings of patriotism and Hindu identity to grow somewhat weak. Perhaps for that very reason, the number of Hindus in the Frontier Province is so small today. You will be astonished to hear that even in that age, there was no dearth of traitors in India. There was one man who had formerly been a paid mercenary of the Persians, and who later became a trusted Hindu general of Alexander. His name was Shashigupta; the Greeks called him Sisicottus. Alongside the Greeks, he too took up the sword against India, and he too was a native of Northern India. After Alexander's arrival in India, many more traitorous Hindus of the frontier joined—or were compelled to join—the Greek army. In that era, a famous kingdom of the frontier was Takshashila. Twenty or twenty-two miles from the modern city of Rawalpindi, the ruins of ancient Takshashila can still be seen today. Yet even though one is overwhelmed at the sight of these ruins, we cannot begin to guess from them the story of Takshashila's past glory. For in the ancient Eastern world, Takshashila was one of the foremost cities. According to the Jataka tales, Takshashila was a city belonging to the kingdom of Gandhara; Gandhari, the queen of King Dhritarashtra and mother of Duryodhana in the "Mahabharata", was a daughter of this very land. Modern Peshawar was also another place within that same Gandhara, though its name then was "Purushapura"—the City of Men. That the physiques of the people there were like those of true men can still be surmised by looking at the people of Peshawar today. Takshashila had also earned immense renown for the pursuit of knowledge and science. Even Varanasi, one of the premier seats of learning in ancient India, was indebted to Takshashila for various branches of knowledge. Especially to learn the science of medicine, students from all over India had to travel to Takshashila in those days. Jivaka, the court physician of King Bimbisara of Patna or Pataliputra, had to live in Takshashila for seven years to complete his education. Later, in the era of Emperor Kanishka, Takshashila prospered even further, because Kanishka's capital was located right in Purushapura. By the way, let me mention that Kanishka, the Buddhist Emperor of India belonging to the Saka dynasty, established a wondrous temple in Purushapura that was counted among the wonders of the ancient world. The temple was made of wood. Thirteen stories high. And four hundred feet in height—which is to say, nearly three times as tall as the Monument in Kolkata. Built in the second century, that temple no longer exists today; Mahmud, the Muslim conqueror of Ghazni, destroyed it.

Input: We entered the scene of the crime by way of Kali Biswas Lane. First of all, Hemanta walked all around the entire house, inspecting everything. Then, standing on the veranda in front of Matibabu's bedroom, he examined the imprint of the rubber shoes. Seeing us, the mastiff dog glared at us angrily and kept growling from time to time. Stepping inside the room, we saw Matibabu's dead body. Sitting down beside the corpse, Hemanta said, "Mr. Datta, you are a doctor. What is your belief? Did someone throttle Matibabu to death?" —"What else can I say?" —"Then what is that blue mark across his throat? That isn't the mark of fingers! At first glance, it looks as though it were some transparent bandage. Finger marks do not look like that." —"I think the finger marks have faded away. That is the mark of a bruise." "Hmm, I see that a bit of the glove has been cut by the broken glass of the tumbler too." —page 29 —"Possible. It will be known for certain once the post-mortem is carried out. Tell me, Satishbabu, does any Bengali in Bengal wear gloves on his hands even in winter?" Satishbabu said, "Not so far as I know. At the very least, I have ascertained that no one in this household has ever used gloves." Picking up the glove from the floor, Hemanta said, "An exceedingly thick white woolen glove. There are bloodstains on this as well. Hmm, I see that a bit of the glove has been cut by the broken glass of the tumbler too. The glass tumbler is broken as well, and there are bloodstains on the shards of glass—astonishing!" Satishbabu asked, "Why, what makes you so astonished?" First Hemanta lifted the corpse slightly and examined the floor underneath it. Then, looking toward the bed, he asked, "Did this glass tumbler belong to Matibabu?" —"Yes, the tumbler used to sit over the mouth of the water-pitcher in that corner of the room. Just look—the mouth of the pitcher is bare now." —"From the signs of a struggle on the bed, it is clear that Matibabu grappled with the murderers for a little while. Nowhere else in the room are there any signs of a struggle. Suppose the murderers seized Matibabu by the throat, and struggling wildly, Matibabu tumbled onto the floor and was overpowered—yet the tumbler had broken even before that, because there is broken glass underneath the back of the corpse as well. ... Still, why did the tumbler break? And why was the murderer's hand cut by the glass of the tumbler? Surely the tumbler didn't suddenly come alive, spread wings like a bird, leave the mouth of the water-pitcher, and fly over to attack the murderers? Even if we say that one of the murderers was holding the tumbler in his hand during the struggle, the question still arises: what connection does a glass tumbler have with throttling a man?" In an admiring voice, Satishbabu exclaimed, "Exactly! Hemantababu, you have discovered a tremendous clue! I hadn't thought of that until now!" Hemanta said, "I see the bottom part of the tumbler is still intact. Its inside, however, is completely dry. Even so, it ought to be sent over to the police laboratory once. Perhaps there is some trace of poison inside it. It is also possible that the murderer's fingerprints are on its surface." Then Shankar slowly opened the door and came out to stand on the platform. The moment he stood there and looked around, the exquisite beauty of the night cast a spell over him. The moon had risen on the far edge of the sky—the long shadows of the yucca trees stretched from east to west, and the sea of grass looked mysterious, motionless. The lion was roaring within five hundred yards behind the station quarters. But the roaring of lions had become a familiar thing to Shankar these days—it no longer frightened him as before. The beauty of the night drew him in so deeply that he seemed to forget the lion's proximity. He turned back and entered the station room. Dong, dong—the clock struck two. Entering the room, he saw the patient sitting up in bed. He said, "Give me a little water, I want to drink."

The man spoke English quite well. Shankar took water from the tin and gave him a drink.

The man's fever seemed to have subsided a bit by then. He said, "What were you saying? Did you think I was afraid? Diego Alvarez, afraid? Young man, you don't know Diego Alvarez." A strange smile mingling despair, sadness, and mockery appeared at the corner of the man's lips. He sank back exhausted against the pillow. At that smile, it struck Shankar that this was no ordinary man. Then Shankar's eyes fell upon his hands. Short, thick fingers—veined, rope-like hands; beneath the coppery beard, the set of his chin bespoke a man of iron. After all this time, as the fever ebbed a little, the real man seemed to be emerging slowly.

The man said, "Come closer. You have done a great deal for me. Even if I had a son of my own, he could not have done more. But let me tell you one thing—I will not live. My heart tells me my days are numbered. I want to do you a good turn before I go. Are you Indian? How much pay do you get here? Since you have left your country and come this far for such a meager salary, you have courage and the strength to endure hardship. Listen carefully to what I say, but promise me that the things I am going to tell you today—you will not reveal them to anyone before my death?"

Shankar gave him that assurance. Then, as that strange night slowly wore on, he listened to a tale so wondrous and unbelievable—the kind one ordinarily reads only in novels.

"Young man, how old would you be? Twenty-two?... When you were a babe in your mother's arms—twenty years ago today, around the years 1888–89, I was wandering among the hills and jungles north of Cape Colony searching for gold mines. I was young then, and I didn't care a straw for any danger in the world.

"Buying supplies from the town of Bulawayo, I set out all alone, with only two donkeys to carry my gear! Crossing the Zambezi River, I moved on; the way and the land were completely unknown—nothing but low hills, grass, and every now and then a Kaffir kraal. Gradually human habitation grew sparser, until I arrived at a place where no European had ever set foot before.

"Wherever I saw a river or a stream—or a hill—first of all I looked for gold-bearing strata. How many people had struck it rich in South Africa! How many tales I had heard about this since childhood—and it was the lure of those stories that had brought me to Africa. Yet for two years I wandered about in vain. What unbearable hardships I endured during those two years! Once, even after finding a trace, I lost it again."

লোকটা বল্লে—সরে এসো কাছে। তুমি আমার যথেষ্ট উপকার করেচ। আমার নিজের ছেলে থাকলে এর বেশি করতে পারতো না। তবে একটা কথা বলি—আমি বাঁচবো না। আমার মন বলছে আমার দিন ফুরিয়ে এসেচে। তোমার উপকার করে যেতে চাই। তুমি ইণ্ডিয়ান? এখানে কত মাইনে পাও? এই সামান্য মাইনের জন্যে দেশ ছেড়ে এত দূর এসে আছ যখন, তখন তোমার সাহস আছে, কষ্ট সহ্য করবার শক্তি আছে। আমার কথা মন দিয়ে শোনো, কিন্তু প্রতিজ্ঞা করো আজ তোমাকে যেসব কথা বলবো—আমার মৃত্যুর পূর্ব্বে তুমি কারো কাছে তা প্রকাশ করবে না?

শঙ্কর সেই আশ্বাসই দিলে। তারপর সেই অদ্ভুত রাত্রি ক্রমশঃ কেটে যাওয়ার সঙ্গে সঙ্গে সে এমন এক আশ্চর্য্য, অবিশ্বাস্য ধরনের আশ্চর্য্য কাহিনী শুনে গেল—যা সাধারণতঃ উপন্যাসেই পড়া যায়।

ইয়্যাং ম্যান্, তোমার বয়স কত হবে? বাইশ?…তুমি, যখন মায়ের কোলে শিশু— আজ বিশ বছর আগের কথা, ১৮৮৮-৮৯ সালের দিকে আমি কেপ কলোনির উত্তরে পাহাড়-জঙ্গলের মধ্যে সোনার খনির সন্ধান করে বেড়াচ্ছিলাম। তখন বয়েস ছিল কম, দুনিয়ার কোনো বিপদকেই বিপদ বলে গ্রাহ্য করতাম না।

বুলাওয়েও সহর থেকে জিনিষপত্র কিনে একাই রওনা হলাম, সঙ্গে কেবল দুটী গাধা, জিনিষপত্র বইবার জন্যে! জাম্বেজী নদী পার হয়ে চলেচি, পথ ও দেশ সম্পূর্ণ অজ্ঞাত, শুধু ছোটখাটো পাহাড়, ঘাস, মাঝে মাঝে কাফিরদের বস্তি। ক্রমে যেন মানুষের বাস কমে এল, এমন এক জায়গায় উপস্থিত এসে পৌঁছনো গেল, যেখানে এর আগে কখনো কোনো ইউরোপীয়ান আসেনি।

যেখানেই নদী বা খাল দেখি—কিংবা পাহাড় দেখি—সকলের আগে সোনার স্তরের সন্ধান করি। লোকে কত কি পেয়ে বড় মানুষ হয়ে গিয়েচে দক্ষিণ আফ্রিকায়, এ সম্বন্ধে বাল্যকাল থেকে কত কাহিনীই শুনে এসেছিলুম—সেই সব গল্পের মোহই আমায় আফ্রিকায় নিয়ে এসে ফেলেছিল। কিন্তু বৃথাই দু’ বৎসর নানাস্থানে ঘুরে বেড়ালুম। কত অসহ্য কষ্ট সহ্য করলুম এই দু’ বছরে। একবার তো সন্ধান পেয়েও হারালুম।

Meanwhile, Rupa's mother had still not recovered from her fluster—the children from the babus' house had come to her home, and what did she have to welcome them with? She brought out two piris and a torn rush mat for them to sit on, fetched larus and placed them in everyone's hands, and kept scurrying in and out of the room in a flurry.
The two mongooses were no less lively; in playful mock-fighting they tumbled together, darted across to the far end of the courtyard, came running back at Rupa's call, and then in the blink of an eye vanished inside the room again. Calling them back once more, Rupa held out both her arms, and the two of them scampered right up her arms onto her shoulders. While traveling along this road, Alvarez said, "Passing through Tanganyika is a very dangerous business. There is a kind of fly here whose bite causes sleeping sickness. Tanganyika has become depopulated by the plague of sleeping sickness. On the road from Mwanza to Tabora, the danger from lions is also very great. In fact, this region of Africa too may well be called the 'Kingdom of Lions.'"

Ten miles from the town, beside the road, stood a small thatched bungalow. A European hunter had taken shelter there. He welcomed Alvarez warmly. Looking at Shankar, he said, "Where did you find him? He's a Hindu! Your coolie?"

Alvarez said, "My son."

Astonished, the sahib said, "How is that?"

Alvarez recounted everything from beginning to end—his illness, and how Shankar had nursed him. The only thing he did not mention was where they were going and for what purpose.

The sahib smiled and said, "Very good indeed. Looking at his face, it seems he has both courage and kindness in his heart. The Hindus of the East Indies are good people indeed. Once in Uganda a Sikh showed me such wonderful hospitality that I shall never be able to forget it. Come in today; night is falling, so spend the night right here with me. This is a government dak bungalow; like you, I too walked all day and put up here in the afternoon."

The sahib had a small gramophone; after evening fell and they had finished their supper of tinned English tomato soup and sardines, everyone lay back in camp chairs outside the bungalow listening to record after record, when the roar of a lion was heard not far off. It sounded as if the lion were roaring with its mouth lowered close to the ground—for the earth itself seemed to tremble. The sahib said, "There is a terrible menace of lions in Tanganyika. And they are fiercely savage. Almost all of them are man-eaters. Having once tasted human blood, they now want nothing other than human flesh."

Shankar thought to himself that this was fine news indeed. During the building of the Uganda Railway, he had seen all too well what the menace of lions meant.

The next morning they set off again; the sahib warned them to be very careful once the sun was up. The sleeping sickness fly wakes as soon as the sun shines. They must not let it settle on their bodies.

A narrow footpath wound through forests of tall grass. Alvarez said, "Be very careful, these tall grass forests are the haunt of lions; don't fall too far behind."

Alvarez had a gun—that was one comfort. Another comfort was that Alvarez was what they call a "crack shot"—that is to say, his bullet rarely missed its mark. Yet even with such an unerring marksman beside him, Shankar did not feel very reassured, for he knew from his experience in Uganda that when a lion takes someone, it strikes so completely without warning that it does not even give a man time to undo the leather strap of the rifle on his back.

That day, about an hour before nightfall, they had to choose a spot in the middle of the vast plain to rest for the night. Alvarez said, "There is no village ahead. It is not wise to travel here after dark."

Under a huge baobab tree, two pieces of canvas were slung up to pitch a tiny tent. Gathering twigs and firewood, Shankar lit a fire and sat down to prepare the evening meal. Then, after the day's hard toil, both of them lay down and fell asleep.

Late at night, Alvarez called out, "Shankar, get up."

Shankar started and sat up in bed.

Alvarez said, "Some animal is prowling around the tent—keep your gun ready." Indeed, the sound of some unknown large beast breathing could be heard right outside the thin canvas flap of the tent. In the faint dying glow of the fire that had been lit in front of the tent that evening, the huge baobab tree looked like a fearsome giant. When Shankar tried to get out of bed with his gun, the old man stopped him.

Just then another market vendor, Satish Kolu the oil-presser, arrived on the spot carrying a large earthen pot of mustard oil set inside a bamboo basket on his head. Spotting Nalu by the roadside, he said, "Come on, aren't you coming?"

"Sit down. Have a smoke of tobacco."

"I don't have any tobacco."

"I do. Wait a bit, let Shipton Sahib pass by first."

"Who said the Sahib is coming?"

"Ray Mashay told me as he rode past—sit down—"

Suddenly Satish Kolu looked ahead in terror and scrambled straight down into the low-lying paddy field past a thicket of shanra and sheora bushes. As he went, he called back, "Come on down, the Sahib is out on the road—"

Leaving his bundle of betel leaves lying right there under the tree, Nalu Pal followed Satish Kolu. In the distance, the jingling bells of the tandem horse could be heard. right at Nalu Pal's resting place beneath their banyan tree, directly in front of them.

Seeing the bundle of betel leaves lying unattended under the banyan tree, the Sahib called out loudly, "Hey! Whose bundle is this?"

By then Nalu Pal and Satish Kolu had turned stiff as wood behind the screen of paddy stalks. Neither of them answered.

From the back of the tandem cart, the orderly Nafar Muchi shouted, "Hey, whose bundle is lying here under the tree?"

The Sahib said, "Give an answer—who is there?"

With a sheepish face and folded hands, Nalu Pal climbed back up onto the road and said, "Sahib, it is mine."

The Sahib stared at him and remained silent. He did not say a word.

Nafar Muchi asked, "Is this your bundle?"

"Yes, sir."

"What were you doing down in the paddy field?"

"Sir—sir—"

The Sahib said, "I know. Everyone sees me and hides. Am I a snake or am I a tiger? Eh?"

Since the question was asked looking straight at Nalu Pal's face, Nalu Pal answered timidly, "No, Sahib."

"Right. What is in the bundle?"

"Betel leaves, Sahib."

"Taking it to the Mollahati market?"

"Yes."

"What is your name?"

"Sir, Shri Nalamohan Pal."

"Put it on your head. In future, do not hide when you see me. I am not a tiger, I do not eat people.

Go on—understand?"

"Yes, sir—"

The Sahib's tandem cart drove off. Nalu Pal's heart was still thumping wildly against his ribs. Whew, what a close shave he had managed to survive today! Whistling to himself, he called out, "O Satish Khuro!"

Keeping behind the cover of the paddy plants, Satish Kolu had crept even further away from the road. Coming back toward him, he called out, "Coming!"

"Goodness, how far did you run away? Did you see him calling me and bolt straight through the paddy field?"

However you kept me, it never even crossed my mind to think that I was in sorrow. In the birthing room, death came and stood by my head, and I felt no fear at all. What is this life of ours that we should fear death? Only those whose bonds to life have been strengthened by love and care find it hard to die. That day, had Yama taken hold of me and pulled, I would have come up root and all, just as easily as a clump of grass is pulled from loose soil. A Bengali woman goes to her death over the smallest thing. But what bravery is there in dying like that? One feels ashamed to die—for us, it is all too easy.

My little daughter rose like the evening star for a brief moment and then set. Once again I threw myself into my daily chores and my cows and calves. Life would have rolled along just like that until the very end; there would have been no need for me to write you this letter today. But the wind blows in a tiny seed, and a peepal sprout shoots up inside a solid brick building; in the end, from that tiny thing, the very ribs of brick and timber are torn apart. Right in the middle of the solid arrangements of my household, a tiny little speck of life blew in from somewhere and fell; and from then on, the crack began.

After her widowed mother died, when my elder sister-in-law's sister Bindu came to take shelter with her elder sister in our house because of the mistreatment of her paternal cousins, all of you thought that day: Where did this nuisance come from now? What can I do about my wretched nature, tell me—when I saw that all of you were inwardly irritated, my whole heart seemed to gird its loins and stand firmly beside this helpless girl. To come and take shelter in another's house against their wishes—what a terrible humiliation that is! Even someone whom you are forced to take in out of obligation—can she just be pushed aside into a corner?

Then I saw the plight of my elder sister-in-law. Out of sheer compassion, she had brought her sister to live with her. Yet once she saw her husband's displeasure, she began to act as though this girl were a dreadful nuisance to her, as if she would be relieved just to be rid of her. She did not have the courage to show open, heartfelt affection to this orphaned sister of hers. She is a devoted wife.

Seeing her predicament, my heart ached all the more. I watched as my elder sister-in-law, making sure everyone noticed, arranged such coarse food and clothing for Bindu and set her to every kind of maidservant's drudgery in the house that I felt not only sorrow, but shame. She was anxious to prove to everyone that our household had struck a great bargain in getting Bindu practically for nothing. She did a vast amount of work, while in terms of expense she was dirt cheap.

My elder sister-in-law's father's family had little else besides noble lineage—neither beauty nor money. You know full well how her family begged and pleaded at my father-in-law's feet to get her married into your house. Rushing up in a great hurry, the old man took a puff or two at his hukka and asked, 'Well, is the calculation done?'

The crow glanced this way and that for a moment and said, 'It's just about done.'

The old man said, 'How astonishing! Nineteen days have gone by, and the calculation still isn't finished?'

Looking very solemn, the crow sucked on its pencil for two or three minutes and then asked, 'How many days did you say?'

The old man said, 'Nineteen.'

At once the crow craned its neck and called out loud, 'Going, going, going—twenty!'

The old man said, 'Twenty-one.' The crow said, 'Twenty-two.' The old man said, 'Twenty-three.' The crow said, 'Twenty-three and a half.' Just as if they were bidding at an auction.

In the middle of calling out bids, the crow suddenly looked at me and asked, 'Why aren't you bidding?'

I said, 'Why on earth should I bid for no reason?'

The old man hadn't noticed me until now; the instant he heard my voice, he spun around eight or ten times like a top and stopped facing me.

Then he held the hukka up to his eyes like a telescope and stared at me for a long time. After that, he pulled a few pieces of colored glass out of his pocket and peered at me through them again and again. Next, producing an old tailor's tape measure from somewhere, he began taking my measurements while calling out loud, 'Height twenty-six inches, sleeve twenty-six inches, cuff twenty-six inches, chest twenty-six inches, neck twenty-six inches!'

I objected vehemently and said, 'That cannot be! My chest is twenty-six inches and my neck is twenty-six inches too? Am I a pig?'

The old man said, 'If you don't believe me, look for yourself.'

I saw that almost all the numbers and markings on the tape had worn off; only the number 26 was faintly legible, so whatever the old man measured came out to twenty-six inches.

Then the old man asked, 'What is your weight?'

I said, 'I don't know!'

Pinching me lightly with two fingers, the old man said, 'Two and a half seers.'

I said, 'How can that be? Even Patla weighs twenty-one seers, and he's a year and a half younger than me!'

The crow immediately chimed in hurriedly, 'Your way of calculating is different from ours.'

The old man said, 'Then write it down—weight two and a half seers, age thirty-seven.'

I said, 'Nonsense! I am eight years and three months old, and he says thirty-seven!'

After pondering something for a moment, the old man asked, 'Going up or going down?'

I asked, 'Now what does that mean?'

The old man said, 'I mean, is your age increasing right now or decreasing?'

I said, 'How can anyone's age decrease?'

The old man said, 'Why, is it supposed to just keep going up forever? Then we'd be done for! One day we'd find our age had kept climbing until it passed sixty, seventy, eighty years, and in the end we'd grow old and die!'

I said, 'Well, of course that's what happens. When people reach eighty years of age, won't they grow old?'

The old man said, 'What brains you have! Why would anyone become eighty years old? The moment we reach forty, we turn our age around. Then it doesn't become forty-one or forty-two anymore—it starts coming down: thirty-nine, thirty-eight, thirty-seven. When it comes down like that all the way to ten, we let the age go up again. When he was hungry, Charan Majhi had refused to give him two bananas, and for a moment Naga felt like telling Madhabbabu the real price of the bananas. Right after that, he remembered that among the poor boatmen, Charan Majhi was poorer still. Was it for pleasure that he had ripened the bananas over a fire without giving them time to ripen on the tree? What fun was there in taking revenge by making him, his wife, and his children starve?
Madhabbabu's wife said, 'You're busy buying this and that, but where is Thakurpo? Where is the boat?' Forgetting his triumph over buying the bananas, Madhabbabu grew worried and said, 'That's true, I don't see Jadab anywhere. Didn't he write that he would bring a boat?'
Naga gave him the news about Jadabbabu. Hearing it, Madhabbabu's wife said, 'Do you see that? Do you see your brother's antics? We are arriving today, coming after all these years, and today of all days he had to go get his palm read!'
Madhabbabu said, 'Come, let's go sit in the boat. Who are you, boy?' Naga smiled and said, 'Me? I'm nobody, Karta!'
'Trying to be cheeky, are you?' said Madhabbabu angrily, and walked ahead with his family. Only then did it probably occur to him that he had no idea where his brother's boat was. Having no choice, he called upon Naga himself to point out the boat.
Naga had not understood the reason for Madhabbabu's anger, and being scolded for nothing had made him angry too. He said indifferently, 'Who knows where the boat is!'
Madhabbabu then said in a sweet voice, 'Come now, my boy, come—why are you angry?'
More than the sweetness of his tone, hearing Madhabbabu speak in their own local dialect at last made Naga's anger melt away like water. Not only did he point out the boat, he also helped them get the children and the luggage aboard; when the eldest girl lost her footing the moment she stepped onto the boat and was about to topple into the river, he steadied her, and at the request of Madhabbabu's wife he even held the one-and-a-half-year-old boyin his arms for a while. Then he went and sat on the prow of his own boat. Sitting there, he watched their goings-on. Probably for fear of having to disembark at any moment, even though they had nibbled on this and that on the steamer, their morning breakfast had been put off. As soon as they had settled in a little, preparations for it began. And what preparations! Even though the planks of the boat were clean, a satranji was spread out; from a large cane basket came tinned plates, glasses, teacups, a kettle, and a huge covered aluminum dekchi. A massive tiffin carrier was also separated from the pile of luggage and brought out. Madhabbabu's wife served food to everyone. From the dekchi she served luchi, and from the tiffin carrier she served begun bhaja, alur dom, and several kinds of sweets.
Over on that boat they went on eating, while on this boat Naga thought to himself: goodness, they are no ordinary gluttons! Coming from so far away, they have brought along a wedding or sacred-thread feast just for their morning breakfast!
The thin, fair-complexioned boy of Naga's own age suddenly remarked, 'Look how he's staring at us eating with his mouth wide open!'

"The stone belonged to South Africa's famous class of yellow diamonds. Of course, there was no reason for great rejoicing yet, because this only proved that in some unknown, inaccessible part of this vast mountain range there was a mine of yellow diamonds. A fragment from one of its strata had been washed down by the river current. To track down that parent mine would require superhuman labor, patience, and courage.

"We would not have lacked that labor, courage, and patience, had not the monster that guards the priceless diamond mine of those mysterious forested mountains thwarted us in a completely unexpected way.

"One day toward evening we were sitting resting in a clearing inside the forest; in front of us in that clearing stood a palm tree, and around the base of the trunk beneath the palm tree was a very thick tangle of brushwood. Suddenly we saw something shaking that huge palm tree so violently that its dry fronds up top were rattling and rustling just as they do when a storm hits. The trunk itself was swaying along with them.

"We were astonished. There was no wind anywhere, yet why was the palm tree shaking? It seemed to us as if someone were grasping the trunk of the palm tree and giving it a shake. Right away, Jim went into that thicket at the base of the trunk to see what was going on.

"Shortly after he entered it, I heard a scream and came running with my rifle. Plunging into the bushes, I saw Jim lying in the brush covered in blood—some terribly powerful beast had ripped and torn him open with sharp claws from the front of his face down to his chest—just as one rips open an old pillow and pulls out the cotton. Jim only gasped, 'The devil himself—the devil incarnate—'

"Motioning with his hand, he said, 'Run—run—'

"Right after that, Jim died. Looking at the trunk of the palm tree, I saw what looked like thick, coarse bristles stuck to the bark. It occurred to me that some terribly powerful animal had been rubbing its body against the trunk of the palm tree, and that was why the tree had been shaking like that. I found no trace of the beast. After carrying Jim's body out into the clearing, I went with rifle in hand to the other side of the thicket. Going there, I saw the footprints of some unknown animal on the ground; it had only three toes on each foot. I went some distance following the footprints; a little way into the jungle, the tracks led into the mouth of a cave. On the dry sand near the entrance of the cave lay the large three-toed paw prints of that unknown, terrifying beast.

"By then it had grown dark. Standing alone in that uninhabited forest and mountain-ringed unknown valley, I was tracking a still more unknown and terrifyingly powerful beast. Looking to my right in the gathering dusk, I saw a towering wall of basalt rising sheer for nearly four thousand feet, densely clothed in forest, while high up on the tips of the mountain bamboo groves lingered a faint touch of reddish sunlight—or perhaps it was a trick of my eyes, the afterglow of the boundless sky.

"I thought it would not be wise to enter the cave or stand there at such an hour. Taking Jim's body, I returned to the tent. All night long I sat by his dead body with the fire burning and my rifle held ready.

"The next day, after burying Jim, I set out again in search of that beast. But the trouble was that search as I might, I could not even find that cave or that palm tree again. There were many such caves in various parts of the mountains. Who knew which cave I had seen in the evening darkness?

"It was impossible to stay alone without a companion in the forests of that perilous Richtersveld mountain range. Walking for fifteen days, I reached that Kaffir kraal. They recognized me and treated me with great hospitality. I told them the story of Jim's death.

"Hearing it, their faces turned pale with terror—their small eyes grew wide with fear. They said, 'Good heavens! The Bunyip! It is out of that very fear that nobody goes there.'"

Almost all the lights in the village had gone out; village folk do not stay up at night burning oil. The light of a half-moon lay spread across the earth like the smile of a sorrowful man. Naga preferred darkness to this. Haru Majhi's home consisted of two rooms beside the dirt road, with a bamboo grove behind it, a huge pond to the right, and Nakul Saha's tin-roofed house to the left. On other nights, everyone would be asleep by the time he came home, and Naga would go in by himself and eat whatever was left of the cooked food. Tonight, Haru Majhi's wife and daughter were sitting up awake just for Naga. Haru Majhi must have told them before leaving.
'Why are you so late tonight, Naga? You went to Ramtala, didn't you? Sit down and eat your rice. Oh Kali, set out a pira for your dada to sit on.'
Such a warm welcome was something new. Naga's heart sank even further. The moment they heard about his job, everyone had started fussing over him! Couldn't they have waited at least two days before starting all this hospitality—couldn't they have let two days pass before making it so plain: all this time we didn't care whether you lived or died, and today, because you have a fine job, we are showering you with affection and care?
Kali whispered, 'Baba left two annas for you, Dada.'
Naga felt like running away at once. Lying down on his rush mat, he kept turning all these thoughts over in his mind. He had already decided earlier that he would take his few little belongings and leave the house at dawn. He would send half of his wages to Haru Majhi, but he himself would never come back. As he thought about it, a strange feeling stirred within Naga. It was neither sorrow nor joy; he could not understand at all how he felt. It only seemed to him as though his new life had already begun even before he left home; the whole world around him had changed, and he was spending his days among many people who all loved him with simple, genuine affection.
What belongings did Naga have, after all? Everything fit into one small bundle. He did not take the rush mat he slept on, and though he thought of taking the rag-wrapped bolster beside him, in the end he left that behind too. The old, thick kantha that he used to wrap around himself in winter lay folded on top of a wooden box; he merely wrapped his small bundle inside that kantha.
Something kept nagging at Naga's mind. He did not feel like taking anything at all with him. It seemed to him that it would be best to begin his new life without carrying a single thing from here. Just as touching a clean, shining object with soiled hands leaves a smudge on it, taking anything from this place would leave a stain upon his new life.
Daylight had not yet broken properly. After walking a short distance from the house along the dirt road, he turned back. He set the kantha-wrapped bundle down on the veranda and walked out again.
No, he would take nothing at all with him from here.
Not that the bundle had been particularly heavy, yet as he walked along now, Naga felt lighter inside himself. A little way ahead, the road curved to the right, and just past the bend stood the house of Kailash Chakrabarti, who had read Jadabbabu's palm the morning before.

Today is Poila Boishakh. For other nations in other lands, the first day of the new year is a day of joy and festivity. We, however, know that day only through our halkhata. On New Year's Day, we settle the accounts of the past year's debts and dues, profits and losses; we open a new ledger, and onto its very first page we carry forward the balance of the old ledger.
Year after year goes by, and another year comes round; yet in our new ledger there is never any entry of new profit. From one halkhata to the next, we go on steadily swelling the column of losses alone. There is no doubt that if things continue in this way much longer, our race will have to declare bankruptcy. When the profit side stands at zero and the figures on the loss side keep mounting higher and higher, why don't we wind up the business altogether? Because in the marketplace of this world, no one shuts up shop of his own accord—and besides, there is always hope. As people say, hope never dies until we die.
It is not that we are altogether indifferent toward our own people. Last year, a debate arose over whether, as a caste, the Kayastha is superior or the Baidya is superior. Since by every measure we are smaller than others, we have no recourse left but to quarrel and bicker among ourselves over who is smaller and who is greater. We cannot let go of the fond illusion of introducing ourselves as great. The Kayastha says, 'I am superior'; the Baidya says, 'I am superior.' When the scriptures offer as many opinions as there are sages, it is nearly impossible to settle the matter definitively through subtle hair-splitting. The Baidya's profession is medicine—saving lives; the Kshatriya's profession is slaying—taking lives. Therefore, the Kshatriya is undoubtedly superior to the Baidya. Concluding that in order to outrank the Baidya it was necessary to become Kshatriyas, a handful of leaders of the Kayastha community became dead set on turning themselves into Kshatriyas. Upon hearing this auspicious news, I felt particularly elated.
For, in the first place, I am a partisan of progress; whenever I see or hear that a particular individual or a particular community has taken the initiative to improve its own condition through its own efforts, it is only natural for me to rejoice—especially when the thing is so altogether novel for Bengal. Whose heart is not drawn to what is new, at least for a moment or two? Decline requires no effort from anyone; slacken your grip ever so slightly, and it happens all by itself. The chief mark of inert matter is inactivity, and the chief law of inert matter is downward motion—gravitation. Recently, I hear, Professor J. C. Bose has demonstrated before the scientific world that our perception of a difference between the inanimate and the animate is nothing but an illusion. The root of that illusion lies in the gross vision of our mortal eyes. By the light of electricity, he has shown that, depending on circumstances, the responses and behavior of inanimate matter are identical to those of living matter. Professor Bose himself says that for the people of India this is no new truth or fact; this truth had been grasped by our ancestors long ago and could not escape their divine sight—in a word, it is our ancestral, hereditary truth. I say, what doubt can there be of that! To prove this truth, we have no need of the aid of science, nor do we need to go back to our ancestors.

কারণ, প্রথমত আমি উন্নতির পক্ষপাতী; কোনো লোকবিশেষ কিংবা জাতিবিশেষ আপন চেষ্টায় আপনার অবস্থার উন্নতি করতে উদ্যোগী হয়েছে দেখলে কিংবা শুনলে খুশি হওয়া আমার পক্ষে স্বাভাবিক। বিশেষত বাংলার পক্ষে যখন জিনিসটে এতটা নূতন। নৃতনের প্রতি মন কার না যায়, অন্তত দুদণ্ডের জন্যও। অবনতির জন্য কাউকেই আয়াস করতে হয় না। ও একটু ঢ়িলে দিলে আপনা হতেই হয়। জড়পদার্থের প্রধান লক্ষণ নিশ্চেষ্টতা, আর জড়পদার্থের প্রধান ধর্ম অধোগতি- গ্র্যাভিটেশন। সম্প্রতি প্রোফেসর জে. সি. বোস, শুনতে পাই, বৈজ্ঞানিকসমাজে প্রমাণ করেছেন যে, জড়ে ও জীবে আমাদের ভেদজ্ঞান শুধু ভ্রান্তিমাত্র। সে ভ্রান্তির মূল আমাদের চর্মচক্ষুর স্থূলদৃষ্টি। তিনি ইলেকট্রিসিটির আলোকের সাহায্যে দেখিয়ে দিয়েছেন যে, অবস্থা অনুসারে জড়পদার্থের ভাবভঙ্গি ঠিক সজীব পদার্থের অনুরূপ। প্রোফেসর বোস নিজে বলেন যে, ভারতবাসীর পক্ষে এ কিছু নতুন সত্য বা তথ্য নয়; এ সত্য আমাদের পূর্বপুরুষদের কাছে বহুপূর্বে ধরা পড়েছিল, তাদের দিব্য চক্ষু এড়িয়ে যেতে পারে নি; এক কথায় এটা আমাদের খানদানী সত্য। আমি বলি, তার আর সন্দেহ কী। এ সত্যের প্রমাণের জন্য বিজ্ঞানের সাহায্যও আবশ্যক নয়, এবং আমাদের পূর্বপুরুষদের কাছেও যাবার দরকার নেই।

Jadabbabu took a great liking to Naga. Seeing Naga's well-built, muscular body brought back memories of the days when he himself had been passionate about wrestling. What a fondness he had had for physical culture back then! At Naga's age, he had been as thin as a jute stalk, constantly suffering from one illness or another. All the strength he had built up after starting at an older age and wrestling for several years—Naga had grown into an even bigger wrestler all on his own, perhaps without ever doing a single day of squats and push-ups in his life. Naga knew a boatman's trade well, too. That had been proved within the four hours of his rowing from Atkhawar to Ramtala.
So Jadabbabu thought of making Naga a permanent boatman on his boat. Who knew when Chand Majhi would recover; and he needed a boatman anyway. He brought up the matter with Naga himself. By then, through close questioning, he had already found out a great deal about Naga. So he said plainly, 'I'll give you as much food as you want to eat, and for clothes and wages I'll give you what I used to give Chand's son. What do you say, will you stay?'
Naga fell into deep thought. If he took the job here, Haru Majhi would be in a tight spot; he would have to hire someone else and either pay the man wages or give him a share of the boat's earnings. Yet on the other hand, living with Haru Majhi was a great hardship for Naga. He never gave him enough to fill his stomach, refused to buy him new clothes when his old ones tore, and flew into a temper if he asked for so much as a single pice. Naga had just finished eating a meal of rice here; not once had he needed to ask for anything—how many times they had come of their own accord and served dal and curry onto his plate! Toward the end, he had felt downright bashful. Most of all, he was amazed that everyone was genuinely happy to see him eat heartily. At home, if he asked more than once or twice for a little more dal as thin as water, Haru Majhi's wife would snap at him, whereas here, serving various dishes onto his plate again and again of her own accord, Jadabbabu's wife had said, 'Only when someone can eat well is there joy in cooking and serving them.'
He would get food to eat, clothes to wear, and wages besides. Could one pass up a job like this? Yet on the other hand, however he might have done it, Haru Majhi had fed and clothed him and raised him since childhood—how could he suddenly abandon him like a selfish ingrate? —'I'll come tomorrow and tell you, Karta.'
In the boat of a boatman he knew, Naga went back to Atkhawar. There is never any shortage of familiar boatmen going to nearby places. By then, evening had already passed. Evening falls upon the river with grand pageantry—a silent, colorful pageantry. The colors that the sun scatters as it sets remain only in the sky for people on land. People of the river see those colors in the river as well. Taking on the hues of the sky, the river seems to vie with the heavens in painting itself crimson.
The evening steamer would arrive before long, and Haru Majhi had surely gone to the jetty. Naga quietly climbed into their boat and sat waiting.

নাগাকে যাদববাবুর খুব পছন্দ হয়ে গেল। নাগার সুগঠিত জোরালো শরীর দেখে নিজের কুস্তির নেশার দিনগুলির কথা তাঁর মনে পড়তে লাগল। দেহ-চৰ্চার দিকে কি ঝোঁকটাই তখন তাঁর ছিল! নাগার বয়সে তিনি ছিলেন পাকাটির মত রোগা, ক্রমাগত অসুখেই ভুগতেন। আরও বেশী বয়সে আরম্ভ করে কয়েক বছর কুস্তি চালানোর পরে তাঁর গায়ে যতটুকু জোর হয়েছিল, জীবনে হয়তো একটা দিন ডন বৈঠক না দিয়েও আপনা থেকেই নাগা তার চেয়ে বড় পালোয়ান হয়ে উঠেছে। মাঝির কাজও নাগা ভালই জানে। আটখামার থেকে রামতলা পর্যন্ত তার ঘণ্টাচারেকের মাঝিগিরির মধ্যেই তার প্রমাণ মিলেছে।
যাদববাবু তাই ভাবলেন, নাগাকে স্থায়িভাবেই তাঁর নৌকার মাঝি করা যাক। চাঁদ মাঝি কবে ভাল হবে কে জানে; মাঝি তো একজন তাঁর চাই। নিজেই তিনি নাগার কাছে কথাটা পাড়লেন। খুঁটিয়ে খুঁটিয়ে নাগার সম্বন্ধে অনেক কথাই ততক্ষণে তিনি জেনে ফেলেছেন। তাই তিনি স্পষ্ট করেই বললেন, ‘খাওন দিমু যত খাওন চাস, পরন আর বেতন দিমু চাঁদের পোলারে যা দিতাম। কি কস, থাকবি?’
নাগা বড় ভাবনায় পড়ে গেল। সে এখানে কাজ নিলে হারু মাঝি মুশকিলে পড়বে, অন্য একজন লোক তাকে রাখতে হবে এবং হয় লোকটিকে দিতে হবে বেতন, নয় দিতে হবে নৌকার আয়ের ভাগ। কিন্তু এদিকে হারু মাঝির কাছে থাকতে নাগার বড় কষ্ট। পেট ভরে খেতে দেয় না, কাপড় ছিঁড়লে কিনে দিতে চায় না, একটা পয়সা চাইলে পর্যন্ত মেজাজ তার গরম হয়ে ওঠে। নাগা সবে ভাত খেয়ে উঠেছে, একবার তাকে কিছু চাইতে হয়নি, যেচে যেচে কতবার যে তার পাতে ডাল তরকারি দিয়ে গেছে। শেষের দিকে তার রীতিমত লজ্জা করছিল। সবচেয়ে সে অবাক হয়ে গেছে তার খাওয়া দেখে সকলে সত্য সত্যই খুশি হয়েছে বলে। বাড়িতে একবারের বেশী দুবার জলের মত পাতলা ডাল একটু চাইলে হারু মাঝির বৌ মুখ ঝামটা দিয়ে ওঠে, আর এখানে নিজে থেকে নানা ব্যঞ্জন বার বার তার পাতে দিয়ে যাদববাবুর বৌ বলেছেন, ‘খাইতে পারলে তবে স্যান্‌ মাইনষের রাইন্ধা বাইড়া খাওয়াইয়া সুখ।’
খেতে পাবে, পরতে পাবে, বেতন পাবে। এ কাজ কি ছাড়া যায়? এদিকে যেভাবেই হোক খাইয়ে পরিয়ে হারু মাঝি তাকে ছেলেবেলা থেকে মানুষ করেছে, স্বার্থপরের মত তাকেই বা হঠাৎ ত্যাগ করা যায় কি করে? —‘কাইল আইসা কমু, কর্তা।’
একজন চেনা মাঝির নৌকায় নাগা আটখামারে ফিরে গেল। চেনা মাঝির অভাব কাছাকাছির জায়গায় কখনো হয় না। তখন সন্ধ্যা পার হয়ে গেছে। নদীতে সন্ধ্যা হয় মহাসমারোহে, নিঃশব্দ রঙীন সমারোহ। অস্ত যাবার সময় সূর্য যে রঙ ছড়িয়ে দেয়, ডাঙ্গার মানুষের কাছে সে রঙ থাকে শুধু আকাশে। নদীর মানুষ নদীতেও রং দেখতে পায়। আকাশের রং নিয়ে নদী যেন আকাশের সঙ্গে পাল্লা দিয়ে নিজেকে রাঙ্গিয়েছে।
সন্ধ্যার স্টীমার আসতে দেরি নেই, হারু মাঝি নিশ্চয় জেটিতে গিয়েছে। নাগা চুপচাপ নিজেদের নৌকায় উঠে বসে রইল।

From that day on, we all began keeping an eye on him. But before two days had passed, there was another theft. Poor Pagla Dashu had brought a meat chop from home and hidden it under the bench in the tiffin room; someone came along, ate half of it, and ruined the rest by dropping it in the dirt. In a fit of rage, the madcap yelled and cursed until he brought the whole school building down around our ears. We all told him, "Hey, hush, hush, don't shout so much! How will the thief get caught if you do?" But would the madcap listen to that? Then Jaladhar tried to reason with him, saying, "Just be patient for two more days, I'll catch that new fellow red-handed—all of this is his handiwork." Hearing this, Dashu said, "What brains you have! Those people are upcountry Brahmins—do they ever eat meat? Go ask Darwanji if you want!" True enough! That hadn't occurred to any of us. For days on end that young fellow rolls out ruti and eats it; why, we had never once seen him eat fish or meat. Madcap or whatever else Dashu might be, everyone had to admit he was right. Jaladhar, however, was not the sort of boy to be embarrassed. With a broad grin, he said, "I misled you guys on purpose. Come on, you're not supposed to say anything until the thief is caught—no seasoned detective ever does that. Only I know who I've marked as the thief in my mind."

For the next few days we stayed very alert; for eight or ten days, no theft occurred. Then Jaladhar said, "You guys made a ruckus and ruined everything. The thief figured out that I'm on his trail. Would he dare steal anymore? Still, it's a good thing I didn't let the real name slip to you." Yet that very day, word got around that the Headmaster-mahashay's own tiffin had been stolen right out of his room! We said, "Well, hey? Wasn't the thief supposed to be too scared of you to steal? Looks like his fear has vanished!"

For the next two days, not a smile was seen on Jaladhar's face. Brooding constantly over the thief, his studies got into such a muddle that he came within an inch of getting a beating in Panditmashai's class. Two days later, he called us all together and announced that his arrangements for catching the thief were completely ready. At tiffin time, he would leave a paper packet containing sarbhaja, luchi, and alur dom in the tiffin room and walk away. After that, nobody was to go near that side. From the gymnastics room outside the school building, one can secretly watch the tiffin room. A few of us would pretend to go home and hide in there. And a few others would stay in the little room in the western corner of the courtyard. These people favor doing everything slowly, steadily, and coolly. Just because they do not want to charge ahead with fiery resolve, no one should think they want to turn back. Staying right where we are is what they consider the mark of intelligence. In fact, they do approve of moving forward a little, but ever so slowly, ever so cautiously. That quintessential Bangali temperament which lies unspoken within most people is expressed by some of them in clear, fine English. In short, their argument is this: float the clumsy cargo boat of life on the faint current of progress; it will inch forward bit by bit, even though to the eye it may look as if it is not moving at all. But mind you, do not push with a pole, do not drop an oar, do not haul a towline, do not hoist a sail—just sit quietly and hold the rudder. The name of this doctrine is prudence. In our country, prudence is held in great fondness and high esteem. Seeing the cargo boat standing still, people wonder what unfathomable riches must be loaded inside it.
This thing called prudence is merely a product of our present condition. In English, this condition is called a transition period—that is to say, our nation has now reached its adolescence. Bidyapati Thakur described adolescence by saying, 'Lakhaite na para jetha ki kanetha'—one cannot tell whether it is the elder or the younger. Consequently, in our deeds and words, we show either childishness, or precociousness, or both at once. This attitude of the precocious child is especially to our liking. We do not care at all for the restless spirit of a little child. Hearing overly mature talk from a young mouth is what pleases us. The polite name for this precociousness is prudence.
Mistaking the whole earth for a mere clay saucer is something we all consider ridiculous, but mistaking a clay saucer for the whole earth is, to us, a noble thing. For without that mindset, one cannot become prudent. Why other people shouldn't laugh when the views Burke expressed in his critique of that vast political upheaval, the French Revolution, are applied in favor of forcibly keeping child widows widowed and preserving the practice of Kulinism, is something I cannot understand.
Our society and social rules have been running for a very long time; in custom and conduct, we are slaves to habit. Our education is new, and that education has changed our minds. There is no harmony between our social conduct and our state of mind. Those who believe the mind to be the supreme part of a human being naturally wish to bring conduct into line with the mind. On the other hand, those who are weak, timid, and incapable, yet clever, try to use argument and logic to bring the mind into line with conduct. The arguments and logic dug up for this purpose are what go by the name of prudence. We Bangalis are by nature weak, timid, and incapable; therefore, by force of nature, we bow down before the prudent without a second thought—that is the sum and substance of it.

Yet this noble example of hers has made things very difficult for the rest of us. I cannot shrink myself so impossibly small in every way. When I understand something to be good, it is not in my nature to accept it as bad just to please someone else—you too have had plenty of proof of that.

I drew Bindu into my own room. Didi said, "Mejobou is set on spoiling a poor family's girl." She went around complaining to everyone as though I had brought about some dreadful calamity. Yet I know for certain that deep down she breathed a sigh of relief. Now the burden of blame fell squarely upon my shoulders. By getting me to show her sister the affection she could not show herself, her heart grew lighter. My elder sister-in-law used to try to subtract a few figures from Bindu's age. Even so, if one were to say in private that she was no less than fourteen, it would not be unfair. As you well know, she was so plain to look at that if she were to fall and crack her head open, people would worry more about the floor of the room. Consequently, without a mother or father, there was no one to arrange her marriage, and besides, how many men had the strength of mind to marry her?

Bindu came to me in great fear and trepidation, as though I would not be able to bear it if her touch brushed against my body. It was as if she had no right to be born into this wide world; so she always sidled past and kept out of sight. In her father's house, her paternal cousins had not wanted to spare her even a tiny corner where an unwanted object might lie. Unwanted rubbish easily finds space around a house because people forget about it; an unwanted woman, however, is not only unwanted, she is also hard to forget, and so there is no room for her even on the rubbish heap. And yet one could hardly claim that Bindu's paternal cousins were indispensable beings in this world. Still, they are getting along just fine.

So when I called Bindu into my room, her heart began to tremble inside her chest. Seeing her fear, I felt deep sorrow. With a great deal of tenderness, I made her understand that there was a little place for her in my room.

However, my room is not mine alone. So my task was far from easy. After she had stayed with me for just a few days, some red spots broke out on her skin. Perhaps it was prickly heat, or perhaps something else; all of you declared it was smallpox. After all, it was Bindu. A quack doctor from your neighbourhood came and said it was impossible to tell for sure until another day or two had passed. But who had the patience to wait those one or two days? Bindu was nearly dying of shame over her own illness. I said, "Even if it is smallpox, so be it—I will stay with her in that birthing room of ours, and no one else will have to do a thing." While all of you were up in arms against me over this, and even Bindu's own elder sister was feigning extreme irritation and proposing to send the ill-fated girl to the hospital, every single red mark on her skin vanished completely. I saw that this made all of you even more agitated. You said the smallpox had surely sunk inward into her body. After all, it was Bindu.
