বিন্দকে আমি আমার ঘরে টেনে নিলুম। দিদি বললেন, “মেজোবউ গরিবের ঘরের মেয়ের মাথাটি খেতে বসলেন।” আমি যেন বিষম একটা বিপদ ঘটালুম, এমনি ভাবে তিনি সকলের কাছে নালিশ করে বেড়ালেন। কিন্তু, আমি নিশ্চয় জানি, তিনি মনে মনে বেঁচে গেলেন। এখন দোষের বোঝা আমার উপরেই পড়ল। তিনি বোনকে নিজে যে স্নেহ দেখাতে পারতেন না আমাকে দিয়ে সেই স্নেহ করিয়ে নিয়ে তাঁর মনটা হালকা হল। আমার বড়ো জা বিন্দুর বয়স থেকে দু-চারটে অঙ্ক বাদ দিতে চেষ্টা করতেন। কিন্তু, তার বয়স যে চোদ্দর চেয়ে কম ছিল না, এ কথা লুকিয়ে বললে, অন্যায় হত না। তুমি তো জান, সে দেখতে এতই মন্দ ছিল যে, পড়ে গিয়ে সে যদি মাথা ভাঙত তবে ঘরের মেজেটার জন্যই লোকে উদ্‌বিগ্ন হত। কাজেই পিতামাতার অভাবে কেউ তাকে বিয়ে দেবার ছিল না, এবং তাকে বিয়ে করবার মতো মনের জোরই বা কজন লোকের ছিল।

বিন্দু বড়ো ভয়ে ভয়ে আমার কাছে এল। যেন আমার গায়ে তার ছোঁয়াচ লাগলে আমি সইতে পারব না। বিশ্বসংসারে তার যেন জন্মাবার কোনো শর্ত ছিল না; তাই সে কেবলই পাশ কাটিয়ে, চোখ এড়িয়ে চলত। তার বাপের বাড়িতে তার খুড়ততো ভাইরা তাকে এমন একটি কোণও ছেড়ে দিতে চায় নি যে কোণে একটা অনাবশ্যক জিনিস পড়ে থাকতে পারে। অনাবশ্যক আবর্জনা ঘরের আশে-পাশে অনায়াসে স্থান পায়, কেননা মানুষ তাকে ভুলে যায়; কিন্তু অনাবশ্যক মেয়েমানুষ যে একে অনাবশ্যক আবার তার উপরে তাকে ভোলাও শক্ত, সেইজন্য আঁস্তাকুড়েও তার স্থান নেই। অথচ বিন্দুর খুড়তুতো ভাইরা যে জগতে পরমাবশ্যক পদার্থ তা বলবার জো নেই। কিন্তু, তারা বেশ আছে।

তাই, বিন্দুকে যখন আমার ঘরে ডেকে আনলুম তার বুকের মধ্যে কাঁপতে লাগল। তার ভয় দেখে আমার বড়ো দুঃখ হল। আমার ঘরে যে তার একটুখানি জায়গা আছে সেই কথাটি আমি অনেক আদর করে তাকে বুঝিয়ে দিলাম।

কিন্তু, আমার ঘর শুধু তো আমারই ঘর নয়। কাজেই আমার কাজটি সহজ হল না। দু-চারদিন আমার কাছে থাকতেই তার গায়ে লাল লাল কী উঠল। হয়তো সে ঘামাচি, নয় তো আর-কিছু হবে; তোমরা বললে বসন্ত। কেননা, ও যে বিন্দু। তোমাদের পাড়ার এক আনাড়ি ডাক্তার এসে বললে, আর দুই-একদিন না গেলে ঠিক বলা যায় না। কিন্তু, সেই দুই-একদিনের সবুর সইবে কে। বিন্দু তো তার ব্যামোর লজ্জাতেই মরবার জো হল। আমি বললাম, বসন্ত হয় তো হোক্, আমি আমাদের সেই আঁতুড়ঘরে ওকে নিয়ে থাকব, আর কাউকে কিছু করতে হবে না। এই নিয়ে আমার উপরে তোমরা যখন সকলে মারমূর্তি ধরেছ, এমন-কি বিন্দুর দিদিও যখন অত্যন্ত বিরক্তির ভান করে পোড়াকপালি মেয়েটাকে হাসপাতালে পাঠাবার প্রস্তাব করছেন, এমন সময় ওর গায়ের সমস্ত লাল দাগ একদম মিলিয়ে গেল। তোমরা দেখি তাতে আরও ব্যস্ত হয়ে উঠলে। বললে, নিশ্চয়ই বসন্ত বসে গিয়েছে। কেননা, ও যে বিন্দু।

Input: How did Alexander come as a world-conqueror to an India that was the fatherland of such sons, and return to his homeland with his glory undimmed? Naturally, this question may arise in your minds. In reply, this may be said: in the historical era, the very first sole sovereign of a vast Indian empire whom we see is Chandragupta. Although he was a contemporary of Alexander, at the time of the Greek invasion of India he was an exile from his homeland, a man without allies or resources. Had the kingdom been in his hands, Alexander might not have been able to make much headway. Alexander occupied only a small portion of Northern India, and even that was divided at the time into tiny states whose kings lacked unity among themselves. At that time, far more famous and powerful than King Puru—Alexander's principal adversary—was the king of the Nanda dynasty of Pataliputra (modern-day Patna). His standing army consisted of eighty thousand cavalry, two hundred thousand infantry, eight thousand war-chariots, and six thousand war-elephants. If needed, their numbers could have been increased many times over; for just a few years later, immediately upon the founding of the Maurya dynasty, we see the army of Pataliputra standing thus: six hundred thousand infantry, thirty thousand cavalry, nine thousand war-elephants, and countless chariots. Therefore, had there been a trial of strength between King Nanda of Pataliputra and Alexander, there is no telling what would have happened! Alexander did indeed propose marching toward Pataliputra, but at the mere mention of that proposal the entire Greek army showed signs of mutiny—and the chief reason for it was that the bitter taste of Indian valor the Greeks had already experienced in the realm of the minor king Puru had proved more than enough for them. Then comes another question. Is the history of Greek valor in India that we receive exaggerated in many places, fabricated in some, and utterly baseless in others? My belief is, yes. Because in this case, the historical painter painted his own portrait himself. Even in this age of newspapers, in the realm of ever-vigilant radio, telegraph, and telephone, we see every day how both sides engaged in a war strive with all their might to conceal the truth—claiming when defeated that they were not defeated, and calling a minor victory extraordinary! How then can we say that in those myth-loving ancient times, the Greeks wrote history like truthful Yudhishthira? And how can we believe that the Greeks were never defeated anywhere? Modern European writers themselves have pointed out several exaggerated and untrue statements made by the Greek historians. Another point worth noting is that although so great a storm swept across the bosom of India, not the slightest hint or mention of it is to be found anywhere in Hindu, Buddhist, or Jain literature! This too is unnatural or suspicious. And proof that the Greeks did not grow afraid for no reason was found not long afterward. Not now—I shall tell you of that in due time. Right now, I want to acquaint you with the condition at that time of the region that served as the theater where the Greeks and the Indians first met in a tryst of death. Many of you may perhaps grow angry with me for pausing the story to talk of extraneous matters. However, people's acquaintance with the ancient history of our country is so slight that without giving a brief introduction to the time and place, the true flavor of this historical tale will never come alive at all.
Target Output: এমন সব সন্তানের পিতৃভূমি যে ভারতবর্ষ, আলেকজাণ্ডার দিগ্বিজয়ীরূপে সেখানে এসে কেমন ক’রে অম্লান গৌরবে স্বদেশে ফিরে গেলেন? তোমাদের মনে স্বভাবতই এই প্রশ্নের উদয় হ’তে পারে। এর জবাবে বলা যায়ঃ ঐতিহাসিক যুগে বিরাট ভারত-সাম্রাজ্যের একছত্র অধিপতিরূপে সর্বাগ্রে দেখি চন্দ্রগুপ্তকে। তিনি আলেকজাণ্ডারের সমসাময়িক হ’লেও গ্রীকদের ভারতআক্রমণের সময়ে ছিলেন স্বদেশ থেকে নির্বাসিত, সহায়-সম্পদহীন ব্যক্তি। তাঁর হাতে রাজ্য থাকলে আলেকজাণ্ডার হয়তো বিশেষ সুবিধা ক’রে উঠতে পারতেন না। আলেকজাণ্ডার উত্তর-ভারতের এক অংশ মাত্র অধিকার করেছিলেন, তাও তখন বিভক্ত ছিল ক্ষুদ্র ক্ষুদ্র রাজ্যে এবং সে-সব রাজ্যের রাজাদের মধ্যে ছিল না একতা। তখন আলেকজাণ্ডারের প্রধান শত্রু রাজা পুরুর চেয়েও ঢের বেশী বিখ্যাত ও শক্তিশালী ছিলেন পাটলিপুত্রের।(বর্তমান পাটনার) নন্দবংশীয় রাজা। তাঁর নিয়মিত বাহিনীতে ছিল আশী হাজার অশ্বারোহী, দুই লক্ষ পদাতিক, আট হাজার যুদ্ধরথ ও ছয় হাজার রণহস্তী। দরকার হ’লে এদের সংখ্যা ঢের বাড়তে পারত, কারণ এর কয়েক বৎসর পরেই দেখি, মৌর্য বংশের প্রতিষ্ঠার সঙ্গে সঙ্গেই পাটলিপুত্রের ফৌজ দাঁড়িয়েছে এইরকমঃ ছয় লক্ষ পদাতিক, ত্রিশহাজার অশ্বারোহী, নয় হাজার রণহস্তী এবং অসংখ্য রথ। সুতরাং পাটলিপুত্রের রাজা নন্দের সঙ্গে আলেকজাণ্ডারের শক্তিপরীক্ষা হ’লে কি হ’ত বলা যায় না! আলেকজাণ্ডার পাটলিপুত্রের দিকে আসবার প্রস্তাবও করেছিলেন বটে, কিন্তু সেই প্রস্তাব শুনেই সমগ্র গ্রীকবাহিনী বিদ্রোহের ভাব প্রকাশ করেছিল এবং তার প্রধান কারণই এই যে ক্ষুদ্র রাজা পুরুর দেশেই গ্রীকরা ভারতীয় বীরত্বের যেটুকু তিক্ত আস্বাদ পেয়েছিল, তাদের পক্ষে সেইটুকুই হয়ে উঠেছিল যথেষ্টের বেশী। তারপর আর এক প্রশ্ন। ভারতবর্ষে আমরা গ্রীক-বীরত্বের যে-ইতিহাস পাই, তা বহু স্থলেই অতিরঞ্জিত, কোথাও কল্পিত এবং কোথাও অমূলক কিনা? আমার বিশ্বাস, হাঁ। কারণ এক্ষেত্রে ঐতিহাসিক চিত্রকর নিজের ছবিই নিজে এঁকেছেন। এই খবরের কাগজের যুগে, সদা-সজাগ বেতার, টেলিগ্রাফ ও টেলিফোনের রাজ্যেও নিত্যই দেখছি যুদ্ধে নিযুক্ত দুই পক্ষই প্রাণপণে সত্যগোপন করছে, হেরে বলছে হারিনি, সামান্য জয়কে বলছে অসামান্য! সুতরাং সেই কল্পনাপ্রিয় আদ্যিকালে গ্রীকরা যে সত্যবাদী যুধিষ্ঠিরের মতো ইতিহাস লিখেছিল, তা কেমন ক’রে বলি? গ্রীকরা যে কোথাও হারে নি, তাই বা কেমন ক’রে মানি? আধুনিক য়ুরোপীয় লেখকরাই গ্রীক ঐতিহাসিকদের কোনো কোনো অতিরঞ্জিত ও অসত্য কথা দেখিয়ে দিয়েছেন। আর একটা লক্ষ্য করিবার বিষয় হচ্ছে, ভারতের বুকের উপর দিয়ে এত-বড় একটা ঝড় ব’য়ে গেল, তবু হিন্দু, বৌদ্ধ বা জৈন সাহিত্যে তার এতটুকু ইঙ্গিত বা উল্লেখ দেখা যায় না! এও অস্বাভাবিক বা সন্দেহজনক। এবং গ্রীকরা যে অকারণে ভয় পায় নি, তার কিছুদিন পরেই সেপ্রমাণ পাওয়া যায়। সে এখন নয়, যথাসময়ে বলবো। গ্রীকদের সঙ্গে ভারতবাসীদের প্রথম মৃত্যু-মিলন হয় যে-নাট্যশালায়, এখন সেই অঞ্চলের তখনকার অবস্থার সঙ্গে তোমাদের পরিচিত করতে চাই। গল্প-বলা বন্ধ রেখে বাজে কথা বলছি ব’লে তোমাদের অনেকেই হয়তো রাগ করবে। কিন্তু আমাদের দেশের পুরাণো ইতিহাসের সঙ্গে লোকের পরিচয় এত অল্প যে, স্থান-কাল সম্বন্ধে একটু ভূমিকা না দিলে এই ঐতিহাসিক কাহিনীর আসল রসটুকু কিছুতেই জমবে না।

I quickly interrupted and asked, 'What kind of calculation is that?'

The cat said, 'It's terribly difficult. Would you like to see how it works?' Saying this, it took a twig, drew a long scratch on the grass, and said, 'Suppose this is Gechodada.' Right after saying that, it sat in solemn silence for a good while.

Then it drew another scratch just like the first one and said, 'Suppose this is you,' and cocked its head to one side and fell silent again.

Then it suddenly drew yet another scratch and said, 'Suppose this is a chandrabindu.' In this way, it would ponder something for a while, draw another long scratch each time, and say, 'Suppose this is Tibet'—'Suppose this is Gechoboudi cooking'—'Suppose this is a hole in the tree trunk—'

Listening to all this, I finally began to lose my temper. I snapped, 'Oh, rubbish! What nonsense are you babbling on about? I don't like this one bit.'

The cat said, 'Alright, then let me explain it a little more simply. Close your eyes, and calculate in your head whatever I tell you.' I closed my eyes.

I kept my eyes closed, and kept them closed, and there wasn't a sound or peep from the cat. Suddenly growing suspicious, I opened my eyes and saw the cat with its tail held high, leaping over the garden fence and running away while snickering nonstop—'Phyach, phyach!'

What else could I do? I sat down on a stone under the tree. The moment I sat down, someone spoke up in a cracked, gravelly voice, 'How much is seven times two?'

I wondered, now who on earth is this? As I was looking around this way and that, the same voice sounded again, 'Well, why aren't you answering? How much is seven times two?' It would not be amiss to paint a small historical picture here of a banquet of the Greeks of those days. In the center of the pavilion stand several silver-inlaid wooden couches, their woodwork adorned with colorful designs. Leaning against cushions or bolsters upon the couches, the guests recline with their legs stretched out or half-lying down. It was from the Persians and other Eastern peoples that they had learned to eat and drink in this half-reclining posture. In front of the couches stand even lower small tables, their legs crafted from ivory. Upon these small tables are arrayed food, delicacies, and drinking vessels. The Greeks of that era were exceedingly fond of meat. They ate fish as well, though compared to meat they regarded fish as trifling. They used very few greens and vegetables. Drinking wine was not considered reprehensible among them; everyone drank wine openly. Along with wine, they ate onions. In Alexander's hand is a painted drinking cup shaped like the head of a bull. জানো আমি তোমার জীবনরক্ষক? গ্রানিকাশের যুদ্ধের কথা কি এখনি ভুলে গেছ? আমি না থাকলে পারসীরা তো সেই দিনই তোমাকে টুক্‌রো টুক্‌রো ক’রে ফেলত, তারপর কোথায় থাকত তোমার দিগ্বিজয়ের দুঃস্বপ্ন? শঠ, কপট, নট! আমাদের প্রাণ নিয়ে তুমি ছিনিমিনি খেলতে চাও?

He said, "The people of ancient Egypt, along with their civilisation and many secret mysteries, have vanished from the earth forever, it is true, and no one today knows the art of turning mummies into living human beings either; yet even in this scientific age, many British scholars who are experts on Egypt cannot help expressing the suspicion that bodiless souls still remain alive inside the ancient burial grounds of Egypt! Even in British newspapers, one often reads that curious European travellers who bought mummies from Egypt and took them to Britain have witnessed all sorts of supernatural occurrences and fallen into strange dangers! That a mummy brings a curse when taken out of its tomb has now practically become a common English proverb! Everyone also knows that many of the famous European scholars who dig up the earth and ransack the tombs of ancient Egypt later die unnatural deaths in various freak accidents! Seeing and hearing all this, one has to admit that the souls of those whose mummies we see today have not yet died; they still love their earthly bodies and, given the chance, want to return into those bodies again! We are Hindus, we too are an ancient race, and we too believe in the immortality of the soul. Perhaps out of the very fear that if attachment to the body remains, the soul might not wish to leave the earth, the scriptures of the Hindus have ordained that the dead body be burned in fire and utterly destroyed!" From time to time, it seemed to Dilip that the early symptoms of insanity had appeared in Bhairab! One day, in the middle of a conversation, he suddenly cried out in an exultant voice, "To be able to bring both good and evil under one's own control—oh, what good fortune that would be! If I could get the gods of heaven and the demons of hell within the grasp of my fist, I could rule the earth!" On another day he said, "I shall marry Abani's sister, it is true, but Abani is good for nothing! Of course, as a human being Abani is a good fellow, but he can never be a true friend to someone who has high ambitions. He is not worthy of being my friend!" For the past few days now, a new malady had taken hold of him. From downstairs, Dilip could often hear Bhairab sitting alone in his upstairs room and talking to himself! Late at night, while Dilip was studying and there was not a single outsider in the upstairs room, amidst the surrounding silence one could clearly hear Bhairab speaking to himself in a very low voice—almost in a whisper! Annoyed by this strange habit of his, Dilip said one day, "Bhairabbabu, do you very much enjoy chatting with yourself?" Startled, Bhairab said, "Do I chat with myself? No, no, you have heard wrong!" But Dilip had not heard wrong, and proof of that was soon found. Keshto was Dilip's old servant. One day he said, "Babu, may I ask you something?" —"What is it?" —"Has the gentleman in the upstairs room gone out of his mind?"

Professor Hushiar is terribly angry with us. We have printed all sorts of accounts about prehistoric creatures, yet nowhere have we made any mention of his extraordinary hunting adventures. Truly, this is very unfair of us. We knew nothing at all about those stories. However, Professor Hushiar has copied out a few excerpts from his hunting diary and sent them to us. So we have printed some of them here. Whether these accounts are true or false is for you to judge.

"June 26, 1922. Karakoram, ten miles north of Mount Bandakush. There are ten of us in all now—myself, my nephew Chandrakhai, two hunters (Chhakkar Singh and Lakkar Singh), and six coolies. My dog is trotting along with us too.

"Pitching our tent on the riverbank and leaving all our baggage in the charge of the coolies, I set out with Chandrakhai and the two hunters. With us we carried guns, a map, and a huge box containing our instruments and food supplies. After walking for two hours, we arrived at a place where everything looked strangely unfamiliar. There were huge trees, not a single one of which we could name. From one tree hung enormous red fruits the size of giant wood-apples; we saw a flowering tree bearing yellow and white blossoms, each a cubit and a half long. From another tree hung things shaped like ridge gourds, giving off a pungent smell from twenty-five cubits away. While we stood marvelling at all this, a dreadful hubbub suddenly broke out from up on the mountain with a loud 'hop-hop, gub-gab' sound.

'The two hunters and I immediately stood ready with our guns. But Chandrakhai pulled two tins of jam out of the box and sat down calmly to eat. That is a great fault of his; once he gets hold of food, he loses all sense of danger or trouble. For the rest of their walk after that, Kanika kept a sullen face, and on the way back she suddenly burst out, 'What a quarrelsome girl! Well, she's a low-class man's daughter, what else can you expect! Just because I asked for a mongoose—'
Naga himself had felt ashamed of Rupa's outburst, yet to defend Rupa he said, 'No, no, it wasn't because of the mongoose—it was because Khokababu laughed, wasn't it?'
Growing angrier still, Kanika snapped, 'Of course you'll take her side—you're people of the same sort, after all!' Up until then, Naga had been walking along with the rest of them, but stung by the insult in Kanika's words, he strode rapidly ahead a good distance. He felt like marching straight back to the house by himself, but having taken on the responsibility of looking after the children, he could not very well leave them all behind and walk off. Foolish and greedy-eyed as these children were, if they spotted water lilies blooming in a pond and went down to pluck them, one or two of them might well drown and die. Keeping a little distance between himself and them, he brought everyone safely home at dusk. And the moment he reached the house, he went straight to his own room.
With a face as sour as a curd-pot, Paresh was smoking a bidi; the instant he saw Naga, he twisted his face into a sneer and greeted him: 'Come right in, O truthful Yudhishthir!'
Why a sudden urge to smoke a bidi came over Naga, who knew—perhaps because his mood was so dark. Holding out his hand, he said, 'Give me a bidi, Paresh.'
Paresh nearly choked with rage: 'Oh, what fond regard I have for him! Give his lordship a bidi, indeed! Can't you smoke Karta's cigars? Doesn't Karta tip you with cigars? You filthy spy, you scoundrel!'
Understanding what was going on now, Naga said, 'I'll thrash you, Parsha, I'm warning you.'
Paresh said, 'Why will you thrash me—aren't you a spy? Didn't you tell Karta? To my face he says he won't tell, and behind my back he goes and tells Karta—does any human being do such a thing?'
'I didn't tell him.'
But Paresh refused to believe it—who else besides Naga knew the secret of his setting the cowshed on fire? He cursed Naga again, calling him the king of liars, a number-one devil, and an inhuman spy—why didn't he go work as a spy for the police and become a rich man? Without any further warning, Naga started thrashing him then and there, and between one hand throttling his neck and the other raining punches and slaps upon him, within a single minute Paresh was seeing stars before his eyes. How could he have known that Naga would start beating him before the quarrel had even warmed up properly? How many quarrels like that he had had with people before! When a quarrel reaches its peak and the exchange of curses becomes unprintable, a fistfight breaking out is no surprise—but by then one has plenty of time to sense it coming and slip away from the spot to avoid blows. A fellow who doesn't follow the rules of a war of words, who starts bashing you right at the outset—what sort of countryman is this!
Once let go, Paresh went weeping to Madhabbabu to lodge a complaint, and a little while later Kanika came to summon Naga.
'Jethamashai is calling you, Naga.'
Seeing Naga walk toward the inner courtyard without a word, she put on the grave air of a solemn mistress of the house and said, 'Listen, Naga, listen—are you angry because I scolded you? You don't listen to me, and that's why I scold you.'
Kanika had thought that this little bit of coaxing would make Naga melt with gratitude, but Naga's anger only grew hotter.

Right at that moment, a new photo popped up at the top of the gallery.

Nila's fingers were trembling. She opened the photo.

In the photo was she herself. Sitting on the bed, her back against the wall, the phone in her hand, the glow of the screen on her face. The photo had been taken from directly behind her, over her right shoulder. And peeking out beside her shoulder was another face. So close that their cheeks were touching. That face was staring at the phone's screen, just the way she was staring at it.

The face was smiling.

Below it, the timestamp: 3:17.

Nila looked at the clock. The time on the phone was 3:16. Between the time in the photo and reality, there was a gap of just one minute.

She couldn't move. Her right shoulder suddenly felt unnaturally cold. Near her neck, at the roots of her hair, something stirred faintly, as if someone were breathing out ever so softly.

She knew that if she turned her head, she would see it. And she also knew that she had seen her own face in the photo. In the photo, her eyes were facing forward, toward the phone. She hadn't turned back.

The time on the phone's screen didn't change. 3:16. As if the clock were stuck waiting for something.

And in the air of the room, right beside her ear, a very low whisper was heard, as though someone were happy to finally talk to another person after a very long time:

"Now you stay awake with me."

What a wretched fate poor Bindi had indeed! For as long as she lived, she never won any praise for beauty or virtue—and even when it came time to die, it never entered her head to think things through and die in some novel fashion that would make the menfolk of this country clap their hands in delight! Even by dying, she only annoyed people!

Didi wept in secret behind closed doors. Yet in that weeping there was a sense of relief. Whatever might be said, at least it was over and done with. She was dead, after all; had she lived, who knows what else might have happened!

I have come on a pilgrimage. Bindu no longer needed to come, but I did.

What people ordinarily mean by suffering was something I never had in your household. In your house there is no shortage of food or clothing; whatever your elder brother's character may be, there is no such flaw in your character for which I could blame the Almighty. Indeed, even if your nature had been like your elder brother's, my days would probably have gone by in much the same way on the whole, and like my chaste and devoted elder sister-in-law, instead of blaming my husband-god, I would have tried to blame the God of the universe. Therefore, I do not wish to raise any complaint against you—this letter of mine is not for that.

But I will never return to that Number Twenty-Seven Makhan Baral Lane of yours. I have seen Bindu. I have discovered what a woman's true standing is in the midst of this worldly household. I have no need of any more.

And then I have seen this too: though she was only a girl, God did not abandon her. Whatever power all of you might have held over her, there was an end to that power. She was greater than her own wretched mortal life. Your feet are not long enough to keep her life crushed forever beneath your soles according to your own whims and your own customs. Death is greater than all of you. Within that death, she is great—there Bindu is not merely the daughter of a Bengali home, not merely the cousin of her father's brother's sons, not merely the cheated wife of an unknown madman. There she is infinite.

The day that flute of death sounded through this young girl's broken heart and echoed across to the other bank of the Yamuna of my life, at first it felt as if an arrow had pierced my chest. I asked the Creator, why is it that whatever is most trivial in this world is also the hardest to break through? Why is this tiny, joyless bubble, walled in on all four sides inside this narrow lane, such a terrifying obstacle? However much Your universe may call out to me holding the nectar-cup of its six seasons in its hands, why cannot I cross the tiny threshold of these inner quarters even for a single moment? Why, having such a life within such a world of Yours, must I die inch by inch behind that paltry screen of brick and wood? How trivial is this daily round of my existence; how trivial are all its fixed rules, its fixed habits, its fixed phrases, its fixed blows—shall the stranglehold of that pettiness triumph in the end, and shall that world of joy, Your own creation, suffer defeat?

Yet the flute of death kept playing—where now are the walls built by masons, where now is the thorny fence woven out of your domestic laws? What sorrow, what humiliation has the power to keep a human soul imprisoned? Look there—in the hand of death flies the victory banner of life! O Mejobou, have no fear! It does not take even the blink of an eye for your Mejobou shell to be torn away.

Input: Out of the footsteps of everyone else in the house, she could unerringly recognise the sound of my footsteps. I noticed this myself. The moment she heard my tread, she would lift her face and listen intently. Yet she could tell that I despised her. For whenever I came near her, she would move away; or else she would sit huddled up somehow, like someone guilty of a crime. And here is another strange thing: in all this time, she had never spoken a single word to me. Like a blind, dark silence, she weighed heavily upon my heart and mind. Nor was I in any hurry to make her speak. I did not speak to her either. A whole year went by like this. In all that year, neither of us spoke a single word to the other. Before this, I had no idea that such a silence could exist between husband and wife. Oh! You cannot even begin to imagine it. This silence is unbearable—unbearable—unbearable!—Yes, unbearable indeed—and yet neither of us had the courage to break this silence. I was busy enjoying life. A huge void had been left inside my youth. Not everyone can understand the anguish of a man whose hot bloodstream of full youth is squandered against his will. My friends advised me: compensate yourself for the loss. Leaving fifty thousand rupees in Company promissory notes locked inside his iron safe, Father (whether unwillingly or not, I cannot say!) had departed for the next world.—Unfortunately for him, however, he had not been able to take the key to the safe along with him tucked into his waistband. With those fifty thousand rupees, I tried to fill up the void in my life. Before long, in my drawing room, the clinking of wine goblets began to ring out in time to the baiji's song of "Hili-mili-paniya". As a result, the more the void in my life began to fill up, the emptier Father's iron safe gradually became. Benu had no eyes, but she had ears. Even though she could see nothing, she could hear everything. Though she never uttered a word to me, I could see quite clearly from her face that a storm was raging inside her heart. Yet even seeing it, no pity awoke in my heart—instead, a cruel sense of satisfaction rose within me. At night I rarely stayed at home. And even when I was at home, I never went near Benu. My revulsion and anger toward her were growing day by day. Then one day I suddenly came down with a fever. Shivering with fever in the outer sitting room, I lost consciousness. After that, when my bosom cronies decided that staying by my side was unnecessary and quietly slipped away one by one, and when the servants carried me inside to the inner quarters and laid me down on my bed, I had no awareness at all. * * * * In the dead of night, the clock in the room suddenly began to strike. At that sound, I regained consciousness. I counted: one, two, three, four! Startling the heavy stillness of the late night awake all of a sudden, the chimes stopped again. Only, like the beating heart of the night itself, that ever-wakeful clock kept murmuring softly without cease: tick-tick-tick!

"That day I had hunted a deer in the morning. Pitching my tent, I cooked the meat and lay down at noon—because walking in the midday sun in those places is practically impossible; in summer the temperature rises from 115 degrees to 130 degrees. After resting, when I went to clean my gun, I saw that the foresight at the end of the barrel had somehow been lost. Without the foresight, a rifle cannot be aimed properly. Despite searching all over, the sight was nowhere to be found. Nearby there was a mound of rock, and on its surface some hard whitish substance caught my eye. That substance was present in several spots on the mound. Picking out a single grain of it, I rubbed and shaped it, and for the time being fitted it onto the tip of the rifle barrel as a makeshift sight. Then in the afternoon I set off northward from there again, and gradually forgot where I had pitched my camp.

"Fifteen days later, I met an Englishman who, like me, was wandering in search of gold. He had two Matabele coolies with him. We were glad to find each other; his name was Jim Carter—a rover just like me, though older in years. One day, while examining my gun, Jim suddenly saw something and was astonished. He asked me, 'Why is your gun's foresight like this?' Then, after hearing my story, he grew excited. He said, 'Didn't you realize this stuff is pure silver—native silver? Where this is found, there is usually a silver mine. My guess is that from one ton of rock there, at least nine thousand ounces of silver will be obtained. Come, let us go to that place right now! This time we shall become millionaires!'

"Let me tell it briefly. Taking Carter with me, I retraced the path by which I had come. But after trying hard for four months, suffering unbearable hardships, losing our way again and again in the vast, trackless, desert-like veld, and coming to the very door of death, by no means could I locate that spot. When I had struck camp there that time, I had not paid close attention to the surroundings. On the African veld there are hardly any landmarks by which one can find an old spot again—everything looks the same. Worn out after many attempts, we finally gave up hope of the silver mine and headed toward the Gwai River. Jim Carter never left me again. Right up until his death, he stayed with me. Even now it pains me to think of his tragic death.

"During these travels, the torment of thirst seemed to us worse than any other hardship. So it was decided that from then on we would follow the course of rivers. We hunted wild animals for food, and whenever we came across a Kaffir kraal now and then, we procured sweet potatoes, chickens, and the like from there."

Late at night everyone fell asleep, while under the foreign sky filled with unfamiliar stars, mysterious wild nature seemed to awaken—the calls of all kinds of wild beasts drifted from the direction of the jungle; there was no sleep in Shankar's eyes, and entranced by this beauty, he sat awake defying the night chill of Central Africa.

There shone the glittering Great Bear—far away in the sky above his own little village, the same Great Bear had risen tonight, along with that same slender crescent moon of the dark fortnight late at night. Leaving those familiar skies behind, how much further would he have to go, and who knew how it would all end?

Two days later, the boat reached Sankini. From there they set out on foot once more—there was not much jungle on this side, only a horizon-spanning, uninhabited plain and countless hills large and small; most of the hills were rugged and treeless, while on some grew thickets of euphorbia trees. Yet to Shankar it seemed that the scenery of this part of Africa was singularly beautiful. Finding so much open space, his mind seemed to breathe a sigh of relief; the colors of the sunset and the magic of the moonlit nights turned this land in the afternoons and at night into a fairyland out of a storybook.

Alvarez said, "Because every place in this veld region looks alike, the danger of losing one's way is very great."

The very day those words were spoken, an incident occurred. When the sun set over the uninhabited veld, they pitched their tent in the lee of a small hill and lit a fire—and Shankar went out to look for water. He took Alvarez's gun along with him, but with only two cartridges. Wandering this way and that for half an hour, the last of the daylight faded, and a thin darkness slowly veiled the entire plain. Shankar could swear that he had not walked for more than half an hour. Suddenly, looking around him, Shankar felt a strange uneasiness, as if some danger were approaching and it would be best to return to the tent. Far away stood hills large and small; every direction looked exactly the same—there was no landmark, everything looked identical!

After walking for just five or six minutes, Shankar realized he had lost his way. Then he remembered Alvarez's words. Yet even then, owing to his inexperience, he failed to grasp the gravity of the danger. He kept walking and walking—one moment it seemed the camp lay ahead, the next moment to the left, and the next to the right. Why could the campfire not be seen? Where was that small hill?

After walking for two hours, Shankar grew terribly afraid. By then he understood that he had completely lost his way and was in dire peril. All alone, he would have to spend the night in this uninhabited, lion-infested, unknown wilderness of Rhodesia—without food, and in this biting cold without a blanket and without a fire. He did not even have a single matchbox with him.

In short, what happened was that before evening the next day—that is, twenty-four hours after losing his way—Alvarez rescued Shankar, delirious and half-dead with thirst, from beneath a euphorbia tree about seven miles from their tent and brought him back to camp.

Alvarez said, "The way you were heading, Shankar, if I hadn't been able to track you down today, you would have wandered deeper and deeper into the desert wilderness and died of thirst by noon tomorrow. Many men like you have died that way before on the Rhodesian veld. These are terrible places. Never go out from the tent like that again, because you are a novice. You don't know the art of traveling in the desert. You'll die for sure."

Shankar said, "Alvarez, twice you have saved my life; I shall never forget this."

Input: On the ground floor of Hemanta's house, there were two large halls side by side. One of them is his laboratory. In it stands a long table arrayed with all sorts of scientific apparatus, while shelves along the walls are lined with glass jars, phials, and bottles filled with various liquid and powdered chemicals. The other room serves as both his drawing room and his library. Bookcases tall and short, narrow and wide, packed with books, stand covering all four walls, while in the center are arranged cots spread with snow-white sheets and soft bedding, chairs, sofas, couches, small tables, and the like. Entering the drawing room that day, I saw Hemanta sitting on a couch, staring intently at a book open in his lap. Dropping into a chair, I asked, "Well, old chap, what book are you reading with such deep concentration?" Lifting his face, Hemanta said, "I'm not reading a book, brother—I'm looking at a picture! This is the Calcutta Police Journal." —"A picture in the Police Journal? Then it must surely be the face of one of your cronies—that is to say, some thief or murderer?" —"No, Rabin, your joke has fallen flat. Looking at this picture, I am thinking of a world-famous, immortal artist." —"Good heavens! Has the baleful eye of Saturn of the police fallen even upon artists nowadays?" —"Rabin, don't be so needlessly unkind toward the police. And tell me, why shouldn't the eye of the police fall upon artists? Does being an artist automatically make a man a saint? Wasn't Villon, the famous poet of France, a thief and a murderer? Have you heard the name of Sigismondo Malatesta of Italy?" —"No. Who was he?" —"A poet, a scholar, a worshipper of the fine arts. He was born in the Middle Ages. Yet you wouldn't find a more depraved criminal than him even if you searched every coffee-house and slum in Kolkata. Let all that go! Do you know what I am looking at right now? The panja—the handprint—of Badshah Shah Jahan, the creator of the Taj Mahal." —"Let me see." Taking the book in my hand, I saw printed in an illustration the impression of Emperor Shah Jahan's right hand. Hemanta said, "In those days, all valuable documents of the Mughal Empire bore the impression of the Emperor's panja. Because the Mughals knew that a royal seal or a handwritten signature could be forged, whereas the impression of an entire palm along with all five fingers is impossible to forge. No two people in the world can have the exact same handprint. Sir William Herschel of the Bengal Police was the very first in the world to adopt the system of taking the fingerprints of accused persons just the other day—in the year 1877 AD. Today this system is prized in country after country across the world. Yet in India, this method was born ages ago. Not only the panja impressions of the Mughals, but Hindus too, since ancient times, have been putting their thumb-impressions on deeds instead of signing their names. So there is nothing at all to boast of in the discovery of the modern police. ... But Rabin, looking at the impression of Badshah Shah Jahan's panja, doesn't anything strike you?" —"Indeed it does! It strikes me that looking at this handprint does not remind one of Shah Jahan at all!" —"You've hit the nail on the head. When one stands in the shadow of the many palaces, mosques, and mausoleums of Delhi and Agra, one is overwhelmed by the love of beauty of that artist Shah Jahan—yet is this really the print of his own hand? Modern experts say that by looking at the shape of a person's fingers, one can tell his nature and profession. Just look at the shape of Shah Jahan's fingers! The fingers of an artist ought not to be shaped like this—the handprint of any ordinary man could look like this. That is the very thing I was sitting here thinking about."

Input: Abani said, "I do not know. When I came into the room, I found him in that very condition." Dilip placed his hand on Bhairab's chest and said, "His chest is heaving up and down like a pair of bellows! It is quite clear that he was terribly frightened after seeing something dreadful." Abani said, "Then perhaps the root of all this mischief is that 'mummy'!" —"'Mummy'? How so?" —"Who wouldn't be frightened at the sight of a corpse several thousand years old? It is not good for living human beings to meddle with such ghostly matters. Some time ago, I saw him in this same condition once before. On that day too, he was lying unconscious in just this way at the feet of that ghostly figure." Stretched out full-length lay the body of Bhairabchandra. —"What does he want to do with the 'mummy'?" —"Who knows! Bhairabbabu probably has a touch of madness in his head. Meddling with these things is his obsession! How often I forbid him—I tell him, keeping company with the dead is neither good nor proper for the living! Hearing that, he laughs and says, 'This is my shava-sadhana!'" —"Hush! The patient is regaining consciousness." Bhairab's face had looked white and pale all this while; now, little by little, a hint of colour was returning to it. His breathing, too, gradually became normal. A little later, he opened his eyes and looked around the room. Suddenly his eyes fell upon the 'mummy'; immediately he sat up, and the very next instant he sprang forward in a single bound, snatched up that rolled-up 'papyrus' manuscript, and hurriedly stuffed it inside a drawer of the table. Then he turned around and said in an angry voice, "Why are there outsiders in my room? What do you want?" In a hurt voice, Abani said, "We want nothing at all! You were screaming and groaning, and hearing that, we came to help." In an embarrassed tone, Bhairab said, "Oh, Dilipbabu! My head is not right at the moment; I have blurted out I know not what—please forgive me. It is fortunate that you came, otherwise I do not know what would have happened! Oh, what a fool I am, what a fool I am!"—and saying this, he went back, sat down on the sofa, and buried his face in both hands. Abani went up to Bhairab, placed a hand on his head, and said, "Bhairabbabu, you are playing with fire! In the dead of night, a man ought not to meddle with a 'mummy'. There is no telling what might happen." Lifting his face, Bhairab said in a low voice, "Abanibabu, if you too had seen what I saw, you would surely have gone mad by now." —"What did you see?" Bhairab suddenly changed his tone and said, "No, nothing much. What I mean is, not many people would have the courage to stay with a 'mummy' at midnight!... What is this, are you leaving already? No, no, do not go right away; sit a little longer!" Abani said, "What is this smell inside the room? It feels as if I am suffocating!" Picking up something like dried leaves from a vessel on the table and tossing them into a burning dhunuchi, Bhairab said, "This is the sacred dhuno of the Egyptian priests... In an alert voice, Subandhu said, "Greek soldiers!" Chitrarath said, "They've reached the ferry-landing and dismounted quickly! They mean to cross the river!" Puranjan asked, "Have they struck such a huge camp so quickly and begun their march already?" Shaking his head, Subandhu said, "The main army is probably still busy trying to strike camp." —"Then are they an advance guard?" —"Possibly. But my belief is that they are looking for us. They have surely guessed our purpose—they have surely come to capture us!" —"But we will not be captured. It will take them time to cross the river. By then we'll be able to ride far ahead. On the far bank, the urgency of the Greeks grew more frantic still as they saw the prey snatched once again from their very jaws. Once more day gives way to night, and night gives way to day. Once they can plunge into the fastnesses of the Hindu Kush, who will ever be able to catch them? From beyond the Hindu Kush, the ancient soul of their Great India is calling out to them! Beneath the hooves of the homeward-bound horses awakes the rhythm of lightning speed! A vast, flat plain—lying utterly helpless, scorching under the fiery midday sun. Coming very close to the mountain, Puranjan's horse suddenly stopped first—and then sank down onto the ground. Twitching once or twice, it lay completely still! Puranjan dropped to his knees on the ground to examine the horse, while Subandhu and Chitrarath dismounted from their own horses as well. Lifting a face as pale as death, Puranjan said in a choked voice, "My horse will never rise again in this life!" Subandhu said, "Losing a horse right now means falling captive into the enemy's hands. Anxiously Subandhu said, "What do we do now? How can we possibly flee, leaving Puranjan behind here?" In a resolute voice Puranjan said, "Listen, Subandhu! I have settled upon a plan. Right now, this plan is our only way." Spurring their horses, the Greeks were now galloping forward at an even faster pace. Keeping his eyes fixed in that direction, Subandhu said, "Whatever you have to say, say it quickly. Otherwise we'll be taken captive standing right here." Drawing a deep breath and squaring his chest, Puranjan said, "A son of India is not taken captive so easily! Listen, Subandhu! Before us stands the high mountain, and behind us are the Greek troops—even on horseback we couldn't escape anywhere else! But do you see that narrow path winding up the mountain? Two men cannot climb that path side by side! Come, let us leave the horses behind and climb up that path. The Greeks too will have to leave their horses and climb up that path one by one. Chitrarath and I will climb the mountain, stand across that path, and hold the enemy back." In an astonished voice Subandhu asked, "And what about me?" —"With God's blessing, you run on toward India. Alone, you will be able to slip ahead under cover for a few days. Then, buying a fresh horse, you will rouse India from her carefree slumber in time." —"And the two of you?" —"We will hold the enemy at bay for as long as we can. And then, with a smile on our lips, we will lay down our lives for our homeland." —"That cannot be, Puranjan! Why should I be deprived of the joy of laying down my life for our homeland?" In a harsh voice Puranjan said, "Do not argue, Subandhu—there is no time for bandying words now. The Greeks are marching on India; you will get plenty of chances to lay down your life for our homeland! Fulfill the greatest duty of all right now, while we hold back the enemy.—Chitrarath! Why are you silent? Are you afraid?" Proudly Chitrarath replied, "Afraid! Does a Kshatriya fear death? I am keeping quiet because silence is the mark of consent!" Unsheathing his sword and running toward the mountain, Puranjan cried, "Then come with me! Say—Victory, victory to India!" Filling the sky and air with cries of victory in India's name, the three sons of India raced at full speed toward the mountain ahead. As soon as they reached the spot, Subandhu realized that Puranjan had made no mistake—by standing firm across this narrow path, just two men could hold off a multitude for a long time! About seventy or eighty feet higher up, the path grew narrower still. Puranjan said, "This is the place where we make our stand! Now press onward, Subandhu, along the sacred path of our fatherland! Victory, victory to India!" In a heavy voice Subandhu said, "Fortunate friends! In a few days' time, vast India will raise cries of victory in your names with a grateful heart! Come, give me one last embrace! Then I shall go along the path of sleeping India, while you tread the path of waking death!" Sitting upon the throne of Persia then was Darius the Third, Codomannus. He was known as the Great Emperor, it is true, but he lacked military genius. On the battlefield of Issus, the strength of the East and the West was first put to the test (332 BC). With six hundred thousand troops, Darius attacked Alexander. In numbers, the Greeks were considerably weaker, and had Darius possessed military genius, Alexander's dream of world conquest would have vanished that very day. Instead, with utter foolishness, Darius maneuvered his vast army into a narrow defile. As a result, despite being far superior in numbers, the Persians could accomplish nothing. They perished in droves like locusts, and the remainder fled across the Euphrates River. Winning one battle after another in succession, Alexander captured the greater part of the Persian Empire. Persepolis, the famous capital city of Persia, was offered up to the flames, and Darius himself was slain at the hands of a traitorous countryman. The victorious Alexander then gazed proudly around the world. Yet across the civilized world of Europe and Africa at the time, he could see no worthy rival to himself. Rome had been born, but as I have said before, she was then an infant. Suddenly, Alexander remembered India. The fame of Indian civilization had crossed many lands and seas to reach Greece as well. Along the trade routes, too, Indian goods were held in no small esteem. A part of the Persian Empire also lay within India. Moreover, on the battlefield itself, Alexander had had the opportunity to witness with his own eyes the prowess of the tall, strong-armed North Indian Aryan warriors fighting on the side of the Persians. Alexander declared, "I shall conquer India. I shall not leave even the last trace of the Persian Empire standing!" Alarmed, his generals said, "What are you saying, Emperor! That is so far away! In your absence, rebellion will break out in Greece!" Alexander could never brook any protest. In an impatient voice he said, "Be silent, all of you! What the Persians have achieved is not impossible for me. I shall conquer India!" Before the wrathful gaze of the young world-conqueror, the veteran generals silently bowed their heads. Yet was Alexander truly able to conquer India? He won a few battles on the banks of the Five Rivers, it is true, but wounded in the battle of Multan, he came close to the jaws of death. And most historians remain silent about the fact that it was here in India that he was forced to endure the humiliation of his first defeat. Without having conquered India, the Greeks were forced to turn back—or flee—toward their homeland once more. Alexander had set foot upon only one corner of India. And when departing for his homeland, he left behind great generals and numerous troops to guard that occupied portion of Northern India. Yet not even Western historians have been able to conceal the story of the unforeseen disaster that befell them when they fell into the clutches of the great heroes of Eastern India. All these matters will be told to you in due course. Bear in mind that in Alexander's time, Vedic Hinduism prevailed in India. Hindus then neither worshipped idols nor built temples to the gods; according to some historians, Hindus and Buddhists learned to fashion images and build temples from the Greeks themselves. How much truth there is in this I do not know, though there is no doubt whatsoever that before the coming of the Greeks to India, no one had ever fashioned an image of Lord Buddha.
Target Output: পারস্য-সাম্রাজ্য তখন পারস্যেরও বাইরে এসিয়া-মাইনরে, মিশরে, বাবিলনে ও ভারতে সিন্ধুনদের তট পর্যন্ত বিস্তৃত। পারস্যের সিংহাসনে বসেছেন তখন তৃতীয় দরায়ুস কোডোমেন্নাস। তিনি মহা-সম্রাটরূপে পরিচিত বটে, কিন্তু তাঁর যুদ্ধপ্রতিভা ছিল না। ইস্‌সাস্ রণক্ষেত্রে প্রথমে প্রাচ্য ও প্রতীচ্যের শক্তি পরীক্ষা হয় (খৃঃ পূঃ ৩৩২)। ছয় লক্ষ সৈন্য নিয়ে দরায়ুস আক্রমণ করলেন আলেকজাণ্ডারকে। সংখ্যায় গ্রীকরা যথেষ্ট দুর্বল ছিল এবং দরায়ুসের যুদ্ধপ্রতিভা থাকলে সেইদিনই মিলিয়ে যেত আলেকজাণ্ডারের দিগ্বিজয়ের স্বপ্ন। কিন্তু অতিশয় নির্বোধের মতো দরায়ুস একটি সংকীর্ণ ক্ষেত্রের মধ্যে নিজের বিপুল বাহিনী চালনা করলেন। ফলে সংখ্যায় ঢের বেশী হয়েও পারসীরা কিছুই করতে পারলে না। তারা পঙ্গপালের মতো দলে দলে মারা পড়ল, বাদবাকী ইউফ্রেটেস্ নদী পেরিয়ে পালিয়ে গেল। পরে-পরে আরো অনেকগুলি যুদ্ধে জয়লাভ ক’রে আলেকজাণ্ডার পারস্য সাম্রাজ্যের অধিকাংশ দখল করলেন। পারস্যের রাজধানী বিখ্যাত নগর পার্সিপোলিস্‌কে অগ্নিশিখায় আহুতি দেওয়া হ’ল এবং এক স্বদেশী বিশ্বাসঘাতকের হস্তে দরায়ুসও মারা পড়লেন। বিজয়ী আলেকজাণ্ডার তখন সগর্বে পৃথিবীর চতুর্দিকে দৃষ্টিপাত করলেন। কিন্তু য়ুরোপে ও আফ্রিকায় তখনকার সভ্য-জগতে নিজের কোনো যোগ্য প্রতিদ্বন্দ্বী দেখতে পেলেন না। রোমের জন্ম হয়েছে, কিন্তু আগেই বলেছি, সে তখন শিশু। হঠাৎ আলেকজাণ্ডারের মনে পড়ল ভারতবর্ষের কথা। ভারতীয় সভ্যতার খ্যাতি তখন দেশ-দেশান্তর অতিক্রম ক’রে গ্রীসেও গিয়ে উপস্থিত হয়েছে। বাণিজ্য-পথেও ভারতীয় পণ্যদ্রব্যের আদর কম নয়। ভারতে ও পারসীদের সাম্রাজ্যের অংশ আছে। এবং যুদ্ধক্ষেত্রেও পারসীদের পক্ষে উত্তর ভারতীয় দীর্ঘদেহ সবলবাহু আর্য বীরদের পরাক্রম আলেকজাণ্ডার স্বচক্ষে দেখবার সুযোগ পেয়েছিলেন। আলেকজাণ্ডার বললেন, “আমি ভারত জয় করবো। পারস্যসাম্রাজ্যের শেষ-চিহ্নও আর রাখবো না!” সেনাপতিরা ভয় পেয়ে বললেন, “বলেন কি সম্রাট! সে যে অনেক দূর! আপনার অবর্তমানে গ্রীসে যে বিদ্রোহ উপস্থিত হবে!” আলেকজাণ্ডার কোনোদিন প্রতিবাদ সহ্য করতে পারতেন না। অধীর স্বরে বললেন, “স্তব্ধ হও তোমরা! পারসীরা যা পেরেছে, আমার পক্ষে তা অসম্ভব নয়। আমি ভারত জয় করবো!” যুবক দিগ্বিজয়ীর ক্রুদ্ধ দৃষ্টির সামনে প্রাচীন সেনাপতিরা নীরবে মাথা নত করলেন। কিন্তু আলেকজাণ্ডার কি সত্যসত্যই ভারত জয় করতে পেরেছিলেন? পঞ্চনদের তীরে কয়েকটি যুদ্ধে জয়লাভ করেছিলেন বটে, কিন্তু মূলতানের যুদ্ধে আহত হয়ে তিনি প্রায় মৃত্যু-মুখে এগিয়ে গিয়েছিলেন। এবং এই ভারতেই তিনি যে প্রথম পরাজয়ের অপমান সহ্য করতে বাধ্য হন, অধিকাংশ ঐতিহাসিকই সে সম্বন্ধে নীরব। ভারত জয় না ক’রেই গ্রীকরা আবার স্বদেশের দিকে ফিরতে—বা পলায়ন করতে বাধ্য হয়েছিল। আলেকজাণ্ডার ভারতের মাত্র এক প্রান্তে পদার্পণ করেছিলেন। এবং স্বদেশে প্রস্থান করবার সময়ে বড় বড় সেনাপতি ও অনেক সৈন্যসামন্ত উত্তরভারতের ঐ অধিকৃত অংশ রক্ষা করবার জন্যে রেখে গিয়েছিলেন। কিন্তু পূর্ব-ভারতের মহাবীরদের কবলে প’ড়ে তাদের যে অভাবিত দুর্দশা হয়, পাশ্চাত্য ঐতিহাসিকরাও সে কাহিনী গোপন রাখতে পারেন নি। এ-সব কথা যথাসময়েই তোমাদের কাছে বলা হবে। মনে রেখো, আলেকজাণ্ডারের যুগে ভারতে বৈদিক হিন্দুধম প্রচলিত ছিল। হিন্দুরা তখন মূর্তি-পূজাও করতেন না, দেবমন্দিরও গড়তেন না, কোনো কোনো ঐতিহাসিকের মতে, হিন্দু ও বৌদ্ধরা মূর্তি ও মন্দির গড়তে শেখেন গ্রীকদের কাছ থেকেই। এ কথা কতটা সত্য জানিনা, তবে গ্রীকদের ভারতে আসবার আগে বুদ্ধদেবের মূর্তি যে কেউ গড়েনি, সে-বিষয়ে কোনোও সন্দেহ নেই।

Input: For nearly twelve or thirteen minutes they kept running like this, and in all that time the stream of laughter did not cease even once. Then suddenly the laughter stopped, the forest path came to an end, and right in front of them stood a towering wall blocking the way. Stopping in despair, Kumar said, "The way ahead is blocked! What do we do now?" Helplessly, Bimal and Jayanta looked this way and that. Suddenly, inside the forest, the groan of dry leaves crushed under hundreds of feet rose once again. Jayanta said, "This time the footsteps are coming from both sides and from behind us. In front of us is a sheer wall. There's no way left for us to escape." With a faint smile, Bimal said, "We aren't escaping—we're making a retreat." Trying to smile as well, Jayanta said, "Fine, I grant you these are our tactical movements; but which way do we march now?" Bimal said, "Look closely straight ahead—set into the wall in front of us is a small door. And its leaves aren't shut either." Stepping two paces forward and looking closely, Jayanta saw that Bimal was right! Then he said, "I see your eyes work better in the dark than ours! But if we go inside there, will we ever be able to get out again? It's quite clear that the invisible enemies on either side and behind us are using their booming laughter and footsteps to herd us right this way. Just as hunters drive tigers or lions along a set path into a trap, our enemies have adopted the exact same trick." Bimal said, "Exactly. I've figured out their intention too. And to make it convenient for us to enter, they have kindly left both leaves of the door open! So, thanking them kindly, we have no choice now but to stick our heads through that doorway, because the footsteps aren't far off anymore!" Kumar asked, "What if there's a new danger waiting on the other side of the door?" —"We will welcome that danger fearlessly," said Bimal, and raising his gun at the ready, he stepped through the doorway first. Kumar and Jayanta followed close behind him! Stepping inside, they saw in astonishment a small open ground devoid of trees or grass, enclosed on all four sides by a wall nearly four stories high. At first glance, it looked as if someone had raised walls there to imprison the bleak, terrifying silence of an utterly desolate desert! Jayanta asked, "What is the meaning of this? Why has an open field been enclosed by such a high wall?" After a brief silence, Bimal said, "A long time ago, we went to Champa-Dwip. Kumar, hearing this roaring today, doesn't it remind you of certain creatures from that place?" Kumar asked, "Do they mean to keep us imprisoned in here?" As if in answer to his question, the two leaves of the door behind them slammed shut with a loud clang. Bimal ran back, tugged hard at the door, and said, "Yes, Kumar, having come to Amrita-Dwip, the Island of Nectar, it seems our lot will be pure poison. This door is so solid that even a rutting elephant couldn't do a thing to it! I hadn't noticed until now, but this is a thick iron door, and this wall is made of stone. To break through this door and wall, one would need a cannon!"

"What else could I do, tell me? We're poor, humble folk. If he laid Shyamachand across my back, what could I possibly do, tell me that! What did the Sahib say to you?"

"He spoke quite kindly."

"And what was Ray Mashay saying to you earlier?"

"He was saying that the Sahib was coming, and told me to sit up straight."

"Why wouldn't he say that? Men like him are the Sahib's brokers, after all! Working as the Dewan of the indigo factory, Ray Mashay has made a pretty penny for himself! Look at that huge two-courtyard brick mansion he built the other year."

Ray Mashay's full name was Rajaram Ray. He was the Dewan of the Mollahati indigo factory. For his sycophancy toward the Sahib and his oppression of the tenant farmers, the people of this region hated him every bit as much as they feared him. Yet no one had the courage to say a word to his face. His home was in the nearby village of Panchpota.

The afternoon sun had slanted down behind the dense green of the orchards when Rajaram Ray rode into his own compound and dismounted from his horse. Bhaja Muchi, a paternal cousin of Nafar Muchi, came up and took hold of the horse. Glancing toward the chandimandap pavilion, Rajaram saw that a large crowd of people had gathered there. In the chandimandap of the indigo factory's Dewan,

such a crowd was a constant sight all twelve months of the year. People from various villages had come to plead all sorts of cases: in someone's field, standing crops had been ploughed under by force and sown with indigo; in someone else's, instead of marking off the plot originally agreed upon for the indigo advance, the factory's amin surveyor had gone and marked off another, far more fertile plot for sowing indigo—complaints of every description like these.

And those complaints did get redressed; otherwise, crowds would not have gathered day after day at the Dewan's chandimandap. There was no system of cash bribes for this. Rajaram Ray was not a man to take money as a bribe from anyone; however, once a matter had been settled, if someone sent over a rohu fish, or a large mankachu arum root, or two earthen pots of fresh nolen gur date-palm jaggery as a token gift of respect, he was never known to send it back.

Rajaram's wife Jagadamba had been quite a beauty in her day; wearing an unbleached handloom sari with a red border, bauti and poiche bracelets on her arms, and an iron kharu bangle and conch-shell shakha on her wrists, with a broad streak of vermilion across her forehead, she was a well-built, capable matron of the house.

Jagadamba stepped forward and said, "Don't go back out right now. Finish your evening sandhya-ahnik prayers first."

Smiling, Rajaram handed his wife a small cloth pouch and said, "Put this away. Why, is there some light refreshment ready?"

"Of course there is. I've puffed some muri and fried some chhola chickpeas."

"Wonderful, wonderful! Wait, let me wash my hands and feet first. Where are Tilu, Bilu, and Nilu?"

"They're chopping vegetables."

"I'm coming. Tell Tilu to bring me water."

After dusk had fallen, Rajaram sat down at one end of the raised veranda to perform his evening prayers. Tilu had already come and spread out a kusha-grass mat for him there. He performed his sandhya-ahnik prayers for a long time—nearly an hour—reciting a great many hymns and invocations.

The reason it took so long was that, after completing the evening Gayatri mantra, Rajaram made a habit of reciting hymns to various

deities. Among the gods and goddesses, those whom he considered essential to keep pleased every single day were Lakshmi, Saraswati, Rakshakali, Siddheshwari, and Mother Manasa. It would not do to offend any of them; his mind would feel uneasy. It was by their grace that he was earning his livelihood. Moreover, lest any goddess fail to hear him, he always chanted the hymns clearly in a loud, drawn-out voice.

Tilu came up and asked, "Dada, will you have a green coconut now?"

"No. Isn't there any rock-candy water?"

"There's no rock candy in the house, Dada."

"Leave the coconut then; go bring my snack."

In a large bell-metal bowl—a jambati big enough to hold at least half a katha of puffed rice—Tilu brought muri and fried chhola thoroughly soaked and tossed in mustard oil. Bilu brought a bell-metal plate heaped with firm khaja jackfruit cloves. Nilu brought a metal pot of water and about half a poya of date-palm jaggery in a stone bowl.

Rajaram said affectionately to Nilu, "Sit down, Nilu—will you have some jackfruit?"

"No, Dada. You eat—I've already eaten plenty."

"Will you take some, Bilu?"

"You eat, Dada."

—কি করি বলো। আমরা হলাম গরীব-গুরবো নোক। শ্যামাচাঁদ পিঠে বসিয়ে দিলে করচি কি তাই বলে দিনি। কি বললে সায়েব তোমারে?

রায় মশায়ের পুরো নাম রাজারাম রায়। মোল্লাহাটি নীলকুঠির দেওয়ান। সাহেবের খয়েরখাঁই ও প্রজাপীড়নের জন্যে এদেশের লোকে যেমন ভয় করে, তেমনি ঘৃণা করে। কিন্তু মুখে কারো কিছু বলবার সাহস নেই। নিকটবর্তী পাঁচপোতা গ্রামে বাড়ি।

বিকেলের সূর্য বাগানের নিবিড় সবুজের আড়ালে ঢলে পড়েচে, এমন সময় রাজারাম রায় নিজের বাড়িতে ঢুকে ঘোড়া থেকে নামলেন। নফর মুচির এক খুড়তুতো ভাই ভজা মুচি এসে ঘোড়া ধরলে। চণ্ডীমণ্ডপের দিকে চেয়ে দেখলেন অনেকগুলো লোক সেখানে জড়ো হয়েচে। নীলকুঠির দেওয়ানের

চণ্ডীমণ্ডপে অমন ভিড় বারো মাসই লেগে আছে। কত রকমের দরবার করতে এসেছে নানা গ্রামের লোক, কারো জমিতে ফসল ভেঙে নীল বোনা হয়েচে জোর-জবরদস্তি করে, কারো নীলের দাদনের জন্যে যে জমিতে দাগ দেওয়ার কথা ছিল তার বদলে অন্য এবং উৎকৃষ্টতর জমিতে কুঠির আমীন গিয়ে নীল বোনার জন্যে চিহ্নিত করে এসেচে— এই সব নানা রকমের নালিশ।

নালিশের প্রতিকার হোত। নতুবা দেওয়ানের চণ্ডীমণ্ডপে লোকের ভিড় জমতো না রোজ রোজ। তার জন্যে ঘুষ-ঘাষের ব্যবস্থা ছিল না। রাজারাম রায় কারো কাছে ঘুষ নেবার পাত্র ছিলেন না, তবে কার্য অন্তে কেউ একটা রুই মাছ, কি বড় একটু মানকচু কিংবা দু’ভাঁড় খেজুরের নলেন্‌ গুড় পাঠিয়ে দিলে ভেটস্বরূপ, তা তিনি ফেরত দেন বলে শোনা যায় নি।

রাজারামের স্ত্রী জগদম্বা এক সময়ে বেশ সুন্দরী ছিলেন, পরনে, লালপেড়ে তাঁতের কোরা শাড়ি, হতে বাউটি পৈঁছে, লোহার খাড়ু ও শাঁখা, কপালে চওড়া করে সিঁদুর পরা, দোহারা চেহারার গিন্নিবান্নি মানুষটি।

রাজারাম হেসে স্ত্রীর হাতে ছোট একটা থলি দিয়ে বললেন— এটা রেখে দাও। কেন, কিছু জলপান আছে বুঝি?

I thought for a moment and asked, 'Then what shall I call you now? You aren't a real cat; actually, you are a handkerchief.'

The cat replied, 'You can call me a cat, you can call me a handkerchief, or you can call me a chandrabindu.'

To your lotus feet,

We have been married for fifteen years today, and until today I have never written you a letter. I have always been right there beside you—you have heard many spoken words from me, and I have heard many from you too, so there was never space enough between us to write a letter.

Today I have come on a pilgrimage to Shrikhetra, while you are back at your office work. Your relationship with Kolkata is like a snail's with its shell—it has become fused to your body and mind. That is why you did not apply for leave at your office. Such was the Creator's design; He has granted my application for leave instead.

I am the Mejobou—the second daughter-in-law—of your family. Today, after fifteen years, standing by the shore of this sea, I have come to realise that I also have another relationship with my world and with the Lord of the World. That is why I have gathered the courage to write this letter today; this is not a letter from your family's Mejobou.

In my childhood, when no one knew of the possibility of my bond with your family except the One who had written it on my forehead, my brother and I fell ill with typhoid fever at the very same time. My brother died, and I survived. All the women of the neighbourhood began to say, "Mrinal is a girl, after all—that's why she lived; if she had been a boy, would she ever have been spared?" Yama is a master at the art of stealing; his greed is always for the precious things.

There is no death for me. It is to explain that very thing clearly that I have sat down to write this letter.

The day your distant maternal uncle brought your friend Nirod to inspect the prospective bride, I was twelve years old. Our home was in a remote country village where jackals called even in the daytime. One had to travel seven krosh from the station in a hackney carriage and then cover the remaining three miles of unpaved dirt road in a palki just to reach our village. What an ordeal you all went through that day! And on top of that, our Bangal country cooking—Uncle still hasn't forgotten the farce of that meal.

Your mother was dead set on making up for your Barobou's lack of beauty through the Mejobou. Otherwise, why would you go to such trouble to travel to that village of ours? In Bengal, no one has to go searching for an enlarged spleen, a bad liver, dyspepsia, or a bride; they come and latch onto you on their own and refuse to let go no matter what.

Father's heart pounded with dread, and Mother began chanting the name of Durga. With what could a village priest please a city god? Their only hope rested on their daughter's beauty; yet the girl herself had no pride in that beauty—whatever value the man who had come to inspect her chose to place upon her, that alone was her worth. That is why, even with a thousand beauties and virtues, a woman's diffidence never goes away.

This terror of the entire household—and indeed, of the entire neighbourhood—sat heavy as a stone upon my chest. All the light in the sky that day and all the forces in the world seemed to be acting like bailiffs to hold a twelve-year-old village girl firmly up for inspection before the two pairs of eyes of two examiners—I had nowhere to hide.

The wedding flutes began to play, making the whole sky weep—and I came to live in your house. Even after examining all my flaws in great detail, the matrons of the household all admitted that, on the whole, I was indeed beautiful. Hearing that, my elder sister-in-law's face grew solemn. Yet I wonder what need there ever was for my beauty. If some old-fashioned pandit had fashioned beauty out of sacred Ganga clay, it would have been cherished; but because the Creator fashioned it purely out of His own joy, it has no value in your pious household.

আজ পনেরো বছর আমাদের বিবাহ হয়েছে, আজ পর্যন্ত তোমাকে চিঠি লিখি নি। চিরদিন কাছেই পড়ে আছি—মুখের কথা অনেক শুনেছি, আমিও শুনেছি, চিঠি লেখবার মতো ফাঁকটুকু পাওয়া যায় নি।

আজ আমি এসেছি তীর্থ করতে শ্রীক্ষেত্রে, তুমি আছ তোমার আপিসের কাজে। শামুকের সঙ্গে খোলসের যে সম্বন্ধ কলকাতার সঙ্গে তোমার তাই, সে তোমার দেহ-মনের সঙ্গে এঁটে গিয়েছে। তাই তুমি আপিসে ছুটির দরখাস্ত করলে না। বিধাতার তাই অভিপ্রায় ছিল; তিনি আমার ছুটির দরখাস্ত মঞ্জুর করেছেন।

আমি তোমাদের মেজোবউ। আজ পনেরো বছরের পরে এই সমুদ্রের ধারে দাঁড়িয়ে জানতে পেরেছি, আমার জগৎ এবং জগদীশ্বরের সঙ্গে আমার অন্য সম্বন্ধও আছে। তাই আজ সাহস করে এই চিঠিখানি লিখছি, এ তোমাদের মেজোবউয়ের চিঠি নয়।

তোমাদের সঙ্গে আমার সম্বন্ধ কপালে যিনি লিখেছিলেন তিনি ছাড়া যখন সেই সম্ভাবনার কথা আর কেউ জানত না, সেই শিশুবয়সে আমি আর আমার ভাই একসঙ্গেই সান্নিপাতিক জ্বরে পড়ি। আমার ভাইটি মারা গেল, আমি বেঁচে উঠলুম। পাড়ার সব মেয়েরাই বলতে লাগল, “মৃণাল মেয়ে কি না, তাই ও বাঁচল, বেটাছেলে হলে কি আর রক্ষা পেত।” চুরিবিদ্যাতে যম পাকা, দামি জিনিসের ’পরেই তার লোভ।

আমার মরণ নেই। সেই কথাটাই ভালো করে বুঝিয়ে বলবার জন্যে এই চিঠিখানি লিখতে বসেছি।

যেদিন তোমাদের দুরসম্পর্কের মামা তোমার বন্ধু নীরদকে নিয়ে কনে দেখতে এলেন তখন আমার বয়স বারো। দুর্গম পাড়াগাঁয়ে আমাদের বাড়ি, সেখানে দিনের বেলায় শেয়াল ডাকে। স্টেশন থেকে সাত ক্রোশ শ্যাক্‌রা গাড়িতে এসে বাকি তিন মাইল কাঁচা রাস্তায় পাল্‌কি করে তবে আমাদের গাঁয়ে পৌঁছনো যায়। সেদিন তোমাদের কী হয়রানি। তার উপরে আমাদের বাঙাল দেশের রান্না—সেই রান্নার প্রহসন আজও মামা ভোলেন নি।

তোমাদের বড়োবউয়ের রূপের অভাব মেজোবউকে দিয়ে পূরণ করবার জন্যে তোমার মায়ের একান্ত জিদ ছিল। নইলে এত কষ্ট করে আমাদের সে গাঁয়ে তোমরা যাবে কেন। বাংলাদেশে পিলে যকৃৎ অম্লশূল এবং ক’নের জন্য তো কাউকে খোঁজ করতে হয় না; তারা আপনি এসে চেপে ধরে, কিছুতে ছাড়তে চায় না।

বাবার বুক দুর্‌দুর্ করতে লাগল, মা দুর্গানাম জপ করতে লাগলেন। শহরে দেবতাকে পাড়াগাঁয়ের পূজারি কী দিয়ে সন্তুষ্ট করবে। মেয়ের রূপের উপর ভরসা; কিন্তু সেই রূপের গুমর তো মেয়ের মধ্যে নেই, যে ব্যক্তি দেখতে এসেছে সে তাকে যে দামই দেবে সেই তার দাম। তাই তো হাজার রূপে গুণেও মেয়েমানুষের সংকোচ কিছুতে ঘোচে না।

সমস্ত বাড়ির, এমন-কি, সমস্ত পাড়ার এই আতঙ্ক আমার বুকের মধ্যে পাথরের মতো চেপে বসল। সেদিনকার আকাশের যত আলো এবং জগতের সকল শক্তি যেন বারো বছরের একটি পাড়াগেঁয়ে মেয়েকে দুইজন পরীক্ষকের দুইজোড়া চোখের সামনে শক্ত করে তুলে ধরবার জন্যে পেয়াদাগিরি করছিল—আমার কোথাও লুকোবার জায়গা ছিল না।

সমস্ত আকাশকে কাঁদিয়ে দিয়ে বাঁশি বাজতে লাগল—তোমাদের বাড়িতে এসে উঠলম। আমার খুঁৎগুলি সবিস্তারে খতিয়ে দেখেও গিন্নির দল সকলে স্বীকার করলেন, মোটের উপরে আমি সুন্দরী বটে। সে কথা শুনে আমার বড়ো জায়ের মুখ গম্ভীর হয়ে গেল। কিন্তু, আমার রূপের দরকার কী ছিল তাই ভাবি। রূপ-জিনিসটাকে যদি কোনো সেকেলে পণ্ডিত গঙ্গামৃত্তিকা দিয়ে গড়তেন তা হলে ওর আদর থাকত; কিন্তু, ওটা যে কেবল বিধাতা নিজের আনন্দে গড়েছেন, তাই তোমাদের ধর্মের সংসারে ওর দাম নেই।

Pareshbabu made up his mind. In the morning, he revealed the secret of making gold to Priyatosh.

Priyatosh remained unmoved. Handing him the touchstone, Pareshbabu said, "Destroy this today itself—by burning it, dissolving it in acid, or by whatever other means you can." Priyatosh said, "Right-o."

In the afternoon, a darwan came running to Pareshbabu and said, "Come quickly, Huzoor! Biswas Saheb has gone mad and is calling for you." Pareshbabu hurried over and saw Priyatosh lying on the cot in his bedroom, weeping. Pareshbabu asked, "What is the matter?" Priyatosh replied, "Read this letter and see, sir." Pareshbabu read—

Priya, O Priya, farewell. Father does not agree; he has all sorts of objections. You have neither roof nor hearth, you live in someone else's house, you earn a salary of a mere hundred and fifty rupees, and on top of that you are a Christian by caste, and a year younger than I am as well. He said the marriage is out of the question. And listen to another piece of news. Have you heard the name of Gunjan Ghosh? He sings splendidly, has a handsome appearance, and curly hair. He earns a salary of six hundred rupees in the Civil Supply, is his father's only son, and his father has reportedly made crores of rupees in contracting. My marriage has been fixed with that Gunjan. Do not grieve, there's a dear. You know Bakul Mallik, don't you? She is three years junior to me; we studied together at Diocesan. She cannot hold a candle to me, of course, yet you won't find a girl like her in a thousand. Win Bakul over, and you will be happy. Priya darling, this is my last love letter; from tomorrow you are my brother, and I am your affectionate didi. Yours until today—Hindola.

After reading the letter, Pareshbabu said, "You are quite a fool, my boy! Hindola is stepping aside of her own accord—this is wonderful news, why grieve over it? Offering puja at Kalighat won't do for you, of course, so why not light a couple of candles at church instead? Come on, get up now, splash some water on your eyes and face, and come have some tea and a few luchis. Oh, by the way—did you manage to dispose of the stone?"

In a doleful voice, Priyatosh said, "I have swallowed it, sir. I shall not keep this life any longer; your stone will go to the grave with me. Oh, after so many days of love, now it comes to Gunjan Ghosh!"

Astonished, Pareshbabu said, "Why did you swallow the stone? Is it poison?"

Priyatosh said, "Its composition is unknown, sir, but I think it is poison. Even if it is not poison, if I do not die tonight, tomorrow morning I shall certainly take ten grams of potassium cyanide; I have weighed it out and kept it ready. Do not worry, sir; your stone will remain buried right along with me until the Day of Judgment."

Pareshbabu said, "What a madman I have got mixed up with! Give up those foolish notions; I shall try to arrange your marriage with Hindola. Her father, Jagai Majumdar, is my childhood friend—a shrewd old bird. I will give you a handsome dowry, and when he hears that, perhaps he will agree to give his daughter. But you are a Christian—"

—"I will become a Hindu, sir."

—"Now that is what they call love. Get up now, let us go to Dr. Chatterjee; we must get that stone out of your stomach."

প্রিয়তোষ নির্বিকার। পরেশবাবু তাকে পরশপাথরটা দিয়ে বললেন, এটাকে আজই ধ্বংস ক’রে ফেল, পুড়িয়ে, অ্যাসিডে গলিয়ে, অথবা অন্য যে কোনও উপায়ে পার। প্রিয়তোষ বললে, রাইট-ও।

বিকালবেলা একজন দারোয়ান দৌড়ে এসে পরেশবাবুকে বললে, জলদি আসুন হ‍ুজুর, বিসোআস সাহেব পাগলা হয়ে গেছেন, আপনাকে ডাকছেন। পরেশবাবু তাড়াতাড়ি গিয়ে দেখলেন, প্রিয়তোষ তার শোবার ঘরে খাটিয়ায় শুয়ে কাঁদছে। পরেশবাবু জিজ্ঞাসা করলেন, ব্যাপার কি? প্রিয়তোষ উত্তর দিলে, এই চিঠিটা প’ড়ে দেখুন সার। পরেশবাবু পড়লেন —

প্রিয় হে প্রিয়, বিদায়। বাবা রাজী নন, তাঁর নানা রকম আপত্তি। তোমার চাল-চুলো নেই, পরের বাড়িতে থাক, মোটে দেড় শ টাকা মাইনে পাও, তার ওপর আবার জাতে খীষ্টান, আবার আমার চাইতে বয়সে এক বৎসরের ছোট। বললেন, বিয়ে হতেই পারে না। আর একটি খবর শোন। গুঞ্জন ঘোষের নাম শনেছ? চমৎকার গায়, সুন্দর চেহারা, কোঁকড়া চুল। সিভিল সম্পাইএ ছ শ টাকা মাইনে পায়, বাপের একমাত্র ছেলে, বাপ কনট্রাকটারি ক’রে নাকি কোটি টাকা করেছে। সেই গ‍ুঞ্জনের সঙ্গে আমার বিয়ে ঠিক হয়ে গেছে। দঃখ ক’রো না, লক্ষ্মীটি। বকুল মল্লিককে চেন তো? আমার চেয়ে তিন বছরের জুনিয়ার, ডায়োসিসানে এক সঙ্গে পড়েছি। আমার কাছে দাঁড়াতে পারে না, তা হ’ক, অমন মেয়ে হাজারে একটি পাবে না। বকুলকে বাগাও, তুমি সখী হবে। প্রিয় ডারলিং, এই আমার শেষ প্রেমপত্র, কাল থেকে তুমি আমার ভাই, আমি তোমার স্নেহময়ী দিদি। ইতি। আজ পর্যন্ত তোমারই —হিন্দোলা।

চিঠি প’ড়ে পরেশবাবু বললেন, তুমি তো আচ্ছা বোকা হে! হিন্দোলা নিজেই স’রে পড়ছে, এ তো অতি সুখবর, এতে দুঃখ কিসের? তোমার আবার কালীঘাটে পূজো দেওয়া চলবে না, না হয় গির্জেয় দুটো মোমবাতি জ্বেলে দিও। নাও, এখন ওঠ, চোখে মুখে জল দাও, চা আর খানকতক লুচি খাবে এস। হাঁ, ভাল কথা —পাথরটার কোনও গতি করতে পারলে?

প্রিয়তোষ করুণ স্বরে বললে, গিলে ফেলেছি সার। এ প্রাণ আর রাখব না, আপনার পাথর আমার সঙ্গেই কবরে যাবে। ওঃ, এত দিনের ভালবাসার পর এখন কিনা গ‍ুঞ্জন ঘোষ!

পরেশবাবু আশ্চর্য হয়ে বললেন, পাথরটা গিললে কেন? বিষ নাকি?

প্রিয়তোষ বললে, কম্পোজিশন তো জানা নেই সার, কিন্তু মনে হচ্ছে ওটা বিষ। যদি বিষ নাও হয়, যদি আজ রাত্রির মধ্যে না মরি, তবে কাল সকালে নিশ্চয় দশ গ্রাম পটাশ সায়ানাইড খাব, আমি ওজন ক’রে রেখেছি। আপনি ভাববেন না সার, আপনার পাথর আমার সঙ্গেই কবরস্থ হয়ে থাকবে, সেই ডে অভ জজমেণ্ট পর্যন্ত।

পরেশবাবু বললেন, আচ্ছা পাগলের পাল্লায় পড়া গেছে! ওসব বদখেয়াল ছাড়, আমি চেষ্টা করব যাতে হিন্দোলার সঙ্গে তোমার বিয়ে হয়। ওর বাপ জগাই মজুমদার আমার বাল্যবন্ধু, ঘুঘু লোক। তোমাকে আমি ভাল রকম যৌতুক দেব, তা শুনলে হয়তো সে মেয়ে দিতে রাজী হবে। কিন্তু তুমি যে খীষ্টান —

— হিদুঁ, হব সার।

— একেই বলে প্রেম। এখন ওঠ, ডাক্তার চ্যাটার্জির কাছে চল, পাথরটাকে তো পেট থেকে বার করতে হবে।

I am no longer afraid of your narrow lane. Before me today lies the blue sea, and above my head gather the monsoon clouds of Asharh.

You had kept me shrouded in the darkness of your customs. Coming for a brief moment, Bindu caught sight of me through a chink in that veil. And it was that very girl who, by her own death, tore my veil apart from top to bottom before she left. Stepping outside today, I see that there is no room big enough to hold my glory. The Beautiful One, in whose eyes this neglected beauty of mine has found favour, is gazing down at me through the whole expanse of the sky. Now at last the Mejobou is dead.

You think I am going to die—do not be afraid, I will not play such an old joke on all of you. Mirabai too was a woman just like me—her chains were no less heavy, and yet she did not have to die in order to live. Mirabai sang in her song: 'Let my father forsake me, let my mother forsake me, let everyone wherever they are forsake me—yet Mira held fast to You, Lord, come what may.'

This holding fast is what it means to truly live.

I too shall live. I am saved.

When all the high-level talks came to naught, everyone realised that human discussions would achieve nothing; things would have to rise to the divine level. Well-wishers of humanity—sadhus and mahatmas—began to perform penance together. At last, what no one had ever dreamed of became possible: Brahma, God, and Allah assembled on Mount Sumeru, that is to say, the Hindu Kush mountains. Many other gods and demigods had also wished to join the deliberations of this divine assembly, but fearing that too many sannyasis might spoil the Gajan festival, the organisers had invited only the three Creators.

Along with Brahma came Narad, along with God came Saint Peter, and along with Allah descended a Pir as an attendant. Besides them, many uninvited gods, goddesses, rishis, saints, yakshas, nagas, ghosts, ghouls, angels, devils, and others stationed themselves invisibly all around to watch the fun.

Everyone knows the form of Brahma—four arms, four faces; one moment it seems he has a beard and moustache, and the next moment it seems he does not. He wears a white dhoti and chador, a bunch of sacred threads over his shoulder, and a crown on his head. God is formless; there is no way to see Him. Nevertheless, at the special request of His devotees and for the convenience of conversation, He came in the form of the Jehovah of olden times! A chest covered with grizzled beard and moustache, shoulder-length hair, large eyes, knitted brows, a wrathful appearance like Durvasa's, and a long robe on His body. Fifty or sixty years ago, pictures like this used to be sold in the picture shops of Chinabazar for a particular Christian sect; whether they still are, I do not know.

Allah is even more formless than God; despite many entreaties, He did not agree at all to assume a form or to utter a single word. Pir Saheb said, "There is nothing to worry about. Allah is everywhere, and He is here too; I myself shall express His views." But Narad and Saint Peter said, "What proof is there that you won't just speak your own mind?" Pir Saheb replied, "I am setting up this crescent-marked banner right here; standing beneath it and facing west, I shall speak. If Allah is displeased, this sacred banner will fall upon my head." Brahma and God agreed to this proposal, for They are always ready to keep Allah's servant pleased.

A description of Narad, Saint Peter, and Pir Saheb is unnecessary. Their appearances can be seen in jatra performances, in ancient European paintings, and in Islamic gatherings and processions.

Brahma, God, and Allah—the temperaments of these three are not alike. No Hindu deity takes offence at jokes and banter. As for Brahma, it goes without saying—by relation, He is everyone's grandfather. God is exceedingly solemn, though recently He has developed a slight sense of humour, so one may crack a little joke or two with Him. But Allah is not only beyond sight and beyond speech; He is also beyond jest. The declaration of Allah's sovereignty in the preamble to the Pakistani Constitution is no joke at all.

Kalidasa has written that during Mahadeva's penance, at Nandi's command the trees and plants stood motionless, the bumblebees and honeybees kept silent, the birds grew mute, and the deer stopped their frolicking—as if the entire forest were painted in a picture. With the coming together of the three Creators, Mount Sumeru too fell into that same state; but seeing Them launch into an argument instead of sitting in meditation, all creatures stationary and moving took heart and gradually returned to their natural ways.

সমস্ত উচ্চ স্তরের আলাপ অর্থাৎ হাই লেভেল টক যখন ব্যর্থ হ’ল তখন সকলে বুঝলেন যে মানুষের কথাবার্তায় কিছু হবে না, ঐশ্বরিক লেভেলে উঠতে হবে। বিশ্বমানবের হিতার্থী সাধুমহাত্মারা একযোগে তপস্যা করতে লাগলেন। অবশেষে যা কেউ স্বপ্নেও ভাবে নি তা সম্ভব হ’ল, ব্রহ্মা গড আর আল্লা সুমেরু, অর্থাৎ হিন্দুকুশ পর্বতে সমবেত হলেন। আরও বিস্তর দেবতা ও উপদেবতার এই ঐশ্বরিক সভার বিতর্কে যোগ দেবার ইচ্ছা ছিল, কিন্তু অনেক সন্ন্যাসীতে গাজন নষ্ট হ’তে পারে এই আশঙ্কায় উদযোক্তারা কেবল তিন বিধাতাকে আহবান করেছিলেন।
