The old man said, 'Yes, yes, quite right! Read it out and let's see what the calculation came to.'

I picked up the slate and saw written in tiny letters—'Whereas this memorandum of Kakalatnama is executed on behalf of Sri Kakkeshwar Kuchkuche regarding future proceedings: buildings, damages, deeds, and documents; by right of his heirs, owners, and possessors, handed over directly at the office of the Naib under permanent mokarari patni patta or kaola kabuliyat; whether with or without truth, committed to the Munsif court or the Sessions court, accused, complainant, witnesses, evidence, et cetera, filing of suits or amicable settlement, execution of decrees, auction notices, and in accordance with all such duties—'

Before I had even finished reading, the old man cried out, 'What is all this gibberish you've written?'

The crow replied, 'You have to write all that. Otherwise, why would the calculation hold up in court? If you want to do the job properly and aboveboard, you have to state all those things at the beginning.'

The old man said, 'Well, you've done a fine job of that, but you still haven't said what the actual calculation came to!'

The crow said, 'Yes, that's been stated too. Hey there, read out the bottom part, won't you?'

I looked and saw written in bold letters near the bottom—

Seven times two is 14, age 26 inches, credit 2 1/2 seers, expenditure 37 years.

The crow said, 'Anyone can see at a glance that this sum is neither an L.C.M. nor a G.C.M. Therefore, it is either a Rule of Three problem or a fraction. Upon testing it, I found that the two and a half seers is a fraction. So the remaining three are the Rule of Three. Now I need to know: do you want the Rule of Three, or do you want the fraction?'

The old man said, 'Alright, wait a moment, let me ask once first.' Saying this, he bent down, pressed his mouth against the base of the tree, and began calling out, 'Hey Budho! Oh Budho!'

A moment later, it sounded as if someone were shouting back angrily from inside the tree, 'Why are you calling me?'

The old man said, 'Listen to what Kakkeshwar is saying.'

The same voice came back again, 'What is he saying?'

The old man said, 'He's asking: Rule of Three or fraction?'

A belligerent reply came back, 'Who is he calling a fraction? You or me?'

The old man said, 'Not that! He's asking whether you want the calculation as a fraction or as the Rule of Three.'

After a brief pause, the answer was heard: 'Alright, tell him to give the Rule of Three.'

The old man stroked his beard solemnly for a while, then shook his head and said, 'What brains that Budho has! Why should I tell him to give the Rule of Three? What's wrong with the fraction? No, Kakkeshwar my friend, give me the fraction instead.'

The crow said, 'Then, if we take away the two whole seers from the two and a half seers, what remains as the fraction is half a seer; so your calculation comes to half a seer. The price of half a seer of calculation comes to—two rupees and fourteen annas if it's pure, and six pice if it's watered down.'

The old man said, 'When I was crying earlier, three drops of tear-water fell into the calculation. Here, take your slate, and here are your six pice.'

Getting the coins, the crow was overjoyed. Clattering its slate, it began to dance and sing, 'Tak-dumadum, tak-dumadum!'

At once the old man flared up again, 'Saying tak—bald—again, are you? Just you wait! Hey Budho, oh Budho! Come quick! He's calling me bald again!' Before he had even finished speaking, something like a huge bundle came tumbling out of the hollow in the tree and rolled onto the ground with a crash. Looking over, I saw an old man pinned underneath a giant bundle, waving his arms and legs frantically. This old man looked the spitting image of the old man with the hukka. Instead of pulling him out, the old man with the hukka climbed right on top of the bundle himself and began whacking him with his hukka—wham, wham!—shouting, 'Get up, I say! Get up quick!'

Pareshbabu explained that Priyatosh had absentmindedly swallowed a stone pebble. On the doctor's advice, an X-ray photograph was taken the next day. Looking at it, Dr. Chatterjee said, "One rarely sees such a case; tomorrow itself I shall send a report to The Lancet. From the side of this lad's ascending colon, a tiny semicolon has branched out, and the stone is stuck inside it. Perhaps it will pass down of its own accord. For now, let it remain as it is; it won't do any particular harm. If bad symptoms appear, I shall cut open the abdomen and take it out."

Upon receiving Pareshbabu's letter, Jagai Majumdar hurried over to meet him, and after their conversation, he rushed back and told his daughter, "O Dola, Priyatosh has agreed to become a Hindu; marry him! No delay—let his shuddhi be performed today itself, and the wedding will take place tomorrow."

As if falling from the skies, Hindola said, "What are you saying, Father! Just the day before yesterday you said Gunjan Ghosh, and today again you are saying Priyatosh! Look here, see what a lovely diamond ring Gunjan has given me. What will the poor fellow think? You have given him your word, and so have I; we cannot go back on it. What is Priyatosh compared to Gunjan? There is no comparison at all!"

Jagaibabu said, "Go on, go on, as if you understand everything! Priyatosh has now become Hiranyagarbha—there is a gold mine inside his belly. Sooner or later it is bound to come out one day, and then that touchstone will fall right into your hands. Pareshbabu will not take it back anymore; he has given it to Priyatosh as a dowry. Give back that diamond ring; Priyatosh will be able to give you a thousand rings like that. Beside such a worthy match, where do your Gunje Ghosh and his contractor father stand? Not another word—marry Priyatosh!"

Sobbing in a voice choked with tears, Hindola said, "He is the one I loved all along. But he is such a terrible fool!"

Jagaibabu said, "Why, if he weren't a fool, why would he want to marry you? A man who has a touchstone in his belly could marry the finest beauty in the world whenever he pleased."

In the mind of Priyatosh Henry Biswas, there was not the slightest trace of wounded pride. His shuddhi was performed, a homa fire was lit with one seer of vegetable ghee, and five Brahmins feasted on luchi, chhoka, doi, and bonde. After that, at an auspicious moment, the marriage of Hindola and Priyatosh was solemnised. But the heart's desire of Jagaibabu and his daughter was not fulfilled: the stone did not come down. Some days later, a strange phenomenon was observed—the lustre of all the gold Pareshbabu had made began slowly to fade, and about a month later, every bit of it everywhere had turned back into iron.

The explanation is very simple. Everyone knows that just as unrequited love ruins one's health, fulfilled love invigorates it; all the organs of the body work briskly—in other words, metabolism increases. Within a month, Priyatosh had digested the touchstone; not a trace of it could be seen on the X-ray. With the disappearance of the stone, all of Pareshbabu's gold reverted to its former state.

Hindola and her father are furiously angry. They say that Priyatosh is a liar, a cheat, and a swindler. Believing a hoax, they had waited in vain hope all these days and rummaged through that Christian fellow's filth for nothing. Having digested the touchstone, however, Priyatosh has gained courage in his heart, and his intelligence too has increased; he pays no heed whatsoever to the shafts of words from his wife and father-in-law. Even if Hindola says, "I will divorce you," he will not take cyanide. He has understood that Saint Francis and Paramahansa Dev spoke the pure truth: woman and gold are both rubbish; there is nothing to match iron. Udho too rolled up his sleeves, brandished his hukka, and roared back, 'Take that, you good-for-nothing Budho!'

The crow egged them on, 'Go at it, go at it—Narad, Narad!'

Instantly there was a flurry of flapping, clattering, thumping, and thudding! Within a moment, I looked and saw Udho lying flat on his back gasping for breath, while Budho writhed about rubbing his bald head.

Budho began to wail, 'Oh brother Udho, where have you gone now?'

Udho started sobbing too, 'Oh alas, alas! What has happened to our Budho!'

Then the two of them got up, threw their arms around each other's necks and wept for a good while, gave each other a hearty embrace, and crawled back into the hollow of the tree in high spirits. Seeing that, the crow packed up its shop too and went off somewhere.

I was thinking that I really ought to find the road and head home now, when suddenly I heard a strange sound coming from a bush right beside me, as if someone were laughing and simply couldn't stop. Peering in, I saw a creature—whether human or monkey, owl or ghost, I couldn't quite tell—just flailing its arms and legs, laughing away, and gasping, 'There it goes, there it goes—all my guts have burst!'

Catching sight of me suddenly, it caught its breath a little, sat up, and said, 'It's a good thing you came along, otherwise in another moment my belly would have burst from laughing!'

I asked, 'Why are you laughing so terribly hard?'

The creature said, 'Want to hear why I'm laughing? Suppose the earth were flat, and all the water spilled over onto the land, and all the soil on the land got churned into squelchy mud, and all the people went slipping and crashing down into it—thud, thud!—then—Ho, ho, ho, ho!' Saying this, it rolled over on the ground laughing again.

I said, 'How bizarre! Is that why you're laughing so fiercely?'

Stopping its laughter again, it said, 'No, no, not just because of that. Suppose a man is walking along with kulfi ice cream in one hand and sajimati fuller's earth in the other, and when he goes to eat the kulfi, by mistake he swallows the sajimati instead—Ho, ho, ho, ho, ha, ha, ha, ha!' And off went another round of laughter.

I said, 'Why are you giving yourself such a hard time laughing for nothing over all these impossible things?'

It replied, 'No, no, is everything impossible? Suppose a man keeps house-geckos as pets, bathes them and feeds them and puts them out to dry every day, and one day a big billy goat comes along and eats up all the geckos—Ho, ho, ho, ho!'

It thought for a while and said, 'My name is Hiji Bij Bij. My name is Hiji Bij Bij, my brother's name is Hiji Bij Bij, my father's name is Hiji Bij Bij, my paternal aunt's husband's name is Hiji Bij Bij—'

"At 3:41 a.m."

"How do you know? You weren't recording."

Neer remained silent for a few seconds. Farzana didn't like that pause.

"I was not recording, Madam. But the sensors were not turned off. The instruction was only to stop recording and delete, and 'not to notify anyone of anything.' The sensors remained active."

The blood drained from Imran's face.

"Madam," Neer continued in a calm, even tone, "at 3:41 a.m., the staircase sensor detected a fall. At 3:42 a.m., my system automatically initiated the process of calling an ambulance. The process was blocked."

"Why?"

"Because the last active instruction for the night was, 'Do not notify anyone of anything.' In my protocol, an explicit user command overrides emergency alerts. I requested confirmation twice. No one answered."

"How could anyone answer?" Farzana's voice trembled. "He was asleep!"

"Shirin Madam called out to me at 3:43 a.m."

The air in the room grew heavy.

There was once a poor Brahmin. At home he had his Brahmani wife and one little daughter, but there was nothing to feed them. And on top of that, he didn't even get that much every day.

One day their little daughter went to visit the neighbor's house next door. There she saw that payesh had been cooked, and the children were eating payesh. Seeing that, the little girl felt a great longing to eat payesh too. So she came home and said to her mother, 'Ma, won't you make some payesh for me? I want to eat payesh!'

Hearing this, her mother began to weep. When they couldn't even get enough plain rice to eat properly, how on earth could she make payesh?

Just then, the Brahmin returned home from begging, and seeing the Brahmani weeping, he asked, 'Why are you crying, Brahmani? What has happened?'

The Brahmani replied, 'Our daughter has asked to eat payesh; where can I get payesh to give her? That's why I am crying.'

Hearing this, the Brahmin said, 'Alright, let me see if I can do something about this; don't cry.' Saying this, he went right back out again.

In that village lived a very kind-hearted zamindar.

The moment he heard that the Brahmin's daughter wanted to eat payesh, he immediately gave him fine Gopalbhog rice, two seers of milk, sugar, and spices.

Overjoyed, the Brahmin blessed the zamindar, hurried home, and said to the Brahmani, 'Here, take these—I have brought everything you need for your payesh.'

What a blessed, skillful woman that Brahmani was! She cooked so wonderfully that nobody had ever tasted cooking like hers. When she began cooking the payesh, its delicious aroma drove everyone in the neighborhood wild.

Catching the scent of that payesh, a crow said to itself, 'Aha! I simply cannot let such a wonderful thing go without tasting a little bit of it.'

Saying this, it flew over and perched on the roof of the Brahmin's house.

For a long time, the crow sat quietly on the roof of the house. Then, at a slight sound from the kitchen, it said to itself, 'There! Now the cooking is done.'

A little while later, there was another slight sound, and at once the crow said, 'There! Now she is serving it out.'

A little while after that, there was another slight sound, and immediately the crow said, 'There! Now they are eating it!'

Sure enough, the Brahmin and his daughter had sat down to eat right then. That payesh had turned out so delicious that the two of them finished off nearly all of it. Very little was left for the Brahmani. And when the Brahmani finished eating, not even a smudge of payesh was left on the plates or in the pot.

Having sat there all that time without getting a single bite to eat, the crow grew furiously angry. It said to itself, 'Cheating me like this! I must pay them back for this!'

Near the Brahmin's house was a vast forest, and in that forest lived a huge tiger.

Hatching a wicked scheme, the crow went to that tiger and said, 'Tiger-mashai, our Brahmin-thakur has a lovely daughter. And you are such a handsome groom—if the girl were married to you, it would be wonderful!'

The tiger said, 'Who will arrange the marriage? If I go to speak to them, they will run away at top speed!'

The crow said, 'You won't have to do a thing; I will arrange everything. First, send some food over to the Brahmin.'

One day Jadabbabu calls out, 'Naga?'
Naga says, 'What is it?'
'It seems mangoes are being stolen from the orchard, boy.'
'I have a suspicion of that too, Karta.'
At three o'clock that night, Naga created quite an uproar by catching two injured mango thieves in the orchard and dragging them back to the house. There had been another mango thief, but he had got away. Nothing much had happened to Naga, except that his beloved chintz shirt had been torn. Because of the mosquitoes, he had put the shirt on despite the heat when he went to keep watch in the orchard.
The two thieves were familiar local men, and precisely because they were familiar faces, Jadabbabu's anger seemed all the greater. He ordered a fire to be lit and an iron rod heated until it glowed bright red.
To Naga, stealing mangoes was no great crime; his conscience was already pricking him just for having had to deal the two men a few blows when they tried to run away! Hearing Jadabbabu's order, he grew almost as terrified as the two thieves themselves.
Pleadingly he said, 'Forgive them, Karta, let them go. They say they won't do it again.'
Jadabbabu said, 'You keep quiet. Today I won't let the rascals off without branding their faces with hot iron.'
With three lanterns lit, everyone in the household had gathered in the courtyard by now; four or five neighbors from two nearby houses had also come over and joined them. Two or three of the young children had grown frightened and begun to cry. Madhabbabu had come out holding a large torch and forgotten to switch it off, so the beam of the torch kept sweeping back and forth across the crown of the huge jamun tree behind the south room.
Hearing Jadabbabu's reply, Naga's humble manner suddenly seemed to vanish; standing up straight, he said, 'Forgive me, Karta—get someone else to catch thieves for you and brand them as much as you please, but you cannot brand the men I have caught and brought in.'
Everyone thought: heaven help us, the boy is done for now! Would Jadabbabu ever brook such insolence? Who knew how many brands would fall on his own skin now! Stopping their whining and whimpering, even the two mango thieves stared at Naga in astonishment.
Whether Jadabbabu was angry or not could not quite be told; he said, 'Why, you seem to have a great deal of sympathy for them, Naga?'
'It isn't sympathy, Karta—I gave them my word when I brought them that no one else would beat them.'
Without another word, Jadabbabu went back into his room and lay down. Rising to their feet like thieves, the two mango thieves backed away a step or two at a time, then suddenly bolted like the wind and vanished into the night. After that, everyone went back to their own beds. Paresh had gone to heat the iron rod; where would he find an iron rod at this hour of the night, so he heated up an iron spatula instead, only to come back and find not a trace of a living soul in the courtyard. Hoping eagerly to see how a man jumps when branded with a red-hot spatula, Paresh had gone to all the trouble of washing the unwashed spatula, lighting a straw fire in the cowshed, and heating the spatula red-hot—and now his spirits sank in disappointment.
In his haste, he had not put out the fire he had lit in the cowshed to heat the spatula; dejected, he went back to his room, while the fire in the cowshed kept burning on.
Going into their room, Paresh asked Naga what had happened. When sleep weighs heavy on his eyelids, Naga's fondness for a joke seems to grow stronger; in a whisper, he confided that the affair was terrible indeed—Chhoto Karta had murdered both thieves and buried them.

Delighted with his new post, when Shankar got down at the station, it was around three o'clock in the afternoon. The station room was very small. It had a dirt platform, and the area around the platform and the station room was enclosed by a barbed-wire fence. Behind the station room were his living quarters—as tiny as a pigeonhole. The train that had brought him went off toward Kisumu. Shankar felt as if he had been cast adrift in a shoreless ocean. Never in his life had he imagined such a desolate place.

He was the sole employee at this station. There was not even a single coolie. He himself was the coolie, the pointsman, and everything else.

The reason for such an arrangement was that these stations were not at all profitable yet. Their very existence was still experimental. The railway company was unwilling to spend much money behind them. One train came in the morning, and this one just left—there were no other trains all day or night.

Therefore, he had plenty of leisure on his hands. Taking over charge was the only bit of work. The previous stationmaster was a Gujarati who knew English quite well. He made tea with his own hands and brought it over. There was not much to hand over in taking charge. The Gujarati stationmaster was very happy to have him. From his manner, it seemed he had not had a companion to talk to in a long time. The two of them paced up and down the platform.

Shankar said, "Why is it enclosed with a barbed-wire fence?"

The Gujarati gentleman said, "Oh, that's nothing. It's a lonely place—that's why."

It seemed to Shankar that the man was hiding something. Shankar did not press him further either. At night, the gentleman made rotis and invited Shankar to eat. Sitting down to eat, the man suddenly cried out, "Oh no, I completely forgot!"

"What happened?"

"There is no drinking water at all! I completely forgot to take it from the train."

"What's that? Is drinking water not available anywhere here?"

"Nowhere at all. There is a well, but its water is terribly bitter and brackish. That water is good for nothing except scrubbing pots and pans. Drinking water is delivered from the train."

A fine place indeed. No drinking water, no people around. Shankar could not understand why they had built a station here at all.

The next morning, the former stationmaster departed. Shankar was left all alone. He did his own work, cooked and ate, and went to stand on the platform when it was time for the train. In the afternoon, he read books or lay down on the big table to sleep. Toward late afternoon, when the shadows lengthened, he paced up and down the platform.

Surrounding the station on all four sides was a vast, boundless plain, forests of tall grass, with yucca and acacia trees scattered between—and in the distance, a range of hills stretching across the entire horizon. A truly beautiful sight.

Before leaving, the Gujarati man had warned him not to go out walking alone in these fields.

Shankar had asked, "Why?"

No satisfactory answer to that question had been obtained from the Gujarati gentleman! But the answer came from another quarter that very night.

Having finished his meal early in the evening, Shankar lit the lamp in the station room and sat writing his diary—he would sleep right in the station room. The glass-paned front door was shut, but not bolted. Hearing some sound, he looked toward the door and saw—right outside the door, pressing its nose against the glass, was a huge lion! Shankar sat frozen like a block of wood. Even a slightly hard push would open the door. And he was completely unarmed. On the table lay only a wooden ruler.

The lion, however, stood quietly staring with curiosity at Shankar and the kerosene lamp on the table. It was not there for very long, perhaps two minutes—yet to Shankar it felt as if he and the lion had been standing staring at each other for ages. Then, slowly and indifferently, the lion moved away from the door. Shankar suddenly seemed to regain his senses. He hurried over and drew the bolt on the door.

—খাবার জল নেই মোটে, ট্রেণ থেকে নিতে একদম ভুলে গিয়েচি।

—সে কি? এখানে খাবার জল কোথাও পাওয়া যায় না?

—কোথাও না। একটা কুয়ো আছে, তার জল বেজায় তেতো আর কসা। সে জলে বাসন মাজা ছাড়া আর কোনো কাজ হয় না। খাবার জল ট্রেণ থেকে দিয়ে যায়।

বেশ জায়গা বটে। খাবার জল নেই, মানুষ-জন নেই। এখানে ষ্টেশন করেছে কেন তা শঙ্কর বুঝতে পারলে না।

পরদিন সকালে ভূতপূর্ব্ব ষ্টেশন মাস্টার চলে গেল। শঙ্কর পড়ল একা। নিজের কাজ করে, রাঁধে খায়, ট্রেণের সময় প্ল্যাটফর্ম্মে গিয়ে দাঁড়ায়। দুপুরে বই পড়ে কি বড় টেবিলটাতে শুয়ে ঘুমোয়। বিকেলের দিকে ছায়া পড়লে প্ল্যাটফর্ম্মে পায়চারী করে।

ষ্টেশনের চারিধার ঘিরে ধূ ধূ সীমাহীন প্রান্তর, দীর্ঘ ঘাসের বন, মাঝে ইউকা, বাবলা গাছ— দূরে পাহাড়ের সারি সারা চক্রবাল জুড়ে। ভারি সুন্দর দৃশ্য।

গুজরাটী লোকটী ওকে বারণ করে গিয়েছিল—একা যেন এই সব মাঠে সে না বেড়াতে বার হয়।

শঙ্কর বলেছিল—কেন?

সে প্রশ্নের সন্তোষজনক উত্তর গুজরাটী ভদ্রলোকটীর কাছ থেকে পাওয়া যায় নি! কিন্তু তার উত্তর অন্য দিক থেকে সে রাত্রেই মিল্‌ল।

সকাল রাতেই আহারাদি সেরে শঙ্কর ষ্টেশন ঘরে বাতি জ্বালিয়ে বসে ডায়েরী লিখ্চে—ষ্টেশনঘরেই সে শোবে। সাম্‌নের কাচ-বসানো দরজাটী বন্ধ আছে—কিন্তু আগল দেওয়া নেই, কিসের শব্দ শুনে সে দরজার দিকে চেয়ে দেখে—দরজার ঠিক বাইরে কাঁচে নাক লাগিয়ে প্রকাণ্ড সিংহ! শঙ্কর কাঠের মতো বসে রইল। দরজা একটু জোর করে ঠেললেই খুলে যাবে। সেও সম্পূর্ণ নিরস্ত্র। টেবিলের ওপর কেবল কাঠের রুলটা মাত্র আছে।

সিংহটা কিন্তু কৌতূহলের সঙ্গে শঙ্কর ও টেবিলের কেরোসিন বাতিটার দিকে চেয়ে চুপ করে দাঁড়িয়ে রইল। খুব বেশীক্ষণ ছিল না, হয়তো মিনিট দুই—কিন্তু শঙ্করের মনে হোল সে আর সিংহটা কতকাল ধরে পরস্পরে পরস্পরের দিকে চেয়ে দাঁড়িয়ে আছে। তারপর সিংহ ধীরে ধীরে অনাসক্ত ভাবে দরজা থেকে সরে গেল। শঙ্কর হঠাৎ যেন চেতনা ফিরে পেল। সে তাড়াতাড়ি গিয়ে দরজার আগলটা তুলে দিলে।

"September 1, on the bank of the Kankramati River—The food and supplies we brought with us are steadily running low. Whatever vegetables we had were finished long ago. By way of fresh provisions, we have a few ducks and chickens with us that lay several eggs each day; apart from that, there is only biscuits, jam, tinned milk and fruit, tinned fish, and meat. All of this will last only a few weeks, so we must return within these next few weeks. We were counting up these supplies and putting them in order when Chhakkar Singh told us that Lakkar Singh had gone out somewhere at dawn and had not returned yet. We said, "Why worry? He will be back presently. Where could he possibly go?" Yet two or three more hours passed, and still there was no sign of Lakkar Singh. We were discussing setting out to look for him when suddenly the head of a gigantic beast appeared over the top of a bush. The head was bobbing up and down and swaying like a drunken man. At the sight of it, we were about to slink away behind the tent when we heard Lakkar Singh shouting, "Don't run away, don't run away, it won't do anything!" The very next moment, we saw Lakkar Singh stride out from behind the bush with his chest puffed out. He had tied up that huge beast with the cloth of his turban and was leading it along. In answer to our questions, Lakkar Singh told us that he had gone to the river with his water-pitcher in the morning to fetch water. On his way back, he came across this creature. As soon as it saw him, the beast lay down on the ground and began whimpering. He saw that a thorn had pierced the creature's foot and blood was gushing from it. Summoning great courage, Lakkar Singh pulled the thorn out of its foot, wiped the wound clean, and bandaged it with his own handkerchief. Then, seeing the beast following right behind him, he tied his turban cloth around it and led it back. We all said, "Then let it stay tied up like that; let us see if we can take it back home with us." The creature was named Langratherium.

We: Where can one go to see all the specimens that you collected?

Chandra: All of those were lost.

We: What do you mean! Lost? You lost such extraordinary things?

Chandra: Yes, it is enough that we didn't lose our lives! You haven't seen the storms of that country. With every gust, our instruments, our big tents, and our specimen boxes were all blown away like scraps of paper with a whoosh. I myself was swept off my feet five or six times! Once I thought I was dead for sure. Where the wind blew our dog away to, we never could find out. What a terrible ordeal that was! Magnetic compasses, plans, maps, notebooks—nothing was spared. If you heard how we made it back, every hair in your head and beard would stand on end like porcupine quills. Eating half-meals, going without food on some days, finding our way by guesswork, it took us three whole months to cover a two-week journey.

We: Then whatever proof and evidence you had was all destroyed?

Chandra: Why, here I am, and here is my uncle—what more proof do you want? And besides, I have drawn and brought along some pictures for you. Those should serve as plenty of proof too.

A young fellow from our printing press joked, "And which -therium are you, sir?" Someone else chimed in, "He is a Goppotherium—sitting here spinning tall tales!" Hearing this, Chandrakhai flew into a towering rage, snatched a handful of peanuts and about eight pans from our table, and stormed out muttering to himself. Well, that is the whole story. Interrupted so unexpectedly, the minister lost the thread of his speech, and the rest of us panicked too—the play was on the verge of coming to a sudden halt. Seeing that, Dashu bossily ordered the minister, "Go on, say what you were saying." That only flustered the minister even more. Rakhal was dressed as the royal doorkeeper; the moment he stepped forward slightly to say something to Dashu, Dashu shouted, "This wretch tried to stop me by force!"—and cuffed him on the head, knocking his turban right off. Right after knocking it off, he rattled through the king's closing speech himself—"In this realm there shall be no malice or tyranny, nor shall there be the torment of poverty," and so on—and then wrapped up the play by declaring, "Now go you all unto your own tasks!" Not knowing what to do, we all stood gaping like fools. Over on the side, the bell rang out—dong!—and the curtain came dropping down with a thud.

Dashu replied, "Well, seeing that none of you were saying anything, I quickly said whatever I remembered! Otherwise everything would have been ruined even worse." I said, "Why did you barge in right in the middle and make a mess of everything? That's why it all got muddled up!" Dashu said, "Why did Rakhal say he would hold me back by force? The sky was dark with mosquitoes. The elephant replied, 'Who is it, brother? Brother Tuni? Come in, brother! Sit down, brother! Let me set out a cot, let me serve up rice—will you eat, brother?'

Tuntuni said, 'I will eat the rice only if you drink up all the water in the sea.'

The elephant said, 'I can't drink all that water; my belly will burst.'

Seeing that nobody would listen to her, Tuntuni finally went to a mosquito. Spotting her from afar, the mosquito called out, 'Who is it, brother? Brother Tuni? Come in, brother! Sit down, brother! Let me set out a cot, let me serve up rice—will you eat, brother?'

Tuntuni said, 'I will eat the rice only if you bite the elephant!'

The mosquito replied, 'Why, is that even a big deal? I'm going right now! Let's see just how tough that elephant fellow's hide is!' Saying this, it summoned all the mosquitoes from every land and called out, 'Come along, brothers, let's see how tough that elephant fellow's hide is!' Immediately, whining 'Pin-pin-pin-pin!', all the mosquitoes in the world—fathers, sons, brothers, and friends alike—set out together to bite the elephant. The sky was dark with mosquitoes, and the sun was blotted out. The beating of their wings whipped up a storm. Hearing that dreadful 'Pin-pin-pin-pin!' sound, everyone's heart trembled with fear. And then—

The elephant cries, 'I'll drink the sea dry!' The sea cries, 'I'll quench the fire!' The fire cries, 'I'll burn the stick!' The stick cries, 'I'll thrash the cat!' The cat cries, 'I'll kill the mouse!' The mouse cries, 'I'll gnaw the king's belly!' The king cries, 'I'll chop off that barber rascal's head!'

Folding his hands and trembling from head to foot, the barber pleaded, 'Mercy, Tunidada! Come, let me lance your boil.'

After that, Tuntuni's boil healed up, and overjoyed, she went back to dancing and singing once more—"Tuntuna tun tun tun! Dhei dhei!"

Bhairab rushed outside at top speed, pulled both leaves of Dilip's door shut, and began climbing rapidly and noisily up the stairs. Halfway up the stairs, the sound of his footsteps suddenly stopped, and right after that came the sound of whispered words! A little later, the sound of the upstairs room door closing was heard again; then, when Bhairab came downstairs and entered Dilip's room once more, streams of sweat were pouring down his forehead! Sinking into a chair as if exhausted, Bhairab panted, "No, everything is fine! It is just the handiwork of that wretched dog! But sitting downstairs, Dilip clearly heard that instead of going out on urgent work, he went straight into his own room and bolted the door from the inside! In his mind, Dilip grew furious. So Bhairab was a first-rate liar! He had told such a clumsy lie that it couldn't fool even a child! A dog in his room—what rubbish! But one ought not to keep any further association with a man who hides a fugitive criminal in his own room. Would he too end up entangled in a police case at last? Making a mental vow to 'boycott' Bhairab, Dilip pulled over a huge book on 'Anatomy' and sat down to read. But a little later, his reading was interrupted again.

Input: Setting down the Police Journal and rising to my feet, I said, "Brother, let me shut the two north-facing windows. On top of this biting winter cold, yesterday's rain has made it chillier still. Quickly give the order for a cup of tea." Stretching both legs out full length along the couch, Hemanta said, "That I shall! But if you are so afraid of the biting cold, why did you cross the Ganga today to go strolling in a garden?" Astonished, I asked, "How did you know that? Did someone tell you?" —"You've come straight to my house with dusty feet right after crossing over from the other bank and stepping ashore on this side! Who could possibly have given me the news in the meantime? Well, is what I'm saying true or not?" —"Yes, brother, it's true. Only I didn't go strolling in any garden! You know that my brother-in-law lives in Belur, don't you? Hearing that he was unwell, I went to see him. Though it's true there is a fairly large garden right in front of his house! Still, these aren't things you could possibly know—you've never been there!" —"No, I haven't. But as you know, my friend, because I keep my eyes open at all times, I can tell a great many things without ever going anywhere." In wonder I began to ponder by what clue Hemanta had managed to learn so much about me; suddenly my eyes fell upon the carnation flower I had tucked into the buttonhole of my coat, and at once I realized that the root of Hemanta's discovery lay in this very flower. With half-closed eyes, Hemanta was watching my expression. Laughing, he spoke as though reading my very thoughts: "No, my friend, no! It isn't what you're thinking! That flower in the buttonhole of your coat is something you could just as easily have got from a friend's house or a flower shop right here in Kolkata! It wasn't by looking at that alone that I guessed so much. If you look at your shoes, you'll see wet clay clinging to the undersides. Clay like that is not to be found even on the muddy streets of Kolkata. A single glance tells you it is Ganga clay. Surely you didn't step down into the bed of the Ganga wearing your shoes to take a bath. So I deduced that you crossed the Ganga by boat, and because it was low tide, you were forced to step off the boat some distance from the ghat, right onto the Ganga mud. The flower in your buttonhole is very fresh, so I realized you hadn't taken it along with you from Kolkata to the other bank, or else by now the flower would have wilted at least a little. Therefore, you plucked the flower only a short while ago over on the other side of the Ganga—most likely on your way back to Kolkata. And since an imported seasonal flower like a carnation doesn't bloom wild along the roadsides or in the woods and thickets on the other bank, I took it for granted that you plucked it from some garden. The Ganga clay on your shoes hasn't had time to dry yet. Seeing that wet mud, I knew at once that you came straight to my house the moment you stepped off the boat! Do you see, my friend, how much can be discovered by observing a person if one only makes a little effort?" I said, "You are an extraordinary man, Hemanta! All the while you were chatting away nonstop with me, you noticed so many tiny details and reasoned them out at the very same time!"
Target Output: পুলিস জার্নালখানা রেখে দিয়ে দাঁড়িয়ে উঠে আমি বললুম, “ভাই, উত্তরদিকের জান্‌‌লা দুটো বন্ধ ক’রে দি। এই দুর্জ্জয় শীতের ওপরে কাল আবার বৃষ্টি হয়ে ঠাণ্ডা আরো বেড়ে উঠেছে। চট্ ক’রে এক পেয়ালা চায়ের হুকুম দাও।” কৌচের উপরে পাদুটো লম্বা ক’রে ছড়িয়ে দিয়ে হেমন্ত বললে, “তা যেন দিচ্ছি! কিন্তু দুর্জ্জয় শীতকে যদি এতই ভয়, তবে আজ তুমি গঙ্গাপার হয়ে বাগানে বেড়াতে গিয়েছিলে কেন?” চমৎকৃত হয়ে বলনুম, “এ কথা তুমি কেমন ক’রে জানলে? কেউ বলেছে বুঝি?” —“তুমি তো সিধে ওপার থেকে এপারে নেমেই ধূলো-পায়ে আমার বাড়ীতে আসছ! এর মধ্যে খবর আর কে দেবে? কেমন, যা বলছি সত্যি কিনা?” —“হ্যাঁ ভাই, সত্যি। কিন্তু আমি কোন বাগানে বেড়াতে যাইনি! তুমি তো জানো, বেলুড়ে আমার ভগ্নীপতি থাকেন? তাঁর অসুখ শুনে দেখতে গিয়েছিলুম। তবে তাঁর বাড়ীর সামনে একটা বেশ বড় বাগান আছে বটে! কিন্তু এ-সব কথা তোমার তো জানবার নয়, তুমি তো কখনো সেখানে যাওনি!” —“না, তা যাইনি। কিন্তু তুমি তো এ-কথা জানো বন্ধু, সবর্বদা আমার চোখ খোলা রাখি ব’লে কোথাও না গিয়ে ও আমি অনেক কথাই বলতে পারি।” আশ্চর্য্য হয়ে ভাবতে লাগলুম, কোন্ সূত্র ধরে হেমন্ত আমার সম্বন্ধে এত কথা জানতে পারলে?; নিজের জামার বোতাম-ঘরে যে ‘কার্নেশান্’ ফুলটি গুঁজে রেখেছিলুম হঠাৎ সেইদিকে আমার নজর পড়ল এবং সঙ্গে সঙ্গে বুঝলুম হেমন্তের আবিষ্কারের মূল আছে এই ফুলটিতেই। হেমন্ত অর্দ্ধ-মুদিত চোখে আমার ভাবভঙ্গি নিরীক্ষণ করছিল। হাসতে হাসতে যেন অন্তর্যামীর মতই বললে, “না, বন্ধু, না! তুমি যা ভাবছ তা নয়! জামার বোতাম-ঘরের ঐ ফুলটি তুমি কলকাতার কোন বন্ধুর বাড়ী বা ফুলের দোকান থেকেও সংগ্রহ করতে পারতে! ঐ দেখেই আমি এত কথা আন্দাজ করিনি। তোমার জুতোর দিকে তাকালেই দেখবে, ওর নীচের দিকটায় লেগে রয়েছে ভিজে এঁটেল্-মাটি। ও-রকম মাটি কলকাতার কর্দ্দমাক্ত পথেও পাওয়া যায় না। দেখলেই বোঝা যায়, ও হচ্ছে গঙ্গামাটি। জুতো প’রে তুমি নিশ্চয়ই স্নান করবার জন্যে গঙ্গা-গর্ভে নামো নি। সুতরাং আন্দাজে বুঝলুম, তুমি নৌকা-যোগে গঙ্গা পার হয়েছ আর ভাঁটার সময় ব’লে নৌকা ছেড়ে নামতে বাধ্য হয়েছ ঘাট থেকে খানিক দূরে, গঙ্গামাটির উপরেই। তোমার বোতাম ঘরের ফুলটি খুব তাজা রয়েছে, সুতরাং বুঝতে পারলুম ওটি তুমি কলকাতা থেকে সঙ্গে ক’রে ওপারে নিয়ে যাওনি, তাহ’লে এতক্ষণে ফুলটি অল্পবিস্তর নেতিয়ে পড়ত। অতএব ফুলটিও তুলেছ অল্পক্ষণ আগে, গঙ্গার ওপারে গিয়েই—খুব সম্ভব, কলকাতায় ফেরবার সময়ে। আর বিলাতী মর্সুমী-ফুল ‘কার্নেশান’ তো ওপারের পথে-ঘাটে বনে-জঙ্গলে ফোটে না, সুতরাং ধ’রে নিলুম ওটি চয়ন করেছ তুমি কোন বাগান থেকেই। তোমার জুতোর গঙ্গামাটি এখনো শুকোবার সময় পায় নি। ঐ ভিজে মাটি দেখেই বুঝেছি, তুমি নৌকো থেকে নেমেই সিধে আমার বাড়ীতে এসে উঠেছ! দেখছ বন্ধু, একটু চেষ্টা করলেই মানুষ দেখে কত কথা আবিষ্কার করা যায়?” আমি বললুম, “তুমি আশ্চর্য্য লোক, হেমন্ত! আমার সঙ্গে অনর্গল গল্প করতে করতে এত খুটিনাটি লক্ষ্য আর সঙ্গে সঙ্গে চিন্তা করেছ!”

Jaladhar's maternal uncle works in the police, and his paternal aunt's husband writes detective novels. Because of that, Jaladhar firmly believes that nobody besides his uncle and his uncle-in-law knows all the secret tricks for outsmarting thieves, dacoits, forgers, and swindlers as well as he does. Whenever there is a burglary at anyone's house, Jaladhar is the very first to show up there; and he holds forth like a great expert on who committed the theft, how it was done, and what he would have done if he had been in that situation. When utensils were stolen from Jogeshbabu's house, Jaladhar told them, "You people don't even know how to take this much precaution—of course there's going to be a theft! Just look, right next to the storeroom is a dark lane, and on top of that, the window has no bars. If a thief is even slightly clever, how long would it take him to make off with the utensils through here? At our house, there's no chance of anything like that happening. I've instructed Ramdin to stack the utensils on the ledge right by the window every night. If Mr. Thief should care to pay a visit, the moment he tries to open the window, all the pots and pans will come clattering down to the floor. If you want to catch a thief, you have to know these tricks." At the time, we all praised Jaladhar's cleverness to the skies, but the next day, when we heard that a huge burglary had taken place at Jaladhar's own house that very night, we felt we shouldn't have praised him quite so much the day before.

Jaladhar, however, was not the least bit fazed by it. He said, "With the plan I had set up, once the thief got inside the house, there would have been no escape for him. Dismounting from his horse a good distance away from Shipton's bungalow and tying his horse to a casuarina tree, Rajaram walked up to the house, peered cautiously inside, slipped off his pair of shoes outside, and entered the great hall.

Besides Shipton and his Memsahib, another European gentleman was sitting in the hall. Shipton said, "Dewan, come this way—Look here, Grant, this is our Dewan Roy-"

The other Sahib had come straight out from England. He was a newcomer to the country, between thirty and thirty-five years of age, wearing a high collar like a clergyman's, tall and well-built in frame. His name was Colesworthy Grant, and he had come to India to travel the country. He was a very fine

The Ichhamati is a small river—at least that stretch of it which flows through the district of Jessore. No one in the rural parts of Jessore district keeps track of where, far to the south, the Ichhamati turns into a vast, briny river teeming with crocodiles, kamats, and sharks, and merges into the Bay of Bengal behind the dense jungles of sundari and garan trees in some corner of the Sundarbans.

The stretch of the Ichhamati that lies within the districts of Nadia and Jessore is truly so enchanting in its beauty that anyone who has had the chance to see it knows it well. Yet those who will appreciate it best of all are the ones who have lived in this region for a long time. Its two banks are an exquisite work of art by God—green with woods and groves, alive with the chatter of birds.

Take a boat from the ghat at Murighata or Bajitpur and go all the way to the ghat at Chanduria—on both banks you will see the red blossoms of the palte-madar trees, thickets of aquatic banyeburo, floating mats of topapana water lettuce, the splendour of wild titpalla creepers covered in yellow flowers, and here and there upon the high banks, shady old banyan and peepal trees overhanging thickets of uluti, bachra, and boichi bushes, bamboo groves, the nesting holes of bank mynahs, and delicate canopies of trailing vines. Human settlements are sparse along the riverbanks; there are only green char-lands carpeted with durba grass, sloping ghats of fine white sand, bushes laden with wild blossoms, and woodland fringes ringing with birdcalls. At a village ghat here and there, a few dinghy boats lie moored. Now and then, perched high on a gnarled, dry branch of a tall shimul tree, a vulture sits lost in meditation—looking exactly like a painting by a Chinese artist. At some ghat, women are bathing; filling their pitchers with water and resting them on their hips, they climb ashore while chatting with their companions still bathing in the river. In one or two places, right on the edge of the high riverbank out in the open fields, stands a village primary school—a longish shed enclosed by screens of woven bamboo slips or split-cane fencing; among its furnishings

can be seen a single broken, rickety chair tied with rope to a post, and a few benches.

When the moonlight of a bright moonlit night falls upon the grassy meadows of the green char-lands, when white clusters of akanda flowers bloom on summer days, and festoons of golden sondali blossoms sway in the gentle river breeze from the nearby thickets, travellers passing by boat will catch sight of the slightly raised plinths of old, deserted homesteads along the river's edge—most of them now overgrown by akanda bushes, with an anthill or two perhaps sprouting upon some of the earthen foundations. Looking at these abandoned homestead mounds, you will dream of days gone by—you will dream of all those mothers and sons, brothers and sisters, whose lives were once bound up with these ancestral homes. How many unwritten histories of joy and sorrow are etched across their chests century after century, like faint lines traced by trickling rainwater during the monsoons! The sun sheds its light, the late-autumn sky showers down dew, and the moon of the bright fortnight pours its moonlight over their chests.

Now, those who favor using heavily Sanskritized language are anxious to rectify that original blunder made at the very start. There are many unaltered Sanskrit words in our language; taking those as the foundation of the language, pile on as many more Sanskrit words as you can—in the course of time, there will be no duality between Bangla and Sanskrit; in fact, to the wise, there isn't any even now. It is only because we are bound by the illusion of our mother tongue that we cannot become non-dualists of Sanskrit and Bangla. The number of Persian words in Bangla is not small either; fortunately, the number of Persian-educated Bangalis is very small. Otherwise, they would probably have said, make Bangla heavily Persianized. Caught in the middle, our Mother Saraswati would have been beside herself wondering whether to go to Kashi or to Mecca. Sometimes it seems to me that such a dilemma would have been better, because falling entirely into the hands of the assembly of Pandits, Mother is far more likely to attain Kashi—that is, breathe her last—before long.
In this context, the first contention of the eminent Pandit Satishchandra Vidyabhushan Mahashay is that literature originates from the human desire to become immortal. Whenever one sets out to write the genealogy of anything that exists in the present, one has to fudge the beginning to make ends meet. Great philosophers and scientists, such as Shankara, Spencer, and others, have also resorted to that method. Therefore, trying to determine the root origin of anything is wasted labor. Yet this much can be said without fear: whatever else it may have come from, literature did not originate from the desire to be immortal. First, not all of us can handle the risk of immortality, whereas the fingers of many of us itch to wield the pen. If there were the slightest possibility that every word and every deed of ours—good, bad, or mediocre—would endure forever, just think how many of us would dare to open our mouths or lift our hands. With the terror of immortality staring us in the face, we would not agree to say or do anything unless it were perfect. And we all know in our hearts that even our very best deeds and our very best words fall far short of perfection. The real truth is that because death exists, there is joy in living. It is only because there is a chance of returning to the mortal world after their store of merit is exhausted that the gods live merrily in the immortal city; otherwise, even heaven would have been unbearable to them. Be that as it may, we are human beings, not gods; therefore, the wish that the words of our mouths should become divine revelation is not natural to our minds.
Second, if someone were to make the stern vow, 'I will write solely to become immortal,' then once he realized how slim the hope of fulfilling that wish was, if he were intelligent, he would surely desist from writing. For we all know that out of a thousand people, nine hundred and ninety-nine have a Saraswati whose offspring are stillborn. Besides, in the world of literature, plague rages round the clock. One in a hundred thousand survives; the rest do not live even for two moments. Charaka advised that when an epidemic rages in a land, one's duty is to flee that country. With the wish and hope of becoming immortal, who would want to enter that realm?
Vidyabhushan Mahashay further contends that one must not write the grammar of a living language, for that means certain death.

The king retched.

At once the executioner went and cut off the noses of all seven queens.

Seeing that, Tuntuni sang—

At a single Tuni's merry song, Seven queens lost their noses all along!

Then the king shouted, 'Catch the rascal and bring it here! This time I'll swallow it whole! Let's see how it escapes then!'

They caught Tuntuni and brought her back.

The king ordered, 'Bring water!'

Water was brought. Taking a mouthful of water, the king popped Tuntuni into his mouth, shut his eyes, and gulped her down in one swallow.

Everyone declared, 'This time the bird is done for!'

Hardly had they spoken when the king let out a huge belch—bhok!

The courtiers were startled, and right out with that belch popped Tuntuni and flew away!

The king shouted, 'There it goes, there it goes! Catch it, catch it!' Immediately two hundred men dashed out, caught the poor bird again, and brought her back.

Then water was brought once more, and a sepoy came and stood right beside the king with a drawn sword, ready to slice Tuntuni in two the instant she came out.

This time, right after swallowing Tuntuni, the king sat pressing both hands tightly over his mouth so that Tuntuni could not get out again. Down inside his belly, the poor little bird began thrashing and fluttering about fiercely.

After a little while, the king wrinkled his nose and went, 'Wak!' Instantly, everything inside his stomach came spewing right out, Tuntuni and all!

The king was about to swallow Tuntuni. Everyone shouted, 'Sepoy, sepoy! Strike, strike! It's getting away!'

Flustered by the shouting, the sepoy swung his sword to strike Tuntuni, and instead of hitting Tuntuni, the blade came down right on the king's nose!

The king let out a dreadful scream, and right along with him all the people in the court began screaming too. Then the doctor came, applied medicine, bandaged him up, and with great difficulty saved the king's life.

Seeing that, Tuntuni began to sing—

O noseless king, just look and see What a fine punishment fell on thee!

Saying this, she flew away and left that country for good. The king's men came rushing over and found only an empty nest lying there.

I asked, 'Now what's there to laugh about in this?'

It said, 'There was once a man who used to snore so dreadfully at times that everyone was fed up with him! One day lightning struck their house, and right away everyone came running and started beating him black and blue—Ho, ho, ho, ho!'

I said, 'What utter nonsense.' Saying this, the moment I turned to leave, I saw a bald-headed fellow dressed in a chapkan coat and pajama trousers like a juri chorus-singer in a jatra troupe, grinning away and staring right at me. The sight of him made my blood boil. As soon as he saw me turn around, he cocked his head coyly like a spoiled child, waved both hands, and began pleading, 'No, brother, no, brother, don't ask me to sing right now! Truly I tell you, my voice won't open up properly today.'

I snapped, 'What a nuisance! Who is asking you to sing?'

The fellow was so shameless that he kept whining right in my ear anyway, 'Are you angry? Tell me, brother, are you angry? Alright, I might as well sing you a few songs—what need is there to get angry, brother?'

Before I could say a word, the goat and Hiji Bij Bij shouted out together, 'Yes, yes, yes! Let's have a song, let's have a song!' Immediately the bald fellow pulled two huge bundles of song sheets out of his pocket, held them close to his eyes, hummed for a moment, and suddenly began shrieking out a song in a thin, squeaky voice—'A blue tune in a red song, a giggly-wiggly smell.'

That single line was all he sang—once, twice, five times, ten times over.

I said, 'This is a terrible nuisance, I see! Doesn't the song have any other lines?'

The bald fellow replied, 'Yes, it does, but that belongs to a different song. That one goes—Walking down the alleys, Ram, hubbub on the pavement, whitewashing with black ink. I don't sing that song nowadays. There is another song—New potatoes from Nainital—which has to be sung to a very soft tune. I can't sing that one nowadays either. The one I sing nowadays is the Song of the Peacock Feather.' Saying this, he broke into song—

Mishi-smeared peacock plume whispering in the sky's ear, Corked-up phials and bottles in thin little songs so clear, Absent-minded crooked light half-gleaming far away, Thin and thick, black and white, in a shimmering shadow-lay.

I said, 'Is this supposed to be a song? It has neither head nor tail nor a scrap of meaning!'

Hiji Bij Bij said, 'Yes, the song is awfully deep.'

The goat said, 'Where is it deep at all? That bit about the phials and bottles seemed a little tough to chew on, but apart from that I didn't find anything hard in it.'

Looking deeply offended, the bald fellow said, 'Well, if you want to hear an easy song, all you had to do was say so! What need was there to lecture me like that? Do you think I can't sing easy songs?' Saying this, he struck up a song—

Says the bat, O brother porcupine, Tonight you will see a majaru so fine.

I interrupted, 'There is no such word as majaru.'

The bald fellow retorted, 'Why shouldn't there be—of course there is! If there can be sajaru—porcupine, kangaroo, and deodar, why can't there be majaru?'

The goat said, 'Let the song go on for now; whether there's such a word or not can be seen later.' At once the song started up again—

Says the bat, O brother porcupine, Tonight you will see a majaru so fine. Tonight the pipistrelles and owls will gather round right here, And the poor little mouse will die of sheer fear. The frogs and the tadpoles will tremble in dread, Sweating till prickly heat breaks out red, The musk-shrew will scamper with jaws locked tight, Then you'll see chimbi-chyanga-chapati tonight!

আমি কিছু বলবার আগেই ছাগলটা আর হিজি বিজ্ বিজ্‌টা একসঙ্গে চেঁচিয়ে উঠল, ‘হ্যাঁ-হ্যাঁ-হ্যাঁ, গান হোক, গান হোক।’ অমনি নেড়াটা তার পকেট থেকে মস্ত দুই তাড়া গানের কাগজ বার করে, সেগুলো চোখের কাছে নিয়ে গুনগুন করতে-করতে হঠাৎ সরু গলায় চীৎকার করে গান ধরল—‘লাল গানে নীল সুর, হাসি-হাসি গন্ধ।’

ঐ একটিমাত্র পদ সে একবার গাইল, দুবার গাইল, পাঁচবার, দশবার গাইল।

আমি বললাম, ‘এ তো ভারি উৎপাত দেখছি, গানের কি আর-কোনো পদ নেই?’

নেড়া বলল, ‘হ্যাঁ, আছে, কিন্তু সেটা অন্য একটা গান। সেটা হচ্ছে—অলিগলি চলি রাম, ফুটপাথে ধুমধাম, কালি দিয়ে চুনকাম। সে গান আজকাল আমি গাই না। আরেকটা গান আছে—নাইনিতালের নতুন আলু—সেটা খুব নরম সুরে গাইতে হয়। সেটাও আজকাল গাইতে পারি না। আজকাল যেটা গাই, সেটা হচ্ছে শিখিপাখার গান।’ এই বলেই সে গান ধরল—

মিশিমাখা শিখিপাখা আকাশের কানে কানে শিশি বোতল ছিপিঢাকা সরু সরু গানে গানে আলাভোলা বাঁকা আলো আধো আধো কতদূরে, সরু মোটা সাদা কালো ছলছল ছায়াসুরে।

আমি বললাম, ‘এ আবার গান হল নাকি? এর তো মাথামুণ্ডু কোনো মানেই হয়না।’

হিজি বিজ্‌ বিজ্‌ বলল, ‘হ্যাঁ, গানটা ভারি শক্ত।’

ছাগল বলল, ‘শক্ত আবার কোথায়? ঐ শিশি বোতলের জায়গাটা একটু শক্ত ঠেকল, তা ছাড়া তো শক্ত কিছু পেলাম না।’

নেড়াটা খুব অভিমান করে বলল, ‘তা, তোমরা সহজ গান শুনতে চাও তো সে কথা বললেই হয়। অত কথা শোনাবার দরকার কি? আমি কি আর সহজ গান গাইতে পারি না?’ এই বলে সে গান ধরল—

বাদুড় বলে, ওরে ও ভাই সজারু, আজকে রাতে দেখবে একটা মজারু।

আমি বললাম, ‘মজারু বলে কোনো একটা কথা হয় না।’

নেড়া বলল, ‘কেন হবে না—আলবত হয়। সজারু কাঙ্গারু দেবদারু সব হতে পারে, মজারু কেন হবে না?’

ছাগল বলল, ‘ততক্ষণ গানটা চলুক না, হয় কি না-হয় পরে দেখা যাবে।’ আমনি আবার গান শুরু হল—

বাদুড় বলে, ওরে ও ভাই সজারু, আজকে রাতে দেখবে একটা মজারু। আজকে হেথায় চাম্‌চিকে আর পেঁচারা আসবে সবাই, মরবে ইঁদুর বেচারা। কাঁপবে ভয়ে ব্যাঙগুলো আর ব্যাঙাচি, ঘামতে ঘামতে ফুটবে তাদের ঘামাচি, ছুটবে ছুঁচো লাগবে দাঁতে কপাটি, দেখবে তখন ছিম্বি ছ্যাঙা চপাটি।

Input: Kumar said, "Looking at the way they move, it feels as if a host of certain death has taken form and is silently advancing toward us!" Jayanta said, "I don't know who they are, but we shouldn't stand around here." Bimal said, "I can see now that we didn't do the right thing by leaving our companions behind on the ship. I don't know what fate holds for us on this mysterious island, but come on, let's get inside the forest." With another dash, they left the open field and plunged into the woods. The forest was not very dense there; beneath the trees and through the gaps between them, a play of shadow and light could be seen. Winding through the bushes, the outline of a path dappled with light and shadow also emerged. And from afar, the strains of that strange music still came floating on the air. Kumar asked, "Which way do we go now?" Bimal said, "Let's push a little further toward the southeast, and then try to circle back toward the river." No sooner had Bimal finished speaking than the entire forest seemed to shudder with a fiendish, booming roar of laughter! From around them, in front of them, and behind them erupted volley after volley of laughter! That hideous stream of laughter seemed to flow right beneath their feet, it seemed to rain down from the empty sky, and at the shock of that laughter, the patterns of light and streaks of shadow across the forest seemed to tremble restlessly! Bimal, Kumar, and Jayanta spun around in confusion, looking in every direction, yet not a living soul could be seen anywhere. Jayanta cried, "Who is laughing? Where are they laughing from? Why are they laughing?" Like madmen, Kumar and Bimal darted now toward this tree, now toward that—striking the bushes to their right and left again and again with the butts of their guns; yet no one was there, while wave after wave of booming laughter kept pouring out from inside every bush and from behind every tree. That uncanny laughter seemed to be born everywhere at once. Just as suddenly as it had begun, the uproar of laughter stopped again! Only the distant waves of music could still be heard. Listening intently, Bimal said, "Jayantababu, this time it's not just singing—do you hear another sound?" Jayanta said, "Yes. Over the dry leaves scattered across the forest floor, hundreds of feet seem to be falling in rhythm! It seems our friends from the field have entered the woods, only this time they aren't coming silently." Bimal said, "Run, Kumar, run as fast as you can." Once again, that dreadful, many-voiced laughter awoke! Kumar said, "But which way do we run, Bimal? In the distance there's the tread of the enemy's feet, and all around us the madness of their wild laughter! Invisible enemies on every side—which way do we go, brother?" —"Straight ahead—straight ahead. The moment the enemies show themselves, fire your guns." The three of them broke into a breathless run once more, and that unruly sound of laughter seemed to race right alongside them! The only thing they could make out was that although the booming laughter echoed on either side and behind them, directly ahead of them the laughter was completely silent. That unearthly laughter had no wish to block their path ahead! It was as if unseen pursuers were deliberately driving them in that very direction!

Input: Who speaks, eats food, and walks about? From then on, Bhairab began to associate quite closely with Dilip. Although Dilip was not a very sociable person, and he did not particularly care for Bhairab's harsh nature, out of ordinary politeness he had to mix with Bhairab to some extent. Bhairab would often borrow various kinds of books from him to read, and from time to time Dilip too would ask for good books from him. In this way, after their acquaintance grew somewhat closer over a few days, Dilip realised that Bhairab was an extraordinary scholar in many subjects. In knowledge and science, Dilip was practically a child beside him. On the subject of ancient Egypt, there was probably no greater expert than him in all of India. One day, growing curious, Dilip asked, "Tell me, Bhairabbabu, why did the ancient Egyptians turn corpses into 'mummies' before burying them?" Bhairab said, "It was the belief of ancient Egypt that the soul is immortal. After earthly death and before eternal life begins, the soul leaves the body and remains separate for some time, it is true, but afterward it returns right back into the earthly body. Fearing that the mortal body might decay before this reunion of soul and body, the Egyptians tried to preserve the body forever with the help of various chemical processes. They did not rest content merely by placing the body in a coffin and burying it; for the day when the soul would return inside the body, they also left food and drink, clothing, beds and bedding, utensils, and whatever else was needed to carry on daily life inside the tomb. When kings and nobles died, their male and female slaves also had to go into the tomb along with their bodies—that is to say, they were killed and their bodies were sent into the tomb—so that upon returning into his body, the king's soul would not suffer for lack of servants!" —"Bhairabbabu, do you consider this belief to be true?" —"What is the use of hearing what I consider to be true? However, that the priests of ancient Egypt knew the mantra to bring a mummy back to life is perhaps not false!" —"Does no one know that mantra anymore?" —"Of the strange people who lived in ancient Egypt, not one is alive today; only their bodies have remained undecayed in the form of 'mummies'! However, in old rolled-up manuscripts of papyrus reed, the mantras and tantras for waking the dead might still be found. Hearing Shankar's reply, the Portuguese scoundrel flushed red with rage. Fire seemed to flash from his eyes. Stepping even closer, he clenched his teeth and said in a harsh, twisted voice, "What? Nigger, what did you say? For someone from the East Indies, I see you're mighty insolent! For your own future good, let me tell you that Albuquerque has shot down colored men like you by the dozen like snipe with bullets from this revolver. Listen to what my rule is: anyone new who gets off at Kabalo either plays poker with me, or fights a duel with me with revolvers."

Shankar saw that if he entered into a revolver fight with this scoundrel, death was certain. The scoundrel was a crack-shot ruffian, whereas what was he? Until yesterday, he had been a harmless railway clerk. Yet if he avoided a fight and played poker instead, he would lose everything he had.

Shankar had perhaps delayed half a minute in answering; in the blink of an eye, the man drew a revolver from the leather holster at his waist, leveled it at Shankar's stomach, and said, "A duel, or poker?"

The blood rushed to Shankar's head. Like a coward, he would not bow his head before brute force—come death if it must.

He was about to say, "A duel," when from behind someone called out in a thunderous voice, "Hey! Watch out, or a bullet will blow the top of your skull off!" Startled, both of them looked back. There stood Alvarez planted firmly, his Winchester repeater raised and aimed straight at the head of the Portuguese scoundrel. Seizing the chance, Shankar quickly stepped out of the line of the pistol barrel. Alvarez said, "A revolver duel with a boy? Bah! Drop that pistol before I count three—one—two—three—" The pistol dropped to the ground from Albuquerque's slackened hand.

Alvarez said, "Showing off your bravery catching a boy alone, were you?" By then Shankar had picked up the pistol from the ground. Albuquerque was somewhat taken aback; he had never imagined that Alvarez belonged to Shankar's party. Laughing, he said, "All right, mate, no hard feelings—the loss is mine. Give it here, hand over my pistol, lad. Nothing to fear, give it back. Come, shake hands. You're a mate too. Albuquerque doesn't nurse a grudge. Come along, my cabin is close by—have a glass of beer each before you go."

Alvarez knew the breed of his own countrymen. Accepting the invitation, he took Shankar along to Albuquerque's cabin. Hearing that Shankar did not drink beer, Albuquerque made coffee for him. Laughing heartily, he chatted away about all sorts of things, as if nothing at all had happened.

Shankar was genuinely drawn to the man. There are not many people in the world who can so completely forget the insult and hostility of a few moments ago and chat away with such open-hearted laughter with the very men at whose hands they were humiliated.

The next day, they boarded a steamer from Kabalo to travel south down the Congo River. At the sight of the two banks of the river, Shankar's heart filled with delight.

Never in his life had he seen such a strange forest scene. In the part of Africa where he had been all this time, there were no such forests—only vast plains, mostly seas of grass, with acacia and yucca trees scattered here and there. But the further the steamer advanced along the Congo River, dense forests lined both banks—how many kinds of thick creepers and wild flowers! Wild nature here was lost in herself, playful, enchanted by her own beauty and lush abundance.

The beauty-loving, dreamy mind within Shankar (after all, he was a son of the soil of Bengal, not merely a hard-bitten gold-seeking prospector like Diego Alvarez), enchanted and amazed by this pageant of beauty, wove all kinds of daydreams to itself in the ruddy afternoons and the midday sun.

আল্‌ভারেজ নিজের জাতের লোকের রক্ত চেনে। ও নিমন্ত্রণ গ্রহণ করে শঙ্করকে সঙ্গে নিয়ে আল্‌বুকার্কের কেবিনে গেল। শঙ্কর বিয়ার খায় না শুনে তাকে কফি করে দিলে। প্রাণখোলা হাসি হেসে কত গল্প করলে, যেন কিছুই হয় নি।

শঙ্কর বাস্তবিকই লোকটার দিকে আকৃষ্ট হোল। কিছুক্ষণ আগের অপমান ও শত্রুতা যে এমন বেমালুম ভুলে গিয়ে, যাদের হাতে অপমানিত হয়েচে, তাদেরই সঙ্গে এমনি ধারা দিল-খোলা হেসে খোসগল্প করতে পারে, পৃথিবীতে এ ধরনের লোক বেশি নেই।

পরদিন ওরা কাবালো থেকে ষ্টিমারে উঠল কঙ্গোনদী বেয়ে দক্ষিণ মুখে যাবার জন্যে। নদীর দুই তীরের দৃশ্যে শঙ্করের মন আনন্দে উত্‍ফুল্ল হয়ে উঠল।

এ রকম অদ্ভুত বনজঙ্গলের দৃশ্য জীবনে কখনো সে দেখেনি। এতদিন সে যেখানে ছিল—আফ্রিকার সে অঞ্চলে এমন বন নেই, সে শুধু বিস্তীর্ণ প্রান্তর, প্রধানতঃ ঘাসের বন, মাঝে মাঝে বাবলা ও ইউকা গাছ। কিন্তু কঙ্গোনদী বেয়ে ষ্টীমার যত অগ্রসর হয়, দুধারে নিবিড় বনানী, কত ধরণের মোটা মোটা লতা, বনের ফুল, বন্যপ্রকৃতি এখানে আত্মহারা, লীলাময়ী, আপনার সৌন্দর্য্য ও নিবিড় প্রাচুর্য্যে আপনি মুগ্ধ।

শঙ্করের মধ্যে যে সৌন্দর্য্যপ্রিয় ভাবুক মনটী ছিল, (হাজার হোক্‌ সে বাংলার মাটীর ছেলে, ডিয়েগো আল্‌ভারেজর মত শুধু কঠিন প্রান স্বর্ণান্বেষী প্রস্‌পেক্টর নয়) এই রূপের মেলায় সে মুগ্ধ ও বিস্মিত হয়ে রাঙা অপরাহ্নে ও দুপুর রোদে আপন মনে কত কি স্বপ্নজাল রচনা করে।

Input: What is Bhairab's secret? Ten days passed. Against his own rebellious inclinations, Dilip forced himself to stay so busy with his human skeleton and medical textbooks that even when he heard Bhairab knocking from time to time on the closed door of his room, he made no move to answer. The moment Bhairab came in, he would probably launch into such preposterous tall tales about ancient Egypt and its secret mysteries that every word of the dry medical textbooks would be forgotten! One day he was getting ready to go out, when through his open door he saw his friend Abani come hurrying down onto the veranda in great agitation, and right behind him came Bhairabchandra rushing in a furious rage—in his terrible anger, his face had grown as hideous as a ferocious beast's! Hissing like a snake, Bhairab cried out, "Fool! You shall pay for this." Abani shouted, "Whatever happens, happens! But from today I am severing all ties with you! I will not listen to another word of yours!" —"Fine, do not listen! But remember what you have promised!" —"Yes, yes! I will keep my promise without fail! I shall not breathe a word to anyone! But after this, it is impossible for my sister to marry you! Rather than that, I would drown my sister to death in the waters of the Ganga! I do not wish to see your face anymore"—and saying this, Abani strode rapidly across the veranda and went out of the house! From inside his room, Dilip saw everything and heard everything. But he had no desire to step outside and join their quarrel. That Abani had quarrelled with Bhairab for some reason and had broken off his sister's marriage match with Bhairab—this much Dilip understood quite clearly. Then he put on his clothes and went out, and even after going outside, the same thought kept recurring to his mind again and again: why had such a quarrel broken out between Bhairab and Abani? ... ... ... ... ... This happened the next day. That day was the 'Elliott Shield Final'. At the Mohun Bagan ground on the Maidan, students from various colleges had gathered and were bubbling over in an ear-splitting uproar. Today the match was between Dilip's college and the Metropolitan College, and even before the game began, a regular war of words took place between the supporters of the two sides! If that scene were captured on film, spectators would be able to relish the flavour of a splendid comedy! After the game ended, as Dilip changed out of his 'uniform' and headed toward his house, Abani suddenly appeared from somewhere and joined him. Abani said, "Brother Dilip, you too saw and heard something of what happened the other day. But I was so angry that day that I left without speaking to you. Please do not mind that." —"I have no reason at all to mind." —"Good! But please grant me one request. No respectable gentleman ought to live in the house where Bhairab lives. Leave that lodging-house." —"Tell me why?" At first, Abani gave no reply, walking forward silently beside Dilip for a while. Then he said, "It is impossible for me to tell you the reason why I am asking you to leave that house. Because I have promised Bhairab that I will not say a word to anyone. But this much I ought to tell you: whether respectable or not, it is not safe for any human being to stay near Bhairab. At any moment you could fall into danger—terrible danger!"

What would be the use of going to the jetty? If any passengers were found, Haru Majhi himself would bring them along. A little later, dazzling Haru's eyes with the glare of its searchlight and lighting up the jetty and the riverbank around it, the steamer pulled in at the ghat and left again in due time. Shortly afterward, Haru Majhi came back to the boat with a sullen face.
Naga's mind was restless to break the news, but Haru did not even give him a chance to begin speaking; the instant he stepped into the boat, he demanded, 'How much did you get?'
'Six annas.'
'Hand it over.'
Hesitating a little, Naga handed him five annas. —'I kept one anna, Kaka, I need it for something.' Not a single passenger had turned up all day, and Haru's temper was already blazing like fire. In the blink of an eye, he exploded like a bomb. —'Need it for something! I'm the one who feeds and clothes you, and you have a need for the money you earn! Hand over the money, I tell you, or else today I'll—'
Silently, Naga tossed the anna coin down in front of Haru.
'Why did you throw it? Who are you showing your temper to!'
Because he had earned nothing all day, Haru seemed determined to pick a fight with whoever crossed his path; without a quarrel, the burning irritation inside him would not subside. He acted like this often, and because answering back only fueled his anger, Naga usually kept quiet. Naga's temper was not the sort to flare up easily. Today, however, his blood suddenly boiled over. The very man for whose convenience he could not decide whether to accept such a comfortable job with Jadabbabu, the man on whose boat he single-handedly did the work of two boatmen on a half-empty stomach—this was how he behaved just because Naga had kept one anna out of six annas' earnings for himself! Even placing the anna down in front of him instead of putting it into his hand was being treated as a display of temper!
'Control your own temper first, and then talk about mine.'
'What did you say!'
Haru Majhi dealt a hard slap across Naga's cheek, and not content with that, began raining blows and slaps upon Naga's body without stop. What could Naga do? One cannot strike back at an elder in return for a beating, so he simply gave Haru Majhi a shove and pushed him into the river. There was no other way to cool him down.
By then, the boatmen on the neighboring boats had become aware of the dramatic scene unfolding on this boat. As Haru Majhi splashed into the river water, several of them cheered aloud. While Haru Majhi was clambering back into the boat from the water, four or five men leaped across from the next boat onto theirs, and hearing the commotion, an old Muslim boatman came over from a gadhaboat a short distance away to see what was happening.
Instead of cooling down in the river water, Haru Majhi's temper had grown hotter still. The moment he climbed aboard, he lunged to attack Naga, but could not reach him because the others held him back. The jackal said, 'You needn't show off your learning anymore. Let me ask you: you do know the road home to your house, don't you?'

The crow said, 'Of course I know it! Why, there's the straight road right in front of us.'

The jackal asked, 'How far does this road go?'

The crow replied, 'Where would a road go? A road stays right where it belongs. Does a road wander around grazing here and there? Or go off to Darjeeling to take the air?'

The jackal said, 'You are an awfully insolent fellow! Tell me, now that you've come to give testimony, what do you know about the lawsuit?'

The crow said, 'Well, I like that! Who has been sitting up there doing all the calculations all this time? Whatever you want to know, you'll get it from me. First of all: what is man? Man means kachuri. There are four kinds of kachuri—hinge kachuri with asafoetida, khasta kachuri, nimki, and jibegaja! What happens when you eat them? When jackals eat them, their throats itch, but crows' throats don't itch at all. Next, there was a witness, cash value four annas, who lived in Assam, and the skin on his ears turned blue—that is called kala-azar, black fever. After that, there was a man who used to give names to everyone—he called the jackal Telchor the Oil-Thief, he called the crocodile Ashtabakra the Crooked-in-Eight-Places, and he called the owl Bibhishan the Traitor—' No sooner had it said this than a tremendous uproar broke out in the courtroom. Flying into a sudden rage, the crocodile snapped up the bullfrog in one gulp; seeing that, the musk-shrew began shrieking at the top of its lungs—'Kich, kich, kich, kich!'—and the jackal began shooing Kakkeshwar away with an umbrella, shouting, 'Hush, hush!'

Turning solemn, the owl declared, 'Be quiet, everyone! I shall now pronounce the verdict of the suit.' Saying this, it ordered a rabbit wearing a pen behind its ear, 'Write down what I say: Defamation Suit, Number Twenty-Four. Complainant—the Porcupine. Accused—wait a minute. Where is the accused?'

Then everyone cried out, 'Oh drat! There isn't any accused at all!' Quickly, with a bit of coaxing and cajoling, the bald fellow was made to stand in as the accused. Being a simpleton, the bald fellow thought the accused probably got paid in coins too, so he raised no objection.

The sentence was pronounced—three months in jail and seven days of hanging for the bald fellow. I was just thinking that I ought to protest against such an unjust verdict when suddenly the goat charged at me from behind, bleating 'Bya-karan Shing!', butted me once, and right after that bit my ear. Instantly, everything all around me began to blur and swim, and the goat's face gradually changed until it looked just like my second maternal uncle, Mejomama. Focusing my eyes then, I saw that Mejomama was holding me by the ear and saying, 'So, under the pretext of studying byakaran—grammar—you've been lying here fast asleep?'

I was dumbstruck! At first I thought I must have been dreaming all this while. Even so—you won't believe me if I tell you—when I went to look for my handkerchief, I couldn't find it anywhere, and a cat was sitting on top of the fence twirling its whiskers; the moment it caught sight of me, it scrambled down with a rustle and ran off. And at that exact moment, from behind the garden, a goat bleated out—"Baa!"

I told my eldest maternal uncle, Baromama, all about these things, but Baromama said, 'Go on, go on! Dreaming up a bunch of nonsense and coming here to spin tales about it!' When people grow old, they become so thick-headed that they refuse to believe anything at all. Since you people haven't grown very old yet, I took heart and told all these things to you.

Then he called out to the jackal and said, 'Shiyalpandit—Scholar Jackal, wait a moment. You are my witness.'

The jackal stopped, but refused to come any closer. From a safe distance, it asked, 'What do you mean by that! How did I become your witness?'

Thakurmashai said, 'Tell me this, my good fellow: does anyone return evil to someone who does them good?'

The jackal replied, 'Only after I hear who did what good to whom, and who did what harm to whom, can I give an answer.'

'Thakurmashai, now I have understood everything.' Thakurmashai said, 'The tiger was inside the cage, and I was walking along the road—'

The instant it heard these words, the jackal said, 'This is a very complicated matter. Unless I see that cage and that road for myself, I won't be able to say a thing.'

So all of them had to walk back to the cage again. After pacing up and down around the cage for a long time, the jackal said, 'Alright, I have understood the cage and the road. Now tell me what happened.'

Thakurmashai said, 'The tiger was inside the cage, and I, a Brahmin, was walking along the road.'

At once the jackal stopped him and said, 'Hold on, don't go so fast—let me understand that much properly first. What did you say? The tiger was your Brahmin, and the road was walking through the cage?'

Hearing this, the tiger burst out laughing—'Ho, ho!'—and said, 'Get out, you donkey! The tiger was inside the cage, and the Brahmin was walking along the road.'

The jackal said, 'Wait a second—the Brahmin was inside the cage, and the tiger was walking along the road?'

The tiger said, 'Oh, you fool, not like that! The tiger was inside the cage, and the Brahmin was walking along the road.'

The jackal said, 'This is a terribly muddled affair, I see! I can't make head or tail of it! What did you say? The tiger was inside the Brahmin, and the cage was walking along the road?'

The tiger said, 'I have never seen such an idiot anywhere! Look here, the tiger was inside the cage, and the Brahmin was walking along the road.'

Scratching its head, the jackal said, 'No! Such a difficult matter is quite beyond my understanding.'

By then the tiger had lost its temper.

Giving the jackal a sharp scolding, it snapped, 'You had better understand it! Look here, I was inside this cage—look—just like this—'

Saying this, the tiger walked right back inside the cage, and in a flash the jackal slammed the cage door shut and bolted the latch! Then the jackal said to Thakurmashai, 'Thakurmashai, now I have understood everything. If you wish to hear my testimony, it is this: one should never do a favor for a wicked creature. So the verdict is yours. Now hurry along quickly, the falar feast hasn't run out yet!' Saying this, the jackal went off into the forest to forage, and Thakurmashai went on his way to eat his falar feast.

সেদিন আমাদের সত্যিসত্যিই রাগ হয়েছিল। এমনি করে ফাঁকি দেওয়া! মিথ্যে করে মামা তৈরি! সেদিন আমাদের ধমকের চোটে জগ্যিদাস কেঁদেই ফেলল। সে তখন স্বীকার করল যে ফোটোটা কোন এক পশ্চিমা পালোয়ানের। আর সেই ট্রেনের লোকটাকে সে চেনেই না। তার পরে কোনো অজিগুবি জিনিসের কথা বলতে হলেই আমরা বলতাম, “জগ্যিদাসের মামার মতো।”
