Brahma: "We cannot accept cash."

Satan: "Not cash. To please you, they will spend lavishly. They will build temples, churches, mosques, monasteries, and almshouses; they will donate handsome sums to hospitals, the Red Cross, schools, colleges, tols, madrasas, and memorials for great men; they will feed khichuri to the starving and distribute blankets to those shivering in the cold. Tell us who the descendants of your mind-born sons are, and they will be given high posts and motorcars. In exchange for all this, you will keep my clients safe."

Brahma: "How much will they spend?"

Satan: "Say, one per cent of their earnings."

Brahma: "That won't do, my boy."

Satan: "All right, two per cent?"

Brahma: "Do you take me for a broker?"

Satan: "Five per cent? Ten—fifteen—twenty? Very well, let twenty-five per cent be given away in charity for your pleasure. You don't agree even to that? Whew! I see your greed is even greater than that of our patriotic leaders. How many years have you served in jail, Lord? All right, tell me yourself how much it will take to please you."

Brahma: "I want a full one hundred per cent."

Narad: "O Satan, the Lord is saying that one must surrender the entire fruit of one's actions; only then is deliverance gained."

Satan: "Then earning anything at all is in vain! If one has to give up everything, what is the profit in stealing, robbing, looting, and fighting?"

Brahma: "Explain that to your clients. No bargain can be struck while holding something back in hand. What do God and Allah Ta'ala say? Why, where have They all gone?"

Narad: "They have all vanished."

Satan: "Then I too shall take my leave, Grandfather. You have disappointed me."

Brahma: "Wait a moment; one must not return empty-handed. I am granting you a boon.—My son Satan, priest, padre, or mullah, police, army, or the United Nations—none of them will stand in your way; you may consign your clients to hell without hindrance. After that, I shall create human beings anew. Narad, come, let us go now; call for my swan."

Narad: "Lord, it has gone to graze at Lake Manas Sarovar; it did not know the assembly would break up so soon. Come along on my husking-pedal instead."

শয়তান। নগদ টাকা নয়। আপনাদের খুশী করবার জন্য তাঁরা প্রচুর খরচ করবেন। মন্দির গির্জা মসজিদ মঠ আতুরাশ্রম বানাবেন, হাসপাতাল রেড ক্রস স্কুল কলেজ ঢৌল মাদ্রাসায় এবং মহাপুরুষদের স্মৃতিরক্ষার জন্য মোটা টাকা দেবেন, ব‍ুভুক্ষকে খিচুড়ি খাওয়াবেন, শীতার্তকে কম্বল দেবেন। আপনার মানসপুত্রদের বংশধর কে কে আছেন বলুন, তাঁদের বড় বড় চাকরি আর মোটর কার দেওয়া হবে। এইসবের পরিবর্তে আপনারা আমার মক্কেলগণকে নিরাপদে রাখবেন।

ব্রহ্মা। একটু থাম, শ‍ুধু হাতে ফিরে যেতে নেই। একটা বর দিচ্ছি। —বৎস শয়তান, পুরুতে পাদরী মোল্লা, পুলিস সৈন্য বা মিলিত জাতিসংসদ, কেউ তোমাকে বাধা দেবে না, তোমার মক্কেলদের তুমি নির্বিঘ্নে নরকস্থ করতে পারবে। তার পর আমি আবার মানুষ সৃষ্টি করব। নারদ, এখন যাই চল, আমার হাঁসটাকে ডেকে আন।

Near a king's palace lived a fox. His burrow was right behind the king's goat-shed.

The king's goats were very fine and plump.

Whenever the fox saw them, his mouth watered to eat them. But for fear of the king's herdsmen, he could not get near them.

So the fox began digging a tunnel from inside his burrow. He dug and dug until he came right up into the goat-shed, yet even then he did not get to eat a goat.

The herdsmen happened to be sitting there at the time. The moment they spotted the fox, they caught him and tied him up. Then, leaving him tied to a stake, they went away. As they left, they said, 'Tomorrow we will show everyone some fun with this fellow, and then we'll kill him. It has grown late tonight.'

After the herdsmen had gone, the fox was sitting with his head hanging low when a tiger came walking by that way.

Greatly surprised to see the fox, the tiger asked, 'What is this, nephew? What are you doing sitting here?'

The fox said, 'I am getting married.'

The tiger asked, 'Then where is the bride? Where are the wedding guests?'

The fox said, 'The bride is the king's daughter. The people have gone to fetch her.'

The tiger asked, 'Why are you tied up?'

The fox said, 'Well, I didn't want to get married, so they tied me up before leaving, lest I run away.'

The tiger asked, 'Is that really true? You don't want to get married?'

The fox said, 'Truly, uncle. I don't feel like getting married in the least.'

Hearing this, the tiger grew terribly eager and said, 'Why don't you tie me up in your place and go away?'

The fox said, 'Right away! Just untie my ropes, and then I will tie you up before I go.'

Who could measure the tiger's joy at that! He immediately came over and untied the fox's ropes. Without wasting a moment, the fox tied him securely to the stake and said, 'Just one thing, uncle. Your brothers-in-law will come and play jokes and pranks on you. You won't get angry at that, will you?'

The tiger said, 'Oh, no! Would I get angry over that? Do you take me for such a fool?' At these words, the fox went off laughing to himself. The tiger sat wondering when they would bring the bride.

In the morning, the band of herdsmen arrived. Seeing them, the tiger thought, 'Here come my brothers-in-law. They will probably crack jokes with me right now. And then I must laugh heartily too.'

The herdsmen had come to kill the fox. When they arrived, they found a tiger sitting there instead. The tiger went, 'Hee, hee, hihi, hihi!' At once a tremendous commotion broke out. Some of them wanted to run away, while others stopped them and said, 'Hey, don't you see he's tied up? What is there to fear? Go fetch axes, spades, and spears!'

Then one of them brought a huge brick and hurled it at the tiger.

At that, the tiger went, 'Ha, ha, haha, haha!'

Another man jabbed him hard with a bamboo pole.

At that, the tiger went, 'Hee, hee, hihi, hihi!'

Then another man prodded him with a spear.

At that, the tiger went, 'Ooh, hoo, hoo, hoho, hoho, hoho!—I can tell you fellows are my brothers-in-law!'

Again they jabbed him with the spear.

At that, the tiger flew into a furious rage and shouted, 'To hell with it! I won't have such a wretched marriage!' Snapping the rope, he bounded off into the forest.

এক রাজার বাড়ির কাছে এক শিয়াল থাকত। রাজার ছাগলের ঘরের পিছনে তার গর্ত ছিল।

রাজার ছাগলগুলি খুব সুন্দর আর মোটা মোটা ছিল।

তাদের দেখলেই শিয়ালের ভারী খেতে ইচ্ছে হত। কিন্তু রাজার রাখাল গুলির ভয়ে তাদের কাছে আসতে পারত না।

তখন শিয়াল তার গর্তের ভিতর থেকে খুঁড়তে আরম্ভ করল। খুঁড়ে-খুঁড়ে তো সে ছাগলের ঘরে এসে উপস্থিত হল, কিন্তু তবুও ছাগল খেতে পেল না।

রাখালের দল তখন সেখানে বসে ছিল। তারা শিয়ালকে দেখতে পেয়েই ধরে বেঁধে ফেলল। তারপর তাকে খোঁটায় বেঁধে রেখে তারা চলে গেল। যাবার সময় বলে গেল, ‘কাল এটাকে নিয়ে সকলকে তামাশা দেখাব, তারপর মারব। আজ রাত হয়ে গেছে।’

রাখালেরা চলে গেছে, শিয়াল মাথা হেঁট করে বসে আছে, এমন সময় এক বাঘ সেইখান দিয়ে যাচ্ছে।

শিয়ালকে দেখে বাঘ ভারী আশ্চর্য হয়ে বললে, ‘কি ভাগ্নে, এখানে বসে কি করছ?’

শিয়াল বললে, ‘বিয়ে করছি।’

বাঘ বললে, ‘তবে কনে কোথায়? লোকজন কোথায়?’

শিয়াল বললে, ‘কনে তো রাজার মেয়ে। লোকজন তাকে আনতে গেছে।’

বাঘ বললে, ‘তুমি বাঁধা কেন?’

শিয়াল বললে, ‘আমি কিনা বিয়ে করতে চাইনি, তাই আমাকে বেঁধে রেখে গেছে, পাছে আমি পালাই।’

বাঘ বললে, ‘সত্যি নাকি। তুমি বিয়ে করতে চাচ্ছ না?’

শিয়াল বললে, ‘সত্যি মামা। আমার বিয়ে করতে একটুও ইচ্ছে হচ্ছে না।’

তা শুনে বাঘ ভারী ব্যস্ত হযে বললে, ‘তবে তোমার জায়গায় আমাকে বেঁধে রেখে তুমি চলে যাও না।’

শিয়াল বললে, ‘এক্ষুণি। তুমি আমার বাঁধন খুলে দাও, তারপর আমি তোমাকে বেঁধে রেখে যাচ্ছি।’

তখন বাঘের আনন্দ দেখে কে। সে অমনি এসে শিয়ালের বাঁধন খুলে দিল। শিয়ালও আর দেরি না করে, তাকে ভালো মতো খোঁটায় বেঁধে বললে ‘এক কথা মামা। তোমার শালারা এসে তোমার সঙ্গে হাসি-তামাশা করবে। তাতে বা তুমি চটো?’

বাঘ বললে, ‘আরে না। আমি তাতে চটি? আমি বুঝি এতই বোকা।’ এ কথায় শিয়াল হাসতে-হাসতে চলে গেল। বাঘ ভাবতে লাগল, কখন কনে নিয়ে আসবে।

সকালবেলায় রাখালের দল এসে উপস্থিত হল। বাঘ তাদের দেখে ভাবল, ‘এই আমার শালারা এসেছে। এক্ষুণি হয়তো ঠাট্টা করবে। আর তাহলে আমাকেও খুব হাসতে হবে।’

রাখালেরা এসেছিল শিয়াল মারতে। এসে দেখলে বাঘ বসে আছে। বাঘ বললে, ‘হীঃ, হীঃ, হিহি, হিহিঃ!” অমনি তো ভারী একটা হইচই পড়ে গেল। কেউ-কেউ পালাতে চায়, কেউ-কেউ তাদের থামিয়ে বললে, ‘আরে বাঁধা রয়েছে দেখছিস না? ভয় কি? কুড়ুল, খন্তা, বল্লম নিয়ে আয়।’

তখন একজন একটা মস্ত ইট এনে বাঘের গায়ে ছুঁড়ে মারল।

তাতে বাঘ বললে, ‘হাঃ, হাঃ, হাহা হাহা।’

আর একজন একটা বাঁশ দিয়ে গুঁতো মারলে।

তাতে বাঘ বললে, ‘হী, হীঃ, হিহি, হিহি।’

আর একজন একটা বল্লম দিয়ে খোঁচা মারলে।

তাতে বাঘ বললে, ‘উঃ, হূঃ, হূঃ, হোহো হোহো হোহো!—বুঝেছি তোমরা আমার শালা।’

আবার তারা বল্লমের খোঁচা মারলে।

তাতে বাঘ বেজায় রেগে বললে, ‘দুত্তোর! এমন ছাই বিয়ে আমি করব না।’ বলে সে দড়ি ছিঁড়ে বনে চলে গেল।

Tuntuni had gone to dance on a brinjal leaf. While dancing away, she got pricked by a brinjal thorn. From that prick, she developed a huge boil.

Oh dear, what will happen now? How will such a huge boil ever heal?

Tuntuni asked this one and asked that one. Everyone told her, 'Get a barber to lance it for you.'

Now at last he understood why there was a barbed-wire fence all around the station. Yet Shankar had made a slight mistake—he had understood only partially, and getting the rest of the answer was delayed by a couple of days.

That came from another direction.

The next morning, he told the guard of the morning train about the night's incident. The guard was a good man; after hearing everything, he said, "It is like this everywhere in these parts. Twelve miles from here there is another small station just like yours—it's the same story there too. And what happened right here—"

He was about to say something, but suddenly stopped mid-sentence and boarded the train. As he left, he called out from the moving train, "Always be very careful—"

Shankar grew worried—were they trying to hush something up? Was there something else besides lions? Whatever it was, from that day on Shankar kept a fire burning every day on the platform in front of the station room. Before evening fell, he shut the door and went inside the station room—sitting up late into the night studying or writing in his diary. The experience of the night was strange. Thick darkness descended over the vast plain, the night wind caught in the branches of the yucca tree on the platform and made a peculiar sound, jackals howled across the plains at every watch of the night, and on some nights, deep in the dark, the roar of a lion could be heard far away—a strange life indeed!

This was the very life he had wanted. It was in his blood. This uninhabited plain, this mysterious night, the sky filled with unfamiliar stars, this constant threat of danger—this was life! A safe, quiet life might suit a harmless clerk—not him.

That day, after seeing off the afternoon train, he was about to enter the kitchen of his quarters when, spotting something on the wooden post, he leaped back three cubits—seeing him, a huge yellow spectacle cobra had raised its hood and thrust its head out nearly a cubit from the post! Had Shankar's eyes fallen that way just two seconds later—then—no, what could be done now to kill the snake? But the very next moment, the snake climbed up the post and hid inside the thatched roof above. A fine state of affairs indeed. Shankar now had to go into that very room and sit down to cook rice. This was no lion that he could keep out by shutting the door and lighting a fire. After hesitating for a while, Shankar reluctantly entered the kitchen, somehow finished cooking in a hurry, completed his meal before evening fell, and came out of there into the station room. But how could he trust the station room either? When and through what gap a snake might slip into the room—could it ever be kept out?

On the next morning's train, a new coolie came from the guard's van to unload his sack of rations. Twice a week, the railway company sent rice and potatoes from Mombasa for the employees of these remote stations—the cost was deducted from their monthly salary.

The coolie who came to unload the sack of rations was an Indian, from the Gujarat region. After setting down the sack, he looked at Shankar in a strange way, and as if afraid that Shankar might ask him something, he hurriedly climbed back into the train.

That look of the coolie did not escape Shankar's eyes. What mystery was bound up with this place that no one wanted to reveal to him—as if revealing it were forbidden? What was going on?

Two days later, after passing the train, he was about to enter his quarters when he came within an inch of stepping right on a snake's neck. That same spectacle cobra. It could be the snake he had seen before, though there was no proof that it was not a new one either.

পরদিন সকালের ট্রেণে গার্ডের গাড়ি থেকে একটি নতুন কুলী তার রসদের বস্তা নামিয়ে দিতে এল। সপ্তাহে দু’দিন মোম্বাসা থেকে চাল আর আলু রেলকোম্পানী এইসব নির্জ্জন ষ্টেশনের কর্ম্মচারীদের পাঠিয়ে দেয়—মাসিক বেতন থেকে এর দাম কেটে নেওয়া হয়।

যে কুলীটা রসদের বস্তা নামিয়ে দিতে এল সে ইণ্ডিয়ান, গুজরাট অঞ্চলে বাড়ী। সে বস্তাটা নামিয়ে কেমন যেন অদ্ভুত ভাবে চাইলে শঙ্করের দিকে, এবং পাছে শঙ্কর তাকে কিছু জিগ্যেস্ করে, এই ভয়েই যেন তাড়াতাড়ি গাড়ীতে গিয়ে উঠে পড়্‌ল।

কুলীর সে দৃষ্টি শঙ্করের চোখ এড়ায় নি। কী রহস্য জড়িত আছে যেন এই জায়গাটার সঙ্গে, কেউ তা ওর কাছে প্রকাশ করতে চায় না—প্রকাশ করা যেন বারণ আছে। ব্যাপার কী?

দিন দুই পরে ট্রেণ পাশ করে সে নিজের কোয়ার্টারে ঢুকতে যাচ্ছে—আর একটু হোলে সাপের ঘাড়ে পা দিয়েছিল আর কি। সেই খড়িশ গোখুরা সাপ। পূর্ব্বদৃষ্ট সাপটাও হোতে পারে, নতুন একটা যে নয় তারও কোনো প্রমাণ নেই।

Take the sentence, 'Gharer chhele ghare jao, gharer bhat beshi kore kheyo'—'Boy of the house, go home and eat plenty of home-cooked rice'—and try replacing 'ghar' with 'griha' anywhere in it; just see how it sounds to the ear, and how clear the meaning remains!
Is not the real truth this: that at root there is no difference between written language and spoken language? The language of both is one and the same; only the means of expression differs—on the one hand through the voice, on the other through letters. Speech dwells upon the tongue. Only the spoken word is alive. As far as possible, writing comes to life only when we can write in the very language in which we speak. Our chief endeavor should be to preserve unity between speech and writing, not to destroy it. Language comes from the human mouth to the nib of the pen, not from the nib of the pen to the human mouth. If you try to do the reverse, you only end up with ink smeared on your face. Some say that the wealth of our ideas has grown so vast that it can no longer be contained within the language of our fathers and grandfathers. That may well be true, but precious little proof of it is to be found in Bangla literature. According to Kanada, 'abhava'—absence or non-existence—is a substance. I am the child of a Hindu, so I am obliged to accept Vaisheshika philosophy; for that very reason, I am compelled to admit that there is a great deal of 'substance' in current Bangla literature too. The ideas of English literature, the vocabulary of the Sanskrit language, and the grammar of the Bangla language—the khichuri we cook up by mixing these three things is what we call Bangla literature; needless to say, without knowing English, one cannot grasp its meaning. At times I suspect that, caught beneath the dual shelter of foreign ideas and an ancient tongue, Bangla literature is unable to blossom. I do admit, of course, that to some extent we need to bring new words into our language. Whatever has life must be fed every day. And to nourish the body of our language, we must draw new words chiefly from the Amarakosha. But whoever uses a new Sanskrit word ought to keep this in mind: he must breathe life into every single word anew; if he cannot do that, he will only be hanging borrowed gold on the ears of Banga-Saraswati. Piling up a heap of Sanskrit words without judgment will neither enhance the beauty of the language, nor increase the glory of literature, nor express one's thoughts clearly. What the language needs now is to be whetted to bring out its edge, not weighed down with a heavier load. A word that is absolutely indispensable—bring it from wherever you can, provided you can make it fit into your own language. But do not beg, borrow, or steal any more than that. When Lord Pavananandan—Hanuman—went to fetch the Vishalyakarani herb and uprooted the entire Gandhamadan mountain to bring it back, he showed his extraordinary strength—but he did not show intelligence.

Recently, a major dispute has broken out in our small literary circle over Bangla grammar. I am no grammarian, nor have I any wish to become one. People generally lament that the Muslims burned down the famous library of Alexandria, but the attitude of the celebrated French writer Montaigne was that it was a blessing it turned to ashes. For there were a hundred thousand volumes of dictionaries and grammars in it. 'Good heavens! So many words just about words!' I, too, agree with Montaigne. Since I care nothing for grammar, there was no need for me to join this debate to absolve myself of any debt to the ancient sages. But in our country, argument is a liquid substance; its very nature is to flow effortlessly from one subject to another in the blink of an eye. The debate began with grammar, has now reached poetics and rhetoric halfway through, and will probably end in worldly renunciation. Be that as it may, Pandit Sharatchandra Shastri Mahashay has been propagating the view that the more Sanskrit words we import into our writing, the better it will be for our literature. My wish is that Bangla literature be written in the Bangla language. It is the nature of the weak not to be able to stand on their own feet. They want to cling to some external support. We depend on others for our own progress. For the advancement of our homeland, we look eagerly to foreigners, and for the exact same reason, we beg the help of another language for the enrichment of our own. However supreme another language may be, does clinging to the hem of its garment show any self-respect? I say, why don't we test ourselves for once? No one can say what the result will be, for there is no doubt that we have never tried that experiment before. Enough of such idle talk. I love the Bangla language, and I revere Sanskrit. But I do not accept the scripture that says you must perform funeral rites for the very thing you revere. Whether my view is right or Shastri Mahashay's view is right is not what I have sat down to judge. I only wish to examine the arguments by which he has set out to support his opinion.
Someone might ask right at the outset: what do we call the Bangla language? Such a question does not sit well in the mouth of a Bangali. Is not the simple answer to this question that the language we all know, hear, and understand—the language in which we have been expressing our thoughts, reflections, joys, and sorrows effortlessly and painlessly for ages, and probably will continue to express for ages to come—is the Bangla language? The Bangla language lives not inside the Prakritibad dictionary, but in the mouths of Bangalis. Yet I see that many are exceedingly reluctant to admit this very simple truth. I hear that certain scripture-learned Maulvis say that when the Badshah of Delhi sat down to create the Urdu language, his intention was to fashion a completely pure Persian language, but moved to pity by the weeping and wailing of the poor Hindus, he allowed a few Hindi words to enter Urdu. Input: Ever since childhood, I have regarded Hemanta Chowdhury as an extraordinary man. From pathshala to school, and from school to college, the two of us always studied together. Even after climbing to the highest rung of the university, our paths did not part on the journey of life—as usually happens. The reason was that both of us were independent. In many other respects, too, a remarkable similarity can be seen between the two of us. Both of us are the sons of wealthy men, and both of us have lost our parents. Both of us have an intense passion for physical culture—wrestling, jujutsu, boxing (along with a passion for wrestling, quarterstaff, and swordplay), we left nothing unlearned—although in competitions Hemanta always came first and I came second. Both of us love traveling from land to land, and even in our youth we have toured as far as Europe and America. Neither of us has married, and the moment matchmakers set foot across the threshold of our house, we clench our fists and charge at them. However, the ways in which the two of us spend our days and pass our time are not the same. For Hemanta practices amateur detective work, while I pursue literature as a pastime. There is no need to say anything here about my literary pursuits. I have been compelled to take up my pen today for a different reason. Nowadays Hemanta has won such renown in detective work that all sorts of people express the keenest eagerness to hear his stories from my lips. Many people do not hesitate to pester Hemanta himself for this as well. Yet in one respect he is terribly shy—nothing in the world can persuade him to boast of his own exploits with his own mouth. Then everyone starts tugging at me, and having no choice, I have to oblige their requests. Still, how many stories of Hemanta can I go on telling over and over again by word of mouth to different people? So this time I have decided that, to satisfy people's curiosity, I shall publish the stories of Hemanta's exploits in print one by one. I shall begin right from the very beginning. Before anything else, I want to put down in writing the story of the very first case that Hemanta solved to win fame at home and abroad. Yet even before that, I think it necessary to give a little more introduction to Hemanta himself. The magic mango tree sprouts up suddenly right before the spectators' eyes. Hemanta, however, did not turn into a full-fledged detective overnight; for that, he had to undergo rigorous training and dedication. Right from boyhood he had an intense passion for reading fictional detective stories, and there is probably no famous detective story in the world that he has not read to this day. Yet he never tried to become an expert merely by reading those fictional—and often wildly improbable—tales! He went to Europe and America chiefly with a single purpose in mind! He went there to learn firsthand the exact methods by which real detectives in Western countries carry out their work. Having secured several letters of recommendation from some of the highest officials of the police department in this country, he had the opportunity to observe the work of Western police forces from inside their detective departments. Across the countries of Europe, detective police forces have a wide variety of working methods. The most famous among them are the methods of the English, French, German, and Austrian police. Hemanta had the opportunity to study all four of these methods in special detail.

তাই এবারে স্থির করেছি, লোকের আগ্রহ নিবারণের জন্যে হেমন্তের কার্ত্তিকাহিনী ছাপার হরপে প্রকাশ করব একে একে। আমি শুরু করব একেবারে গোড়া থেকেই। হেমন্ত সর্ব্বপ্রথমে যে-মামলার কিনারা ক’রে দেশ-বিদেশে যশস্বা হয়ে ওঠে, আগে তার কথাই লিপিবদ্ধ ক’রে রাখতে চাই। কিন্তু তারও আগে হেমন্তের আরো কিছু পরিচয় দেওয়া দরকার মনে করি। ম্যাজিকের আমগাছ দর্শকদের চোখের সামনে গজিয়ে ওঠে হঠাৎ। কিন্তু হেমন্ত অকস্মাৎ পূরোদস্ত্তর গোয়েন্দা হয়ে পড়েনি, এজন্য তাকে সাধনা করতে হয়েছে দস্তুরমত। ছেলেবেলা থেকেই কাল্পনিক গোয়েন্দা কাহিনী পড়বার জন্যে তার অতিশয় ঝোঁক ছিল এবং আজ পয্যন্ত সে পাঠ করেনি পৃথিবীতে এমন বিখ্যাত গোয়েন্দার গল্প বোধ হয় নেই। কিন্তু এই সব কাল্পনিক এবং প্রায়ই অতি-উদ্ভট কাহিনী প’ড়ে কোনদিনই সে বিশেষজ্ঞ হবার চেষ্টা করেনি! সে য়ুরোপে-আমেরিকায় গিয়েছিল প্রধানত এক উদ্দেশ্য নিয়ে! পাশ্চাত্য দেশের সত্যিকার গোয়েন্দারা কোন্ কোন্ পদ্ধতি অনুসারে কাজ করে, সে গিয়েছিল হাতে-কলমে তাই শেখবার জন্যেই। এদেশের পুলিস-বিভাগের কয়েকজন উচ্চতম কর্ম্মচারীর কাছ থেকে সে খানকয় সুপারিস-পত্র জোগাড় ক’রেছিল, তারই সাহায্যে গোয়েন্দা বিভাগের ভিতর থেকে পাশ্চাত্য-পুলিসদের কাজ দেখবার সুযোগ তার হয়েছিল। য়ুরোপের দেশে দেশে গোয়েন্দা-পুলিসদের কার্য্যপদ্ধতি আছে নানারকম। তারই মধ্যে সবচেয়ে বিখ্যাত হচ্ছে ইংরেজ, ফরাসী, জার্ম্মান ও অস্ট্রিয়ান পুলিসের পদ্ধতি। হেমন্ত এই চার-রকম পদ্ধতি নিয়েই বিশেষ ভাবে আলোচনা করবার অবসর পেয়েছে।

You and we are different. Because you are you, and we are we. If that were not so, Europe and Asia would not be two—they would be one. There would be no distinction between 'I' and 'you.' You and we together would have become either only we, or only you.
We are the East, you are the West. We are the beginning, you are the end. Our land is the nursery of human civilization; your land is human civilization's cremation ground. We are the dawn, you are the twilight. Ours is a rising out of darkness; yours is a dissolution into darkness!
Our color is dark, your color is white. Our garments are white, your garments are black. You keep your white bodies covered; we keep our dark bodies bare. We drink plain water, you drink red liquor. Our sky is fire, your sky is smoke. Blue is in your women's eyes, gold is on your women's heads; blue is in our firmament, gold is beneath our soil. There are many differences of color and caste between you and us. Let us not forget that between your land and ours lies the gulf of the Kalapani, the black waters. If we cross the Kalapani, we lose our caste; if you do not, you cannot keep yours.
You rush around abroad; we lie at home. Our society is stationary; your society is mobile. Your ideal is the animal; our ideal is the plant. Your intoxication is wine; our intoxication is opium. Your happiness lies in restless bustling; our happiness lies in dozing. Happiness is your ideal; suffering is our reality. You want the strength to conquer the world; we want the ruse to evade the world. Your goal is comfort; our goal is repose. The final word of your ethics is labor; ours is the ashram.
Your women are nearly men; our men are nearly women. Even when you grow old, your childishness does not leave you; even in childhood, we are full of old-mannishness. We marry before youth arrives; you marry after youth has passed. Just when you are entering household life, we are heading for the forest.
With you, love comes first and marriage after; with us, marriage comes first and love after. Our marriages 'happen'; you 'do' marriage. In our language, the primary root verb is 'bhu'—to be; in your language, it is 'kri'—to do. Among you, women's beauty is cherished; among us, women's virtues go unappreciated. Your husbands need scholarship in economics; our husbands need scholarship in rhetoric and poetics.
In a word, what you want, we do not want, and what we want, you do not want; what you get, we do not get, and what we get, you do not get. We want the One; you want the Many. In place of the One, we get zero; in place of the Many, you get a one followed by many zeros. Your philosopher seeks reason; our philosopher seeks mukti—liberation. You want the outside; we want the inside. The life of your men is outside the home; the death of our men is inside the home. To your mind, our songs and our music are mere lamentation; to our mind, your songs and your music are mere raving. The aim of your science is to know everything and understand nothing; the aim of our wisdom is to know nothing and understand everything. Your hereafter is heaven; our present world is hell. Therefore, the hereafter is your destination, while this world is ours to renounce. According to your religion, the soul has a beginning but no end; according to our religion, the soul has no beginning but has an end—its culmination is nirvana. As I said before, the East and the West are distinct. We are good, and you are good too—only your good is our bad, and our good is your bad. Therefore, that the 'we' of the past and the 'you' of the present should combine to become the 'they' of the future—that too is impossible.

আমরা পূর্ব, তোমরা পশ্চিম। আমরা আরম্ভ, তোমরা শেষ। আমাদের দেশ মানবসভ্যতার সূতিকাগৃহ, তোমাদের দেশ মানবসভ্যতার শ্মশান। আমরা উষা, তোমরা গোধূলি। আমাদের অন্ধকার হতে উদয়, তোমাদের অন্ধকারের ভিতর বিলয়!
আমাদের রঙ কালো, তোমাদের রঙ সাদা। আমাদের বসন সাদা, তোমাদের বসন কালো। তোমরা শ্বেতাঙ্গ ঢেকে রাখো, আমরা কৃষ্ণদেহ খুলে রাখি। আমরা খাই সাদা জল, তোমরা খাও লাল পানি। আমাদের আকাশ আগুন, তোমাদের আকাশ ধোঁয়া। নীল তোমাদের স্ত্রীলোকের চোখে, সোনা তোমাদের স্ত্রীলোকের মাথায়; নীল আমাদের শূন্যে, সোনা আমাদের মাটির নীচে। তোমাদের ও আমাদের অনেক বর্ণভেদ। ভুলে যেন না যাই যে, তোমাদের দেশ ও আমাদের দেশের মধ্যে কালাপানির ব্যবধান। কালাপানি পার হলে আমাদের জাত যায়, না হলে তোমাদের জাত থাকে না।

তোমাদের মেয়ে প্রায়-পুরুষ, আমাদের পুরুষ প্রায়-মেয়ে। বুড়ো হলেও তোমাদের ছেলেমি যায় না, ছেলেবেলাও আমরা বুড়োমিতে পরিপূর্ণ। আমরা বিয়ে করি যৌবন না আসতে, তোমরা বিয়ে কর যৌবন গত হলে। তোমরা যখন সবে গৃহপ্রবেশ কর, আমরা তখন বনে যাই।
তোমাদের আগে ভালোবাসা পরে বিবাহ; আমাদের আগে বিবাহ পরে ভালোবাসা। আমাদের বিবাহ ‘হয়’, তোমরা বিবাহ ‘কর’। আমাদের ভাষায় মুখ্য ধাতু ‘ভূ’, তোমাদের ভাষায় ‘কৃ'। তোমাদের রমণীদের রূপের আদর আছে, আমাদের রমণীদের গুণের কদর নেই। তোমাদের স্বামীদের পাণ্ডিত্য চাই অর্থশাস্ত্রে, আমাদের স্বামীদেব পাণ্ডিত্য চাই অলংকারশাস্ত্রে।
অর্থাৎ এক কথায়, তোমরা যা চাও আমরা তা চাই নে, আমরা যা চাই তোমরা তা চাও না; তোমরা যা পাও আমরা তা পাইনে, আমরা যা পাই তোমরা তা পাও না। আমরা চাই এক, তোমরা চাও অনেক। আমরা একের বদলে পাই শূন্য, তোমরা অনেকের বদলে পাও একের পিঠে অনেক শূন্য। তোমাদের দার্শনিক চায় যুক্তি, আমাদের দার্শনিক চায় মুক্তি। তোমরা চাও বাহির, আমরা চাই ভিতর। তোমাদের পুরুষের জীবন বাড়ির বাইরে, আমাদের পুরুষের মরণ বাড়ির ভিতর। আমাদের গান আমাদের বাজনা তোমাদের মতে শুধু বিলাপ, তোমাদের গান তোমাদের বাজনা আমাদের মতে শুধু প্রলাপ। তোমাদের বিজ্ঞানের উদ্দেশ্য সব জেনে কিছু না জানা, আমাদের জ্ঞানের উদ্দেশ্য কিছু না জেনে সব জানা। তোমাদের পরলোক স্বৰ্গ, আমাদের ইহলোক নরক। কাজেই পরলোক তোমাদের গম্য, ইহলোক আমাদের ত্যাজ্য। তোমাদের ধর্মমতে আত্মা অনাদি নয় কিন্তু অনন্ত, আমাদের ধর্মমতে আত্মা অনাদি কিন্তু অনন্ত নয়— তার শেষ নির্বাণ। পূর্বেই বলেছি, প্রাচী ও প্রতীচী পৃথক। আমরাও ভালো, তোমরাও ভালো— শুধু তোমাদের ভালো আমাদের মন্দ ও আমাদের ভালো তোমাদের মন্দ। সুতরাং অতীতের আমরা ও বর্তমানের তোমরা, এই দুয়ে মিলে যে ভবিষ্যতের তারা হবে— তাও অসম্ভব।

Input: Bimal pulled out the map of Amrita-Dwip from his pocket and said, "Look here. Look toward the mountain with the highest peak among the five mountains at the northwestern corner of the island. A river comes out from the interior of the island, cuts through the mountain, and empties into the sea. We have to enter the island by rowing a boat up that very river." Sundarbabu said, "I'm letting you know well in advance—don't anyone ask me to get off the ship! ... How about it, Ramhari, you're on my side too, aren't you?" At first Ramhari remained silent. Then, shaking his head, he said, "That cannot be, sir! If the Khokababus go ashore, I must go ashore too." In an astonished voice, Sundarbabu said, "What are you saying, Ramhari? That island is an island of ghouls! Even those who die over there walk around!" Ramhari said, "For the Khokababus, I can even give my life." The sun set. The ship was now very close to the island. The darkness of evening deepened. The ship came to a halt beneath the five peaks of the rocky island. The seabirds were silent now. In the amphitheater of the sky, millions of stars waited in mute anticipation for the first-night moon. Not a single sign of life came from inside the island either. Yet the sea was not mute even there; its surge sounded like a wondrous melody played upon the vina of silence. Then slowly the moon rose, sending waves of silvery light rippling across the black touchstone of the dark. Bimal said, "Jayantababu, our ship has anchored right at the mouth of the river that leads into the island. What if we take a boat right now and make a quick tour inside the island?" Manik exclaimed, "Good heavens, at this hour of the night?" Jayanta said, "Night is the best time for scouting around in secret, Manik! There's bright white moonlight, so we won't have any trouble at all." Bimal said, "Tonight we'll just take a look at a part of the island and come back. Apart from me, Kumar, and Jayantababu, no one else needs to go tonight. After we return, our real expedition will begin tomorrow morning." Pulling a reluctant face, Manik said, "But what if you run into some danger?" —"At the first sign of danger, we'll slip away. Otherwise, all three of us will fire our guns together as a signal. In reply, you too will fire your guns to let us know, and then enter the island in full force with the ship's sailors." * * * * Piercing the dream-web of moonlight, their boat glided along, dancing upon the island's river. Bimal and Jayanta pulled the oars, while Kumar held the rudder. Because they wanted to go about their business quietly, they had not taken the sailors' help either. For a while, along both banks of the river, mountains could be seen standing like eternally silent sentinels. After about an hour, they passed beyond the mountain zone. Along both banks they now caught sight of open spaces here and there, interspersed with small and large thickets and woods. In every direction, the moonlight had painted countless pictures of varied beauty and charm, yet their eyes were not drawn to them then. Nor did they find any evidence that human eyes were enjoying this beauty anywhere on the island. It was as if the island were completely uninhabited—as if this were the private realm of green fields, giant forest trees, and sky-kissing mountains!

Input: The police of olden days worked largely like blind men. Science was then an infant, and even the little that science knew, the police did not think it necessary to call upon for help. Bertillon's system of taking bodily measurements or the method of taking fingerprints had not yet been invented. Nor did the police have anything to gain from the camera, the microscope, or the science of chemistry. Whenever the police saw a stain that looked like blood, they took it for granted that it was blood; whether it was really blood, and even if it was, whether it was the blood of a human being or an animal, or whether it belonged to a particular human being—there was no way at all to find out any of these things. However, the advanced science of the modern age has stepped in to remove much of that blindness of the police. In this field of science, Hemanta was remarkably well advanced! He had passed his M.A. in science with the highest honors. And even now he pursues scientific research regularly. He knows how to apply science to detective work with such ingenuity that one is left amazed at the sight of it. In the story that I have sat down to write today, readers will also get some glimpse of Hemanta's scientific acumen. To gather various kinds of information about the criminals of Bengal, he has struck up friendships with many of the bigwigs of the local police force. It is true that the police of no country look upon outside amateur detectives with much favor, regarding them rather as useless, meddlesome nuisances. Yet if one observes the behavior of certain officers of the Kolkata Police, it becomes quite clear that they have no lack of respect for Hemanta's opinions. There are several reasons for this as well. First, Hemanta never utters a single unreasoned word without thinking it through carefully. Second, he expresses his views with the utmost modesty. Listening to him converse with police officers, one feels as though a student is respectfully submitting his own opinions before his guru. Consequently, even when they come to ask for his help, the pride or self-importance of the police is never wounded. Hemanta does not mingle only with the police. His eagerness to cultivate close acquaintances with the thieves, pickpockets, ruffians, murderers, and hardened old offenders of this country is so great that at times I fear he may fall into terrible danger someday! Disguised as a Muslim, he frequently slips into the slums and coffee-houses of Mechhobazar and other notorious neighborhoods of the city, spending the hours there until late into the night. From time to time, he takes me along with him too. As a result, he has struck up friendships with many scoundrels at the mere sight of whom, lurking in street corners and alleys, respectable folk cannot help trembling with fear! Whenever I ask, "Hemanta, doesn't it disgust you to mix with those people?" Hemanta laughs and says, "Not in the least, brother Rabin. Doctors do not approach patients afflicted with loathsome diseases like tuberculosis and leprosy with hearts full of disgust. I too am like another kind of doctor, and I regard criminals as patients. In ordinary patients, it is the body that is diseased; whereas this disease attacks not the criminal's body, but his mind. Theft, fraud, murder, and robbery are nothing other than mental diseases. If one wishes to gather experience about those diseases, one cannot do without making friends with criminals."

This time, the very sight of the Padma had frightened her, and then the Padma pulled a stunt that terrified her even more.
One day she had gone for a walk along the riverbank with the children, and Naga had gone along as their guard. Here the Padma has been slowly devouring its bank, and in several places the riverbank drops off in a sheer cliff. Ignoring their mother's gentle warnings, Khoka and Kanika had run ahead and just stood on the edge of one such steep bank when, a short distance away, forty or fifty cubits of the bank came crashing down with a roar—and right here, letting out a scream, Kanika tumbled into the water. It looked almost as if she had jumped in on purpose. But would such a slip of a girl, who didn't even know how to swim, deliberately leap into the river like that? Startled and dazed by the sudden thunder of the bank collapsing so close by, perhaps she could not figure out which way to run, or else her foot slipped as she turned to flee and she fell in. However Kanika may have fallen, Naga jumped into the river on purpose and climbed back up carrying Kanika up the slope of the bank right where the earth had just caved in. It was as if the bank had collapsed right at hand just to make it easier for him to climb back up.
After returning home, once the pounding in her chest had subsided, Khoka's mother said to Naga, 'You climbed up through that spot, Naga—what if it had caved in again?' Naga said, 'How would it cave in? Only when the river eats away the earth underneath does the earth on top break off and fall, doesn't it?' Then Khoka's mother said, 'Well, my boy, God has truly saved us. What if the bank had collapsed a little further this way, right where they were standing!'
Naga said, 'That wouldn't have collapsed, Boro-Ma.'
Even though Naga had pulled her daughter out of the river only a short while ago, Khoka's mother grew a little annoyed and said, 'How did you know it wouldn't collapse?'
Naga said, 'The earth underneath hasn't been washed away yet, so why would it collapse? It will break, sure enough, in a few days it'll break, but it won't break right now. If it were going to break now, do you think I would have let our Khokababu and Khuki go near it? I wouldn't have let them.'
Kanika said, 'Why do you call me Khuki, Naga? Haven't I forbidden you to?'
'What should I call you, then?'
'Call me Didimoni.'
'Didimoni? Didimoni?' —Naga did not care for that title. He felt a little insulted. Servants call the daughters of the house Didimoni—the grown-up daughters. And he was not a house servant; he was a boatman. Besides, how could one call a girl of twelve or thirteen Didimoni? Somewhat annoyed, Naga walked away from there, making up his mind that no matter how angry anyone got, he would never call Kanika Didimoni.
Since that day, she never lets the children go anywhere without Naga. She would be happiest if she could stop them from going out anywhere at all, but why would they listen to that! So she treats Naga with great regard and reminds him over and over, 'Keep an eye on them, my boy, keep them safe.'
Naga cannot quite figure out Jadabbabu's wife, yet she is probably the only person in this house whom he fears. Her health is poor; after looking after the household for an hour or two, she lies down in bed, and after an hour or two she gets up again.

এবার পদ্মাকে দেখেই তাঁর ভয় হয়েছিল, তারপর একটা কাণ্ড করে পদ্মা তাঁকে আরও ভয় পাইয়ে দিয়েছে।
একদিন তিনি ছেলেমেয়েদের নিয়ে নদীর ধারে বেড়াতে গিয়েছেন, পাহারাদার হিসাবে সঙ্গে গিয়েছে নাগা। পদ্মা এখানে ধীরে ধীরে তীর গ্রাস করেছে, কয়েক জায়গায় নদীর তীর একেবারে খাড়া। মার মৃদু মৃদু বারণ না মেনে খোকা আর কণিকা ছুটে গিয়ে সবে এরকম একটা খাড়াইএর ওপর দাঁড়িয়েছে, খানিক তফাতে চল্লিশ পঞ্চাশ হাত ডাঙ্গা হুড়মুড় করে ভেঙ্গে পড়ল আর এখানে একটা চীৎকার করে কণিকা পড়ে গেল জলে। মনে হল যেন ইচ্ছে করেই লাফিয়ে পড়েছে। কিন্তু ইচ্ছে করে কি আর অতটুকু মেয়ে সাঁতার পর্যন্ত না জেনে এমন করে নদীতে ঝাঁপিয়ে পড়ে? হঠাৎ এত কাছে পাড় ভেঙ্গে পড়ার শব্দে চমকে উঠে দিশেহারা হয়ে হয়তো কোন্‌দিকে পালাবে ঠিক করতে পারে নি, নয়তো পালিয়ে আসতে গিয়ে পা পিছলে পড়ে গেছে। কণিকা যে ভাবেই পড়ে থাক, নাগা ইচ্ছে করেই নদীতে লাফিয়ে পড়ল এবং কণিকাকে নিয়ে ওপরে উঠে এল যেখানে এইমাত্র ডাঙ্গা ভেঙ্গে পড়েছে সেইখানে তীরের ঢাল বেয়ে। তার ওপরে উঠবার সুবিধার জন্যই যেন হাতের কাছে ডাঙ্গাটা ভেঙ্গে পড়েছিল।
বাড়ি ফিরে বুকের ধড়ফড়ানি কমবার পর খোকার মা নাগাকে বললেন, ‘তুই যে ওখান দিয়ে উঠে এলি নাগা, আবার যদি ভেঙ্গে পড়ত?’ নাগা বলল, ‘ক্যামনে ভাঙ্গবো? নদী তলার মাটি খাইবো তবে স্যান উপরের মাটি ভাইঙ্গা পড়ব?’ ﻿ তখন খোকার মা বললেন, ‘যাক বাবা, ভগবান খুব বাঁচিয়েছেন। আরেকটু এপাশে ওরা যেখানে দাঁড়িয়েছিল সেখানটা যদি ভেঙ্গে পড়ত!’
নাগা বলল, ‘তা পড়ত না, বড়-মা।’
খানিক আগে নাগা তার মেয়েকে নদী থেকে তুলেছে, তবু খোকার মা একটু বিরক্ত হয়ে বললেন, ‘তুই কি করে জানলি পড়ত না।’
নাগা বলল, ‘তলায় ক্ষয় যায় নাই, ভাইঙ্গা পড়ব ক্যান? ভাঙ্গবো, কয়দিন পরে নিয্যস ভাঙ্গবো, অখন ভাঙ্গবো না। ভাঙ্গবোই যদি, আমাগো খোকাবাবু আর খুকীরে যাইতে দিতাম ভাবছেন? দিতাম না।’
কণিকা বলল, ‘আমাকে তুই খুকী বলিস কেনরে নাগা? বারণ করে দিইনি তোকে?’

যাদববাবুর স্ত্রীকে নাগা ঠিক বুঝতে পারে না, কিন্তু এ বাড়িতে একমাত্র তাকেই বোধ হয় সে ভয় করে। শরীরটা তাঁর ভাল নয়, দু’এক ঘণ্টা সংসার দেখাশোনা করে তিনি বিছানায় শুয়ে পড়েন, দু’এক ঘণ্টা পরে আবার ওঠেন।

God: "Listen, Brahma.—I created a pair of sinless man and woman and placed them in the Garden of Eden. They lived in supreme peace, but you people could not bear it. One of your descendants went there, gave them evil counsel, and ruined Adam and Eve."

Brahma: "That was done by Satan, a rebellious attendant of your own."

God: "Satan is an utter scoundrel, but he did not ruin Adam and Eve; it was done by Vasuki, a great-grandson of yours."

Brahma: "Vasuki? Though he is a snake, he is a very good lad; he would never give evil counsel. Well, let us ask him directly. Narad, call Vasuki here."

Narad called out—"Vasuki, O Vasuki—"

Nearby, Vasuki was hanging with his tail wrapped around the branch of a deodar tree. Hearing the call, he slithered swiftly down. Prostrating himself in salute before Brahma, he said, "What is your command, Grandfather?"

Brahma: "Tell me, my boy, is it true that you went to the Garden of Eden and ruined Eve and Adam?"

Biting his forked tongue, Vasuki said, "Fie, fie, could I ever do such a thing? You have heard wrong, Lord. If you grant me assurance of safety, I shall relate what truly happened."

Brahma: "I grant you assurance of safety. Speak out and tell us the whole affair."

Many had come to sell all sorts of things—chira, muri, gur sandesh, boiled-down thick milk, doi made from thick milk, patkhir, fruits and roots, handloom cloth, and gamchhas—and many others had come simply for an outing and to watch the fun. A few beggars had come in the hope of alms.
With so many delicious things to eat all around, Naga had filled his belly by chewing just a handful of khesari dal. Filled his belly? Where—it didn't feel as if his belly was full at all! Even if it had been, by now it must have been digested.
Charan Majhi had brought a whole stalk of ripe bananas to sell. Only two days ago, Naga had seen those very bananas hanging on the tree behind Charan Majhi's house. At the time, it had seemed it would take several more days for the bananas to ripen. How had they ripened so quickly and taken on such a color? He must have forced them to ripen over the heat of a fire. The bananas wouldn't taste half as good.
Walking up to him, Naga said, 'Fine bananas, Charan Kaka. Won't you give me a couple of bananas?'
Charan Majhi said, 'Sure I will. Two bananas cost two pice; to you I'll give them for one pice.'
'Where would I get a pice?'
'If you can't get a pice, why do you have a craving to eat bananas? Go on, clear off!' By now the gangplank had been lowered from the steamer, and people were getting on and off. As soon as a passenger stepped ashore, Haru Majhi competed with the other boatmen, asking in an eager voice, 'Where will you go, Karta? Do you need a boat, Karta?' Everyone who had brought wares to sell was calling out the names of their goods. The whole place was buzzing with the clamor of people. Three times every day, arriving with a blast of its whistle, the steamer wakes up the sleepy jetty. The heart fills with joy and excitement. Today, too, within a few moments Naga forgot the burning ache of his hunger and Charan Majhi's insult.
Loading a huge pile of baggage onto a coolie's head, a gentleman stepped off the steamer. With him were his wife, a boy about Naga's age, a girl the same age as Naga's cousin Kali, and three younger children. Not a single other gentleman had disembarked with a family, so Naga easily figured out that this must be Jadabbabu's elder brother, Madhabbabu. With curious eyes, Naga began watching them. What a mountain of luggage they had with them, and what a grand display of clothes and finery! Who knew from what distant world outside Naga's own world these people came?
Most likely Jadabbabu had not yet managed to return from having the astrologer read his palm. Probably looking around this way and that in search of his brother, Madhabbabu came rushing over the instant his eyes fell on Charan Majhi's stalk of bananas. Almost breathlessly, he asked, 'How much will you take for it, hey?'
Charan Majhi hemmed and hawed and said, 'Give whatever you please. I couldn't take less than two rupees, Karta.' Had it been any local person, he would have walked away without a word, but Madhabbabu said, 'Two rupees my foot! Will you give it for one and a half rupees?'
'Yes, sir, take it.'
Hoisting the stalk of bananas onto the shoulders of the servant accompanying him, Madhabbabu looked all around with pride, as though by buying the bananas at double their price before anyone else could snap them up, he had pulled off a great feat of cleverness.

From Mombasa, the railway line ran all the way to Kimumu on the shore of Lake Victoria Nyanza—and a branch line off it was then under construction. The spot lay three hundred and fifty miles west of Mombasa, and seventy-two miles southwest of Nudsburg Station on the Uganda Railway. Here Shankar had arrived as the clerk and official storekeeper of the construction camp. He lived in a small tent, with many other tents pitched around his. Since no permanent buildings had been erected here yet, everyone lived in tents. The tents were arranged in a circle in an open clearing—and surrounding them on all sides stretched a vast, open plain overgrown with tall grass and dotted with occasional trees. Right beside the tents, at the outer edge of the clearing, stood a huge baobab tree. It was the famous tree of Africa that Shankar had seen so many times in pictures; now, seeing a real baobab tree with his own eyes, Shankar could hardly get his fill of looking at it.

A new land, and Shankar's fresh, young heart—in these lonely plains and wilds of Uganda, he felt as though he had found the fulfilment of his dreams. Every day, the moment his work was done, he would step out of his tent and wander off wherever his eyes led him—east, west, south, or north. In every direction grew tall grass—in some places as high as a man's head, and in others taller still.

One day, the European engineer in charge of the construction camp called Shankar over and said, "Listen, Ray, don't go wandering about like that out here. Don't take a single step outside without a gun. First of all, you can easily lose your way in this sea of grass; people have lost their way in places like this and died of thirst. Second, Uganda is lion country. Right here, the noise of our camp and the clanging of hammers may have driven the lions a little way off for now—but there is no trusting them. Be very careful. These parts are not safe at all."

One afternoon, while work was in full swing, a human cry of agony suddenly rang out from the tall grassland some distance from the tents. Everyone came running toward the spot to see what had happened. Shankar ran too—the grassland was searched thoroughly inch by inch, but there was nothing there.

What had that cry been, then?

The engineer Sahib arrived. A roll call of the coolies was taken, and it was found that one coolie was missing. Upon inquiry, it turned out that he had gone toward the tall grass a little while earlier on some errand, and no one had seen him come back.

As they searched around, the pugmarks of a lion were discovered on a patch of brownish sand just outside the tall grass. Taking his gun and a party of men with him, the Sahib followed the tracks a long way and found the mangled, blood-soaked body of the unfortunate coolie behind a large boulder.

They carried him back to the camp, but no sign of the lion was found. Startled by the shouting of the men, it had abandoned its prey and fled. Before dusk fell, the coolie died.

The very next day, the tall grass all around the tents was cut down and cleared for a good distance. For a few days, nothing was talked of in the camp except the lion. Then, after a month or so had gone by, the incident grew old and faded from everyone's mind. Work went on smoothly once again.

That day had been scorching hot. Shortly after dusk, however, a chill set in. In front of the coolies' tents, a large pile of brushwood and logs had been lit to make a bonfire. Everyone in the camp was sitting around it in a circle, chatting away. Shankar was there too, listening to their stories and reading the 'Kenya Morning News' by the light of the bonfire. The newspaper was five days old; yet out here in this uninhabited wilderness, it still brought some news at least of the outside world.

একদিন দুপুরের পরে কাজকর্ম্ম বেশ পুরোদমে চলচে, হঠাৎ তাঁবু থেকে কিছুদূরে লম্বা ঘাসের জমির মধ্যে মনুষ্যকণ্ঠের আর্ত্তনাদ শোনা গেল। সবাই সেদিকে ছুটে গেল ব্যাপার কি দেখতে। শঙ্করও ছুট্‌ল—ঘাসের জমি পাতি পাতি করে খোঁজা হল—কিছুই নেই সেখানে।

এঞ্জিনিয়ার সাহেব এলেন। কুলীদের নাম-ডাক হোল, দেখা গেল একজন কুলী অনুপস্থিত। অনুসন্ধানে জানা গেল সে একটু আগে ঘাসের বনের দিকে কি কাজে গিয়েছিল, তাকে ফিরে আসতে কেউ দেখে নি।

খোঁজাখুঁজি করতে করতে ঘাসের বনের বাইরে কটা বালির ওপরে সিংহের পায়ের দাগ পাওয়া গেল। সাহেব বন্দুক নিয়ে লোকজন সঙ্গে করে পায়ের দাগ দেখে অনেক দূর গিয়ে একটা বড় পাথরের আড়ালে হতভাগ্য কুলীর রক্তাক্ত দেহ বার করলেন।

তাকে তাঁবুতে ধরাধরি করে নিয়ে আসা হল। কিন্তু সিংহের কোনো চিহ্ন মিল্‌ল না। লোকজনের চীৎকারে সে শিকার ফেলে পালিয়েচে। সন্ধ্যার পূর্ব্বেই কুলীটা মারা গেল।

তাঁবুর চারিপাশের লম্বা ঘাস অনেকদূর পর্য্যন্ত কেটে সাফ্‌ করে দেওয়া হল পরদিনই। দিনকতক সিংহের কথা ছাড়া তাঁবুতে আর কোনো গল্পই নেই। তারপর মাসখানেক পরে ঘটনাটা পুরাণো হয়ে গেল, সে কথা সকলের মনে চাপা পড়ে গেল। কাজকর্ম্ম আবার বেশ চলল।

সেদিন দিনে খুব গরম। সন্ধ্যার একটু পরেই কিন্তু ঠাণ্ডা পড়ল। কুলীদের তাঁবুর সামনে অনেক কাঠকুটো জ্বালিয়ে আগুন করা হয়েচে। সেখানে তাঁবুর সবাই গোল হয়ে বসে গল্পগুজব করচে। শঙ্করও সেখানে আছে, সে ওদের গল্প শুনচে এবং অগ্নিকুণ্ডের আলোতে ‘কেনিয়া মর্ণিং নিউজ্‌’ পড়চে। খবরের কাগজখানা পাঁচদিনের পুরোণো। কিন্তু এ জনহীন প্রান্তরে তবু এখানেতে বাইরের দুনিয়ার যা কিছু একটা খবর পাওয়া যায়।

The bus passed Tongi, cleared the Gazipur traffic jam, and got onto the highway. The night was deepening. The conductor turned off the interior lights. A few passengers fell asleep.

"What work do you do, baba?" Khala asked.

This was the hardest question of all. Tanvir paused for a moment and said, "Actually... I'm not doing anything right now, Khala. I was trying for a job. It didn't work out today."

"Oh."

Khala said nothing more. No consolation, no advice. A little later, she opened the lid of the tiffin carrier. The aroma of dim bhuna drifted out from inside.

"Here, take some."

"No, no, Khala, that's for your daughter..."

"There's plenty for my daughter. Sitting alone on this bus all night on an empty stomach isn't right." She scooped some khichuri onto a steel plate. "Eat up. When your stomach is full, your head clears too."

Tanvir ate. Warm, home-cooked food after such a long time. As soon as he put the first bite into his mouth, something caught in his throat. He kept his head bowed and went on eating.

"Where is your home?" Khala asked.

"In Jamalpur too. Melandaha."

"Then we're travelers on the same road!" Khala was pleased. "Who do you have at home?"

"My mother and my younger sister."

"Does your mother know?"

"Know what?"

"That the job didn't happen."

Tanvir stayed silent. Then he said, "No. I haven't told her. Ma thinks I'm doing fine."

Khala looked out the window. In the darkness, the dim, flickering lights of a shop or two floated past now and then. "My son used to do the same thing, you know. He went to Dubai. For three years he didn't send anything, and didn't tell us what was going on either. I used to think he must be doing well. Later I found out he had no work and was sleeping in a single room with eight other men."

"Where is he now?"

"He came back. Now he's opened a small shop in the bazaar." She turned toward Tanvir. "Do you know what hurt the most? Not that he was suffering, but that he didn't tell me. Mothers can bear anything, baba—the only thing they can't bear is being shut out."

"এখন কোথায় সে?"

"ফিরে এসেছে। এখন বাজারে ছোট দোকান দিয়েছে।" তিনি তানভীরের দিকে ফিরলেন। "জানো, সবচেয়ে কষ্ট কী ছিল? ও যে কষ্টে আছে সেটা না, ও যে আমাকে বলেনি সেটা। মায়েরা সব সহ্য করতে পারে বাবা, শুধু বাদ পড়ে যাওয়াটা পারে না।"

It was the last day of school before the holidays. Right after school, there would be a meeting of the students' union, where the boys were going to put on a play together. Dashu was terribly eager to act in some role too. He even got various people to put in a good word for him, but we all dug our heels in and said, "That is not happening under any circumstances."

After all, the last time we put on a play, Dashu had played the general. That time, he had ruined the play completely. When the spy of Trichur quarreled with the general and challenged him to a duel, saying, "If thou hast courage, draw thy sword," Dashu was supposed to say, "Come then, to open battle!"—and draw his sword right away. But Dashu tugged at it so clumsily that not only could he not get the sword out, he also panicked and forgot to say his lines altogether. Seeing that, the spy roared again, "Draw thy sword!" Dashu is such an idiot that he immediately yelled back at him in a scolding voice, "Wait a second, can't you see the buckle is stuck?" Thankfully, I hurried over and undid the sword for him, or else the play would have come to a halt right then and there. Then toward the end, when the king asked, "What reward dost thou seek, speak, O General," Dashu was supposed to reply, "May my devotion ever remain at the royal feet," but instead of saying that, Dashu started reciting another line from further down, suddenly bit his tongue, blurted out, "Oh drat! I forgot," and looked over at me grinning. When I glared at him, he quickly pulled himself together and started the right line.

So this time, the moment his name came up, we declared firmly, "No, that is out of the question." Bishu said, "Dashu acting? That'll be the end of everything." Tyapa said, "We might as well call in Bhaju the gardener instead." Poor Dashu pleaded a great deal at first, then lost his temper, and finally drooped and sat sulking with a face like a thundercloud. Throughout the days our rehearsals went on, Dashu would come every day, sit quietly in a corner of the hall, and listen to our acting. A few days before the holidays, we noticed that Dashu had struck up a great friendship with little Gansha from the Fourth Class. Gansha is a young boy, but he can recite wonderfully—so he had been given the part of the angel. Every day Dashu brought him all sorts of treats to eat, gave him colored pencils and picture books, and promised to buy him a football on the day of the holidays. We couldn't figure out any reason for Dashu's sudden fondness for Gansha. All we saw was that Gansha, won over by the toys and treats, was fast becoming an ardent devotee of his "Dashuda."

On the day of the holidays, as we were getting ready for the play, the real story came to light. Before it had even struck half past two, brother Dashu was seen walking into the greenroom and starting to put on a costume. We asked, "What's this? What are you doing in here?" Dashu said, "Well, shouldn't I get into costume?" I said, "Why would you get into costume? You aren't acting in the play." Dashu said, "Well, you certainly keep track of things! Don't you know who's playing the angel today?" Hearing this, a sudden suspicion struck our minds, and I asked, "Why, what happened to Gansha?" Dashu replied, "You can go ask Gansha yourself what happened." Looking around then, we saw that everyone had arrived except Gansha. At once, Rampada, Bishu, and I dashed out in search of Gansha.

স্কুলের ছুটির দিন। স্কুলের পরেই ছাত্রসমিতির অধিবেশন হবে। তাতে ছেলেরা মিলে অভিনয় করবে। দাশুর ভারি ইচ্ছা ছিল সেও একটা কিছু অভিনয় করে। একে ওকে দিয়ে সে অনেক সুপারিশও করিয়েছিল, কিন্তু আমরা সবাই কোমর বেঁধে বললাম, ‘সে কিছুতেই হবে না।’

সেই তো গতবার যখন আমাদের অভিনয় হয়েছিল, তাতে দাশু সেনাপতি সেজেছিল। সেবারে সে অভিনয়টা একেবারে মাটি করে দিয়েছিল। যখন ত্রিচূড়ের গুপ্তচর সেনাপতির সঙ্গে ঝগড়া করে তাকে দ্বন্দ্বযুদ্ধে আহ্বান করে বলল, “সাহস থাকিলে তবে খোল তলোয়ার।” দাশুর তখন, “তবে আয়, সম্মুখ সমরে”—বলে তখনি তলোয়ার খুলবার কথা। কিন্তু দাশুটা অনাড়ির মতো টানাটানি করতে গিয়ে তলোয়ার তো খুলতে পারলই না, মাঝে থেকে ঘাবড়ে গিয়ে কথাগুলোও বলতে ভুলে গেল। তাই দেখে গুপ্তচর আবার, “খোলো তলোয়ার!” বলে হুংকার দিয়ে উঠল। দাশুটা এমনি বোকা, সে অমনি, “দাঁড়া, দেখছিস না বকলস আটকিয়ে গেছে” বলে চেঁচিয়ে তাকে এক ধমক দিয়ে উঠল। ভাগ্যিস আমি তাড়াতাড়ি তলোয়ারটা খুলে দিলাম, তা না হলে ঐখানেই অভিনয় বন্ধ হয়ে যেত। তার পর শেষের দিকে রাজা যখন জিজ্ঞাসা করলেন, “কিবা চাহ পুরস্কার, কহ সেনাপতি,” তখন দাশুর বলবার কথা ছিল, “নিত্যকাল থাকে যেন রাজপদে মতি”, কিন্তু দাশুটা তা না বলে, তার পরের আরেকটা লাইন আরম্ভ করেই, হঠাৎ জিভ কেটে, “ঐ যাঃ। ভুলে গেছিলাম” বলে আমার দিকে তাকিয়ে হাসতে লাগল। আমি কটমট করে তাকাতে, সে তাড়াতাড়ি নিজেকে সামলে নিয়ে ঠিক লাইনটা আরম্ভ করল।

তাই এবারে তার নাম হতেই আমরা জোর করে বলে উঠলাম, “না, সে কিছুতেই হবে না।” বিশু বলল, “দাশু একটিং করবে? তা হলেই চিত্তির।” ট্যাঁপা বলল, তার চাইতে ভজু মালিকে ডেকে আনলেই হয়।” দাশু বেচারা প্রথম খুব মিনতি করল, তার পর চটে উঠল, তার পর কেমন মুষড়ে গিয়ে মুখ হাঁড়ি করে বসে রইল। যে কদিন আমাদের তালিম চলছিল, দাশু রোজ এসে চুপটি করে হলের এক কোনায় বসে বসে আমাদের অভিনয় শুনত। ছুটির কয়েকদিন আগে থেকে দেখি, ফোর্থ ক্লাশের ছোটো গণ্‌শার সঙ্গে দাশুর ভারি ভাব হয়ে গেছে। গণ্‌শা ছেলেমানুষ, কিন্তু সে চমৎকার আবৃত্তি করতে পারে—তাই তাকে দেবদূতের পার্ট দেওয়া হয়েছে। দাশু রোজ তাকে নানারকম খাবার এনে খাওয়ায়, রঙিন পেনসিল আর ছবির বই এনে দেয়, আর বলে যে ছুটির দিন তাকে একটা ফুটবল কিনে দেবে। হঠাৎ গণ্‌শার উপর দাশুর এতখানি টান হবার কোনো কারণ আমরা বুঝতে পারলাম না। কেবল দেখতে পেলাম, গণ্‌শাটা খেলনা আর খাবার পেয়ে ভুলে ‘দাশুদা’র একজন পরম ভক্ত হয়ে উঠতে লাগল।

ছুটির দিনে আমরা যখন অভিনয়ের জন্য প্রস্তুত হচ্ছি, তখন আসল ব্যাপারটা বুঝতে পারা গেল। আড়াইটা বাজতে না বাজতে দেখা গেল, দাশুভায়া সাজঘরে ঢুকে পোশাক পরতে আরম্ভ করেছে। আমরা জিজ্ঞাসা করলাম, “কি রে? তুই এখানে কি করছিস?” দাশু বলল, “বাঃ, পোশাক পরব না?” আমি বললাম, “পোশাক পরবি কি রে? তুই তো আর একটিং করবি না।” দাশু বলল, “বাঃ, খুব তো খবর রাখ। আজকে দেবদূত সাজবে কে জান না?” শুনে হঠাৎ আমাদের মনে কেমন একটা খটকা লাগল, আমি বললাম, “কেন, গণ্‌শার কি হল?” দাশু বলল, “কি হয়েছে, তা গণ্‌শাকে জিজ্ঞেস করলেই পার।” তখন চেয়ে দেখি, সবাই এসেছে, কেবল গণ্‌শাই আসে নি। অমনি রামপদ, বিশু আর আমি, ছুটে বেরাম গণ্‌শার খোঁজে।

Then two days passed. Gradually they entered deeper and deeper into the jungle. Nowhere was the path level—only uphill and downhill, with patches of coarse, tall tussock grass every now and then; water was almost unobtainable, and even when an occasional stream or two was seen, Alvarez would not let him so much as touch their water. Crystal-clear water came cascading down the stream, cool and tempting—for a thirsty man it was terribly hard to resist that temptation—yet Alvarez would make him drink cold tea instead of water rather than let him drink the water. Thirst for water is not quenched by cold tea, and the torment of thirst seemed to Shankar the worst suffering of all. At one place, the thicket of tussock grass was terribly dense. On top of that, the fog surrounding them on all sides that day was very thick. Suddenly, as the morning wore on, the lower fog cleared away—looking ahead, it seemed to Shankar that a huge ascent stood blocking their path; how high it was could not be told, for its upper part was completely shrouded in dense fog or cloud. Alvarez said, "The main range of the Richtersveld."

Shankar asked, "Is it necessary to cross this?"

Alvarez said, "It is necessary because that time Jim and I had come to the foot of this mountain range from the south, without crossing the main range. The river on whose bank the yellow diamond was found flows from east to west. This time we are going from north to south, so unless we cross the mountain to the other side, how can we locate that river?"

Shankar said, "Seeing how foggy it is today, why don't we wait a little? Let the day advance a bit more."

Pitching the tent, they finished their meal. Even as the day wore on, the fog did not clear much. Shankar fell asleep inside the tent. When he woke up, the daylight was gone. Rubbing his eyes as he came out of the tent, he saw Alvarez sitting with a worried face, the map spread open before him. Seeing Shankar, he said, "Shankar, we still have a lot of suffering ahead of us. Look in front of you."

At Alvarez's words, Shankar looked straight ahead and a solemn sight met his eyes. The fog had cleared at some point, and before him the main tier of the vast Richtersveld mountains rose step by step until it seemed to touch the very sky. The waist of the mountain was wrapped in dense, lightning-charged masses of cloud, while the highest peaks stood rearing their heads far up into the blue void in the ruddy light of the setting sun, like golden temples of the gods.

Yet the section of the mountain directly in front of them was completely unscalable—nothing but sheer, towering crags, without a single gentle slope anywhere. Alvarez said, "It isn't possible to climb the mountain from here, Shankar. You can surely see that for yourself. Come, let us follow the foot of the mountains westward. Wherever we find a lower, gentler slope, we shall have to cross the mountain there. But to find such a spot along this hundred-and-fifty-mile-long mountain range will take more than a month, I can see."

However, after going westward for five or six days, they found a spot where the mountainside sloped quite gently, and by which the mountain could be climbed.

The next day, they began climbing the mountain very early in the morning. By Shankar's watch it was then half past six. Before it was even half past eight, Shankar could walk no further. Where they were climbing, the steep incline of the mountain rose six thousand feet within four miles—so even if the slope was gradual, one can easily imagine how terribly exhausting the climb was. Moreover, the higher they climbed, the denser the forest grew, with thick darkness all around; the day had advanced and the sun was up, yet sunlight did not penetrate into the jungle—not even the sky could be seen, let alone the light of the sun.

Her days pass getting into bed and getting up again, yet she manages every single affair of the household. She has a remarkable gift for getting work done by people. Naga, too, runs many errands for her. A wooden chest has to be moved from this room to that room, a few logs of firewood have to be split quickly from a huge mango-tree trunk, the unruly cow has snapped its rope and run off and needs to be caught and tied up again—who else would do all these things if not Naga? And she asks him to do these chores in such a way that the question never even crosses Naga's mind: who used to do all this work when he wasn't here?
Among the boatmen, Naga and Paresh stay at Jadabbabu's house, Jitu stays on the boat, and Nakul stays at his own house in this village. Naga has known Nakul for a long time; if one racks one's brains hard enough, some sort of distant kinship can supposedly be traced between the two of them. Yet it is such a tangled relationship that there is no way for Naga to figure out what to call him. In polite society, calling him 'Nakulbabu' would have served well enough, but neither of them is a gentleman; so Naga simply calls him Mamu, and Nakul calls him Bhaigna.
At all hours, Naga drops by Nakul's house, and however happy he may be at Jadabbabu's house, here he feels an extra measure of ease on top of that happiness. It feels as though this is his own world—a poor boatman's home. Just as there are Haru Majhi, his wife, and Kali in the house at Atkhawar, so too here there are Nakul Majhi, his wife, and Rupa. Only the neglect of the house in Atkhawar is missing.
Pleased to see him, Nakul says, 'Come in, Bhaigna, sit down. What's the news?' Even if they have stepped off the boat together an hour ago, Nakul still asks for the news, and it does not sound out of place at all. Meeting on the boat and meeting at home are two very different things. Naga does not have to give any news; Nakul himself rattles off all the joys and sorrows of his own life and of everyone in the world from start to finish. Nakul dearly loves to talk.
Nakul is blind in one eye. Nakul had a son named Panchu, older than Naga; about two years ago, after blinding his father in that eye, he ran away from home. Since then, he has never returned to the village nor sent any word. People say he is now working in the police force in the district town, but Nakul says no, he is not alive. If someone sees Panchu with his own eyes in the district town and hurries back to give Nakul the news, Nakul flies into a terrible rage. He is not alive, not alive—not once, but a hundred times over, Panchu is not alive! Whoever the man saw was not Panchu!
On the other hand, if someone agrees with him and says that Panchu is truly dead, he does not look particularly pleased at that either. He just sits there with a heavy, gloomy face.
Seeing Naga, Nakul's wife says, 'I've made fresh larus, Bhaigna—who knows how they've turned out!'
Naga says, 'How can I tell without tasting them, Mami?'
Rupa asks, 'Have you brought my puppy?'
'I'll bring one as soon as the litter is born.'
'All right, all right, don't bring one then! I have my Ram and Lakshman.'
Ram and Lakshman are two tame mongooses. Rupa loves them dearly. Now she needs a puppy to shower her love on as well.

There is no one in the room, yet who does he talk with?" —"What business is that of yours, Keshto?" —"None of my business, it is true, but isn't it strange? Do you know what is stranger still? When the gentleman locks the door of his room with a key and goes out of the house, someone still walks about inside his room with heavy footsteps on the floor! Babu, these are not good matters; I feel terribly afraid!" —"What nonsense are you babbling!" —"It is not nonsense, Babu; I have heard it with my own ears! Not only inside the room, Babu—on some days I hear footsteps outside as well. Do you know what happened one day? I was sitting in front of my room in the corner of the courtyard, preparing tobacco. Dusk had already passed, and the other side of the courtyard was dark. Because there was no one in the house, I had bolted the front door. Suddenly I heard someone coming down the stairs! There was no one in the house, yet someone was coming down the stairs! I asked—'Who goes there?' I got no reply, but in the dark part of the courtyard, I heard someone's footsteps! Right after that, with a thud, the bolt of the front door slid open, and the door opened and closed again! What kind of business is this, Babu!" —"Keshto, Bhairabbabu was surely in the house without your knowledge, and it was he who went out!" —"Then why didn't he answer?" —"That is his pleasure." "It is not nonsense, Babu; I have heard it with my own ears." —"Then let me tell you one more thing, listen. Bhairabbabu's food comes every day from the hotel, as you know, don't you? All this time, food used to come twice a day for one person only, but I heard from the mouth of the hotel servant that nowadays, every night, food comes for two people! Bhairabbabu is alone, so why does food for two go to his room at night? Who eats that food?" —"Bhairabbabu himself. Perhaps he has a big appetite, and food for one is not enough." —"But does his appetite increase only at night? In the morning, food for two doesn't come! And earlier he didn't have such a ravenous appetite, did he? Why did his nighttime appetite suddenly increase, either? Ever since I have been hearing these strange footsteps, his appetite has increased from that very time!" —"Keshto, you are an utter rubbish!" —"You do not believe me; what more can I say!"—Saying this, Keshto went away. Astonished, Dilip began to think—when Bhairab is not in his room, who could be walking about in there? Has Bhairab hidden some other person inside his room? Who is he? And why would he remain in hiding? What is this business about food for two that Keshto mentioned today? Even if we suppose that someone is hiding in Bhairab's room and that is why food for two comes, why doesn't food for two come every morning as well? Does he fast in the morning?... All of this is as baffling as a riddle! I laughed Keshto off with a joke, it is true, but it has set me thinking too!

There is one great virtue in being brought up in neglect: it makes the body utterly immune to age and death. Illness simply refuses to take hold; the main highways to death are completely closed off. So disease merely mocked her and went its way; nothing came of it at all. Yet one thing became very clear: giving shelter to the most insignificant person in the world is the hardest thing of all. The greater her need for shelter, the more formidable the obstacles in its way.

Once Bindu's fear of me broke, another obsession took hold of her. She began to love me so fiercely that it frightened me. I had never seen such a passion of love anywhere in real life. I had read of it in books, to be sure, and even that was between men and women. For a very long time there had been no occasion for me to remember that I had beauty—and now, after all these years, this plain-looking girl became infatuated with that beauty of mine. Her eyes could never get their fill of looking at my face. She would say, "Didi, no one else has ever truly seen this face of yours except me." On days when I tied up my own hair myself, she would be deeply hurt. She loved running both her hands through the thick mass of my hair. Except when going out to an invitation somewhere, I had no need to dress up. Yet Bindu would pester me relentlessly and make me put on some little adornment or other every single day. The girl became utterly mad about me.

In your inner quarters there is not a single patch of bare earth anywhere. Against the northern wall, beside the drain, a gab tree had somehow sprouted on its own. Whenever I saw the new leaves of that gab tree turn a bright, fiery red, I knew that spring had truly arrived upon the earth. And the day the heart of that neglected girl blossomed with such colour through and through amidst my daily household routine, I realised that there is a spring breeze in the world of the heart as well—it blows in from some heaven, not from the corner of the lane.

The unbearable intensity of Bindu's devotion made me restless. At times I would get angry with her, I admit, yet through this love of hers I saw a true self of mine that I had never seen before in my life. That was my free self.

Meanwhile, the fact that I was lavishing so much love and care on a girl like Bindu struck all of you as terribly excessive. There was no end to the fussing and grumbling over it. The day an armlet was stolen from my room, you felt no shame in hinting that Bindu had some hand in the theft. When people's houses began being searched during the Swadeshi disturbances, you readily suspected that Bindu was a female spy in the pay of the police. There was no other proof of it—only the proof that she was Bindu.

The maidservants of your house objected to doing any work for her—and if I ordered any of them to do something for her, the girl herself would stiffen up with embarrassment. For all these reasons, my expenses on her account went up. I hired a separate maidservant specifically for my room. None of you liked that. Seeing the clothes I gave Bindu to wear made you so angry that you stopped my allowance for pocket money. Starting the very next day, I began wearing coarse, unbleached mill-made dhotis that cost five sikas a pair. And when Moti's mother came to clear away my used dinner plate, I forbade her to touch it. I went down to the tap in the courtyard myself, fed my leftover rice to the calf, and scrubbed my own dishes. One day, catching sight of that scene by chance, you were none too pleased. That it does not matter whether I am pleased, whereas it is imperative that all of you be pleased—this piece of good sense has not entered my head even to this day.

Input: Lifting his face at the sound of footsteps, he saw that Pratap had made his appearance in the room. Sitting down beside him, Pratap said, "Dilip, you are a complete bookworm! Day and night, nothing but studying and studying and studying! Meanwhile, the day after tomorrow is our 'Elliott Shield' match—have you forgotten about that?" —"Am I on the team?" —"Of course! The 'selection' took place today itself. You will play on the right line. Go to the field tomorrow and get some 'practice'." —"I shall go. But take your leave today, please, and let me study. There isn't any other news, is there?" —"There is one piece of news. Do you remember I told you the other day about the quarrel between Nandalal and Bhairab? Yesterday, Nandalal fell into terrible danger." —"What danger?" —"Yesterday evening, Nandalal was returning home along the road across the field, when suddenly someone attacked him!" —"Who attacked him?" —"That is what is so difficult to say! According to Nandalal, it was not a human being! Of course, the deep wounds on his throat made by fingernails could not possibly be caused by human nails either!" —"Then what? Did a ghost jump onto Nandalal's shoulders?" —"Pshaw! Who says that? It is no ghost or anything of the sort! It is my belief that a large ape, like an orangutan or a chimpanzee, has escaped from the zoo or from some showman's troupe. This is its handiwork!... Every day at that exact time, Nandalal returns home along that road. Right over the road there, a bushy banyan tree leans down, creating darkness. Just as Nandalal was passing underneath it, that unknown creature suddenly pounced upon his neck—Nandalal believes it descended onto his shoulders right from the branch of that tree. The moment it landed on his back, the creature gripped his throat with both hands with all its might! To Nandalal, it felt as if someone had clamped bands of steel around his throat! He could not see anything at all; only those two dreadful hands kept pressing harder and harder around his throat. Fearing for his life, he let out an ear-splitting scream, and hearing his cry, two men came running from somewhere! The moment it saw them, that creature leapt over a wall with the swiftness of a leopard and vanished! Nandalal only felt the death-grip of a pair of iron hands and a huge phantom shadow—apart from this, he knows nothing else." Dilip said, "Perhaps he fell into the hands of some murderous thug." "Suddenly pounced upon his shoulders." —"It could be. But Nandalal says it was not so. According to him, the two hands of the one who attacked him and throttled his neck were as icy cold as frost!—the touch of no living creature is ever that cold! Surely this is a delusion of his mind, but the poor fellow is completely shaken with fear... Oh, by the way! Given how fondly your friend Bhairabchandra regards Nandalal, if he hears this news he will probably start dancing with joy! I know him very well; he never forgives any enemy. Therefore, be careful—never provoke him!" Dilip said, "He is neither my friend nor my enemy. I have only a slight acquaintance with him; what need do I have to provoke him?"
