The spot where Tirumal had been lying was now examined closely. Clear across the ground ran the unmistakable drag-marks of some heavy object being pulled away. It did not take anyone long to understand what had happened. Near the baobab tree, a torn shred of the sleeve of Tirumal's shirt was found. Gun in hand, the engineer Sahib led the way in front, and Shankar walked beside him. The coolies followed closely behind them. In the dead of night, they searched a wide area across the plain far from the tents, but no trace of Tirumal's body was found. Then once again the roar of the lion rang out—further away this time, sounding like the blood-curdling shriek of some mysterious demoness presiding over this desolate wilderness.

The Masai coolie said, "The lion is carrying the body away. We are going to suffer badly on account of this beast. It won't stop until it has struck down many more men. Everyone be on your guard! Once a lion starts eating human flesh, it becomes terribly cunning."

It was nearly three o'clock in the morning when everyone returned to the tents. The whole plain was bathed in bright, clear moonlight. In this part of Africa, birds were rarely seen during the daytime, but at night the call of a certain nocturnal bird could be heard—a melody of unearthly sweetness. Just at that moment, from the top of some distant tree, that bird called out, filling the heart in an instant with a wistful melancholy. Shankar did not go to sleep. Everyone else went inside their tents to lie down, for none of them had been spared exhausting labour that night. In front of the tents, brushwood and logs were piled high to make a huge bonfire. Naturally, Shankar did not dare sit outside alone—there was no sense in such reckless bravado. Instead, lying inside his own tent, he gazed out through the window opening across the vast, moonlit expanse of the unknown plain.

A strange feeling came over his mind. Perhaps it was for this very end that the decree of fate had drawn Tirumal all the way to Africa. And for what purpose had his own destiny brought him here—who knew the answer to that?

Africa was extraordinarily beautiful to behold—yet Africa was terrifying! What if it looked just like the open meadows of Bengal dotted with babla groves—Africa was teeming with unseen death! Everywhere, at every step, cruel traps of sudden death lay waiting in ambush... What would happen in the very next moment, no one could tell in this moment.

Africa had claimed its first sacrifice—the young Hindu youth Tirumal. It demanded blood sacrifices.

Tirumal was gone, and from the very next day the situation in the camp became such that it was well-nigh impossible to stay there on account of the lion's depredations. A man-eating lion is a most terrifying beast—every bit as bold as it is cunning. Let alone after dusk, even in broad daylight no one could venture far alone. Before evening fell, huge bonfires were lit at various spots across the camp clearing. Huddling close to the fires, the coolies chatted, cooked their meals, and ate right there. Rifle in hand, the engineer Sahib patrolled around the tents three or four times every night and fired blank warning shots into the air—and yet, despite all these precautions, the lion carried off another coolie at nightfall just two days after killing Tirumal. The day after that, a Somali coolie went out at midday to break stones at a rocky mound within three hundred yards of the tents—and by evening he had not returned.

That very night, past ten o'clock, Shankar was walking back from the engineer Sahib's tent; hardly anyone was out of doors, as everyone had retired early to their own quarters, leaving only one or two dying bonfires smouldering here and there. In the distance, jackals were calling—and whenever Shankar heard the call of jackals, he felt as if he were back in his own country village in Bengal; closing his eyes, he would try to picture his village, try to picture that bilati amra hog-plum tree at the corner of their house—and tonight, too, he halted abruptly in his tracks and quickly shut his eyes.

সেই রাত্রেই, রাত দশটার পরে—শঙ্কর এঞ্জিনিয়ার সাহেবের তাঁবু থেকে ফিরচে, লোকজন কেউ বড় একটা বাইরে নেই, সকাল সকাল যে যার ঘরে শুয়ে পড়েচে, কেবল এখানে ওখানে দু একটা নির্ব্বাপিত প্রায় অগ্নিকুণ্ড। দূরে শেয়াল ডাক্‌চে—শেয়ালের ডাক শুনলেই শঙ্করের মনে হয় সে বাংলাদেশের পাড়াগাঁয়ে আছে—চোখ বুঁজে সে নিজের গ্রামটা ভাববার চেষ্টা করে, তাদের ঘরের কোণের সেই বিলিতি আমড়া গাছটা ভাববার চেষ্টা করে—আজও সে একবার থম্‌কে দাঁড়িয়ে তাড়াতাড়ি চোখ বুঁজলে।

At eleven fifty-five at night, the order came through on the app. Sajib had parked his bike at the Lalbagh intersection and was having tea. Earnings hadn't been good today; just one more order and he could head home.

Order: kacchi biryani, two packets. Customer's name: Motaleb Hossain. Address: 47/A, an old three-story house in an inner lane of Lalbagh. Written in the remarks below: "Do not knock on the door. Leave it in front of the door and go."

Sajib frowned. Nearly midnight, kacchi, two packets, and knocking was forbidden. Still, an order was an order.

The lane was so narrow that a bike couldn't fit. He parked the bike and walked in. On both sides stood old houses pressed shoulder to shoulder, clothes hung out to dry on their verandas. Somewhere, a cat yowled. The front gate of 47/A was wide open, and there was no light on the stairs inside. Sajib turned on his phone's flashlight.

Climbing up to the third floor, he froze. A heavy padlock hung on the door of the flat, and dust had gathered thick on the lock. Advertising flyers piled at the bottom of the door had turned yellow. You didn't need to be a detective to tell no one had lived here for a long time.

He called the customer through the app. It rang. And right at that moment, from the other side of the padlocked door, an old-fashioned ringtone began to play. That monotonous tune from an old button phone.

Something cold trickled down Sajib's spine. He ended the call, and the ringtone stopped too.

Input: Standing silently right there and pondering Abani's words in astonishment, Dilip kept hearing the muffled, choked groans of Bhairab! Right after that came Abani's frantic voice from upstairs—"Dilip, Dilip! Quick, come upstairs quickly! Bhairabbabu is at death's door!" In three or four bounds, Dilip cleared the stairs to the upper floor and stood before Bhairab's room. Through the open door, in the bright glare of the electric light, the interior of the room rose clearly before his eyes. Seeing the room, his eyes truly froze in amazement! Never in his life had he seen such a sight! Dilip had seen countless pictures in many books of the strange figures that scholars had unearthed from ancient tombs and temples while excavating the soil of ancient Egypt. Standing in front of the walls of the room were many such large and small wooden figures! The figures had bodies like humans, but some had heads like bulls, some had heads like storks, and others had heads like cats or owls! These were the gods and goddesses of ancient Egypt! Hanging from the rafters of the room was the carcass of a crocodile—Dilip knew that the crocodile, too, was regarded as a deity by the ancient Egyptians. In the middle of the room, upon a large table, rested an ancient Egyptian 'coffin' or 'mummy'-case with its lid open. And standing right inside it was an Egyptian 'mummy', or preserved human corpse! Dilip had seen a 'mummy' at the Calcutta Museum. That was the corpse of an Egyptian woman from several thousand years ago! Having come into Calcutta's damp climate, the body of that corpse had quickly deteriorated, so although it used to be kept standing earlier, now it had to be laid down. That 'mummy' in the museum was a woman's corpse, and various parts of her body had crumbled away; but the preserved body of an ancient human that he saw before his eyes today was that of a man, and it looked so intact and lifelike that it was impossible even to imagine it as a corpse! Although by the grace of thousands of years the colour of its skin had turned unnaturally black, and its entire body had been reduced to mere skin and bone, still, looking at its shrivelled, gruesome face filled the mind with an unearthly dread. Right at the feet of the 'mummy', stretched out full-length upon the floor of the room, lay the body of Bhairabchandra, and in his hand was a half-open, long sheet of paper rolled up like a horoscope scroll. Dilip understood that it was an ancient Egyptian manuscript made of 'papyrus' reed! Abani cried out in a distressed voice, "Bhairabbabu will probably not survive!" Dilip was a student of the Medical College, not a man to lose his nerve so easily. He stepped forward slowly, sat down beside Bhairab, examined his body, and said, "Do not fear, Abani; Bhairabbabu has merely fainted. Come forward and take hold of his feet; I am holding the head end. Now come, we must lay him down on that sofa. Bring the water pitcher and splash some water on Bhairabbabu's face and chest... But why did he fall into such a state?"

Input: Who screams?—Why does he scream? After Pratap drank his tea and left, Dilip was trying to concentrate properly on his studies again, when suddenly rain came pouring down in a fierce torrent. The emptiness of that lonely and dark field in Tollygunge filled with the roar of rain and storm. Dilip got up, shut the windows, and was about to close the door of the room as well, when Abani came hurrying down from upstairs and said anxiously, "Why are you shutting the door, my friend? Where will I go in this rain?" Dilip said, "Who is asking you to go? Come inside the room. Lie back in the easy-chair and listen quietly to the song of the rain, while I do my studying by myself." Entering the room and sitting down in the easy-chair, Abani said, "Put aside your studies in this rainy weather! Come, let us have a chat for a while." Reluctantly closing his book, Dilip said, "Once you incarnations of Shani made your appearance today, I knew right from the start that my studying would not happen! Very well, let your wish be fulfilled!" Outside, the rain kept pouring, and inside, the two friends' chatting went on. Even after an hour, there was no sign of either the rain outside or the chatting inside coming to a stop. When the clock in the room struck eleven with a 'tung-tung', it dawned upon Abani that he had to return home today. 'He was cursing and abusing me.'
In the dim light of the lantern, Naga's face could not be seen clearly; had it been daylight, one look at his face would have frightened Madhabbabu. His mood had already been soured by one thing after another, and now on top of that came this humiliation. To be made to stand like a prisoner in front of ten people while someone sat in judgment over him—that was something Naga could never endure, no matter who the judge might be. Once, in Atkhawar, he had been put on trial before ten respectable gentlemen for administering a beating just like this, and the moment the president began questioning him in a harsh tone, Naga had said, 'If you glare at me when you ask questions, Karta, I won't answer. Am I guilty already? Only when everyone says I'm guilty will I be guilty.' Hearing that, the president and several of the other gentlemen had flown into a towering rage! They looked ready to strike Naga any second, yet one look at his build kept them from daring to touch him. In the end, without a proper trial, he was declared guilty and handed a punishment: the man he had beaten was to give him seven slaps across the cheek and seven blows on the back—right in front of everyone. The gentlemen all approved, but the boatmen objected. What sort of justice was this? If his guilt was proved, let him be fined—why slaps and punches? Because Naga himself accepted the punishment, however, no one could say anything more. The man he had beaten came forward timidly and gave him seven slaps on the cheek and seven blows on the back—more gently than a mother pats her child to put him to sleep or thumps him in playful affection.
Since that day, a deep disdain for gentlemen had remained awake in Naga's heart. Whenever anyone summoned him to bully and browbeat him, his whole body burned with rage. Kanika pleaded, 'Don't drive him away, Baba! He will never beat anyone again.'
Annoyed, Madhabbabu said, 'You keep quiet.'

Just then the crow looked at me and asked, 'Have you got the advertisement? The handbill?'

I said, 'Why, no—an advertisement for what?' No sooner had I spoken than the crow pulled a printed sheet from a bundle of papers and handed it to me. Reading it, I saw written there—

Salutations unto Sri Sri Bhushandikagaya

Sri Kakkeshwar Kuchkuche

No. 41 Gechobazar, Kageyapati

We carry out all kinds of calculations—accounted and unaccounted, retail and wholesale—by scientific processes. Price: 1 rupee, 6 annas, 0 pai per inch. Upon your sending necessary particulars such as your shoe size, complexion, whether your ears ache, whether you are alive or dead, etc., we dispatch a catalogue by return post.

Beware! Beware!! Beware!!!

We are traditional high-born Darikulin of the ancient Bayas lineage—that is to say, ravens. Nowadays, out of greed for money, various classes of house crows, jackdaws, jungle crows, and other such crows are also running all sorts of businesses. Beware! Do not be deceived by the flashiness of their advertisements.

I said, 'I couldn't quite understand all of it properly.'

Turning solemn, the crow said, 'Yes, it is very deep; not everyone can grasp it. Once a customer came to me who had a bald head—'

The moment it said these words, the old man charged at it in a furious rage, shouting, 'Look here! If you say "bald head" one more time, I'll whack you with my hukka and smash your slate to pieces!'

Taken aback for a moment, the crow thought a bit and then said, 'Not a bald head, a dented head—a head that has got dimpled from being poked and pressed.'

Even that didn't calm the old man down; he sat there grumbling to himself. Seeing this, the crow asked, 'Don't you want to see the calculation?'

Softening a little, the old man said, 'Is it done? Let's see it, then.'

Saying 'Here, look!', the crow immediately dropped its slate with a sharp clack right onto the old man's bald pate. The old man clapped both hands to his head, plopped down on the ground at once, and, pouting his lips like a little child, began kicking his arms and legs and bawling, 'Oh Ma, oh Pisi, oh Shibuda!'

Staring in surprise for a moment, the crow said, 'Did that hurt? Shat-shat—sixty-sixty, may you live long!'

The old man immediately stopped crying and called out, 'Sixty-one, sixty-two, sixty-four—'

The crow called back, 'Sixty-five.'

Seeing that another round of auction-bidding was about to start, I hurriedly spoke up, 'Well, why haven't you looked at the calculation yet?'

Coming to Jadabbabu's house, Naga's whole world seemed to change. He no longer had to worry about his stomach now. For so long it had been as if he were a prisoner locked in the jailhouse of the single thought, 'What will I eat, what will I eat?'—and now, set free at last, he had the chance to look around at the world. From the people to the houses, the fields and ghats, and the river itself, everything seemed to have shed its old skin and become new to him. New, yet not unfamiliar. After all, he had not come to some fairy-tale land across seven seas and thirteen rivers; he had visited Karamtala before. Many of the people here were known to him. It was the change brought about within him by a little simple affection, a full stomach, and respect for his labor that had made the outside world look new to him as well. The starving Naga who had lived amid everyone's neglect and cruelty in Atkhawar seemed not to be the same Naga as Jadabbabu's new boatman.
Naga had arrived with nothing but the cloth on his back—Jadabbabu arranged for all his necessary things, clothes and bedding alike. Not all the items were brand-new, to be sure, and the chintz shirt was a little tight on his frame, yet not a single thing was torn or cast-off rubbish. Jadabbabu even gave him a mattress and a pillow to sleep on; for an hour or so after lying down, he felt wonderfully comfortable on it, but after that he would roll up the mattress and spread out a rush mat to sleep. When a man is used to sleeping on a hard rush mat, how can sleep come on a soft mattress! Besides, a mattress bed seemed to feel much too warm.
Everyone in the household liked Naga well enough, except Madhabbabu. Right from the start, the gentleman was somewhat ill-disposed toward Naga. Why, Naga did not know. To tell the truth, he was annoyed with all the servants of the house. Most likely he did not care for the ways of the hired folk of this country. They did not seem to show enough deference to their masters; instead of standing with their heads bowed in fear, they spoke in an easy, natural manner, and instead of coming running breathlessly the instant they were called, they walked up unhurriedly. Ganesh, an old servant of many years, forgot altogether that he was a servant of the house and even came forward to have his say in family matters. Once upon a time Madhabbabu himself had been used to such easy behavior from servants, and if anyone ever acted overly obsequious and nervous, he would rather grow suspicious that the fellow was up to no good; but living in Calcutta for so many years had soured his mind. There, the master pays wages, the servant does the work, and no other bond exists between them—save the relationship of one side constantly snapping in irritation and the other side silently cursing the master in his heart while playing the meek worm on the outside for a few days before running off one fine morning. Madhabbabu's wife, however, had grown very fond of Naga. She had been born in Calcutta; in the early days after her marriage she had visited her in-laws' home two or three times, and never again since. For twenty years, the only rivers she had seen were the Ganga in Calcutta and two or three calm, narrow rivers crossed on bridges while riding in a train. That one could not see from one bank to the other of the river here, that such huge waves rose upon it, and that at this time of year storms blew up and sank boats—all these things she had nearly forgotten.

বাড়ির সকলেই নাগাকে একরকম পছন্দ করে, মাধববাবু ছাড়া। প্রথম থেকেই নাগার ওপর ভদ্রলোক একটু বিরূপ। কেন, তা নাগা জানে না। সত্য কথা বলতে কি, বাড়ির সমস্ত চাকরবাকরের ওপরেই তিনি চটা। খুব সম্ভব এদেশের মাইনে-করা মানুষগুলির চালচলন তাঁর পছন্দ হয় না। মনিবদের তারা যেন যথেষ্ট পরিমাণে সম্মান দেখায় না, ভয়ে ঘাড় নীচু করে থাকার বদলে সহজভাবে কথা কয়, ডাক দেওয়ামাত্র হন্তদন্ত হয়ে ছুটে আসার বদলে ধীরে সুস্থে কাছে আসে। অনেকদিনের পুরোনো চাকর গণেশ তো একেবারে ভুলেই থাকে যে সে এবাড়ির চাকর, ঘরোয়া ব্যাপারে পর্যন্ত সে কথা বলতে আসে। এককালে চাকরবাকরের এইরকম সহজ ব্যবহারেই তিনি অভ্যস্ত ছিলেন, অতিরিক্ত বিনয়ে কেউ সর্বদা তটস্থ হয়ে থাকলেই বরং তার সম্বন্ধে সন্দিগ্ধ হয়ে উঠতেন, সে ব্যাটার মতলব ভাল নয়, কিন্তু বহুদিন কলকাতায় থেকে মনটা তাঁর বিগড়ে গেছে। সেখানে মনিব মাইনে দেয়, চাকর কাজ করে, আর কোন সম্পর্কই তাদের মধ্যে থাকে না, এক পক্ষের চটাচটি আর অন্য পক্ষের মনে মনে মনিবের মুণ্ডপাত করতে করতে বাইরে কিছুদিন কেঁচো সেজে থেকে একদিন পালিয়ে যাওয়ার সম্পর্ক ছাড়া। মাধববাবুর স্ত্রী কিন্তু নাগাকে খুব পছন্দ করে ফেলেছেন। তিনি জন্মেছেন কলকাতায়, বিয়ের পর প্রথম প্রথম দু’চারবার শ্বশুরবাড়ি এসেছিলেন, তারপর আর আসেন নি। বিশ বছর ধরে নদীর মধ্যে তিনি শুধু দেখেছেন কলকাতার গঙ্গা আর রেলগাড়িতে চেপে পুলের ওপর দিয়ে যাবার সময় দু’চারটে শান্ত ও সঙ্কীর্ণ নদী। এখানকার নদীর যে এপার ওপার দেখা যায় না; এমন বড় বড় ঢেউ ওঠে নদীতে, আর বছরের এ সময়টা ঝড় উঠে নৌকা ডুবিয়ে দেয়, এসব একরকম ভুলেই গিয়েছিলেন।

When Nila went to the office that day, she couldn't focus on her work. At noon, she asked the bhabi on the ground floor, "Do you know why the girl who lived here before left?"

The bhabi stayed quiet for a moment and said, "Toward the end, that girl used to keep the lights on all night. I asked her one day, and she didn't say much. All she said was, 'Bhabi, after three in the morning, I'm scared to be alone.'" She didn't say anything more.

That night, Nila decided she wouldn't sleep. She turned on all the lights and sat on the bed with her back against the wall, her phone in her hand, the gallery open. The clock on the wall read two-fifty a.m.

Time crept by slowly. Three o'clock struck. Three-ten. The flat was dead silent, save for the faint hum of the fridge and a dog barking somewhere outside. Her own heartbeat pounded in her ears.

3:15. 3:16.

She looked at the time on the phone's screen. 3:16. She sat holding her breath. One minute. Just one more minute, and she would know whether all of it had been a trick of her mind.

Atkhawar is a small steamer ghat. The river is very wide here. When there is not a wisp of fog on the breast of the river, if you stand on this bank and look across toward the other side, it feels as though the far bank is receding further and further into the distance, growing blurry before your eyes like a bank of gathered mist.
In the whole day, only three steamers call at Atkhawar—in the morning, at midday, and after evening falls. So few passengers and so little cargo get on and off here that when the directors of the steamer company look at their timetable, they sometimes even think of striking the name of Atkhawar off altogether.
One morning, sitting on the prow of a small boat near the ghat, Haru Majhi's nephew Naga was chewing dry khesari dal. The sun had climbed barely a cubit up the sky; it would be a long time yet before the steamer arrived. A steamer could be seen out in mid-river, but this steamer would not come anywhere near the ghat; it would pass by in the distance. Who knew where it was bound? All day long, how many ships pass down the river, and at night, from how many ships do the piercing beams of searchlights sweep across and dazzle the eyes—how Naga longs to know where they come from and where they go!
A boat pulled up alongside—the boat of Jadabbabu, the talukdar of Karamtala. Jadabbabu emerged hurriedly from under the boat's canopy and leaped ashore, tilting his head slightly with a smile to acknowledge Naga's presence, so the boy would not feel hurt thinking he had been completely ignored. At first glance, Jadabbabu looks fat, and one wonders where the belly to match such a fat man has gone. Then one realizes he is not actually fat; it is his slightly softened, formidable wrestler's build that makes him appear stout. Once upon a time he was said to have been a great wrestler, and after he gave up wrestling, his body grew soft. No sooner had he stepped ashore than Jadabbabu called out, 'Why are you dawdling, Chand?'
'Let's go, Karta, let's go.'
Climbing down quickly, Chand Majhi set off toward the village right behind Jadabbabu. Old Nakul Majhi pushed the boat a few cubits out from the bank, drove a bamboo pole into the riverbed, and tied the boat fast.
Naga asked, 'Why have you come, Mamu?'
Nakul Majhi replied, 'Boro Karta is arriving on the steamer.'
Boro Karta? Who was that again? As Nakul Majhi began to explain, Naga remembered. Ah yes, he had indeed heard rumors that Jadabbabu had an elder brother named Madhabbabu. He lived in Calcutta and never visited his village home. Now he was coming with his family to stay at their country house for a while.
'Where did Karta go, Mamu?'
'Karta has gone to have his palm read—what can I tell you, Naga, Karta is downright crazy about getting his palm read.'
'Yeah.'
Kailash Chakrabarti of Atkhawar is a renowned astrologer; he amazes people by reading their palms. Just so he could go into the village and have his palm read once before the steamer arrived, Jadabbabu had set out from Karamtala in the dead of night and reached the ghat this early.

Fair enough. Let the elder brother arrive from afar, let Jadabbabu have his palm read, let the boatmen wait eagerly with their eyes fixed on the river for the steamer so they can set off with passengers and cargo—Naga's hunger refuses to listen to reason. His is not the sort of hunger that can be appeased by chewing a handful of dry dal. Haru Majhi had gone off somewhere; the moment he returned a little later, Naga made his plea: 'Will you give me the pice, Kaka? I want to eat some muri.'
'Let the steamer come first.'
'My belly's crying out with hunger, Kaka.' 'Why wouldn't it? With you, it's nothing but hunger and more hunger! All day long you have no other business than eating.'
Tossing a pice toward him, Haru sat down to prepare his tobacco. That the coin had slipped past Naga's hand and fallen into the river water seemed not to have caught his eye at all. Naga remained silent. Haru was supposed to give him one pice every morning, and Haru had given the pice. He could easily have reached out and placed the coin right in Naga's hand, but when giving it to Naga and throwing it into the water were all the same to Haru, what was the use of complaining? Haru himself would probably turn around and complain instead: why doesn't a clumsy, half-witted, good-for-nothing fool who lets a pice slip through his fingers into the water just drop dead?
What Haru Majhi said is not untrue; all day long Naga is ravenous for food. He has quite a bad reputation as a glutton. And he has another bad reputation—for stealing food. From home, from other people's shops, and from fields and farmyards, he gathers chira, muri, tiluri, patali, raw rice and dal, fruits and roots—whatever he can lay his hands on—and sends it straight down into his belly. Out in the fields and by the ghats, he milks cows and goats and gulps the milk down on the spot. And without bothering his head over whether he has been invited or not, he turns up at feast houses and sits down with a banana leaf before him. There is no end to the ways Naga tries to fill his stomach.
People call this Naga's gluttony; yet isn't real gluttony just greed for delicacies—sweating and straining to stuff ten more rosogollas down one's throat when one's belly is already so full there isn't room for even one? Naga only wants to fill his stomach; he only wants to soothe the burning ache of his hunger. Perhaps it is because of this very gluttony that Naga's body has grown much taller and broader than the sons of other boatmen, and that there is a touch of healthy grace in his build. It is because they do not get enough to eat that boatmen's sons cannot grow properly; toiling away at back-breaking labor, their muscles merely harden and twist like knotted rope. Without knowing anything of such matters, in his eagerness to satisfy his hunger, Naga has managed to find himself some nourishing food here and there and given his body a chance to thrive. At seventeen or eighteen years of age, therefore, Naga has greater physical strength than many a grown boatman.
Then, half an hour late, the steamer finally arrived. As if it had no wish to dock at the ghat at all, it steamed a little way past, swung around in a wide circle, and pulled up alongside the jetty. By then, a small crowd had gathered on the jetty. There were not many steamer passengers, boatmen, or people from the atchala shops; most of the crowd had come from the surrounding villages.

Input: Not far from Takshashila lies the kingdom of Maharaja Hasti. The name of Maharaja Hasti has found an honorable place in the histories of the Greeks, though the name of his capital has been swallowed up by the womb of the past. Even so, I can see his capital clearly before my eyes. Near and far rise range after range of hills, and upon the bosoms of the mountain rivers dance the green shadows of trees and the deep blue of the sky. Perched atop the peaks of several hills, well-fortified mountain citadels raise their sky-kissing heads—among their eyeless, mute stones seems to awake the frown of something terrible! The houses of the capital are made of wood. In those days, the people of India used stone or brick at most for laying foundations. Many wooden houses rose three, four, five, or even more stories high. On the wooden walls and doors was eye-soothing carving and craftsmanship. Yet the eyes of the present or the future will never see that craftsmanship again, for the lifespan of wood is not long. However, later on, when India began to build houses and temples of stone, the artisans of that era kept the earlier wood-carved designs before them as their model; some of those old temples still survive today. By looking at them, you can form some idea of the beauty of Indian wooden houses in the centuries before Christ. Neighboring countries of India such as Burma and China still uphold the honor of that time-honored tradition of ancient Eastern civilization by building houses, mansions, and temples of wood even today. It is a lovely June morning in the year three hundred and twenty-seven before the birth of Christ; the winter mist has died away. All around shines the calm brightness of the sun. The streets of the city throng with crowds of citizens. Nowhere in the world had anyone heard the name of the purdah system then, and so the number of women in the crowd is by no means small. Both men and women are tall in stature and fair in complexion, dressed in tunics, upper scarfs, and loose trousers. Weak or stunted figures are scarcely to be seen at all. On every side are the signs of newly awakened life: the bustle of shopkeepers and buyers in the shops and marketplaces, the coming and going of crowds, the press of bathers at the river ghats, groups of girls drawing water and returning home with pitchers balanced on their heads, a royal attendant marching down the street beating a kettledrum to proclaim a new royal decree, knots of people standing here and there discussing the news, and from inside many houses the deep, resonant chanting of Vedic mantras. At the city gate, two guards are chatting about the new war between the kingdoms of Abhisara and Takshashila, while a large group of citizens stands gathered around them to listen. The first guard is saying, "The old king of Takshashila has gone senile in his dotage." The second guard asked, "Why?" —"Just the other day the troops of Takshashila took such a thrashing at the hands of Maharaj Puru and came running back, yet the old king has no shame—already he's picked a quarrel with the king of Abhisara, and word is a huge battle was fought the other day." —"What happened in the battle?" —"Haven't got any firm news yet. But whichever side wins the war, thousands of people in both kingdoms will die, weeping will rise in house after house, and the prices of goods will shoot up." An elderly citizen remarked, "The kings indulge their whims, and it's the subjects who die!" The guard said, "Not all kings are alike, though—under the rule of Maharaja Hasti, we live in supreme happiness! Our Maharaja is a mighty warrior, yet he never fights an unjust war!"

Brahma: "What are you doing, either? Why be in such a hurry, when eternity lies stretched out before us? By performing all sorts of good and evil deeds, man is testing the results and searching for what brings him the greatest profit. When he discovers the means of supreme self-fulfilment, peace will come to human society. Until he can do that, fighting and bloodshed will go on."

God: "Then do you believe in Free Will too?"

Brahma: "Have you gone mad!"

Strumming a chord on his Kachchhapi vina, Narad said, "Ishwarah sarvabhutanam hriddeshe 'rjuna tishthati, bhramayan sarvabhutani yantrarudhani mayaya—O Arjuna, the Lord dwells in the hearts of all creatures and, casting His illusion, mounts them upon a wheel and spins them around."

Saint Peter said, "Our Lord is all-loving, supremely compassionate, omnipotent—"

Narad: "Yet He cannot get the better of Satan."

Pir: "Allah is Meherban, all-merciful; it is a sin to probe into His designs. In Allah's domain, nothing bad ever happens."

Brahma: "Listen, Brother God—when man himself becomes loving and compassionate, we too shall become so. Before that, there is nothing to be done."

Saint Peter: "What are you saying! If you give up hope, people will lose their faith in God. Since the three of you have come here, please be gracious and make some arrangement so that harmony may prevail among men."

Pir: "Kabhi nahi ho sakta—that can never be! Allah's subjects are sweet sharbat, and God's subjects are fiery wine. Between them there can be union, for sharbat and wine blend together seamlessly. But the subjects of this Hazrat Brahma are foul-smelling coal tar."

Suddenly the sky grew dark, and a flapping sound was heard, as if someone were beating huge wings. Brahma said, "Is Vishnu coming, then? I hear the sound of Garuda's wings."

Narad said, "It is not Garuda. Don't you see—wings like a bat's, black complexion, horns on his head, hooves on his feet, and a tail as well. Sri Satan is arriving."

Saint Peter shouted, "Avaunt, begone!" Waving his hand, Pir Saheb said, "Gum sho, stay back!" God slipped His hand into the pocket of His robe and began searching for a thunderbolt.

Brahma said, "Ah, let him come; we are not little babies to be frightened at the sight of a bogeyman."

Alighting on the spot, Satan gave a military salute and said, "Lords, if you grant permission, I would like to submit a few words." God sat with a sullen face. Saint Peter and Pir Saheb shut their eyes and plugged their ears with their fingers. With a smile, Brahma said, "What do you wish to say, my son?"

Satan sat down and said, "Grandfather, the three of you Creators have come here together, and such an opportunity will never come again; therefore, I have come to strike a bargain with you. All the rich, respectable, and influential people of the world have sent me as their envoy. They want freedom of action, but in such a way that no harm befalls them in this world or the next as a result. For this, they are ready to gratify you."

Brahma: "In other words, they want to commit misdeeds with impunity. What price will they pay? An offering of rice and bananas? Will they pour ten seers of vegetable ghee into the homa fire?"

Satan: "No, Lord; they understand that you can no longer be appeased with such things. They will give you a share of whatever they earn."

That very day, Shankar thoroughly inspected the station room, his own quarters, and the surrounding ground. All over the place there were large holes in the earth—in the courtyard of the quarters, in the kitchen walls, and here and there across the dirt platform, everywhere there were holes, cracks, and rat burrows. Even so, he could not make sense of it.

One night he was sleeping in the station room; it was very late. The room was dark when Shankar suddenly woke up. Beyond the five senses, some sixth sense seemed to awaken for a moment and warn him that he was about to fall into terrible danger. In the pitch darkness, Shankar's whole body shuddered. Why could he not find the torch by groping around? In the darkness, a faint sound seemed to be coming from somewhere inside the room. Suddenly his hand touched the torch, and like a mechanical doll he swung it forward and switched it on.

Instantly, frozen with fear and astonishment, he sat right there on the bed holding the torch.

Halfway between the wall and his bed, rearing its head high and temporarily dazzled by the glare of the torchlight, stood Africa's cruelest and most ferocious serpent—the black mamba! The snake had raised itself nearly two and a half cubits off the floor of the room—which was nothing surprising, since the black mamba usually chases a man and strikes him on the neck! Shankar had also heard that escaping from a black mamba is nothing short of a second birth.

Shankar had possessed one quality since childhood: he did not easily lose his wits in danger—and even in dire peril, he could maintain control over his nerves.

Shankar realized that if his hand trembled even slightly—the moment the light shifted away from the snake's eyes—its daze would break at once and it would attack immediately. He understood that his life now depended on holding the torch steady and unshaking directly on the snake's eyes. As long as he could keep holding it like that, he was safe. But what if the torch shifted even a little to one side or the other...?

Shankar kept holding the torch. The snake's two eyes glittered like two beads of light. What terrifying power and rage showed in its jet-black, slender body, reared upright like a whip!....

Shankar forgot all the furniture around him, the continent of Africa, his railway job, the line from Mombasa to Kisumu, his homeland, his father and mother—the entire world had emptied out and shrunk into those two glittering beads of light in front of him... Beyond them was nothingness! Darkness! Empty as death, dark as the universe after the final dissolution!

The only reality was this ferocious serpent with its poised hood, capable of injecting 1,500 milligrams of deadly venom into a wound with every strike, waiting poised to deliver it....

Shankar's hand was tingling, his fingers were growing numb, and from his elbow to his armpit his arm seemed to have lost all feeling. How much longer could he keep holding the torch? Perhaps those two beads of light were not a snake's eyes... fireflies, or stars... or... was the battery of the torch losing its strength? Was the white light turning yellow and dim?... Yet the two fireflies or stars burned just the same. Was it night or day? Would dawn break, or evening fall?

After crossing the vast veld between Rhodesia and Angola for about two months, a mountain range was finally seen in the distance looking like a bank of clouds. Checking the map, Alvarez said, "That is our destination, the Richtersveld mountains—they must still be forty miles from here. In these open spaces of Africa, things can be seen from a great distance."

There were many baobab trees in this region. Shankar liked this tree very much—from afar it looked like a banyan or peepul tree, but on coming closer one saw that the baobab tree gave scant shade yet was huge and gnarled, as if covered all over with large warts or growths, looking like a squat, ugly, hunchbacked genie from the Arabian Nights. Across the vast plain, here and there and almost everywhere, near and far, stood huge baobab trees.

One evening, sitting before the campfire in the bitter cold, Alvarez said, "This Rhodesian veld region that you see—diamonds are scattered everywhere here; this is a land of diamond mines. You have surely heard the name of the Kimberley mine. There are many other smaller mines too; how many people have found large and small diamond fragments here and there, and still find them today."

Hardly had he finished speaking when he exclaimed, "Who are those people?"

Sitting in front of him listening, Shankar said, "Where? Who?"

But Alvarez's keen eyesight was as unerring as a bullet from the gun in his hand; a little later, Shankar caught sight of several indistinct figures advancing toward them through the darkness far from the tent. Alvarez said, "Shankar, bring the gun—go quickly, load the cartridges—"

Coming outside with the gun in hand, Shankar saw Alvarez smoking calmly, while some distance away those unknown figures were still coming through the darkness. A little later, they came and stood just outside the circle of the campfire. Looking at them, Shankar saw that the newcomers were dark-skinned and tall—they had nothing in their hands, wore loincloths, had lion's mane around their necks and feathers on their heads—with well-built bodies that in the glow of the campfire looked like so many bronze statues.

Alvarez asked in the Zulu language, "What do you want?"

Some talk passed among them, after which they all sat down on the ground; Alvarez said, "Shankar, give them food—"

Then in a low voice he added, "Great danger. Be very careful, Shankar."

Tinned food was opened. Shankar placed food in front of everyone. Alvarez too sat down to eat with them again, even though he and Shankar had already finished their evening meal at dusk. Shankar realized that Alvarez either had some plan in mind, or else it was the custom of this country to eat along with one's guests.

While eating, Alvarez chatted with the newcomers in the Zulu language; after a long time, having finished their meal, they left. Before they left, each of them was given a cigarette.

Once they had gone, Alvarez said, "They belong to the Matabele tribe. Terribly fierce—they have fought the British government many times. They don't fear even the devil himself. They suspected that we have come to their land in search of diamond mines. The place where we are now is the territory of one of their chiefs. The law of no civilized government holds sway here. They will seize us and take us away to burn us alive. Come, let us strike camp and set off."

Shankar said, "Then why did you ask me to bring the gun?"

Alvarez laughed and said, "Look, I thought that if they weren't won over even after eating, or if I gathered from their talk that their intentions were bad, I would shoot them right while they were eating. Look here—I sat down to eat with my revolver tucked behind me. I would have finished this lot off. My name is Alvarez; once upon a time I didn't fear even the devil, and I don't fear him now either. Before the fish in their hands could reach their mouths, bullets from my pistol would have blown their skulls apart."

The porcupine said, 'Oh, rubbish! There's no telling what on earth he's reading.'

The crocodile said, 'Then which one is it, this one?—Whey and curds, sour broth, tattered kantha and blanket are all foolish Bhombol has to his name—Not this one either? Alright, wait then, let me see—In the dead of the silent night, lying alone on the third floor, why do I keep feeling hungry for nothing?—What did you say?—None of those? A poem about your missus?—Well, you should have said so earlier! Here it is—Rambhajan's missus, good grief, she's just like a lioness! She clatters the pots and pans—jhanar-jhan!—and pounds the laundry—damaddam!—That doesn't match either? Then it must surely be this one—

A ticklish cough, a low simmering fever, a hole in your lungs—die, old man, die! An ache in your back, rheumatism in your ribs—tonight, old man, you'll be knocked flat!'

The porcupine began weeping bitterly, 'Alas, alas! All my money has gone down the drain! What a blockhead of a lawyer—you hand him the documents and he can't even find the right one!'

The bald fellow, who had been standing stiff all this while, suddenly spoke up, 'Which one do you want to hear? That one—Says the bat, O brother porcupine—that one?'

Eagerly, the porcupine cried, 'Yes, yes, that's the one, that's the one!'

At once the jackal bristled up again, 'What does the bat say? Your Honor, let orders be given to summon Badurgopal the bat as a witness!'

Puffing out its cheeks and throat, the bullfrog called out loud, 'Is Badurgopal present?'

Everyone craned their necks to look this way and that, but there was no bat anywhere. Then the jackal said, 'In that case, Your Honor, let orders be given to hang the whole lot of them!'

The crocodile protested, 'Why should that be? We will file an appeal right now!'

With its eyes still shut, the owl said, 'Let the appeal proceed! Call a witness.'

Glancing around this way and that, the crocodile asked Hiji Bij Bij, 'Will you give evidence? You'll get four annas.' At the mention of money, Hiji Bij Bij hopped right up into the witness box and immediately burst out cackling—'Phyak, phyak!'

The jackal asked, 'Why are you laughing?'

Hiji Bij Bij replied, 'Someone had coached a fellow, saying, "You will testify that the book has a green cover, blue leather near the corners, and a red ink stamp on top." The moment the lawyer asked him, "Do you know the accused?" he blurted right out, "Yes, sir—a green cover, blue leather near theears—and a red ink stamp on top!"—Ho, ho, ho, ho!'

The jackal asked, 'Do you know the porcupine?'

Hiji Bij Bij said, 'Yes, I know the porcupine, I know the crocodile, I know them all. The porcupine lives in a burrow and has long quills all over its body, and the crocodile has round bumpy knobs on its back, and they catch goats and things and eat them up.' No sooner had it said this than Byakaran Shing burst into dreadful bleats and sobs—'Baa, baa!'

I asked, 'Now what happened?'

The goat sobbed, 'A crocodile ate up half of my third maternal uncle, and so the other half died too!'

I said, 'Well, if he's gone, he's gone—good riddance! Now keep quiet.'

The jackal asked, 'Do you know anything about this lawsuit?'

Hiji Bij Bij said, 'Of course I know! One person files a complaint and has a lawyer, and they bring another person from Assam, who is called the asami—the accused. He has a lawyer too. On each side there are ten witnesses. And there is a judge, who sits there and sleeps.'

The owl snapped, 'I am certainly not sleeping! I have an ailment in my eyes, which is why I am keeping my eyes shut.'

Hiji Bij Bij said, 'I have seen plenty of other judges too, and every single one of them had an ailment in his eyes!' Saying this, it began cackling away furiously—'Phyak, phyak!'

সজারু বলল, ‘দূর ছাই! কি যে পড়ছে তার নেই ঠিক।’

কুমির বলল, ‘তা হলে কোনটা, এইটা?—দই দম্বল, টোকো অম্বল, কাঁথা কম্বল করে সম্বল বোকা ভোম্বল—এটাও নয়? আচ্ছা তা হলে দাঁড়াও দেখছি—নিঝুম নিশুত রাতে, একাশুয়ে তেতালাতে, খালি খালি খিদে পায় কেন রে?—কি বললে?—ওসব নয়? তোমার গিন্নীর নামে কবিতা?—তা, সে কথা আগে বললেই হত। এই তো—রামভজনের গিন্নীটা, বাপ রে যেন সিংহীটা! বাসন নাড়ে ঝনার্‌ঝন, কাপড় কাচে দমাদ্দম্—এটাও মিলছে না? তা হলে নিশ্চয় এটা—

খুস্‌খুসে কাশি ঘুষ্‌ঘুষে জ্বর, ফুস্‌ফুসে ছ্যাঁদা বুড়ো তুই মর্‌। মাজ্‌রাতে ব্যথা পাঁজ্‌রাতে বাত, আজ রাতে বুড়ো হবি কুপোকাত।’

সজারুটা ভয়ানক কাঁদতে লাগল, ‘হায়, হায়! আমার পয়সাগুলো সব জলে গেল। কোথাকার এক আহাম্মক উকিল, দলিল দিলে খুঁজে পায় না!’

ন্যাড়াটা এতক্ষণ আড়ষ্ট হয়ে ছিল, সে হঠাৎ বলে উঠল, ‘কোনটা শুনতে চাও? সেই যে—বাদুড় বলে ওরে ও ভাই সজারু—সেইটে?’

সজারু ব্যস্ত হয়ে বলল, ‘হ্যাঁ-হ্যাঁ, সেইটে, সেইটে।’

অমনি শেয়াল আবার তেড়ে উঠল, ‘বাদুড় কি বলে? হুজুর, তা হলে বাদুড়গোপালকে সাক্ষী মানতে আজ্ঞা হোক।’

কোলাব্যাঙ গাল-গলা ফুলিয়ে হেঁকে বলল, ‘বাদুড়গোপাল হাজির?’

সবাই এদিক-ওদিক তাকিয়ে দেখল, কোথাও বাদুড় নেই। তখন শেয়াল বলল, ‘তাহলে হজুর, ওদের সক্কলের ফাঁসির হুকুম হোক।’

কুমির বলল, ‘তা কেন? এখন আমরা আপিল করব?’

প্যাঁচা চোখ বুজে বলল, ‘আপিল চলুক! সাক্ষী আন।’

কুমির এদিক-ওদিক তাকিয়ে হিজি বিজ্ বিজ্‌কে জিগগেস করল, ‘সাক্ষী দিবি? চার আনা পয়সা পাবি।’ পয়সার নামে হিজি বিজ্ বিজ্ তড়াক্ করে সাক্ষী দিতে উঠেই ফ্যাক্‌-ফ্যাক্ করে হেসে ফেলল।

শেয়াল বলল, ‘হাসছ কেন?’

হিজি বিজ্ বিজ্ বলল, ‘একজনকে শিখিয়ে দিয়েছিল, তুই সাক্ষী দিবি যে, বইটার সবুজ রঙের মলাট, কানের কাছে নীল চামড়া আর মাথার উপর লালকালির ছাপ। উকিল যেই তাকে জিগগেস করেছে, তুমি আসামীকে চেন? অমনি সে বলে উঠেছে, আজ্ঞে হ্যাঁ, সবুজ রঙের মলাট, কানের কাছে নীল চামড়া, মাথার উপর লাল কালির ছাপ—হোঃ হোঃ হোঃ হো—’

হিজি বিজ্ বিজ্ বলল, ‘হ্যা, সজারু চিনি, কুমির চিনি, সব চিনি। সুজারু গর্তে থাকে, তার গায়ে লম্বা-লম্বা কাঁটা, আর কুমিরের গায়ে চাকা-চাকা ঢিপির মতো, তারা ছাগল-টাগল ধরে খায়।’ বলতেই ব্যাকরণ শিং ব্যা-ব্যা করে ভয়ানক কেঁদে উঠল।

আমি বললাম, ‘আবার কি হলো?’

ছাগল বলল, ‘আমার সেজোমামার আধখানা কুমিরে খেয়েছিল, তাই বাকি আধখানা মরে গেল।’

আমি বললাম, ‘গেল তো গেল, আপদ গেল। তুমি এখন চুপ কর।’

শেয়াল জিগগেস করল, ‘তুমি মোকদ্দমার বিষয়ে কিছু জানো?’

হিজি বিজ্‌ বিজ্‌ বলল, ‘তা আর জানি নে? একজন নালিশ করে তার একজন উকিল থাকে, আর একজনকে আসাম থেকে নিয়ে আসে, তাকে বলে আসামী। তারও একজন উকিল থাকে। এক-একদিকে দশজন করে সাক্ষী থাকে। আর একজন জজ থাকে, সে বসে-বসে ঘুমোয়।’

প্যাঁচা বলল, ‘কক্ষনো আমি ঘুমোচ্ছি না, আমার চোখে ব্যারাম আছে তাই চোখ বুজে আছি।’

হিজি বিজ্‌ বিজ্‌ বলল, ‘আরো অনেক জজ দেখেছি, তাদের সক্কলেরই চোখে ব্যারাম।’ বলেই সে ফ্যাক্‌-ফ্যাক্‌ করে ভয়ানক হাসতে লাগল।

Naga walked up and said, 'What is it?'
Jadabbabu wore two gold rings on two fingers of his left hand and one on a finger of his right hand. Slipping the ring off his little finger, he placed it on Naga's finger right before everyone's eyes.
'Go and sleep.'

Mixing a bellyful of muri with five or six of the mangoes that the mango thieves had stolen and piled into their basket, Naga ate his fill and went off to sleep. Jadabbabu then asked Paresh, 'How did the fire start, Parsha?'
Paresh's face had gone dry and pale; trembling with fear, he said, 'How would I know, Karta? Hearing the cows and calves stamping about—'
'You don't know?'

'Save me, Naga, don't tell Karta! Karta asked me how the fire started, and he'll ask you too. Don't tell Karta, Naga—I'll give you a rupee.'
Though his eyes were heavy with sleep, Naga felt like laughing; even a few days ago, when he could not always get a single pice from Haru Majhi for the asking, hearing Paresh's offer would probably have made him laugh.

Then, lowering his voice, Chandra Chattujye said, "Let me tell you something. It is my wish to have Bhabani settle down right here. Go home and give all three of your sisters in marriage to him—and let the whole burden be lifted once and for all. You can give him five bighas of brahmottar land as dowry. I'll settle everything right now—"

With a thoughtful face, Rajaram said, "I can't give you any final word without asking at home first, Kaka. I will let you know tomorrow."

"Go ahead and get them married without a second thought! I'm not saying this just because he is my nephew. He is a Banruri of Katadaha-Bandighati, only one generation removed from unbroken status—I'll have the ghatak matchmaker recite his kuluji pedigree to you later. A shining Kulin family, known to everyone at a single call."

"How old would the groom be?"

"Somewhere close to fifty. Your sisters aren't young anymore either. Had Bhabani not run off to become a sannyasi, he would have been the father of seven sons by now. Just take a look at him first—every day he performs his evening sandhya-ahnik prayers by the riverbank for an hour and then strolls about by himself—what a build he has! What muscles on his arms!"

"Will Bhabani agree to marry all three sisters at once?"

"Leave that arrangement in my hands, my boy. You may rest completely assured."

It had grown quite dark along the path through the bamboo grove. Fireflies were glimmering in the dense tangle of kunch creepers and babla trees. The fragrance of chhatim blossoms came drifting on the breeze from the direction of the woods.

Late that night, Tilottama heard the news. The waning moon of the dark fortnight had risen behind the bamboo groves along the river. Calling her younger sister Bilu, she asked, "O Bilu, has Boudidi said anything to you?"

"Why wouldn't she? About the marriage, you mean?"

"Oh, go on, you shameless girl—don't you feel shy at all?"

"What's there to be shy about? As if remaining an overgrown unmarried maid all these years was something to be proud of!"

"All three of us are to be bundled onto the same head—you've heard that too, haven't you?"

"I know all of it."

"Do you agree?"

"If I am to speak the honest truth, my view is that if it's going to happen, let it happen."

"That is what I think too. We'll have to ask Nilu's opinion tomorrow morning."

"What could she possibly say? She's just a child—whatever we do, she'll agree to it too."

Until late into the night, Tilu sat on the roof terrace lost in thought. She had turned thirty years old; seeing the face of a husband had been an impossible dream beyond all dreaming. Even now she could hardly believe it: would she truly be married? Would she go to a husband's home? Along with her sisters—well, what of it? That was how things happened in house after house. Chandar Kaka's own father had married seventeen times. In Kulin families, such things were the norm. Who knew what date Dada had fixed for the wedding? Even if the groom was fifty, what of it—was she herself a little girl anymore?

In her excitement, sleep did not come to Tilu's eyes all night. What a fierce droning of mosquitoes rose from the woods and bushes!

Around the very time Tilu was sitting awake alone on the roof terrace, Nalu Pal had just returned from the market at Mollahati, cooked and eaten his meal with his own hands, tallied up his cash, and lain down to sleep.

Nalu had hit upon a plan in his head.

Only today had he come to realise that he had a very sharp head for business. He had sold seven rupees and nine annas worth of betel leaves and betel nuts today. His net profit was one rupee and three annas. As for his expenses, they came to just two annas for two and a half seers of rice, and two pice for a poya of fresh river

khaira fish. He had wanted to buy half a seer of fish, but he didn't have enough oil to fry so much fish. Mustard oil had grown terribly dear in the market lately; what used to cost three annas a seer now stood at fourteen pice—how could he afford to use more oil?

He had to build up the capital in his hand. He would never get ahead just selling betel leaves and betel nuts. Real advancement lay in the piece-cloth trade. Mukunda De was his friend, and Mukunda had explained the ropes to him. Once he had saved up thirty rupees in hand, he would start a cloth business of his own.

For when Persia tested its strength against Greece time and again, even in later ages several Indian kings living along the banks of the Indus were compelled to send troops to aid the Persians... If we change the scene, we see that the very next act takes place in the fourth century before Christ. In India, Buddhism is then trying to raise its head against Vedic Hinduism. In the Punjab, Maharaja Puru enjoys special renown as a brave and true Kshatriya. In Eastern India, the half-Aryan Nanda dynasty is reigning. Chandragupta is then a young man; having learned the art of warfare of both the East and the West, he is gathering strength—his covetous eyes fixed upon the throne of India. The principal theater of the West at that time is Greece. These Greeks, too, were Aryans like the North Indian Hindus and the Persians; their ancestors had also come, in an age beyond memory, from the original Aryan homeland in Central Asia. Most of Europe was then inhabited by uncivilized barbarians, and Rome was still an infant—having not yet parted the curtain of Great Greece's valor, heroism, and civilization, its eyes had not yet glimpsed the vast splendor of the future. In Greece at that time, Macedonia was trying to stage a new drama—much like the half-Aryan Chandragupta of Eastern India in Aryavarta. And the aristocratic Greeks likewise regarded the inhabitants of Macedonia as half-Greek and half-barbarian. Philip, the ruler of Macedonia, had won nobility in the Greek world by the strength of his own arm. When Philip met an untimely, violent death at the hands of an enemy, his son Alexander inherited along with the throne a formidable, vast army trained by his father's own hand. He was only twenty years old at the time. Yet even at that young age, he had inherited his father's political acumen and military genius, as well as his mother Olympias's religious fanaticism, passionate intensity, and power of imagination. The high-born, proud Greeks rose in rebellion against the half-civilized boy-king. But Alexander at once drew his sword from its scabbard, marched out with his troops like a tempest incarnate, and crushed the entire rebellion with effortless ease—showing them that though he was a boy, he was neither weak nor foolish! In this world, there is no greater Kshatriya than the one who possesses strength of arm and valor. It was during the decline of pure Hindu culture and civilization that the half-Aryan Chandragupta, Emperor Ashoka, and others appeared in India. Their genius has kept Indian culture and civilization a wonder of the world to this day. And it was during the age of decline of original Greek culture and civilization that Alexander, regarded as a half-Greek, made his appearance. It was he who took upon himself the task of spreading the message of Greek civilization across the entire world. The aristocratic Greeks despised him, it is true, yet without him the glory of Greek civilization could never have become so peerless today. Through his genius, the fame of Greek culture crossed the boundaries of the West and spread to the banks of India's Five Rivers and into Central Asia. Greece's neighbor at that time was Persia, the mightiest empire of the East. The Persians had invaded Greece more than once. Although the Greeks had somehow managed to defend themselves, they had suffered untold misery. যার বাহুবল ও বীরত্ব আছে, পৃথিবীতে তার চেয়ে বড় ক্ষত্রিয় আর কেউ নেই। খাঁটি হিন্দু সংস্কৃতি আর সভ্যতার অধঃপতনের সময়েই ভারতবর্ষে অর্ধ-আর্য চন্দ্রগুপ্ত ও সম্রাট অশোক প্রভৃতির আবির্ভাব। তাঁদের প্রতিভা ভারতীয় সংস্কৃতি আর সভ্যতাকে আজও ক’রে রেখেছে বিশ্বের বিস্ময়। এবং আদিম গ্রীক ও সংস্কৃতি ও সভ্যতার অধঃপতনের যুগেই অর্ধ-গ্রীকরূপে গণ্য আলেকজাণ্ডার আত্মপ্রকাশ করেন। গ্রীক সভ্যতার বাণী সারা পৃথিবীতে প্রচার করবার ভার নিলেন তিনিই। কুলীন গ্রীকরা তাঁকে ঘৃণা করতেন বটে, কিন্তু তিনি না থাকলে গ্রীকসভ্যতার মহিমা আজ এমন অতুলনীয় হ’তে পারত না। তাঁর প্রতিভায় গ্রীক সংস্কৃতির খ্যাতি প্রতীচ্যের সীমা পেরিয়ে ভারতের পঞ্চনদের তীরে ও মধ্য-এসিয়ায় বিস্তৃত হয়ে পড়েছিল। গ্রীসের প্রতিবেশী ছিল তখন প্রাচ্যের সব-চেয়ে পরাক্রান্ত রাজ্য পারস্য। পারসীরা একাধিকবার গ্রীকদের আক্রমণ করেছিল। গ্রীকরা কোনো রকমে আত্মরক্ষা করতে পেরেছিল বটে, কিন্তু তাদের দুর্দশা হয়েছিল যৎপরোনাস্তি। নিজেকে সমগ্র গ্রীসের দলপতিরূপে প্রতিষ্ঠা করবার জন্যে তরুণ বীর আলেকজাণ্ডার বললেন, “গ্রীস আমার স্বদেশ। প্রাচ্যের পারসীরা আমার স্বদেশের উপর যখন অত্যাচার করেছে, আমিও পারস্য সাম্রাজ্য অধিকার ক’রে প্রতিশোধ নেবো।”

Input: "There is a small sketch of Amrita-Dwip on the map—haven't you looked at it closely? The first special feature of that island is that it is surrounded on all sides by hills—hills that are fifteen hundred to two thousand feet high in places. Its second special feature is that right at the northwestern corner of the island, atop the hills, stand five peaks side by side. The height of the tallest peak is two thousand three hundred feet. An island like that won't be hard to recognize even from afar." Saying this, Bimal turned around, put the binoculars to his eyes, and began scanning the sea to the west. Sundarbabu said, "Hmph! Tell me, Bimalbabu, we are heading east. Yet for the last few days I have been noticing that every now and then you put the binoculars to your eyes and try to spot something toward the west! What is the meaning of this?" Opening his mouth after all this time, Jayanta said, "I can tell you what it means. Bimalbabu is checking whether an enemy ship is following behind us!" "What enemy would come out here?" "Why, have you already forgotten the people who gave Kolkata the nightmare of the Dragon?" "What nonsense you talk! That gang has been scattered to the winds." "How do you know?" "Once the ringleader is knocked out, does the gang still hold together?" Lowering the binoculars, Bimal said, "I believe otherwise. Every single man in that gang is desperate; they are all dead set on reaching Amrita-Dwip. But they do not know the location of that island, because the map is in our hands. They surely have word that we have set out for Amrita-Dwip passing close by their country. I do not think for a moment that the people who could raid Bengal all the way from distant China out of greed for the statue of Lao-Tzu and that map will not make one last attempt." Sundarbabu said, "Hmph! What do you mean by a last attempt? Do you mean to say there will be a naval battle between their ship and ours?" "It wouldn't be surprising." With wide eyes and an excited voice, Sundarbabu said, "What do you mean, it wouldn't be surprising? Can a naval battle just happen like that? Where are our sepoys? Where are our cannons? Are we going to fight by throwing punches?" Kumar laughed and said, "Cannons or no cannons, every one of us has an automatic gun in his hand. And we ourselves are our sepoys." Growing even more agitated, Sundarbabu was about to say something further, when suddenly he let out a hideous "Hmph!" and gave a huge leap, landing five cubits away. Manik said, "What happened, Sundarbabu, what happened? Did your potbelly just pop with a bang?" In an angry voice, Sundarbabu said, "Go on, get away! Pretending you didn't see anything, putting on an innocent act! Kumarbabu, chain up that wretched dog of yours from now on. Whenever that rascal sees me, he comes running from goodness knows where, lets out a loud snort right over my feet, and sniffs at something—can you tell me why, sir?" Manik said, "Bagha probably likes the scent of your lotus feet." "Don't wisecrack with me, Manik; your wisecracks are even ruder than Bagha's behavior. I cannot stand that mangy cur at any cost; I am leaving this place!"
Target Output: —“ম্যাপে অমৃত-দ্বীপের ছোট্ট একটা নক্সা আছে, আপনি কি ভালো ক’রে দেখেন নি? সে দ্বীপের প্রথম বিশেষত্ব হচ্ছে, তার চারিপাশই পাহাড় দিয়ে ঘেরা— পাহাড় কোথাও কোথাও দেড়-দুই হাজার ফুট উঁচু। তার দ্বিতীয় বিশেষত্ব, দ্বীপের ঠিক উত্তর-পশ্চিম কোণে পাহাড়ের উপরে আছে ঠিক পাশাপাশি পাঁচটি শিখর। সবচেয়ে উঁচু শিখরের উচ্চতা দুই হাজার তিন শো ফুট। এ-রকম দ্বীপ দূর থেকে দেখলেও চেনা শক্ত হবে না।”—ব’লেই ফিরে দাঁড়িয়ে বিমল চোখে দূরবীণ লাগিয়ে সমুদ্রের পশ্চিম দিকে তাকিয়ে কি দেখতে লাগল। সুন্দরবাবু বললেন, “হুম্! আচ্ছা বিমলবাবু, আমরা যাচ্ছি তো পূর্ব্বদিকে। অথচ আজ ক’দিন ধ’রেই আমি লক্ষ্য করছি, আপনি যখন-তখন চোখে দূরবীণ লাগিয়ে পশ্চিম দিকে কি যেন দেখবার চেষ্টা করছেন! এর মানে কি?” জয়ন্ত এতক্ষণ পরে মুখ খুলে বললে, “এর মানে আমি আপনাকে বলতে পারি। বিমলবাবু দেখছেন আমাদের পিছনে কোন শত্রুজাহাজ আসছে কি না!” —“এখানে আবার শত্রু আসবে কে?” —“কেন, কলকাতাকে যারা ড্রাগনের দুঃস্বপ্ন দেখিয়েছিল, আপনি এরি মধ্যে তাদের কথা ভুলে গেলেন নাকি?” —“কী যে বল তার ঠিক নেই! সে দল তো ছত্রভঙ্গ হয়ে গেছে।” —“কেমন ক’রে জানলেন?” —“পালের গোদা কুপোকাৎ হ’লে দল কি আর থাকে?” দূরবীণ নামিয়ে বিমল বললে, “আমার বিশ্বাস অন্য রকম। সে দলের প্রত্যেক লোকই মরিয়া, তারা সকলেই অমৃত-দ্বীপে যাবার জন্যে দৃঢ়প্রতিজ্ঞ। কিন্তু ও-দ্বীপের ঠিকানা তারা জানে না, কারণ ম্যাপখানা আছে আমাদের হাতে। আমরা যে তাদের দেশের কাছ দিয়ে অমৃত-দ্বীপে যাত্রা করেছি, নিশ্চয়ই এ-সন্ধান তারা রাখে। যারা লাউ-ৎজুর মূর্ত্তি আর ঐ ম্যাপের লোভে সুদূর চীন থেকে বাংলাদেশে হানা দিতে পেরেছিল তারা যে আর একবার শেষ চেষ্টা করে দেখবে না, এ-কথা আমার মনে হয় না।” সুন্দরবাবু বললেন, “হুম্, শেষ-চেষ্টা মানে? Input: —"I will test the blood on the glove." Mr. Datta said in a curious tone, "Will there be any benefit in that?" —"Of course there will, Mr. Datta! You are a doctor, so you surely know that according to medico-legal opinion, human blood can be divided into just four groups. For now, I want to test and see which group or category the blood on the glove falls into. Then, once the murderer is arrested, it will be possible to say with a great deal of certainty whether this blood came from his body or not." Mr. Datta said, "Hemantababu, I did not know that anyone in this country adopts such scientific methods in detective work. I see you have amazed me. We met at a very unfortunate time today; otherwise, I would have gotten to know you better." Hemanta said modestly, "I am no brightly coloured paper balloon, Mr. Datta; please do not lift me so high into the sky. And if you wish to get to know me better, this humble servant is always ready to present himself at your doorstep." Mr. Datta took one of Hemanta's hands and said, "Not at the doorstep, Hemantababu—I want to take you right up to my second-floor drawing room. You are invited to my place for tea tomorrow afternoon. Well, do you agree?" —"It is my good fortune. But I do not know your address." —"Number ten, Paresh Mitra Lane. Six or seven minutes' walk from here." Satishbabu said, "Mr. Datta is quite a fellow, I must say! We have been left out! Different treatment on the same journey!" Mr. Datta said, "Certainly not, certainly not! You will come too, and Rabinbabu will come as well!" My skin, however, began to crawl with revulsion. Lying right in front of us was the dead body of a murdered man, and from inside the house came the muffled sobs of relatives—and standing right here, they were talking of invitations! Right after that, I understood: Mr. Datta is a doctor—having dissected corpses and witnessed people's deaths time and again, his heart has grown thick-skinned; and Satishbabu is a veteran police officer—having rummaged through the gruesome bodies of countless murdered people in his life, such sights have become utterly routine to his eyes, so it is only natural for his mind to remain unperturbed as well. Just like the muddofarashes at the cremation ground; once a corpse is reduced to ashes, they are seen setting a pot right over the funeral pyre to cook their rice! Mr. Datta glanced at his wristwatch and said hurriedly, "It is half past eight! Satishbabu, there is no way I can stay any longer—I have to visit a patient's house before nine. Hemantababu, do you have any further need of me?" Hemanta said, "No, Mr. Datta, you may freely leave." Mr. Datta departed. Hemanta examined the iron safe for a while. Then he said, "Satishbabu, where is the key to this?" —"The key cannot be found. It is probably with the murderer. A bunch of keys. This is yet another proof that someone from inside the house is involved in this murder. Why would an outside murderer take the keys away? Whoever took the keys surely has some other ulterior motive." Hemanta said nothing. He sat silently, staring at one side of the room's floor. Then he got up, stepped forward, picked up something like a piece of dried mud from the floor, examined it for a few moments, and said, "Satishbabu, tell me, what is this?"

Input: —"Will he indeed? Let us see!" Saying this, Hemanta got up, lifted the receiver of the telephone, and gave the number of the police station. —"Who is this? Satishbabu? Make sure a guard is posted in front of the door of that room at all times—let no one enter that room for any reason whatsoever. Why? There is certainly a reason, but the time to reveal it has not yet come. Do not be angry; I will tell you everything in due course... What did you say? The constable who was coming alone with the broken glass tumbler was suddenly attacked on the way by some people? And then? I am glad to hear they could not snatch the glass away. The constable could not recognise anyone? Yes, today's fog in Calcutta is astonishing indeed! Unprecedented! What did you say? Just a couple of minutes earlier, near the corner of the lane, the constable bumped right into another pedestrian? Who was he? Binod? What was he doing there in such heavy fog? He had gone out for a walk because he had a headache? In this foul fog? What a strange excuse! You are wondering whether to arrest him or not? You understand your duty best; what more can I say? In this line of work, I am nothing more than an apprentice!... Yes, I have a piece of new information too. Some people attacked Rabin and me today as well. Rabin's head was split open. Poor fellow. I wasn't hurt very badly, it is true, but that glove was looted—my luck wasn't as good as the constable's. No, I couldn't recognise them. For one thing, there was the fog, and on top of that, they came wearing masks like villains in a novel. No, no, you need not come to see us so late at night; we are quite well. All right, namaskar." Turning toward me, he said, "Rabin, you heard everything, didn't you?" In an overwhelmed voice, I said, "Brother Hemanta, we have fallen into the clutches of terrible people! Murder and the theft of eighty thousand rupees yesterday, and an attack on us and the constable today! Brother, I am a man who fiddles with pen and ink; my constitution will not be able to bear such turmoil!" Hemanta said, "Hmm, I too used to think that such sensational commotion could only happen in Battala detective novels!... But Rabin, do you realise how desperate the murderers have become to remove the evidence against them? That they are trying to turn even a novel into reality? But who are they—who are they? I cannot make out anything at all!" I said, "Tell me, why didn't you breathe a word about one thing to Satishbabu?" Smiling a mischievous smile, Hemanta said, "About what?" —"About Matibabu's diary?" Hemanta suddenly grew serious and said, "Rabin, this secrecy of mine is pardonable. To tell the truth, this will be the first notable 'case' of my life. Before the police, I want to earn all the credit for this entirely on my own. It is my firm belief that I will be able to get to the bottom of this case. Of course, after that, I shall step back behind the curtain—giving the police the opportunity to claim the full sixteen annas of praise from the public."

After drinking the water, the old man began to speak again:—

"Yes, listen to what happened next. We entered the deep forest. What huge trees, giant ferns, and orchids and lianas of such varied colors—in places that forest was dense and impenetrable. The undergrowth beneath the giant trees was so thick, with fishhook-like thorns on the trunks and the leaves overhead so tightly entangled, that it was doubtful whether sunlight had ever entered that jungle since the beginning of time. The sky could not be seen. There was a terrible nuisance of baboons all over the jungle; on the branches of the big trees sat troops of baboons of all kinds—infants, juveniles, old ones, and young adults—and often we saw that they paid no heed to the arrival of humans. They bared their teeth to frighten us—one or two old leader baboons were truly ferocious by nature, and had we not had guns in our hands, they would easily have attacked us. Jim Carter said, 'At least we shall never be short of food in this jungle.'

"Seven or eight days passed in that dense forest. Jim Carter had spoken the truth: every day one baboon laid down its life to supply our food. Large and small streams came cascading down from the high mountain into various parts of the jungle, so there was no shortage of water either. Once, however, danger arose from this very thing. Coming to the bank of a stream at midday, I had lit a fire and was making arrangements to roast the haunch of a baboon, when Jim, driven by thirst, went and drank water from the stream. A little while later, he began vomiting incessantly, with a terrible pain in his stomach. I knew a bit of science; growing suspicious, I tested the water of the stream and found mineral arsenic mixed in it. The stream was surely washing down over a bed of arsenic higher up the mountain. After I gave him an antidote from the homeopathic chest, Jim recovered toward evening.

"After entering the forest, apart from baboons and an occasional venomous snake or two, we encountered no other wild animals. I leave out birds and butterflies, of course—for nowhere outside these tropical jungles can one see birds and butterflies of such varied colors and species. Besides, they do not fall into the category of what one properly calls wild beasts.

"At first, a spur of the Richtersveld mountain range rose before us; it lay parallel to the main range, to be sure, but was relatively low. Crossing it, we descended into a vast wooded valley and pitched our tent. Seeing a river filled Jim and me with joy, for it is often along the banks of such rivers that traces of minerals are found.

"We went around testing the sand along various parts of the river, but found nothing anywhere. There was not even a single grain of gold in the river sand. Gradually we grew disheartened. By then some twenty or twenty-two days had passed. One evening, while drinking coffee, Jim said, 'Look, my heart tells me we shall find gold here. Stay here a few days more.'

"Another twenty days passed. Baboon meat had become unbearable and utterly disgusting. Even a man like Jim began to lose heart. I said, 'Why stay any longer, Jim? Come, let's turn back now. They fooled us at the Kaffir village. There is nothing here.'

"Jim said, 'This mountain range has many spurs; I won't leave without inspecting them all.'

"One day, sitting by the bed of the mountain river and panning the sand, Jim and I simultaneously spotted a small yellow stone half-buried among a heap of pebbles. Our faces lit up with joy and amazement. Jim said, 'Diego, our labor has paid off at last! You recognize it, don't you?'

"I had recognized it too. I said, 'Yes. But this thing has been washed down by the river current. There is no mine right here.'"

In a single breath, Naga poured out his request. He had got a job somewhere, and so he wanted Thakur-mashai to read his palm just once to see whether things would turn out well or ill for him. Looking thoughtful, Chakrabarti said, 'Can a palm be read on credit, you blockhead? Don't you have even a single pice on you?'

Seeing Naga, Jadabbabu said happily, 'You've come? Good lad! Where are your things?'
'I don't have anything, Karta.'

Madhabbabu's wife said, 'Be quiet, Khoka!'
The girl wearing a red dress said, 'Dada is just impossible!'
Naga quickly turned his face away and began watching the preparations for the steamer's departure. On other days, the steamer never stayed at the ghat this long. Such a grown-up boy was named Khoka! Perhaps the girl's name was Khuki too! Besides, what a strange way of talking they had! People from Calcutta came on the steamer from time to time, and Naga had heard them speak. But these people seemed to have mixed that speech with the local dialect and cooked up a strange khichuri! A little later, Khoka's mother called out, 'Hello there, my boy, do you hear me? Come over here.'
Naga did not go over. Staying right where he was, he turned his head and said, 'What is it?'
Khoka's mother said, 'Come and have a little food.' Naga shook his head gravely and said, 'No, I won't eat. I'm not hungry.'
Until Jadabbabu returned, there was no way to cast off the boat. In the end, Chand Majhi's son Banka was sent to look for them. About an hour later, Jadabbabu came back alone. The gentleman's face looked drawn and pale; one look at him showed that he was utterly worn out and exhausted. Before anyone could even ask, he told everyone the reason for such a long delay. Where Chand and his son were also came to light.
It was an astonishing story.
Examining his palm, Kailash Chakrabarti had said many things, and then, suddenly growing grave and remaining silent for a while, he had asked why Jadabbabu had left home today. At the very question, Jadabbabu's heart gave a violent thud. Nervously he asked why—what would happen if one left home today? In reply, Chakrabarti said that nothing would happen to just anyone, but something would happen to Jadabbabu.
At first Chakrabarti did not want to say what would happen at all, until at last, after much pressing from Jadabbabu, he spoke. Some misfortune would befall either Jadabbabu or his companion today. What sort of misfortune? It could be a great disaster of any kind, or it could be a minor mishap. Even loss of life would not be surprising, while on the other hand, merely stubbing and spraining a toe was also possible.
Old Chand Majhi had been listening to everything, and when it was time to return, he suddenly dug his heels in: he would not go with Jadabbabu! After Chakrabarti Mashai's prediction, he was by no means willing to be Jadabbabu's companion anymore. And since there was a chance that the misfortune might pass off onto the companion instead, how could Jadabbabu come back alone without a companion either! Unable to persuade Chand Majhi by reasoning with him, coaxing him, scolding him, or frightening him, he had no choice but to request Chakrabarti Mashai to provide him with a companion. The companion would receive a handsome reward just for walking back with him.
But Chakrabarti Mashai merely smiled. Could fate be cheated that way? The man with whom he had set out from home was Jadabbabu's companion—could companions be swapped now! Instead, there was one thing that might work: within an hour he could prepare a fresh maduli, and Jadabbabu would do better to wear that.
