Like Livingstone and Stanley, like Harry Johnston, Marco Polo, and Robinson Crusoe! From his earliest childhood he had prepared himself for such a life—without ever stopping to consider that what might happen for boys of other countries was virtually impossible for Bengali boys. They were bred to become clerks, schoolmasters, doctors, or lawyers. For them, the hope of setting out along uncharted paths into unknown lands was nothing more than a vain pipe dream.

That night, by the dim light of an earthen lamp, he opened Westmark's great book of geography and sat down to read. There was one passage in this book that fascinated him deeply. It was the extraordinary account written by the famous German explorer Anton Hauptmann of his ascent of a great mountain in Africa—the Mountain of the Moon (Chander Pahar). How many times he had read that passage! And while reading it, how many times he had dreamed that one day, like Herr Hauptmann, he too would go forth to conquer the Mountain of the Moon. A dream! Forever as distant a thing as a real mountain upon the real moon itself... Does the Mountain of the Moon ever come down to earth?

That night he had a most extraordinary dream...

All around him stretched a dense jungle of giant bamboo. A herd of wild elephants was snapping and crushing the bamboo stalks with a loud cracking sound. He and someone else with him—the two of them—were climbing a colossal mountain; the scenery all around was exactly like Hauptmann's description of the Mountain of the Moon: that same dense bamboo forest, those same huge trees festooned with hanging epiphytes, heaps of rotting leaves underfoot, bare rocky flanks of the mountain showing through here and there, and far above, glimpsed through gaps in the foliage, the snow-white, perpetually ice-capped summit washed in moonlight—appearing one moment and hidden behind the forest canopy the next. In the clear sky, a star or two gleamed here and there. Once, he seemed to actually hear the trumpeting roar of a wild elephant... the whole forest trembled with the sound... So real did it feel that the very sound seemed to startle him awake. He sat up in bed; day had broken, and morning light was streaming into the room through the gap in the window.

Oh, what a vivid dream he had just seen! Dreams seen at dawn are said to come true, aren't they? Many people say so, at least.

In their village stood an old, ruined temple from long ago. Legend had it that in olden times Madan Ray, the son-in-law of one of the twelve Bara-Bhuiya chieftains of Bengal, had built this temple. Now there was no one left in Madan Ray's line. The temple had crumbled into ruins, with peepal and banyan trees sprouting from its cornices—yet the arch above the altar where the deity once stood remained intact even now. There was no idol inside; even so, worship was offered there every Tuesday and Saturday, village women smeared vermilion and sandalwood paste upon the altar, and everyone said the deity of the shrine was wide awake and potent—whatever vow anyone made there was always fulfilled. After taking his bath that day, Shankar went to the temple, tied a clod of earth to an aerial root of the banyan tree, and offered up a silent prayer.

In the afternoon, he went back and sat for a long time on the carpet of durba grass in front of the temple. Although the spot lay within the village neighbourhood, it was surrounded by woods, with an abandoned house standing close by; a murder had taken place in that house during Shankar's childhood, and ever since then the owner had left the village to live elsewhere; everyone said the place was haunted by ghosts. Hardly anyone ever came this way alone. Shankar, however, loved sitting quietly in the secluded grove of this lonely temple courtyard.

Today, that dream at dawn had left a deep impression upon his mind. Sitting in the midst of this grove, that picture rose once again before Shankar's eyes—the herd of wild elephants snapping the bamboo thickets with a loud crash, and high above the dense forest of the mountain plateau, glimpsed through gaps in the leaves and creepers, the moon-pale, snow-clad peak of the mountain pointing like a beacon toward the border of some dreamland. He had dreamed so many dreams in his life—never had he seen so vivid a picture in a dream, and never had any dream etched so deep a mark upon his heart...

From the first day of the New Year, the editor of 'Bharati' will open a 'Kheyalkhata'—a Notebook of Whims—for Bharati. With this intention, she has sent invitations to contribute a line or two to many people who write, or can write, or ought to write, or ought to be able to write. Which of the four above-mentioned groups I belong to, I do not quite know. Even so, considering it my duty to honor the gracious invitation of the editor of Bharati, I have set out to compose a few lines. The editor of Bharati has given the assurance that one may write whatever one pleases; there is no need to introduce or discuss any particular subject. How others react to this proposal I cannot say, but in me it inspires more fear than confidence. Both by nature and by training, our minds are so bound to set subjects that once the prop of a topic is taken away, the workings of our mind come to a halt, and we have nothing left to say. Writing on emptiness is about as easy as walking on air. Whatever may be the case in mathematics, in literature you cannot multiply the value of a statement by piling zero upon zero. Ordering a garland strung without thread is easy enough; weaving it is not so easy. Barely one in a hundred knows the secret of that art. The real truth is that we are all sunk in deep slumber; only a few of us dream. The wish of Bharati's editor is to give this latter group a little opportunity to ramble aloud.
This Kheyalkhata is Bharati's subscription book. Whatever anyone gives willingly and with an unburdened heart will be gladly accepted. Half-rupees, quarter-rupees, two-anna bits—nothing will be turned away; only worn-smooth coins and counterfeits will not do. However small the thought may be, it must be genuine—and if it sparkles as well, what more could one ask? An idea that has passed through a thousand hands, whose very features have been worn away almost to nothing, which no longer catches anyone's eye because it is all too familiar, will find no place in this Kheyalkhata. For the expression of thoroughly old thoughts and old sentiments, there is a separate arrangement—writing articles. When our practical words bear no fruit, what harm is there in cultivating flowers of idle talk? When we can find no way to satisfy our hunger, it becomes necessary to try to indulge our whims while daylight lasts. And it goes without saying that where there is no question of buying and selling—where the matter is purely one of giving and receiving—no gentleman, even if he earns his living by the pen, will try to pass off something he does not wholly believe himself or knows to be false. Since we cannot be true in the world of action, it is to be hoped that we shall not practice falsity in the world of imagination. That is why I say, worn coins and counterfeits will not do.
Whimsical writing is a very rare thing. For in this world there is no shortage of wayward, capricious people, but there is a great scarcity of people with true creative whimsy. What most people do requires labor; for ordinary folk, a tiny bit of inspiration is the result of a great deal of hard thought.

In this building in Mirpur, the elevator was often out of order, and on the days it worked, it was even more annoying. That was why Ritu had a grudge against the guy from the elevator. Tall, messy hair, headphones always in his ears. Last Tuesday, he had held the door, and Ritu had come running. She had meant to thank him, but the guy didn't even look up.

"Some people don't see anyone but themselves," she had told her friend over the phone.

That very week, the book arrived. An old novel bought from an online seller in Nilkhet, a twenty-year-old edition. But the delivery boy left the book at the door of 5C, while Ritu's flat was 5B. Three days later, the book came back inside an envelope slipped under her door, along with a yellow sticky note:

"Sorry, it came to the wrong flat. I kept it for three days because I ended up reading it. Pleading guilty."

Ritu tried not to smile, but she smiled anyway. Opening the book, she saw pencil marks from a previous owner in the margins. And underneath them, a new note in a different hand, neat and slightly slanted:

"I stopped at this part. I'd like to know if you stop here too."

She picked up a pencil and wrote, "I stopped. But I think the character is making a mistake."

The book slipped back under the door into 5C.

Sensing disaster, the other generals hurried forward and said, "Cleitus, have you lost your mind? Whom are you speaking to like this? He is our Emperor!" With utter disdain, Cleitus said, "Go on, get away! Alexander may be your Emperor, but he is nothing to me! I will not obey his commands!" The poison of wine had gone to Alexander's head by then, and he could no longer stomach such humiliation in front of everyone. With a terrifying roar of ungovernable fury, he leaped to his feet and, before an eyelid could blink, snatched a spear from beside him and drove it up to the hilt into Cleitus's chest! Cleitus's body rolled over onto the ground, twitched once or twice, and then lay utterly still! At this unimaginable sight, everyone stood stunned and dumbfounded—the melody of the flutes, the song of the singers, the dance of the dancing-girl, and the joyous clamor of the festival all ceased at once! Standing like a statue of stone, Alexander stared with dazed eyes as streams of blood gushed in spurts over Cleitus's lifeless, motionless body! Within moments, Alexander's unblinking, wide-open eyes filled to the brim with tears, and the very next instant, weeping inconsolably like a child, he cried out, "Cleitus—my brother, savior of my life! Speak to me, friend, speak to me!" Yet Cleitus never spoke again. The spear was still embedded in Cleitus's chest. Suddenly Alexander bent down, wrenched the spear out with both hands, and moved to plunge it into his own chest. In a single bound, a bodyguard lunged forward and gripped his hands, spear and all. From all sides, the generals came rushing up with cries of alarm. Struggling wildly, Alexander cried out like a madman, "No—no! Let me go! I have murdered the very friend who saved my life! I am the vilest of sinners! Death is the only thing fit for me!" Old Parmenion, the commander-in-chief, was a man from the days of Alexander's father, King Philip. Stepping forward, he said, "Calm yourself, my son Alexander. What is done cannot be undone. Taking your own life will do no good at all." In an anguished voice, Alexander said, "I want to take my own life and go to Cleitus." Parmenion said, "If you take your own life, what will become of Greece? Who will lead this vast army? Who will conquer formidable India? It was your own high ambition to conquer the whole world—to exalt the glory of our homeland, Greece! Greece cannot do without you—do you have no duty toward her?" Parmenion had struck the exact right chord. Recovering his composure, Alexander spoke out in a firm voice: "You have spoken truly, General; I have a duty toward my homeland—if I take my own life, Greece will never become the Empress of the World. Our duty now is to conquer India! Having come this far and shed so much blood, we cannot turn back! Input: "I'm drowning, I'm drowning, save me!" Sundarbabu screamed out once again. He could distinctly feel two bony, skin-and-bone arms—yet hard as iron and freezing cold as ice—wrapping around him and dragging him down toward the netherworld, dragging him relentlessly! Overcome with terrible dread, he could not look at it properly, to be sure, yet the dim glimpse he caught was quite enough for him. It was the figure of a dead man—a living dead man—and its two eyes were like those of a dead fish! Cutting through the water with both arms as he swam forward, Ramhari saw in terror that with a hideous cry of "Hmph!", Sundarbabu went under with a splash, and at that very instant Bagha too dived beneath the water. Over on the other side, Bimal, Kumar, Jayanta, and Manik had also plunged into the water by then and were swimming forward. But they did not have to come much further; suddenly Sundarbabu was seen bobbing up again and swimming with all his might back toward the shore! Bagha too had surfaced again! Ramhari was very close by. He saw a patch of blood on the water, and Bagha's mouth too was stained with blood. Grasping what had happened, he praised him, saying, "Bravo, Bagha, bravo!" But of that strange and impossible figure, no trace at all could be found. Everyone climbed ashore. Apart from Sundarbabu, Ramhari, and Bagha, no one else had seen that hideous figure, so no one could yet make out what had actually happened. Lying stretched out flat on the sand with his arms and legs sprawled wide, Sundarbabu began panting like a pair of bellows. Bimal asked, "Sundarbabu, did a shark catch hold of you?" Kumar said, "No, Bimal, that cannot be. Had a shark caught him, he wouldn't have come back with his body unscathed like that." Bimal said, "Hmm, that's true. But then who could attack him underwater?" Out of breath, Sundarbabu simply kept panting! Right now he did not even have the strength to utter a single "Hmph!" With a solemn face, Bagha came over and sniffed Sundarbabu all over, presumably inspecting whether his body was intact or not! The result of the inspection must certainly have been satisfactory, for he began wagging his tail briskly to express his delight. Jayanta said, "Could there be an octopus in the water here?" Ramhari asked, "What did you say?" "An octopus." "Does it look like a human being?" "Not at all. To give you some idea, one might rather say it looks a lot like a huge, strange spider. They hide in the seawater and wrap their eight legs around their prey to suck out its flesh and blood." "No, babu, no. That grotesque creature you speak of is surely terrifying, but the thing that grabbed hold of Sundarbabu looked like a human being." Bursting into loud laughter, Bimal said, "What are you talking about, Ramhari! Is man an aquatic creature? After attacking from underwater, could a human stay submerged beneath the water for this long?" Turning his head, Manik saw that the vast, lake-like expanse of water lay completely still. Apart from their ship and the lifeboat, there was not a trace of any living creature upon it. Bimal had spoken the truth. Whatever had attacked Sundarbabu was surely not a human being!

He hardly needed to tell Shankar that, for Shankar had already gathered from the very look of these regions that they were no pleasure park. He asked, "How far is that yellow diamond mine of yours? As far as can be made out from the map, this right here is the Richtersveld mountain range."

The tiger said, 'Alright, ask it; let's see what it says.'

Thakurmashai said, 'My good banyan tree, you are very old and have seen and heard a great deal. Tell me now, does anyone do harm to one who does them good?'

The banyan tree replied, 'Why, that is the very first thing people do! Those people over there sat in my shade to cool themselves off, and then they jabbed into my trunk to draw out my sap. The tiger said, 'Well, Thakurmashai, what does it say?'

Input: Calcutta's English 'fog'! Stepping out onto the street, I saw what a state the city was in today! Everything all around was covered as if under a canopy of fog. I had never imagined that there could be such fog in Calcutta! Lifting one's face, one could not tell that anything like a blue sky studded with a million spangled stars even existed overhead! Whichever way I looked, this way or that—every sight seemed to have vanished into the womb of thick smoke upon smoke. Wherever there were gas-posts, the fog around them had grown slightly translucent, nothing more, while the lights themselves could not be seen. From time to time, the sound of footsteps could be heard, but the pedestrians were invisible! Hemanta said, "O Rabin, what is this, my friend! Has London's famous English 'fog' come to pay a visit to the premier city of the British Empire?" Hemanta was only an arm's length away from me, yet even he looked like a shadowy apparition! For one thing, this narrow lane behind Matibabu's house was ordinarily deserted; on top of that, it was a freezing winter night with this dreadful mist! It felt as though we were walking like blind men through a silent kingdom of darkness! Behind us, the sound of more than one pair of invisible shoes rang out again. I called out, "Who comes there—careful! Do not trip over our bodies." The very next moment, I felt a tremendous blow upon my head, bright yellow mustard flowers scattered in heaps before my eyes, and right after that I lost consciousness!... How long I remained unconscious, I do not know. But the moment my consciousness returned, I heard Hemanta's voice—"Rabin, Rabin!" —"Eh? What are you saying? Ugh." —"Sit up—" Hemanta held me, helped me sit up, and said, "Your head is split open. It needs to be bandaged right away! Can you walk quickly to my house?" —"I think I can. But who attacked me?" —"No talk now, let us go home first." ...Returning to his own house, Hemanta examined my wound and said, "You have had a narrow escape, Rabin; just a little more and the blow would have been fatal." He quickly washed the wound with water, applied medicine, and sat down to tie a bandage. —"But Hemanta, why would hooligans suddenly attack me?" —"Not hooligans, Rabin—murderers!" —"Murderers?" —"Yes. This is the handiwork of Matibabu's murderers! They attacked not only you, but me as well." —"Did you manage to see them?" —"I saw them like shadowy outlines. Even if I had seen them clearly, I wouldn't have recognised them; they came wearing masks." —"But why?" —"They stole that glove from my pocket and fled." Astonished, I began to think. Then I said, "My suspicion falls upon Binod. Surely he was hiding in the next room and overheard your opinion about the glove." —"And then followed us with one of his henchmen?" —"Hmm. Today's foul fog turned out to be a grand opportunity for him." —"It might also turn out to be a disaster for him, Rabin." —"A disaster?" —"Yes, to some extent indeed!" —"Meaning?" —"Look at this!" Laughing, Hemanta pulled a pocketbook out of his pocket and placed it on the table in front of us. —"A pocketbook!" —"Yes." Opening the pocketbook and flipping through a page or two, he said in a slightly surprised tone, "No, it is not what I had thought!"

Input: —"Victory, victory, victory to India!" That full-throated cry of victory echoed right into Alexander's tent. And the very next moment, from the united throats of the Greeks, rose once more that deep roar like the surging sea—"Victory, victory, victory to Alexander!" Alexander did not know the language of India. He asked, "Who is shouting along with my soldiers in a foreign tongue, and what are they saying?" At once an interpreter came in and reported, "Three Indian soldiers were passing this way. Hearing that we are going to invade India, they are raising cries of victory in India's name." In an astonished voice, Alexander said, "What extraordinary courage they have! There are only three of them, and yet they stand before my troops shouting victory to India!" —"Emperor, they are not standing still—they are shouting as they gallop away at full speed on horseback!" Knitting his brows, Alexander reflected for a few moments. Then he asked, "Which way did they gallop off?" —"Toward the south." —"Toward the south? That means toward India!" Suddenly Alexander sprang to his feet in a single bound. Then he shouted at the top of his voice, "Let my soldiers mount swift horses and ride after them at once! Capture them! Slay them! Otherwise we shall fall into grave danger!" The interpreter hurried outside to proclaim the order. Pacing restlessly up and down inside the tent, Alexander said, "My soldiers are fools! Why did they let them get away?" Several Greek commanders were present there. One of them stepped forward and said, "Emperor, why are you getting so worked up over such a trifling matter? What harm can those three lone fugitive soldiers possibly do to us?" Alexander said, "You are no less foolish yourselves! Do you call this a trifling matter? Can you not see that the later India learns of this expedition of ours, the better? Giving the enemy time to prepare is tantamount to attempting suicide! If all of India gets time to take up arms, what will become of us? Those three soldiers are riding hard for India to warn their homeland! Capture them, slay them, silence their voices!" —"Emperor, India lies hundreds upon hundreds of kos away from here! The fugitives will surely be caught long before they can get there!" * * * "True indeed! Samarkand and India! Between them lie hundreds upon hundreds of kos of roads and trackless wastes—rivers like the Amu Darya, mountains like the Hindu Kush, desolate forests, vast desert plains, and how many other formidable obstacles! Pushing through so many hazards and hardships, will the three travelers of that rugged road ever be able to return to the shelter of their homeland? How many suns will set, how many moons will rise, how many stars will blossom; at times the wind will burn like fire and at times freeze like snow; at times the sky will hurl thunderbolts and at times unleash tempestuous storms; fierce beasts will awake roaring in forest after forest; bandits more ruthless still will spring out of ambush from nooks and crannies—and along with all that, riding hard on their trail with grim determination are thirty mounted Greek soldiers! Will the sons of India ever return to India? Of that last danger, they had no inkling at first. Having begun their return journey, their swift horses had had the chance to cover a good deal of ground. Nor had it taken a small amount of time for the thirty Greek soldiers to equip themselves and set out. Moreover, the three fortune-seeking heroes of India knew the roads and passes back to their homeland thoroughly—knowledge that the Greeks did not possess. Stopping at village after village to gather news of when and by which route the three Indians had passed was also causing the Greeks considerable delay.

The jackal asked, 'What happened now?'

Hiji Bij Bij said, 'There was once a man who was touched in the head, and he used to give fancy names to everything he owned. His shoes were named Abimrishyakarita—Rashness; his umbrella was named Pratyutpannamatitva—Presence of Mind; his water-pot was named Paramakalyanabareshu—Unto the Most Auspicious One; but the moment he named his house Kingkartabyabimurha—Utterly Perplexed, an earthquake struck and the house and everything came crashing down! Ho, ho, ho, ho!'

The jackal said, 'Is that so? Let's hear what your name is.'

It replied, 'Right now my name is Hiji Bij Bij.'

The jackal asked, 'What do you mean by "right now" and "back then" for a name?' Hiji Bij Bij said, 'You don't even know that? In the morning my name stays Alu-Narkol—Potato-Coconut, and a little later in the afternoon my name will turn into Ramtaru.'

The jackal asked, 'Where is your nibas—residence?'

Hiji Bij Bij asked, 'Who are you talking about? Srinivas? Srinivas has gone back to his native village.' Immediately, from the middle of the crowd, Udho and Budho yelled out together, 'Then Srinivas must surely have died!'

Udho said, 'The moment people go back to their native village, they all drop dead—hush, hush!'

Budho said, 'No sooner had Habul's uncle gone to his native village than we heard he had died.'

The jackal said, 'Ah, don't all talk at once, it makes a terrible racket.'

Hearing this, Udho snapped at Budho, 'If you all talk at once again, I'll beat you till you're finished!' Budho retorted, 'If you make a racket again, I'll grab you and thrash you flat with my bundle!'

The jackal said, 'Your Honor, these fellows are all lunatics and idiots; their testimony has no value whatsoever.'

Hearing this, the crocodile lashed its tail in anger and said, 'Who says it has no value? We are having him give testimony by spending a proper four annas in hard cash!' Saying this, it immediately counted out sixteen pice—clink, clink!—and handed them over to Hiji Bij Bij.

At once someone called out from overhead, 'Witness No. 1, cash account, value four annas.' Looking up, I saw Kakkeshwar perched up there writing down the accounts.

The jackal asked again, 'Do you know anything else about this matter or not?'

Hiji Bij Bij thought for a bit and said, 'There is a song about jackals; I know that one.'

The jackal said, 'What song is that, let's hear?'

Chanting in a sing-song voice, Hiji Bij Bij began, 'Come, come, come, jackals eat brinjal, where do they get oil and salt at all—'

Before it could go on, the jackal grew terribly flustered and interrupted, 'Enough, enough, that's about some other jackals—your testimony is finished!'

Meanwhile, what had happened was that, seeing witnesses getting paid in coins, a tremendous scramble broke out among everyone to give evidence. Everyone was shoving and jostling everyone else, when suddenly I saw Kakkeshwar hop down from the tree with a thud, take his seat in the witness box, and start giving testimony. Before anyone could ask him a thing, he began rattling off, 'Salutations unto Sri Sri Bhushandikagaya. Sri Kakkeshwar Kuchkuche, No. 41 Gechobazar, Kageyapati. We carry out all kinds of calculations, accounted and unaccounted, retail and wholesale—'

The jackal snapped, 'Stop talking nonsense and answer what I ask you! What is your name?'

The crow replied, 'What a nuisance! That's just what I was telling you—Sri Kakkeshwar Kuchkuche.'

The jackal asked, 'Where is your residence?'

The crow said, 'I just told you, Kageyapati.'

The jackal asked, 'How far is that from here?'

The crow said, 'That is very hard to say. By the hour it is four annas, by the mile it is ten pice, and if you pay cash it's two pice less. If you add it up it's ten annas, if you subtract it's three annas, if you divide it's seven pice, and if you multiply it comes to twenty-one rupees.'

What else do you call a stroke of bad luck? The wretched canine-tooth got off the bus at the Harrison Road crossing. Then he walked a short distance ahead and went into a coffee-house. Scratching his head, Hemanta was pondering what ought to be done next, when an inspector from the Burrabazar police station arrived on the spot. —"Well, well, if it isn't Hemantababu! Why are you standing here basking in the sun at such an odd hour?" Pointing his finger toward the coffee-house, Hemanta said, "I am watching that man! That one over there, wearing a striped lungi and a striped red vest, sitting and gulping down food ravenously!" The inspector looked closely at the man for nearly a minute, and then said in astonishment, "The rascal has no small nerve! Sitting here openly in broad daylight, merrily enjoying his meal! Hailing a taxi to return home, he said, "Well, old chap, did you see the glory of criminology?"... ...That nearly completed house on Paresh Mitra Lane suddenly caught Hemanta's eye. But nowadays I see that even Bengalis are not ashamed to build houses down the streets of Calcutta in imitation of 'skyscrapers'! Look at this new house. এই কনারক মন্দির আর তাজমহলের দেশে এসেও সেই ঢঙে ‘মেট্রো’—সিনেমার বাড়ী তৈরী করেছে। সেটা আমাদের চোখকে আঘাত দিলেও ‘মেট্রো’র কর্তৃপক্ষকে দোষ দিতে চাই না। কারণ তারা হচ্ছে সেই দেশের লোক যারা বিদেশের ঠাকুর ফেলে স্বদেশের কুকুর ধ’রে আদর ক’রে মনুষ্যত্বের পরিচয় দেয়। কিন্তু আজকাল বাঙালীরাও দেখছি কলকাতার পথে পথে ‘স্কাইস্‌ক্রেপারে’র নকলে ঘরবাড়ী তৈরি করতে লজ্জিত হয় ন॥ এই নতুন বাড়ীখানার দিকে চেয়ে দেখ। এই বিদেশ আদর্শের বদ্-হজম সহ্য করা অসম্ভব। এমন অনুকরণপ্রিয় জাতি কোনদিনই স্বাধীন হ’তে পারবে না!” বিরক্ত চোখে হেমন্ত আরো কিছুক্ষন সেইখানে দাঁড়িয়ে রইল। আমি বললুম, “তোমার স্থাপত্যের সমালোচনা রেখে এখন দশ নম্বরের বাড়ী খোঁজো। পাঁচটা বাজে যে, চায়ের সময় উত্তীর্ণ হয়ে যায়!”

None of the coolies wanted to work anymore. Along the long line, the pickaxe-wielding coolies often had to divide into very small groups to work—even during the daytime they did not want to go very far from the camp. Staying inside the tent at night was not safe either. Fear was in everyone's mind—each one thought his turn was next. There was no certainty about whom it would take or when. Work could not go on under such conditions. Only the Maasai coolies remained unshaken—they did not fear even Yama, the god of death. Two miles away from the camp, they alone did the pickaxe work, and the sahib went with a gun four or five times a day to check on them.

So many new measures were taken, yet nothing reduced the lion's menace. Despite every effort, the lion could not be hunted down. Many said there was not just one lion, but many—how many could be killed? The sahib said, "Man-eating lions are not found in large numbers. This is the work of a single lion."

One day the sahib called Shankar and asked him to take the gun and go check on the pickaxe coolies once. Shankar said, "Sahib, give me your Mannlicher."

The sahib agreed. Taking the gun, Shankar mounted a mule and set off—about a mile from the camp there was a small marsh in one place. By the time Shankar caught sight of the marsh from afar, it was nearly three o'clock in the afternoon. There was no one in any direction, and the fierce glare of the sun had created heat waves across the plain.

Suddenly the mule stopped dead in its tracks. By no means would it go any further forward. It seemed to Shankar that the mule was afraid to go toward that spot. A little later, something stirred in the bushes beside the path. But looking that way, he could see nothing. He dismounted from the mule. Even then, the mule refused to budge.

Suddenly it was as if a bolt of electricity shot through Shankar's body. Was the lion not lying in ambush for him inside the bush? He knew that this often happened—hiding in the bushes beside the path, a lion silently stalks its prey for a long distance. Finding a suitable spot in a lonely place, it leaps upon its neck. What if that were the case? Shankar did not think it wise to go any further forward with the mule. He thought he might as well return to the camp. He had just turned the mule's head toward the camp when something stirred in the bushes again. Immediately there came a terrifying roar of a lion, and a huge tawny-grey body crashed down noisily upon the mule. Shankar was about four cubits ahead at the time; he spun around at once, raised his gun, and fired twice in quick succession. Whether the bullets hit or not could not be told, but by then the mule had collapsed on the ground—and the tawny-grey beast had fled. Examining the mule, Shankar saw that a large chunk of flesh near its shoulder was torn to shreds, and the ground was flooding with blood. It was thrashing about in agony. With a single shot, Shankar put an end to its suffering.

Then he returned to the camp. The sahib said the lion must surely have been wounded. If a bullet from that gun hit its body, it would certainly be badly wounded. But had the bullet actually hit it? Shankar said he could not say for sure whether the shots had hit or missed. He had fired the gun, that was all. Even after searching with men for two or three days, no trace of any wounded or dead lion was found anywhere.

From the beginning of June, the rains set in. Partly because of the lion's menace, and partly because the proximity of the marsh made the place unhealthy, the camp was shifted from there.

Shankar no longer had to stay in the construction camp. Getting the job of stationmaster at a small station about thirty miles from Kisumu, he took his belongings and went there.

কুলীরা আর কেহ কাজ করতে চায় না। লম্বা লাইনে গাঁতিওয়ালা কুলীদের অনেক সময়ে খুব ছোট দলে ভাগ হয়ে কাজ করতে হয়—তারা তাঁবু ছেড়ে দিনের বেলাতেও বেশী দূর যেতে চায় না। তাঁবুর মধ্যে থাকাও রাত্রে নিরাপদ নয়। সকলের মনে ভয়—প্রত্যেকেই ভাবে এইবার তার পালা। কাকে কখন নেবে কিছু স্থিরতা নেই। এই অবস্থায় কাজ হয় না। কেবল মাসাই কুলীরা অবিচলিত রইল—তারা যমকেও ভয় করে না। তাঁবু থেকে দু’মাইল দূরে গাঁতির কাজ তারাই করে, সাহেব বন্দুক নিয়ে দিনের মধ্যে চার-পাঁচবার তাদের দেখাশোনা করে আসে।

কত নতুন ব্যবস্থা করা হোল, কিছুতেই সিংহের উপদ্রব কম্‌ল না। কত চেষ্টা করেও সিংহ শিকার করা গেল না। অনেকে বল্লে সিংহ একটা নয়, অনেকগুলো—ক’টা মেরে ফেলা যাবে? সাহেব বল্লে—মানুষ-খেকো সিংহ বেশি থাকে না। এ একটা সিংহেরই কাজ।

একদিন সাহেব শঙ্করকে ডেকে বল্লে বন্দুকটা নিয়ে গাঁতিদার কুলীদের একবার দেখে আসতে। শঙ্কর বল্লে—সাহেব, তোমার ম্যান্‌লিকারটা দাও।

সাহেব রাজী হোল। শঙ্কর বন্দুক নিয়ে একটা অশ্বতরে চড়ে রওনা হোল—তাঁবু থেকে মাইল দূরে একজায়গায় একটা ছোট জলা। শঙ্কর দূর থেকে জলাটা যখন দেখতে পেয়েচে, তখন বেলা প্রায় তিনটে। কেউ কোনো দিকে নেই, রোদের ঝাঁজ মাঠের মধ্যে তাপ-তরঙ্গের সৃষ্টি করেচে।

হঠাৎ অশ্বতর থম্‌কে দাঁড়িয়ে গেল। আর কিছুতেই সেটা এগিয়ে যেতে চায় না। শঙ্করের মনে হল জায়গাটার দিকে যেতে অশ্বতরটা ভয় পাচ্চে। একটু পরে পাশের ঝোপে কি যেন একটা নড়ল। কিন্তু সেদিকে চেয়ে সে কিছু দেখতে পেলে না। সে অশ্বতর থেকে নামল। তবুও অশ্বতর নড়তে চায় না।

হঠাৎ শঙ্করের শরীরে যেন বিদ্যুৎ খেলে গেল। ঝোপের মধ্যে সিংহ তার জন্যে ওৎ পেতে বসে নেই তো? অনেক সময়ে এরকম হয় সে জানে, সিংহ পথের পাশে ঝোপ্‌ঝাপের, মধ্যে লুকিয়ে অনেক দূর পর্য্যন্ত নিঃশব্দে তার শিকারের অনুসরণ করে। নির্জ্জন স্থানে সুবিধা বুঝে তার ঘাড়ের উপর লাফিয়ে পড়ে। যদি তাই হয়? শঙ্কর অশ্বতর নিয়ে আর এগিয়ে যাওয়া উচিত বিবেচনা করলে না। ভাবলে তাঁবুতে ফিরেই যাই। সবে সে তাঁবুর দিকে অশ্বতরের মুখটা ফিরিয়েছে এমন সময় আবার ঝোপের মধ্যে কি একটা নড়ল। সঙ্গে সঙ্গে ভয়ানক সিংহ গর্জ্জন এবং একটা ধূসর বর্ণের বিরাট দেহ সশব্দে অশ্বতরের ওপর এসে পড়ল। শঙ্কর তখন হাত চারেক এগিয়ে আছে, সে তখনি ফিরে দাঁড়িয়ে বন্দুক উঁচিয়ে উপরি উপরি দু’বার গুলি করলে। গুলি লেগেচে কিনা বোঝা গেল না, কিন্তু তখন অশ্বতর মাটীতে লুটিয়ে পড়েচে—ধূসর বর্ণের জানোয়ারটা পলাতক। শঙ্কর পরীক্ষা করে দেখলে অশ্বতরের কাঁধের কাছে অনেকটা মাংস ছিন্ন ভিন্ন, রক্তে মাটী ভেসে যাচ্চে। যন্ত্রণায় সে ছট্‌ফট্‌ করচে। শঙ্কর এক গুলিতে তার যন্ত্রনার অবসান করলে।

তারপর সে তাঁবুতে ফিরে এল। সাহেব বল্লে সিংহ নিশ্চয়ই জখম হয়েচে। বন্দুকের গুলি যদি গায়ে লাগে তবে দস্তুর মত জখম তাকে হতেই হবে। কিন্তু গুলি লেগেছিল তো? শঙ্কর বল্লে গুলি লাগালাগির কথা সে বলতে পারে না। বন্দুক ছুঁড়েছিল, এইমাত্র কথা। লোকজন নিয়ে খোঁজাখুঁজি করে দু তিন দিনেও কোনো আহত বা মৃত সিংহের সন্ধান কোথাও পাওয়া গেল না।

জুন মাসের প্রথম থেকে বর্ষা নাম্‌ল। কতকটা সিংহের উপদ্রবের জন্যে, কতকটা বা জলাভূমির সান্নিধ্যের জন্যে জায়গাটা অস্বাস্থ্যকর হওয়ায় তাঁবু ওখান থেকে উঠে গেল।

শঙ্করকে আর কনষ্ট্রাক্‌সন তাঁবুতে থাকতে হোল না। কিসুমু থেকে প্রায় ত্রিশ মাইল দূরে একটা ছোট ষ্টেশনে সে ষ্টেশন মাষ্টারের কাজ পেয়ে জিনিষ পত্র নিয়ে সেইখানেই চলে গেল।

I said, 'Instead of all that, you might as well just say your whole clan is called Hiji Bij Bij.'

Thinking again for a bit, it said, 'Why, no, my name is Takai! My maternal uncle's name is Takai, my paternal uncle's name is Takai, my maternal aunt's husband's name is Takai, my father-in-law's name is Takai—'

I scolded it, 'Are you telling the truth, or making it up?'

Looking rather flustered, the creature said, 'No, no, my father-in-law's name is Biscuit.'

I got terribly angry and snapped at it, 'I don't believe a single word of yours!'

Right then, out of the blue, a huge bearded goat poked its head out from behind the bush and asked, 'Are you talking about me?'

I was about to say 'No,' but before I could utter a word, it rattled on at top speed, 'No matter how much you people argue, there are plenty of things that goats do not eat. So I would like to deliver a lecture, and its subject is—What Goats Do Not Eat.' Saying this, it suddenly stepped forward and began its lecture—

'O assembly of boys and my dear Hiji Bij Bij, simply by looking at the certificate hanging around my neck, you can see that my name is Sri Byakaran Shing, B.A., Khadyabisharad—Expert in Food. I can bleat "Baa" splendidly, which is why my name is Byakaran, and as for Shing—horns—you can see them for yourselves. When I write it in English, I write B.A., which stands for "Baa." Which things are edible and which things are not—I have tested them all myself, and therefore my title is Khadyabisharad. When you people say, "What will a madman not say, what will a goat not eat"—that is gross injustice. Why, just a moment ago that rascal over there was claiming that billy goats eat geckos. That is an utter and complete falsehood! I have licked many kinds of geckos to see, and there is nothing worth eating in them at all. Input: Ha! Ha! Ha! Ha! What are you saying?—Why am I laughing? Huh—why am I laughing!—Who knows! Perhaps I am laughing simply because I cannot cry! A sandbank has formed inside my chest, you see! All the water has dried up, I tell you, completely dried up. Nothing comes out. So instead of crying, no tears come from my eyes anymore—I just laugh and laugh! — Yes, as I was saying. Father refused to even lift his head and look at me. When Mother tried to speak up on my behalf, she only got scolded by him instead. Father said, "I have never even seen fifty thousand rupees with my own eyes. The girl is blind—so what! Can one let go of so much money?" The girl cannot see with her eyes, and Father too had never seen fifty thousand rupees with his eyes. Once the marriage took place, even though the girl still wouldn't be able to see, Father would at least get to see all that money with his own eyes!—There, that was enough, quite enough! Just so that he could feast his eyes on that money, I had to get married. Mother is terribly naive. A woman, after all! She said, "Still, you have to consider the boy's side of it too!" Father grew angry and said, "One ought to look first toward the person whom God has struck down! Don't you know she is blind!" Ha! Ha!—What a sense of religious duty Father had! Yet Father deliberately refused to understand this simple point of mine: that there were plenty of other people in the world besides me to look after the one whom God had struck down. This Bengal of ours is overflowing with compassion! If you can put down fifty thousand rupees here, a marriage never gets held up even if the bride is blind; if the father of a Bengali groom gets money, he can drag a dead girl straight off the funeral pyre to the chhadnatala! Father went on to say, "If only I were young enough, I would have married this girl myself—" Mother hastily cut him short and said, "Hush, hush! What on earth are you saying!" Father was quite right, though. Twice a day he performs his sandhya-ahnik prayers, wears a tiki on his head and a sacred poite thread around his neck—should he not look kindly upon one whom God has struck down? Ha! Ha!—I didn't have any objection to that either. Sadly enough, Father did not get much time to feast his eyes on those fifty thousand rupees. Death came and, making Father just as blind as this blind bride of mine, led him away into the darkness. I do not know whether he can still hear the clink of those fifty thousand rupees of this mortal world from across the river Baitarani. Ha! Ha!—And, and—the sound of this laughter of mine! Is that reaching his ears too? Is the sound of this laughter striking blow after blow against every bone in his chest, against every rib of his—striking, striking, striking? I want to know that. Can anyone tell me? Benu is not merely blind. By making her as dark as darkness itself, God has filled the cup of poison to the brim and set it right before my face. Yet who gave her that name—Benu, the bamboo flute? Never have I seen a name ring so true! Astonishing! All her lack of beauty, all her lack of sight seemed to have found perfection inside that sweet, soft, yet sorrow-laden voice of hers. Still, she was blind. She was dark. Looking at her filled me with revulsion, filled me with rage. Why did she plunge me into her own eternal darkness and darken my life as well? Why did she do it—why?

Input: "On the banks of the Five Rivers, coiling their hair upon their heads, before one's very eyes, at the Guru's mantra, awoke the Sikh—ruthless, fearless." Surely all of you know Rabindranath's wonderful ballad. Yet it was not only the Sikhs who awoke on the banks of the Five Rivers; it was here, first of all, that the great soul of Aryan India awoke. On the banks of the Five Rivers, time and again, India has risen and fallen. How many—oh, how many times has India risen only to fall, and fallen only to rise again! She has been wounded, never slain. On the banks of these Five Rivers, in some age beyond memory, wave after wave of Aryan expeditions broke like a flood over non-Aryan settlements! And thereafter, on the banks of these very Five Rivers, age after age witnessed the procession of nation after nation—Persian, Greek, Saka, Hun, Tatar, Mughal, and Pathan! The path by which they set forth to greet Great India—that ever-famous Khyber Pass—still stands immovable today with the same haughty frown! How many epics could every grain of dust there recite! Only the roar of the British Lion came floating from across the Indian Ocean. Yet in one sense, the India of those days never looked upon the ocean as a great barrier—because the sea-route was her own path of world conquest. By that route she herself set out from land to land to trade, to preach religion, to conquer kingdoms, and to establish colonies—in Cambodia, in Java, and in Egypt! And from Alexandria in Egypt to Greece and Rome! That anyone else could come by that route to conquer her was a tale that never entered ancient India's dreams. What are you thinking? Am I telling a story, or repeating history? Bear with me a little. You love to hear tales of adventure. The extraordinary adventure I am going to tell you about this time is the great adventure of Great India and Great Greece! When the Aryan migration began southward from Central Asia, one group of them came to India, while another went to Persia. That is to say, the Aryans of India and the Aryans of Persia were originally the very same people. Even within the religions of ancient India and ancient Persia, ample evidence of this unity can be discovered. However, after living in different lands for many centuries, the Indians and the Persians completely forgot their shared ancestry. The Aryan Hindus lived in Northern India. And they deeply despised the southern regions of India as non-Aryan lands. They did not even deign to regard Anga, Banga, and Kalinga; if any orthodox Brahmin came to this region, he was considered fallen. That old attitude has not entirely vanished even today. Even today, the Brahmins of Northern India do not look upon Bengali Brahmins with respect. Yet by such an irony of fate, it was the mixed-caste Kshatriyas of this despised non-Aryan land, or Eastern India, who later became foremost across all of India in religion and in valor! Right around Bengal rose the Sisunaga dynasty, the Nanda dynasty, the Maurya dynasty (in which Chandragupta and Ashoka were born), the Gupta dynasty, and others; though not pure Aryans, the heroes of these dynasties gradually extended their empires across the whole of India. In religion, too, we see the rise of Buddhism in this region in the seventh century before Christ, and Lord Buddha himself was not a pure Kshatriya. It was around this time, on the banks of the Five Rivers held by the Indian Hindus, that the first foreign enemy—King Darius the First of Persia—appeared with a drawn sword in his hand. Ancient India had no written history. Therefore, what actually happened cannot be known for certain. The Persians, however, claim that they conquered India. Yet the opinion of historians is that the Persians could not advance very far beyond the lands bordering the Indus River! Outside of that, throughout most provinces of the rest of India, the powerful kings and princes who ruled at the time kept their independence and strength intact.

Sanskrit is a dead language because, bound in the serpent-noose of grammar, Sanskrit gave up the ghost. He further contends that spoken language has no grammar, whereas written language cannot do without grammar. The proof: Sanskrit alone has attained immortality, while Prakrit languages such as Pali have died out forever. Put in a single sentence, for any language whatsoever, to live forever it must first die. If that is so, then if Bangla wishes to hang itself with the rope of grammar, what objection can Vidyabhushan Mahashay have? According to his view, one must enter the city of immortality through the gates of Yama, the god of death. He also says that thousands upon thousands of books were composed in Prakrit languages like Pali, yet because Prakrit is not Sanskrit, Pali and such languages have vanished. Therefore, the closer we can bring Bangla to Sanskrit, the better for it. If Vidyabhushan Mahashay's view is true, then why write in Sanskritized Bangla—it is our duty to write directly in the Sanskrit language itself! Because then there would be no doubt left about becoming immortal. But there is one thing I cannot quite understand: it is true that Pali and such languages are dead, but is not Sanskrit dead too? That language of the gods may be immortal, but not in this mortal world. In this world, no one can escape the hand of death; Pali could not, Sanskrit could not, and our mother tongue will not be able to either. Why, then, impose this harsh sentence of hard labor upon Bangla—that for the few days it remains alive, it must carry the corpse of Sanskrit around on its shoulders? Bangla has only a tiny breath of life; it will not bear such a crushing weight.
On this matter, if I have not misunderstood Shastri Mahashay's argument, his view in brief comes down to this: if we make Bangla nearly Sanskrit, learning the Bangla language will become a very easy affair for outsiders such as the Assamese and Hindustanis. Second, Bangla has an advantage that no other language possesses—no matter what Sanskrit word you drop into writing or where you place it, the Banglaness of the Bangla language is not spoiled. In other words, so that those who do not know our language may understand it easily, we must make our written language incomprehensible to ordinary Bangalis. The proposition is so bizarre that one is at a loss how to answer it. So let us see whether his other point is valid. In our country, little boys believe that if you tack an anusvara onto the end of a Bangla word, it becomes Sanskrit; and grown-ups hold the view that if you trim the anusvara and visarga off a Sanskrit word, it becomes Bangla. Both beliefs are equally true. Does docking a monkey's tail turn it into a human being? By way of example, Shastri Mahashay says that in Hindi, 'ghar me jayega' works, but 'griha me jayega' does not—that would be bad Hindi. Yet in Bangla, 'griha' can be used anywhere and everywhere in place of 'ghar.' That is to say, every language has rules, except the Bangla language. Anyone can write whatever they please, and the language is bound to be Bangla. The chief virtue of the Bangla language, then, is that a Bangali can be completely arbitrary in speech and writing. Using the very example Shastri Mahashay chose, that misconception of his can be dispelled.

Input: "The moment Matibabu heard of it, he flew into a towering rage! He was a terribly stern man to begin with, and on top of that, what he hated most in life was anyone who bet on the races or gambled. Binodlal was summoned at once. After receiving a fierce scolding and tongue-lashing from his uncle, he too lost his patience and gave Matibabu a piece of his mind in return. Beside himself with fury, Matibabu shouted, 'I will not leave a single paisa of my property to a gambler! I shall make a new will!' All this took place yesterday around midday. After that, Matibabu went out to his attorney's office. Bringing eighty thousand rupees from there, he returned home in the afternoon. After evening fell, he felt somewhat unwell. He retired to bed a little early, and before going to sleep he bolted the door of his room from the inside with his own hands. Do you know about the unseasonal downpour that came on yesterday evening? It rained for about an hour. The rain stopped at nine o'clock at night. In accordance with the household rule, at half-past ten at night the gatekeeper came and locked the door on the Kali Biswas Lane side before leaving. This morning, Matibabu's dead body was found lying on the floor, and the door of the room was standing open. Yet all the doors leading out of the house into the street were locked. When I received the news and went there, what I saw was this: Binodlal was weeping inconsolably like a child, while Mr. Datta was trying to comfort him. Matibabu's dead body was lying right beside the bedstead. On his face were the marks of terrible agony and fear—along with a hint of utter astonishment! Across his throat was a blue mark. On the bed were signs of a struggle. Scattered beside Matibabu's body lay large and small shards of a broken glass tumbler—some of the pieces stained with blood. And I found another strange thing as well: a very thick woolen glove! On the floor of the room there are muddy footprints—made by two different pairs of shoes. However, none of the prints is clear or complete enough for an exact measurement or cast to be taken. Even so, there is not the slightest doubt that two men entered this room after the rain. That one man stood waiting for a while right outside the door of the room can be deduced from the clear imprint of a pair of shoes left there. Looking at the impression of its grooved soles, one can tell further that he had come wearing rubber-soled shoes. Inside on the floor of the room, too, there are partial prints of those same rubber shoes. Thus it takes no time to realize that after the first man went into the room, he too stepped inside. I have taken a cast of those rubber shoe-prints outside the door. Looking at Matibabu's dead body, it appears that someone—or several people—throttled him to death. His iron safe is standing open; it was unlocked with Matibabu's own key. It isn't only the eighty thousand rupees in notes that have vanished from inside. Matibabu was also fond of lending out money at interest. He used to lend money against promissory hand-notes as well. There were several hand-notes inside the safe, and those too are gone. Nor can Matibabu's pocketbook be found! He had the habit of writing a diary every day."

বৃষ্টি হয় ঘণ্টাখানেক ধ’রে। বৃষ্টি থামে রাত ন’টার সময়। বাড়ীর নিয়মমত রাত সাড়েদশটার সময় দরোয়ান এসে কালী বিশ্বাস লেনের দিকের দরজা বন্ধ ক’রে দিয়ে যায়। আজ সকালে দেখা যায়, মেঝের উপরে মতিবাবুর মৃতদেহ প’ড়ে রয়েছে এবং ঘরের দরজা খোলা। কিন্তু বাড়ী থেকে রাস্তায় বেরুবার সব দরজাই বন্ধ। খবর পেয়ে আমি গিয়ে যা দেখলুম তা হচ্ছে এই। বিনোদলাল বালকের মত অধীর হয়ে কাঁদছেন আর মিঃ দত্ত তাঁকে সান্ত্বনা দেবার চেষ্টা করছেন। মতিবাবুর মৃতদেহ প’ড়ে রয়েছে ঠিক খাটের তলায়। তাঁর মুখের উপরে দারুণ যাতনা ও ভয়ের চিহ্ন—সেই সঙ্গে রয়েছে বিষম বিস্ময়েরও আভাস! তাঁর গলার উপরে একটা নীল দাগ। বিছানার উপরে ধবস্তাধবস্তির চিহ্ন। মতিবাবুর দেহের পাশে ছড়ানো রয়েছে একটা ভাঙা কাঁচের গেলাসের ছোট-বড় টুক্‌‌রো—কোন কোন কাঁচ রক্তাক্ত। আর একটা আশ্চর্য্য জিনিষও পেয়েছি। খুব পুরু পশমের একটা দস্তানা! ঘরের মেঝেতে কাদা-মাখা জুতোর দাগ আছে—দু-রকম জুতোর। কিন্তু কোন দাগ এমন স্পষ্ট বা সম্পূর্ণ নয় যে নিখুঁত মাপ বা ছাঁচ নেওয়া যেতে পারে। তবে দুজন লোক যে বৃষ্টির পরে এই ঘরের ভিতরে এসেছিল, সে বিষয়ে কোনই সন্দেহ নেই। ঘরের দরজার ঠিক বাইরেই যে একজন লোক দাঁড়িয়ে কিছুক্ষণ অপেক্ষা করেছিল, তার একজোড়া জুতোর স্পষ্ট ছাপ দেখেই সেটা অনুমান করা যায়। তার খাঁজ কাটা সোলের ছাপ দেখলে আরো বোঝা যায়, সে এসেছিল রবারের জুতো প’রে। ঘরের মেঝেতেও এমনি রবারের জুতোর আংশিক ছাপ আছে। সুতরাং বুঝতে দেরি লাগে না যে, প্রথম একজন ঘরে ঢোকবার পরে সেও ঘরের ভিতরে ঢুকেছিল। দরজার বাইরেকার এই রবারের জুতোর ছাপ আমি নিয়েছি। মতিবাবুর মৃতদেহ দেখলে মনে হয়, কেউ বা কারা গলা টিপে তাঁকে মেরে ফেলেছে। তাঁর লোহার সিন্দুক খোলা, মতিবাবুর নিজের চাবি দিয়েই সেটা খোলা হয়েছে। ভিতর থেকে কেবল আশী হাজার টাকার নোটই অদৃশ্য হয়নি। মতিবানুর টাকা খাটানোর ঝোঁকও ছিল। হ্যাণ্ডনোটেও তিনি টাকা ধার দিতেন। সিন্দুকের ভিতরে কতগুলো হ্যাণ্ডনোটও ছিল, সেগুলোও আর নেই। আর পাওয়া যাচ্ছে না মতিবাবুর পকেট-বইখানা! তাঁর রোজ ডায়ারি লেখার অভ্যাস ছিল।

I said, "How do you know it didn't fall off the shoe of one of us?" —"For two reasons. First, since this morning the streets and lanes of the city have been bone-dry. None of those who entered this room had to walk along a muddy road. Second, as far as I can see with the naked eye, there is something slightly unusual inside this mud." Satishbabu said, "One of the murderers was wearing rubber shoes. Their heels are flat, so there is no way such a lump of mud could collect there." —"Right. Satishbabu, would it be convenient to meet Binodlal once?" —"Certainly it will!" At Satishbabu's order, a man immediately went to inform Binodlal. A little later, a young man entered the room looking extremely nervous and shrunken, glancing all around like a frightened deer. He had a fair complexion, a slender build, and handsome features. One could tell at a glance that the young man was very fond of luxury. But today, the neatly styled hair on his head was dishevelled and dull for lack of a bath and a comb. He was wearing an expensive silk shirt and fine country-made dhoti, but those too were rumpled and untidy. His eyes were swollen, and there were streaks of dried tears on both his cheeks—just like the 'hero' in the final scene of a tragedy! Hemanta stared silently at the young man with a piercing gaze—for a long time. Looking at his eyes, it seemed as though they wanted to bore right into the young man's mind! Shankar was a boy from a remote country village. Having just passed his F.A. examination, he was currently sitting idle at home in the village. His daily routine consisted of dropping by his friends' houses in the morning for a chat, taking a long nap after his midday meal, and going fishing in the Palghat baor oxbow lake in the afternoon. After the entire month of Baishakh had passed in this manner, his mother called him one day and said, "Listen to me, Shankar. Your father's health is not good. Under these circumstances, how can you continue your studies any further? Who will pay the expenses? Start looking for some kind of job now."

His mother's words set Shankar thinking. Truly, his father's health had been going very badly for the past several months. Paying for Shankar's upkeep in Kolkata was becoming more and more impossible for him. Yet what could Shankar do? Would anyone give him a job right now? And whom did he even know?

At the time we are speaking of, the Great War in Europe was still five years away. This was the year 1909. Back then, the job market was not as bad as it is today. A gentleman from Shankar's village worked at a jute mill in Shyamnagar or Naihati. Shankar's mother went and spoke to the gentleman's wife about a job for her son, asking her to speak to her husband so that he might find Shankar a post at the jute mill. The very next day, the gentleman came over to their house himself to say that he would try his best to get Shankar a job.

Shankar was no ordinary boy. Throughout his school days, he had always come first in sports and athletics. That year, at the subdivisional exhibition, he had won first place and a medal in the high jump. In football, there was no centre-forward in the entire region to match him at the time. In swimming, it was hard to find his equal. At climbing trees, riding horses, and boxing, he was extraordinarily skilled. During his student days in Kolkata, he had practised boxing regularly at the Y.M.C.A. Because of all these pursuits, he had not done quite so well in his academic examinations, passing in the second division.

In one subject, however, he possessed remarkable knowledge. He had a passion for poring over maps of every description and reading thick books on geography. He was very strong in geographical calculations. Almost all the constellations that rise in the sky of our country were familiar to him—that one is Kalpurush (Orion), that one is Saptarshi (the Great Bear), that one is Cassiopeia, that one is Vrishchik (Scorpio); which constellation rises in which month and in which quarter of the sky—all of it was at his fingertips. One glance at the sky and he could tell you on the spot. It can be said without a doubt that most boys in our country know nothing of these things.

This time, while returning home from Kolkata after sitting for his examination, he had bought and brought back a whole stack of such books; he often sat reading them in solitude, and what thoughts ran through his head only he knew. Then came his father's illness, the poverty of the household, and along with it, his mother's plea that he take up a job at the jute mill. What was he to do? He was utterly helpless. He could not bear to see the drawn, careworn faces of his mother and father. Left with no choice, he would have to take the job at the jute mill after all. Yet it was not as if he did not realise that all the dreams of his life would be shattered if he did. Was Shankar—the renowned football centre-forward, the district high-jump champion, the celebrated swimmer—to end up at last as a clerk-babu in a jute mill? With snacks or paan tucked inside a book-shaped nickel tin box and a duster stuffed in his pocket, would he have to go running to the mill the moment the morning siren blew—hurry home at twelve o'clock to bolt down two mouthfuls of rice and rush straight back again—and only get off work when the six o'clock siren sounded in the evening? His fresh, young heart simply could not bear the thought of it! At the mere thought, his whole body and mind rose up in rebellion—was a racehorse to end up pulling a rickety hackney carriage? Dusk was not far off. Sitting alone by the riverbank, Shankar was turning all these thoughts over in his mind. His heart longed to fly away to the far, distant lands of the earth, right into the midst of a hundred daring adventures.

Rahim Saheb brought out two plates. He placed one in front of himself, and the other toward his friend's empty chair. Then he looked at Sajib. "Will you have a plate? It's very late, and it'll take you a while to get home."

Sajib was hungry, but he shook his head. "No, Chacha, I'll get going. You eat."

Reaching the door, he looked back. The old man was quietly opening the packets, spooning the first serving of rice onto the plate in front of the empty chair.

Down in the lane outside, Sajib reached his bike. The app chimed on his phone. Order delivered; a rating had come in. Five stars. Along with a tip: five thousand taka. And below it, a short comment:

"Thank you on my father's behalf. For giving him a little of your time."

Sajib stared at the screen for a long time. Somewhere in the early morning in Canada, he thought, someone was sitting there, using five stars and a single sentence on a phone to say what he had never been able to say to his father.

He started his bike and headed for home. The road was empty, a pale moon in the sky. But tonight didn't feel ghostly to him anymore.

For human beings, making an effort is what is natural, and therefore easy. Spontaneous, overflowing thought or feeling comes only to one or two people by virtue of their own nature. What happens of itself is so supreme and so wondrous that we attribute divine power to its root. This creation of the universe is so vast precisely because it is the lila—the effortless play—of God, and the things made by our hands are so narrow precisely because they are wrought with toil. Still, there is no denying that all sorts of thoughts and worries arise unbidden in the minds of every one of us. But the cause of those thoughts and worries is clear, while their form is indistinct. Worries arise in us from various obvious worldly causes—illness, grief, poverty, and the like; yet those thoughts are so tangled that, let alone others, we ourselves cannot find their thread. What we cannot grasp ourselves, it is impossible to convey to others; a feeling we cannot express cannot be called a 'kheyal'—a true whimsy or caprice of art. For no definable reason, a kheyal appears within the mind wearing a wonderfully clear, coherent form. A kheyal has form; anxious worry does not.
Before practicing kheyal, it is necessary to determine its true nature, because once its nature is understood, the uninitiated will not practice it in vain. In our written treatises, one hardly finds examples of kheyal, so we must take its model from the art of music. Put in a word, the desire to break free from the bondage of dhrupad is the cause of kheyal's birth. Beyond the slow, solemn, pure, and tranquil form of dhrupad, there are many other forms of emotion in the world. Not every memory or every regret of the heart can be expressed through a slow tempo. Therefore, what has no place within the strict discipline of dhrupad—such as taan, gitkiri, and the like—is the real business of kheyal. Yet although the free spirit of kheyal is unbridled, it is not lawless. However much virtuoso flair a kheyal singer may display, he has no right to fall out of taal—the beat—or stray from the raga. Just as matter is the vessel of consciousness, and the body is the dwelling place of beauty, so too is the raga the foundation of kheyal. The purpose of arranging notes and embellishments is to bring out the form, not to bury it. Just because the movement of kheyal is not straight like dhrupad does not mean it staggers crookedly like a drunkard; it is varied and graceful like a dancer. However much kheyal may cast off the fetters of dhrupad, it never casts off the bonds of melody; though its pace is at times exceedingly swift and light, it never loses its rhythm. Writing is governed by the exact same laws as music. One whose mind knows how to walk only along a straight path, whose imagination does not play of its own accord, who cannot let himself go completely—or, once having let go, can no longer keep himself under control—had better not try to write kheyal. Doing so will only diminish his dignity. Trying to fatten a lean body, even if often in vain, is never harmful; but trying to make a heavy, bulky body delicate puts one's very life in peril. He nearly jumped. The door of the neighboring flat had cracked open a little, and an old man in a white panjabi and thick-lensed glasses was peering out from inside.

The old man stayed silent for a moment. Then he opened the door all the way. "Oh, so today is that date."

"What do you mean?"

"Come inside, baba. Bring the packets in."

Sajib hesitated. But there was such a tired, gentle note in the old man's voice that he stepped forward. The room was small and tidy. An old clock on the wall, a teacup on the table. The old man asked him to sit.

"I'm Rahim. Motaleb was my neighbor, and my friend too. Three years ago on this very day, he passed away." He took off his glasses and wiped them. "And every year on this day, just before midnight, an order for kacchi comes in under the name of this house. Two packets."

"Who places it?"

"His son. He lives in Canada—it's morning there now. He had a falling-out with his father, long ago. The boy went abroad and never came back. Never even called. Motaleb wouldn't say anything out loud, but every Friday he would order kacchi and eat it with me. He used to say, 'The boy loved kacchi. When I eat it, it feels like he's eating too.'"

Sajib set the two packets on the table. You could still feel the warmth inside them.

"The day Motaleb died, his son came, but too late. He didn't get to see him one last time." Rahim Saheb's voice trembled slightly. "Ever since then, he places an order every year on this day. He writes in the note to leave it in front of the door. I take it in. His father's phone is still plugged into the charger in that room—the son wouldn't let anyone turn it off. His number was saved in that phone under the name 'My Son.' So when a call comes through the app..."

"The phone rings," Sajib said slowly. He wasn't afraid anymore.

"Yes. It rings."

The bus stopped in front of a tea stall. A few people got off. Tanvir didn't get off. He sat quietly, still holding the plate in his hands.

Her words settled somewhere deep inside him, a place nothing else had reached all day.

The bus started moving again. Khala had her eyes closed—maybe asleep, maybe reciting a dua. Tanvir took out his phone. Battery at six percent.

He opened his mother's number. It was one o'clock in the morning; Ma was surely asleep. Even so, he typed:

"Ma, I'm coming home tomorrow morning. There's something I need to tell you. Nothing to be scared of. Just... I need to tell you."

He hit send. The screen went black; the phone died. Strangely, though, the inside of his chest felt lighter than before.

At four-thirty in the morning, the bus entered Jamalpur town. Gray light touched the edge of the sky. Khala woke up, adjusted her anchal, and pressed the tiffin carrier to her chest.

"Get off here, baba."

Stepping down at the bus stand, Tanvir said, "Khala, I never got to know your name."

"Rahima." She smiled. "And yours?"

"Saying that, he nonchalantly turned over on his side and fell asleep. I came outside the tent and saw that the fire had gone out. There was firewood and brushwood lying beside it, so I built up a blazing fire again with that. Then I came back inside and lay down.

That flat land inside the forest is terribly dangerous; the Bunyip lives there. Once you fall into the hands of the Bunyip, there is no coming back. Nobody goes there. It did not take you long to forget that I had beauty. But you were forced to remember at every step that I had intelligence. That intelligence of mine is so innate to me that even after spending all this time amidst your household chores, it has survived to this day. My mother used to be terribly worried about this intelligence of mine—for a woman, it is a curse. If someone who is meant to live by obeying restrictions tries instead to follow her own intelligence, she is bound to stumble at every step and break her own forehead. But tell me, what could I do? The Creator, in a moment of carelessness, gave me far more intelligence than is needed for a daughter-in-law of your house—to whom can I give it back now? Morning and evening, all of you called me a forward, over-smart girl. Bitter words are the consolation of the powerless; therefore, I forgave you all for that.

There was one thing of mine that remained outside your domestic world, and none of you ever knew of it. I used to write poetry in secret. Whatever rubbish it may have been, the walls of your inner quarters never rose around it. There lay my freedom; there, I was myself. Whatever was in me that went beyond your family's Mejobou, you neither liked nor recognised; that I am a poet has never been discovered by any of you in all these fifteen years.

Among my earliest memories of your house, the one that rises most vividly in my mind is your cowshed. Right next to the staircase leading up to the inner quarters was the room where your cows were kept; apart from the tiny courtyard in front, they had nowhere else to move. In the corner of that courtyard stood the wooden trough for their fodder. In the morning, the servant had many chores to do; until then, the starving cows would lick and chew at the edges of that trough, biting off splinters of wood. My heart would weep for them. I was a village girl—the day I first arrived as a new bride in your house, those two cows and three calves seemed to my eyes like the only long-familiar kin I had in the entire city. For as long as I was a new bride, I used to go without eating myself and feed them in secret; when I grew older, seeing my open affection for the cows, my relatives by marriage who were entitled to tease me began to voice doubts about my caste lineage.

My baby girl died as soon as she was born. As she left, she called me to go with her too. Had she lived, she would have brought into my life everything that is great, everything that is true; from being the Mejobou, I would have become a mother outright. A mother, even while living within a single household, belongs to the whole wide world. I bore the pain of becoming a mother, but I did not gain the freedom of being one.

I remember how the English doctor came and was astonished to see our inner quarters, and how annoyed he got when he saw the birthing room, scolding everyone. Out in front, you have a little garden. The outer rooms have no shortage of furnishings and decorations. Yet the inner quarters are like the underside of a piece of woollen embroidery; on that side there is no modesty, no grace, no adornment. On that side, the lamps burn dimly; the breeze creeps in like a thief; the rubbish in the courtyard refuses to budge; the stains upon the walls and floors abide forever. Yet the doctor made one mistake: he thought that this must cause us sorrow day and night. It is quite the opposite; neglect is like ash—that ash may keep the fire smouldering deep inside, but it does not let the heat be felt from without. When self-respect diminishes, neglect no longer feels unjust. That is why it causes no pain. And that is why a woman feels ashamed even to feel sorrow. So I say, if your arrangement is that a woman must suffer, then it is best to keep her in neglect as much as possible; tenderness only makes the pain of suffering grow sharper.

আমার একটা জিনিস তোমাদের ঘরকন্নার বাইরে ছিল, সেটা কেউ তোমরা জান নি। আমি লুকিয়ে কবিতা লিখতুম। সে ছাইপাঁশ যাই হোক-না, সেখানে তোমাদের অন্দরমহলের পাঁচিল ওঠে নি। সেইখানে আমার মুক্তি; সেইখানে আমি আমি। আমার মধ্যে যা-কিছু, তোমাদের মেজোবউকে ছাড়িয়ে রয়েছে সে তোমরা পছন্দ কর নি, চিনতেও পার নি; আমি যে কবি সে এই পনেরো বছরেও তোমাদের কাছে ধরা পড়ে নি।

তোমাদের ঘরের প্রথম স্মৃতির মধ্যে সবচেয়ে যেটা আমার মনে জাগছে সে তোমাদের গোয়ালঘর। অন্দরমহলের সিঁড়িতে ওঠবার ঠিক পাশের ঘরেই তোমাদের গোরু থাকে, সামনের উঠোনটুকু ছাড়া তাদের আর নড়বার জায়গা নেই। সেই উঠোনের কোণে তাদের জাবনা দেবার কাঠের গামলা। সকালে বেহারার নানা কাজ; উপবাসী গোরুগুলো ততক্ষণ সেই গামলার ধারগুলো চেটে চেটে চিবিয়ে চিবিয়ে খাব্‌লা দিত। আমার প্রাণ কাঁদত। আমি পাড়াগাঁয়ের মেয়ে—তোমাদের বাড়িতে যেদিন নতুন এলম সেদিন সেই দুটি গোরু এবং তিনটি বাছুরই সমস্ত শহরের মধ্যে আমার চিরপরিচিত আত্মীয়ের মতো আমার চোখে ঠেকল। যতদিন নতুন বউ ছিলুম নিজে না খেয়ে লুকিয়ে ওদের খাওয়াতুম; যখন বড়ো হলুম তখন গোরুর প্রতি আমার প্রকাশ্য মমতা লক্ষ্য করে আমার ঠাট্টার সম্পর্কীয়েরা আমার গোত্র সম্বন্ধে সন্দেহ প্রকাশ করতে লাগলেন।

আমার মেয়েটি জন্ম নিয়েই মারা গেল। আমাকেও সে সঙ্গে যাবার সময় ডাক দিয়েছিল। সে যদি বেঁচে থাকত তা হলে সেই আমার জীবনে যা-কিছু বড়ো, যা-কিছু, সত্য, সমস্ত এনে দিত; তখন মেজোবউ থেকে একেবারে মা হয়ে বসতুম। মা যে এক সংসারের মধ্যে থেকেও বিশ্ব-সংসারের। মা হবার দুঃখটুকু পেলুম, কিন্তু মা হবার মুক্তি পেলুম না।

মনে আছে, ইংরেজ ডাক্তার এসে আমাদের অন্দর দেখে আশ্চর্য হয়েছিল এবং আঁতুড়ঘর দেখে বিরক্ত হয়ে বকাবকি করেছিল। সদরে তোমাদের একটুখানি বাগন আছে। ঘরে সাজসজ্জা-আসবাবের অভাব নেই। আর অন্দরটা যেন পশমের কাজের উলটো পিঠ; সে দিকে কোনো লজ্জা নেই, শ্রী নেই, সজ্জা নেই। সে দিকে আলো মিট্‌মিট্ করে জ্বলে; হাওয়া চোরের মতো প্রবেশ করে; উঠোনের আবর্জনা নড়তে চায় না; দেয়ালের এবং মেজের সমস্ত কলঙ্ক অক্ষয় হয়ে বিরাজ করে। কিন্তু, ডাক্তার একটা ভুল করেছিল; সে ভেবেছিল, এটা বুঝি আমাদের অহোরাত্র দুঃখ দেয়। ঠিক উল্‌টো; অনাদর-জিনিসটাই ছাইয়ের মতো, সে ছাই আগুনকে হয়তো ভিতরে ভিতরে জমিয়ে রাখে কিন্তু বাইরে থেকে তার তাপটাকে বুঝতে দেয় না। আত্মসম্মান যখন কমে যায় তখন অনাদরকে তো অন্যায্য বলে মনে হয় না। সেইজন্যে তার বেদনা নেই। তাই তো মেয়েমানুষ দুঃখ বোধ করতেই লজ্জা পায়। আমি তাই বলি, মেয়েমানুষকে দুঃখ পেতেই হবে এইটে যদি তোমাদের ব্যবস্থা হয় তা হলে যত দূর সম্ভব তাকে অনাদরে রেখে দেওয়াই ভালো; আদরে দুঃখের ব্যথাটা কেবল বেড়ে ওঠে।

Input: Philip said, "I see this is a terribly ill-tempered horse! Get rid of this nuisance at once." Little Alexander, just a slip of a boy, stepped forward then and said, "Maharaj, your horsemen do not know horses, and that is why they cannot mount such a splendid steed." Annoyed, Philip said, "Alexander! Such big talk does not become so young a mouth! Do you consider yourself more skilled than even my horsemen?" In a firm voice Alexander replied, "Yes indeed, Maharaj! I am willing to lay a wager and mount that horse right now!" Hearing a child boast like that, the seasoned horsemen of the regiment burst into amused, booming laughter. Philip said, "Very well, try and see." Alexander walked toward the horse. All this while he had been noticing that the horse was shying again and again at the sight of its own shadow on the ground! First he patted its back and coaxed it gently. Then, taking hold of the reins, he turned the horse's face toward the sun so that it could no longer see its own shadow. After that, he mounted the horse's back with effortless ease and made it gallop about in every direction at will. The faces of the veteran troopers and horsemen turned ashen, their heads hanging low in shame! For a moment Philip stood speechless with wonder; then, in an overwhelmed voice, he called Alexander to him and said, "My son, go and conquer some great kingdom for yourself—this tiny Macedonia of mine is not worthy of you!" That very day Philip had realized that his son was no ordinary boy! And his surmise proved true. For it was riding upon the back of that very Bucephalus that Alexander later conquered the entire world. Today, outside the tent, that same Bucephalus was neighing from time to time to let his master know that he ought not to be forgotten for so long—that his hooves were itching to go galloping across fields and roads with his master on his back! Yet Alexander, immersed in the nectar of poetry, had drifted away into another world—roaming the realms of imagination had always been his nature. It was this very imagination that had shown him the dream of world conquest! Imagination always shows dreams to every human being. Yet ninety-nine people out of a hundred remain content merely with dreaming, unwilling to step into the field of action to make those dreams come true. Alexander's nature was cast in a different mold. He did not dream by shirking action; rather, within his dreams lay the seeds of his ever-new deeds. Suddenly, outside the tent, a tremendous uproar arose from a crowd. Lifting his eyes from his book, Alexander tried to guess the cause of the commotion. He heard many voices shouting—"We do not want to go to India!"—"We have nothing to gain by invading India!" "Who knows what fate awaits us there?" Startled, Alexander thought—is this mutiny? This supremely brave Greek army, forged by his own hands and victorious in countless battles, for whose sake he himself had made so many sacrifices, and who by his grace had never once seen the face of defeat—were even they terrified of India today, unwilling to obey his word? A memory from just the other day came back to him. Treading the scorching bosom of Asia burning under the fierce rays of the sun, he had been marching forward with his army—the searing heat of fire in the wind, the waterless road lost no one knew where at the farthest edge of the sky, barren rocky hills here and there, and not the slightest trace of human habitation!

The tiger said, 'Very well! I will go to the village, kill a dog, and leave it at the Brahmin's house.'

Hearing that, the crow bit her tongue and said, 'No, no! They won't eat a dog! Send some lemons from the lemon tree at your house. I will take the lemons over right now.'

Saying this, she took a few lemons, delivered them to the Brahmin's house, and came back to say, 'Mr. Tiger, they were delighted to eat the lemons. If you keep giving them lemons like this for a few days, they will hand over their daughter.'

Hearing this, the tiger began rolling on the ground in sheer joy.

In this way, the crow took lemons every day and told the tiger, 'They will give their daughter in marriage.' In truth, that was a lie, but the tiger believed the Brahmin had really promised to give him his daughter.

Then one day the tiger said, 'Well, the lemons have all run out, yet they haven't given their daughter in marriage.'

The crow said, 'Of course they will! Whenever you ask for her, they will hand her over at once.'

The tiger said, 'Then go and tell them that if they don't give their daughter in marriage tomorrow night, I will chew every one of them up.'

That was just what the crow wanted. She went straight to the Brahmin's house and said, 'Hello there, do you hear? Tomorrow night the tiger is coming to marry your daughter. If you don't give her in marriage, he will chew everyone up.'

No sooner had they heard this than the Brahmin and his wife began beating their chests and wailing out loud.

Hearing their cries, the villagers came running and asked, 'What has happened?'

Weeping, the Brahmin said, 'Tomorrow the tiger is coming to marry our daughter. If we don't give her in marriage, he will chew us all up.'

Hearing this, the villagers said, 'So that's what it is! Well, we'll see how the rascal gets married, or chews us up if we don't give her to him! Don't be afraid at all; we will take care of everything.'

Saying this, they sent word to the tiger: 'Mr. Tiger, could there ever be as fine a groom as you! Come dressed in your wedding clothes, (The crow said, 'Of course they will!') sit in the middle of the gathering, listen to the singing and music, eat the wedding feast, and then marry her properly and go home.'

Then they all got together, dug three hundred stoves in the Brahmin's courtyard, and set three hundred pots of oil on them to boil. Over the well, they spread out a splendid bed. Then they began beating dhaks and dhols and raising a great commotion.

Hearing all the noise, the tiger said, 'Aha, the grand celebrations for my wedding have begun!'

He quickly put on his wedding attire, tied a turban on his head, and came dancing all the way to the Brahmin's house.

At once everyone cried out, 'Oh, the groom has arrived! Play the music, play!' and showed Mr. Tiger to the bed spread over the well. No sooner had Mr. Tiger leaped onto it to sit down than, with a loud 'Gheyao!', he plunged right into the well along with the bed, and at that very instant all the villagers brought the boiling oil from the three hundred pots and the fire from the three hundred stoves and poured them into the well.

'Oh, the groom has arrived! Play the music, play!'

In the blink of an eye, the foolish tiger was burned to ashes, and the Brahmin's trouble was over too.

The crow was sitting on the roof of the house to watch the fun, and the boys of the neighborhood threw stones at her and smashed her head to pieces.
