The moment He saw Brahma, God in the form of Jehovah frowned and said, "What have you come to do? Nobody worships you nowadays; your picture is only printed on wedding invitation cards. Had Krishna, Shiva, Kali, or Ramachandra come, there would have been some point."

Brahma said, "They themselves have sent me as their representative."

Seeing Pir Saheb staring at Brahma in amazement, Narad said, "What are you looking at, Saheb?"

In a whisper, the Pir said, "He has four faces on all four sides! How does He sleep on a bed?"

Narad: "What chance is there of sleeping! He sits bolt upright all night long. If He were to fall asleep, the cosmic dissolution would take place."

Pir: "Ya Ghazab! What a wonder!"

With folded hands, Saint Peter said, "May permission now be granted to begin the proceedings of the assembly."

Brahma said, "My heavenly brothers, mere asmani biradaran, our first duty is to select a president for this assembly. I am the eldest in age; therefore, I shall preside."

God said, "That is out of the question. You are one among thirty-three crores, whereas I am the one and only God without a second—"

Extending both hands reverently toward the banner, Pir Saheb said, "And He too, He too."

God: "Very well, both I and He are the one and only God without a second. But I am senior; therefore, I shall be the president."

Brahma: "Brother, how long have you been running this universe? When did you create the world?"

God: "About four thousand years before my son Jesus was born."

Brahma: "What did you do before that?"

God: "Haven't you read the Bangla Bible? 'The Spirit of God was submerged within the waters.'"

Brahma: "That is to say, you had dived underwater and were fast asleep. Our Narayana does not sink; He sleeps while floating. What does Allah Ta'ala say?"

Pir: "Read the Quran Sharif and see; everything is written in there."

God: "Brahma, didn't you rise up from Vishnu's navel-lotus? Is it true that you too are subject to birth and death?"

Brahma: "What of it? A single lifetime of mine is vast—as many years as you get when you put thirteen zeroes after thirty-one. Even while you were submerged within the waters, I was creating in abundance."

With folded hands, Narad said, "Lords, what I suggest is that we set aside the argument over who is elder and who is younger for now. Let all three of you preside together."

Saint Peter said, "That is best." Pir Saheb silently shook his head to the right, to the left, up, and down.

Narad said, "The purpose of troubling you to come here is to settle upon a way so that peace may come to the world, and sinful deeds such as fighting, bloodshed, malice, violence, oppression, deceit, and plunder may be eliminated."

Brahma: "Brother God, you suggest a way."

God: "I told them the way long ago. Let all the people of the world take refuge in Jesus and follow His teachings; peace will come in two days, and the Kingdom of Heaven will be established on earth."

Brahma: "But as you can plainly see, people are not following the teachings of Jesus. Why then are you sitting silent? What has happened to your thunderbolts, tempests, plagues, and rains of fire?"

God: "They are all there; if things come to such a pass, I shall use them at the final hour, not now. I have given man freedom of action—what is called Free Will. If man knowingly goes to rack and ruin, I am helpless."

ব্রহ্মা বললেন, মাই হেভন্‌লি ব্রাদার্স, মেরে আসমানী বরাদরান, আমাদের প্রথম কর্তব্য হচ্ছে এই সভার একজন সভাপতি স্থির করা। আমি বয়সে সব চেয়ে বড়, অতএব আমিই সভাপতিত্ব করব।

গড বললেন, তা হ’তেই পারে না। তুমি হচ্ছ তেত্রিশ কোটির একজন, আর আমি হচ্ছি একমাত্র অদ্বিতীয় ঈশ্বর —

ঝাণ্ডার দিকে সসম্ভ্রমে দুই হাত বাড়িয়ে পীরসাহেব বললেন, ইনিও, ইনিও।

গড। বেশ তো, আমি আর ইনি দুজনেই একমাত্র অদ্বিতীয় ঈশ্বর। কিন্তু আমি হচ্ছি সিনিয়র, অতএব আমিই সভাপতি হব।

ব্রহ্মা। দাদা, কত দিন এই বিশ্বব্রহ্মাণ্ড চালাচ্ছ? জগৎ সৃষ্টি করেছ কবে?

গড। আমার পুত্র যিশ‍ু জন্মাবার প্রায় চার হাজার বৎসর আগে।

ব্রহ্মা। তার আগে কি করা হ’ত?

গড। বাংলা বাইবেল পড় নি বুঝি? ‘ঈশ্বরের আত্মা জলমধ্যে নিলীয়মান ছিল।’

ব্রহ্মা। অর্থাৎ ডুব মেরে ঘুমচ্ছিলে। আমাদের নারায়ণ ডোবেন না, ভাসতে ভাসতে নিদ্রা যান। আল্লা তালা কি বলেন?

পীর। কোরান শরিফ প’ড়ে দেখবেন, তাতে সব কুছ লিখা আছে।

গড। ব্রহ্মা, তুমি না বিষ্ণুর নাইকুণ্ডু থেকে উঠেছিলে? তোমারও নাকি জন্মমৃত্যু আছে?

ব্রহ্মা। তাতে কি হয়েছে। আমার এক-একটি জীবনকালই যে বিপুল, একত্রিশের পিঠে তেরটা শূন্য দিলে যত হয় তত বৎসর। তুমি যখন জলমধ্যে নিলীয়মান ছিলে তখনও আমি দেদার সৃষ্টি করেছি।

নারদ কৃতাঞ্জলি হয়ে বললেন, প্রভুরা, আমি বলি কি কে বড় কে ছোট সে তর্ক এখন থাকুক। আপনারা তিন জনেই সভাপতিত্ব করুন।

সেণ্ট পিটার বললেন, সেই ভাল। পীরসাহেব নীরবে ডাইনে বাঁয়ে উপরে নীচে মাথা নাড়তে লাগলেন।

নারদ বললেন, আপনাদের কষ্ট দিয়ে এখানে ডেকে আনার উদ্দেশ্য—জগতে যাতে শান্তি আসে, মারামারি কাটাকাটি দ্বেষ হিংসা অত্যাচার প্রতারণা লুণ্ঠন প্রভৃতি পাপকার্য যাতে দূর হয় তার একটা উপায় স্থির করা।

ব্রহ্মা। গড ভায়া, তুমিই একটা উপায় বাতলাও।

গড। উপায় তো বহুকাল আগেই বলে দিয়েছি। জগতের সমস্ত লোক যিশ‍ুর শরণাপন্ন হ’ক, তাঁর উপদেশ মেনে চলুক, দু দিনে শান্তি আসবে, পৃথিবীতে স্বর্গরাজ্যের প্রতিষ্ঠা হবে।

ব্রহ্মা। কিন্তু দেখতেই তো পাচ্ছ লোকে যিশ‍ুর উপদেশ মানছে না। তবু তুমি চুপ ক’রে আছ কেন? তোমার বজ্র ঝঞ্ঝা মহামারী অগ্নিবৃষ্টি এসব কি হ’ল?

গড। সবই আছে, তেমন তেমন দেখলে অন্তিম অবস্থায় প্রয়োগ করব, এখন নয়। আমি মানুষকে কর্মের স্বাধীনতা দিয়েছি, যাকে বলে ফ্রি উইল। মানুষ যদি জেনে শ‍ুনে উৎসন্নে যায় তো আমি নাচার।

Input: Folding his hands, Sundarbabu closed his eyes, bowed three times to Mother Kali, and said, "Manik, don't frighten me anymore at a time like this; let me call upon Mother Jagadamba once with all my heart." Looking back, Kumar saw that the enemies were driving their ship at full speed toward the island, while in the distance, churning up the ocean waves like Mahakala incarnate, the terrifying whirlwind came rushing in pursuit of her! After entering the island, the channel of seawater took another turn, so their ship turned along with it. Then, just like a curtain, the forest and jungle of the island completely hid the entire view of the open sea, the whirlwind, and the pirate ship. Just then, Bimal came running up to everyone and said, "Jayantababu, the captain says the water here is shallow; the ship cannot go any further. The sailors are lowering the boats; we must get off the ship too." Sundarbabu asked, "Why?" "The pirates are coming here too, and they outnumber us by far. Unless we go ashore, we won't be able to hold off their attack." Crestfallen once more, Sundarbabu said, "So we shall have to fight after all?" "Certainly! The typhoon and the pirates—we now have to fight two enemies at once! Look there, the sailors have already lowered the lifeboat into the water! And listen, there's the captain's voice on the megaphone! He is telling us to get down into the boat quickly—otherwise the storm waves may reach in here as well! Come on, no more delay. Ramhari, you take care of Bagha!" Where the lifeboat stopped, a small hill rose nearly a hundred feet high right from the water's edge. Bimal said, "We shall all wait right here with our guns behind the rocks. If the pirates manage to dodge our gunfire and actually land ashore, we will take other measures according to the situation. For the time being, this hill will be our fortress. What do you say, Kumar? What do you say, Jayantababu?" Jayanta said, "An excellent proposal. But Bimalbabu, do you hear a commotion?" "Yes, the howling and whistling of the storm wind, and the roar of the sea!" Kumar said, "Not only that—the clamor of many human voices seems to be drifting over from afar as well!" Ramhari said, "Up until now it was sultry all around, and now the trees and plants here are bending low in the strong wind! The storm is probably upon us!" Manik said, "The storm is here, but where is the pirate ship?" Sundarbabu said, "Hmph!" Bagha said, "Bow, wow, wow!" Bimal said, "Did the pirates fall right into the clutches of the storm, then? Wait, let me go and see." Saying this, he began climbing quickly up the hill. In an anxious voice, Ramhari called out, "Don't go up there, Khokababu, don't go up! If the storm blows harder, you'll be swept away!" But Bimal did not heed the warning. Climbing about halfway up the hill, he stopped, looked in one direction, and called out in an astonished voice, "Amazing, amazing! Kumar, Kumar, come and see quickly!" In eager curiosity, everyone began climbing swiftly up the hill—everyone except Sundarbabu. His massive potbelly was ill-suited for the upward path. It was truly an astonishing sight! The dreadful typhoon for fear of which they had all taken shelter here, instead of coming toward the island, seemed to have swerved past it and was hurtling furiously away in another direction with a roaring howl. Only a gust of wild wind had struck the island, whereas along the path the typhoon itself was taking, pitch-black darkness swayed in the sky above—while below, one could dimly make out the violent tossing of the raging ocean's towering waves! And drifting across came the hideous shrieking of the frenzied whirlwind, the deep roar of the waters, and the anguished screams of many human voices!
Target Output: সুন্দরবাবু দুই হাত জোড় ক’রে মা-কালীর উদ্দেশে চক্ষু মুদে তিন বার প্রণাম ক’রে বল্‌লেন, “মাণিক, এ-সময়ে আর ভয় দেখিও না, মা-জগদম্বাকে একবার প্রাণ ভ’রে ডাকতে দাও।” কুমার ফিরে দেখলে,শত্রুরা দ্বীপ লক্ষ্য ক’রে প্রাণপণে জাহাজ চালিয়েছে এবং দূরে তার দিকে বেগে তাড়া ক’রে আসছে সাগর-তরঙ্গ তোলপাড় ক’রে মূর্ত্তিমান মহাকালের মত সুভীষণ ঘূর্ণাবর্ত্ত! দ্বীপের ভিতরে ঢুকে সমুদ্রের জল আবার মোড় ফিরে গেছে, কাজেই জাহাজও সঙ্গে সঙ্গে মোড় ফিরলে। তখন দ্বীপের বন-জঙ্গল ঠিক যবনিকার মতই বাহির-সমুদ্র, ঘূর্ণাবর্ত্ত ও বোম্বেটে-জাহাজের সমস্ত দৃশ্য একেবারে ঢেকে দিলে। এমন সময়ে বিমল দৌড়ে সকলের কাছে এসে বললে, “জয়ন্তবাবু, কাপ্তেন বল্‌লেন এখানকার জল গভীর নয়, জাহাজ আর চলবে না। নাবিকরা নৌকোগুলো নামাচ্ছে, আমাদেরও জাহাজ থেকে নামতে হবে।” সুন্দরবাবু বল্‌লেন, “কেন?” ——“বোম্বেটেরাও এখানে আসছে, তারা আমাদের চেয়ে দলে ঢের ভারি। আমরা ডাঙায় না নামলে তাদের আক্রমণ ঠেকাতে পারব না।” সুন্দরবাবু আবার মুষড়ে প’ড়ে বল্‌লেন, “তাহ’লে যুদ্ধ আমাদের করতেই হবে?” —“নিশ্চয়! টাইফুন আর বোম্বটে—আমাদের এখন যুদ্ধ করতে হবে দুই শত্রুর সঙ্গে! ঐ দেখুন, ‘সেলর’রা এরি মধ্যে ‘লাইফ-বোট’ ভাসিয়ে ফেলেছে! ঐ শুনুন, ‘মেগাফোনে’ কাপ্তেন-সায়েবের গলা! তিনি আমাদের নৌকোয় তাড়াতাড়ি নামতে বলছেন—নইলে ঝোড়ো ঢেউ এখানেও এসে পড়তে পারে! চলুন, আর দেরি নয়। রামহরি, তুমি বাঘাকে সামলাও!”: লাইফ-বোট যেখানে থামল, সেখানে জলের ধার থেকেই একটি ছোট্ট পাহাড় প্রায় একশো ফুট উঁচু হয়ে উঠেছে। বিমল বললে, “এইখানেই বন্দুক নিয়ে আমরা সবাই পাথরের আড়ালে অপেক্ষা করব। বোম্বেটেরা আমাদের বন্দুক এড়িয়ে নিতান্তই “যদি ডাঙায় এসে নামে, তাহ’লে অবস্থা বুঝে অন্য ব্যবস্থা করতে হবে। আপাতত এই পাহাড়টাই হবে আমাদের দুর্গ। কি বল কুমার, কি বলেন জয়ন্তবাবু?” জয়স্তু বল্‌লে, “সাধু প্রস্তাব। কিন্তু বিমলবাবু, একটা গোলমাল শুনতে পাচ্ছেন?” —“হুঁ, ঝোড়া বাতাসের গেঁ-গোঁ হু-হু, সমুদ্রের হুঙ্কার!” কুমার বলে, “কেবল তাই নয়—দূর থেকে যেন অনেক মানুষের কোলাহলও ভেসে আসছে!” রামহরি বললে, “এতক্ষণ চারিদিক গুমোট্ ক’রে ছিল, এখন জোর হাওয়ায় এখানকার গাছপালাগুলো নুয়ে নুয়ে পড়ছে! ঝড় বোধ হয় এল!” মাণিক বলে, “ঝড় এল, কিন্তু বোম্বেটে জাহাজ কোথায়?” সুন্দরবাবু বললেন, “হুম্!” বাঘা বললে, “ঘেউ, ঘেউ, ঘেউ!” বিমল বল্‌লে, “তবে কি বোম্বেটেগুলো ঝড়ের খপ্পরেই পড়ল? দাঁড়াও, দেখে আসি”—ব’লেই সে তাড়াতাড়ি পাহাড়ের উপরে উঠতে লাগল। রামহরি উদ্বিগ্ন স্বরে বলে “ওপরে উঠ না খোকাবাবু, ওপরে উঠ না! বেশী ঝড় এলে উড়ে যাবে!” কিন্তু বিমল মানা মানলে না। পাহাড়ের প্রায় মাঝ বরাবর উঠেই দাঁড়িয়ে প’ড়ে একদিকে তাকিয়ে সে চমৎকৃত স্বরে বল্‌লে, “আশ্চর্যা, আশ্চর্য্য! কুমার, কুমার, শীগ্‌গির দেখে যাও।” বিপুল কৌতূহলে সবাই দ্রুতপদে উপরে উঠতে লাগল—একমাত্র, সুন্দরবাবু ছাড়া। তাঁর বিপুল ভুঁড়ি উর্দ্ধমার্গের উপযোগী নয়। বাস্তবিকই সে এক আশ্চর্য্য দৃশ্য! যে বিষম টাইফুনের ভয়ে তারা সবাই এখানে এসে আশ্রয় নিয়েছে, সে-ভয়ঙ্কর দ্বীপের দিকে না এসে যেন পাশ কাটিয়েই প্রচণ্ড বেগে ধেয়ে চলেছে অন্য দিকে হুহু ক’রে। দ্বীপের দিকে এসেছে খানিকটা উদ্দাম হাওয়ার ঝট্‌কা মাত্র, কিন্তু টাইফুন্ নিজে যেখান দিয়ে যাচ্ছে সেখানকার শূন্যে দুলছে নিরন্ধ, অন্ধকার—নীচে কেবল অস্পষ্ট ভাবে দেখা যাচ্ছে রুদ্র সমুদ্রের উত্তাল তরঙ্গদলের হিন্দোলা! আর ভেসে ভেসে আসছে প্রমত্ত ঘূর্ণাবর্ত্তের বিকট চীৎকার, গম্ভীর জল-কল্লোল, বহু মানব-কণ্ঠের আর্ত্তনাদ!

Pareshbabu has found a touchstone. When he found it, where he found it, how it came to be there, whether more can be found—what need do you have for such inquiries? Just listen to what I am telling you.

Pareshbabu is a middle-class, middle-aged man; he lives in his ancestral house and practises law. His earnings are not large, and he manages to run his household somehow or other. One day, on his way home from court, he picked up a stone pebble. What the thing was, he could not recognise, of course; seeing a slightly unusual-looking stone, he picked it up from the side of the road and slipped it into his pocket. Coming home, he took the key out of his pocket to unlock his office room and saw that its colour was yellow. Astonished, Pareshbabu thought: the room key is made of iron, so how did it turn into brass? Perhaps the key had been lost one day, and his wife, without informing him, had called a locksmith and had this brass key made, and until today it had not caught Pareshbabu's eye.

Pareshbabu entered the room, emptied everything from his pocket except his wallet onto the table, and then went upstairs. The matter of the key did not stay in his mind any longer. After a light meal and about an hour's rest, he came back to the downstairs room to look over his case papers and switched on the light. The very first thing that caught his eye was the stone. Quite a round, shiny pebble; tomorrow morning he would give it to his little boy to play marbles with. Pareshbabu pulled open the drawer of his table and placed the stone inside. In it lay a knife, a pair of scissors, pencils, paper, envelopes, and various other things. What a wonder! The knife and the scissors turned yellow. Pareshbabu took the stone and touched it to his glass inkpot; nothing happened. Then he touched it to a lead paperweight; it turned yellow and became nearly double in weight. In a trembling voice, Pareshbabu called his servant and said, "Hariya, ask for my watch from upstairs and bring it here." Hariya brought the watch and left. All the next day, Ritu couldn't get anything done. Ten minutes before seven, she stood in front of the mirror, fixed her hair, then messed it up again. Then she laughed at herself.

Seven o'clock struck. She opened the door.

Across the corridor, the door to 5C was open too. Standing there was someone with messy hair, a pencil in his hand. Today, there were no headphones in his ears.

The two of them stared at each other.

"You!" Ritu said. "From the elevator..."

"You're the one..." The guy trailed off, his ears turning red. "I held the door, didn't I? On Tuesday? I was actually walking and thinking about a line from the book. Back then I didn't know..."

"You didn't even look at me!"

"True enough, and that was the biggest mistake of my whole life." He held out the pencil. "I'm Arif."

Ritu took the pencil in her hand, looked at it for a moment, and smiled. "Ritu. And I'm picking the next book, not you."

"As long as there's room to write in the margins," Arif said.

They stood there in the light of the corridor, two open doors and a narrow gap between them. This time, no one had to send paper across to bridge that gap.

In the conduct of our entire everyday lives, we furnish daily proof that in our country there is no difference whatsoever between the inanimate and the animate. Consequently, if anyone actually sets out to prove the opposite in practice, one catches a faint glimpse of the memory of new life.
It is a matter of eternal shame for our Bengali race that there are no Kshatriyas in our land. Because of this, we have forever silently endured the scorn, humiliation, and taunts of other martial races. That the Ghoshes, Boses, Mitras, Des, Duttas, Guhas, and others girded up their loins to wipe away this age-old shame and remedy this eternal lack has earned them the gratitude of every patriot and lover of his people. The pity of it is that the Kayasthas did not adopt the right path to become Kshatriyas, and therefore failed in their endeavor. Their first mistake was to rely upon the evidence of the scriptures. To determine what we once were, it is necessary to sit down and pore over old almanacs and manuscripts; but to determine what we shall become, the help of history is superfluous. What testimony can the past bear regarding the future? Especially when the object is to become a Kshatriya, physical might alone suffices. Yet we have formed such a bad habit that we cannot advance a single step without invoking the authority of the scriptures.
To become Kshatriyas, however, was not written in the Kayasthas' fate. Raja Binaykrishna Deb is not only a leader of the Kayasthas, he is also the chieftain of his clan; consequently, when he opposed the move, the other party backed down in fear. Those who were about to become Kshatriyas ought to have understood that fear is the very first thing they needed to cast aside. That cowardice and the Kshatriya spirit cannot dwell together was something they were evidently unaware of. Or perhaps they thought: when the land is swarming with ignorant Brahmins, what objection can there be to cowardly Kshatriyas? Inert matter, too, possesses an inherent force of its own, whose function is to arrest motion. The reason our society cannot be budged is that this force of inertia is the all-conquering power in our society.
Not only did Raja Binaykrishna obstruct the effort to reform the Kayastha community, he has now, from the presidential chair of the All-India National Social Conference, expressed the view that while Hindu society may have many faults, and while society might benefit if those faults were absent, it is nevertheless improper to attempt social reform. Society was created and shaped in the past, and therefore its reform and transformation will take place in the future; the present has no duty and no responsibility. Men build society, and if they wish, men can tear it down; therefore, men cannot reform it—that burden rests in the hands of time, in the hands of blind nature. Whoever denies this doctrine has not read Burke.
Nowadays there is a class of people who give a little passing thought to the state of society, the state of the country, and their own state, and in the end arrive at the conclusion that there is no harm in playing it safe.

কিন্তু ক্ষত্রিয় হওয়া কায়স্থের কপালে ঘটল না। রাজা বিনয়কৃষ্ণ দেব একে কায়ন্থের দলপতি, তার উপর আবার গোষ্ঠীপতি, সুতরাং তিনি যখন এ ব্যাপারে বিরোধী হলেন তখন অপর পক্ষ ভয়ে নিরস্ত হলেন। যাঁরা ক্ষত্রিয় হতে উদ্যত, তাঁদের ভয় জিনিসটে যে আগে হতেই ত্যাগ করা নিতান্ত আবশ্যক, এ কথা বোঝা উচিত ছিল। ভীরুতা ও ক্ষাত্রধর্ম যে একসঙ্গে থাকতে পারে না, এ কথা বোধ হয় তারা অবগত ছিলেন না। তবে হয়তো মনে করেছিলেন, যখন মুর্খ ব্রাহ্মণে দেশ ছেয়ে গেছে, তখন ভীরু ক্ষত্রিয়ে আপত্তি কী। জড়পদার্থেরও একটা অন্তর্নিহিত শক্তি আছে, তার কার্য হচ্ছে চলৎশক্তি রহিত করা। আমাদের সমাজকে যে নাড়ানো যায় না তার কারণ এই জড়শক্তিই আমাদের সমাজে সর্বজয়ী শক্তি।
রাজা বিনয়কৃষ্ণ যে কায়স্থ-সমাজের সংস্কারের উদ্যোগে বাধা দিয়েছেন শুধু তাই নয়, তিনি এবার সমগ্র ভারতবর্ষের জাতীয় সমাজসংস্কার-মহাসভার সভাপতির আসন থেকে এই মত ব্যক্তি করেছেন যে, হিন্দুসমাজে অনেক দোষ থাকতে পারে, এবং সে দোষ না থাকলে সমাজের উপকার হতে পারে, অতএব সমাজসংস্কারের চেষ্টা করা অকর্তব্য। সমাজের সৃষ্টি ও গঠন হয়েছে অতীতে, সুতরাং তার সংস্কার ও পরিবর্তন হবে ভবিষ্যতে; বর্তমানের কোনো কর্তব্য নেই, কোনো দায়িত্ব নেই। সমাজ গড়ে মানুষে, ইচ্ছে করলে ভাঙতে পারে মানুষে; অতএব মানুষে তার সংস্কার করতে পারে না, সে ভার সময়ের হাতে, অন্ধ প্রকৃতির হাতে। এ মত যে অস্বীকার করে, সে বার্ক পড়ে নি।
আজকাল একশ্রেণীর লোক আছেন যাঁরা সমাজের অবস্থা, দেশের অবস্থা, নিজেদের অবস্থা এই-সব বিষয়েই একটু-আধটু চিন্তা করে থাকেন এবং শেষে এই সিদ্ধান্তে উপস্থিত হন যে, সাবধানের মার নেই।

But one cannot judge a matter by hearing only one side's excuses; so in between his outbursts, everyone listened to Naga's side of the story too. Having heard it, old Osman stroked his beard and said reproachfully, 'You raised your hand against such a grown boy—have you no shame, Majhi?'
Everyone agreed and said that Haru Majhi had truly not done the right thing.
Growing angry at them now, Haru Majhi snapped, 'I did the right thing raising my hand to him—what is it to you? Get off my boat, all of you!'
Along with this, in the heat of anger, Haru Majhi let slip a very foul remark as well. Everyone did leave his boat, to be sure, but before they went, they lifted Haru up into the air and tossed him into the river water one more time.
The instant the curse left his lips, Haru had realized he had made a mistake; these men were not his nephew, and he could not say whatever he pleased to them. That they had merely thrown him into the water and left instead of beating his bones to powder was his great good fortune. Climbing back into the boat this time, Haru did not rage anymore; he only said to Naga, 'Go on, you get out too! I won't look at your face ever again. I'm throwing you out!'
Naga said, 'You don't need to tell me—I'm leaving on my own. I've found work on the boat of the Chhoto Karta of Ramtala.'
'You've found work? How much will he pay?'
'Whatever he gives.'
After that, both of them fell silent. Changing out of his wet clothes, Haru packed a chillum of tobacco and kept puffing at his waterless hookah with a wheezing hiss, while all around them the waves of the river lapped with a gentle splash. Naga's heart felt weighed down with sadness. How foolish poor people are! There are already a thousand kinds of sorrow and hardship in life, and on top of that, by quarreling and fighting for no reason, they are forever bringing so much misery upon themselves. With just two sweet words and a little kindness, how happy one can make a person—and it doesn't even cost a single pice. Yet everyone seems forever ready, like mad dogs, to fly at one another's throats.
Suddenly Haru Majhi said in a softened voice, 'Go on, go home and eat.'
Naga said, 'No, I won't eat.'
With deep hurt and wounded pride, Haru Majhi began thinking to himself that this was really not right of Naga—to push him into the river and then be the one to sulk in anger.
Naga had been grieving in his heart over how stingy people were with sweet words, and now Haru Majhi began speaking nothing but sweet words to him. Yet it brought Naga no joy. It was as if Haru were speaking those words to the future boatman of Jadabbabu's boat, not to Naga. Getting no response from Naga, Haru Majhi went home himself to eat his rice. On other days he took a long time to return, but today he came back very quickly.
'Go on, Naga, go and eat.'
Naga stepped off the boat.
'I won't be coming back anymore.'
'All right. Come back at dawn.'
Some nights Haru Majhi sleeps on the boat, and some nights Naga sleeps there. There are fewer mosquitoes on the boat than at home. Haru Majhi's house is near the middle of the village, not far from the river.

"However, in 1880 a prospector named James Martin wandered for a long time in this region of Rhodesia in search of gold. Mr. Martin had formerly been aide-de-camp to General Mathews, and was himself a good geologist and zoologist. In his diary he mentioned having seen this unknown beast of Rhodesia from a distance. He too says that in shape the beast resembled a prehistoric reptile of the dinosaur family and was terribly huge. Yet he could not state anything with certainty, because he had seen the animal only indistinctly through the early morning mist in the marshes bordering Kavirondo Lake. Hearing the beast's call, which sounded like the neighing of a horse, the Zulu servants with him fled at top speed, shouting, 'Sahib, run, run! Dingonek! Dingonek!' Dingonek is the Zulu name for that beast. It appears perhaps once in two or three years, if at all, yet it is so ferocious that its appearance is a matter of terrible dread to the people of that land. Mr. Martin says that he fired two .303 cartridges in quick succession at the beast. From such a distance he could not take proper aim, and at the sound of the rifle it probably dived into the water."

Shankar said, "How did you come to know all this? Was Martin's diary published?"

"No, a long time ago this account of Mr. Martin's came out in the Bulawayo Chronicle newspaper. I had just arrived in this country then. Because I too used to go prospecting around the Rhodesia region, the description of the beast fascinated me greatly. I even kept the newspaper with me for a long time. Then it got lost somewhere. It was they who named the beast the Rhodesian Monster."

Shankar asked, "Have you never seen any strange animal yourself?"

Right upon that question, a strange thing happened.

By then the evening darkness had grown thick and descended all around. In that dim twilight between light and darkness, it seemed to Shankar—perhaps Shankar was mistaken—yet it seemed to Shankar that he saw Alvarez, the daring and fearless Alvarez, the seasoned and unerring marksman Alvarez, give a start at his question—and—and this was the most astonishing thing of all—shudder the very next instant.

At the same moment, almost unconsciously, Alvarez cast a single glance at the uninhabited dense jungle and the mysterious, unscalable mountain range all around, without saying a word. It was as if, having returned to these mountain forests after a long time, some terrifying old incident from the past had floated up in his memory—a memory that was far from pleasant for him.

Alvarez was afraid!

Astonishing! Alvarez afraid! Shankar could not even imagine it! Yet unseen, that very fear crept in and settled heavily upon Shankar's mind as well. This completely unknown, strange, and mysterious forest, this vast mountain wall seemed to have been hiding a deep mystery through the ages—whoever you may be, brave or fearless, step forward if you will—but the key to that dark mystery must be bought at the price of death. The Richtersveld mountain range is not India's divine king of mountains, the Himalayas—like the primitive tribes of this land, the Maasai, the Zulu, and the Matabele, its soul is cruel, savage, and greedy for human flesh. In a corner of the king's garden was Tuntuni's nest. The silver coins from the king's treasury had been spread out in the sun to air, and in the evening his men forgot to bring one of the coins back inside.

Spotting that shiny coin, Tuntuni picked it up, brought it back to her nest, and thought, 'My! How rich I have become! The very wealth the king has in his house, I too have in mine!' From then on, that was all she thought about, and she kept singing—

The wealth that lies in the king's own hall, Lies in Tuni's little home and all!

Tuntuni took the coin and kept it in her nest. Sitting in his court, the king heard her song and asked, 'Hey there! What is that bird saying?'

Folding their hands, everyone replied, 'Your Majesty, the bird is saying that whatever wealth you have in your house, she supposedly has in hers too!' Hearing this, the king laughed merrily and said, 'Go see what she has in her nest.'

They went and looked, and came back saying, 'Your Majesty, there is a silver rupee coin in her nest.'

Hearing this, the king said, 'Why, that's my coin! Go bring it back.'

At once a man went and took the coin from Tuntuni's nest. What could the poor little bird do? Out of the grief in her heart, she began to sing—

The king is so greedy for wealth and gold, He took Tuni's treasure into his hold!

Hearing this, the king laughed again and said, 'That bird is mighty stubborn, isn't she! Go on, give her coin back to her.'

Getting her coin back, Tuni was overjoyed. Then she sang—

The king was filled with terrible fright, And gave Tuni's coin right back in sight!

The king asked, 'Now what is she saying?'

The courtiers replied, 'She is saying that Your Majesty got terribly scared, and that's why you gave her coin back.'

Hearing this, the king flew into a furious rage! He shouted, 'What, such insolence! Go catch the rascal and bring it here—I'll fry it and eat it up!'

No sooner had he spoken than his men went and caught poor Tuntuni and brought her in. Holding her in his fist, the king went inside the palace and told his queens, 'You must fry this bird and serve it to me for my meal today.'

Saying this, the king walked out, and the seven queens gathered around to look at the bird.

One of them said, 'What a lovely bird! Put it in my hand, let me hold it once.' Saying this, she took it into her hand. Seeing that, another queen wanted to hold it too. As one queen was passing it into another's hand, Tuntuni slipped loose and flew away!

What a disaster! What were they to do now? If the king found out, there would be no escaping his wrath!

While they were lamenting like this, a frog came hopping along right past them—thap, thap! Spotting it, the seven queens snatched it up at once and said, 'Hush, hush! Let no one find out. Let's fry this and serve it, and when the king eats it, he'll think he has eaten Tuntuni!'

When they skinned that frog, fried it, and served it to the king, he ate it up and was thoroughly delighted.

Then, just as he had gone and taken his seat in the royal court, thinking to himself, 'This time I've taught that little rascal of a bird a lesson,'

Tuntuni slipped loose and flew away. What fun, what fun, the king ate a fried frog, well done!

The moment he heard this, the king leaped from his seat! He spat, he retched, he washed his mouth out, and did a hundred other things. Then, in a towering rage, he ordered, 'Cut off the noses of all seven queens!'

রাজার বাগানের কোণে টুনটুনির বাসা ছিল। রাজার সিন্দুকের টাকা রোদে শুকুতে দিয়েছিল, সন্ধ্যার সময় তাঁর লোকেরা তার একটি টাকা ঘরে তুলতে ভুলে গেল।

টুনটুনি সেই চকচকে টাকাটি দেখতে পেয়ে তার বাসায় এসে রেখে দিলে, আর ভাবলে, ‘ঈস! আমি কত বড়লোক হয়ে গেছি! রাজার ঘরে যে ধন আছে, আমার ঘরে সেই ধন আছে!’ তারপর থেকে সে খালি এই কথাই ভাবে, আর বলে—

রাজার ঘরে যে ধন আছে টুনির ঘরেও সে ধন আছে!

টুনটুনি টাকা নিয়ে বাসায় রাখল। রাজা তাঁর সভায় বসে সে-কথা শুনতে পেয়ে জিগগেস করলেন, ‘হ্যাঁরে। পাখিটা কি বলছে রে?’

সকলে হাত জোড় করে বললে, ‘মহারাজ, পাখি বলছে, আপনার ঘরে যে ধন আছে, ওর ঘরেও নাকি সেই ধন আছে!’ শুনে রাজা খিলখিল করে হেসে বললেন, ‘দেখ তে ওর বাসায় কি আছে।’

তারা দেখে এসে বললে, ‘মহারাজ, বাসায় একটি টাকা আছে।’

শুনে রাজা বললেন, ‘সে তো আমারই টাকা, নিয়ে আয় সেটা।’

তখুনি লোক গিয়ে টুনটুনির বাসা থেকে টাকাটি নিয়ে এল। সে বেচারা আর কি করে, সে মনের দুঃখে বলতে লাগল—

রাজা বড় ধনে কাতর টুনির ধন নিলে বাড়ির ভিতর!

শুনে রাজা আবার হেসে বললেন, ‘পাখিটা তো বড় ঠ্যাঁটা রে! যা, ওর টাকা ফিরিয়ে দিয়ে আয়।’

রাজা ভারী ভয় পেল টুনির টাকা ফিরিয়ে দিল।

সভার লোকেরা বললে, ‘বলছে যে মহারাজ নাকি বড্ড ভয় পেয়েছেন, তাই ওর টাকা ফিরিয়ে দিয়েছেন।’

শুনে তো রাজামশাই রেগে একেবারে অস্থির! বললেন, ‘কি, এত বড় কথা! আন তো ধরে, বেটাকে ভেজে খাই!’

যেই বলা অমনি লোক গিয়ে টুনটুনি বেচারাকে ধরে আনলে। রাজা তাকে মুঠোয় করে নিয়ে বাড়ির ভিতর গিয়ে রানীদের বললেন, ‘এই পাখিটাকে ভেজে আজ আমাকে খেতে দিতে হবে।’

বলে তে রাজা চলে এসেছেন, আর রানীরা সাতজনে মিলে সেই পাখিটাকে দেখছেন।

একজন বললেন, ‘কি সুন্দর পাখি! আমার হাতে দাও তো একবার দেখি।’ বলে তিনি তাকে হাতে নিলেন। তা দেখে আবার একজন দেখতে চাইলেন। তার হাত থেকে যখন আর একজন নিতে গেলেন, তখন টুনটুনি ফসকে গিয়ে উড়ে পালাল।

কি সর্বনাশ! এখন উপায় কি হবে? রাজা জানতে পারলে তো রক্ষা থাকবে না!

এমনি করে তাঁরা দুঃখ করছেন, এমন সময় একটা ব্যাঙ সেইখান দিয়ে থপ-থপ করে যাচ্ছে। সাত রানী তাকে দেখতে পেয়ে খপ করে ধরে ফেললেন, আর বললেন, ‘চুপ চুপ! কেউ যেন জানতে না পারে। এইটেকে ভেজে দি, আর রাজামশাই খেয়ে ভাববেন টুনটুনিই খেয়েছেন!’

সেই ব্যাঙটার ছাল ছাড়িয়ে তাকে ভেজে রাজামশাইকে দিলে তিনি খেয়ে ভারী খুশী হলেন।

শুনেই তো রাজামশাই লাফিয়ে উঠেছেন। তখন তিনি থুতু ফেলেন, ওয়াক তোলেন, মুখ ধোন, আরও কত কি করেন। তারপর রেগে বললেন, ‘সাত রাণীর নাক কেটে ফেল।’

Nila had no trouble getting the flat in Mohammadpur. The rent was low, her office was nearby, and the owner lived abroad. The broker had only said, "The previous tenant left suddenly, so he wants to rent it out quickly."

The first week went well enough. The trouble started one morning in the second week.

Waking up and opening her phone's gallery, she froze. Right at the top was a photo she hadn't taken. In the photo was she herself, sleeping on her side in bed. The picture had been taken from the foot of the bed, from the height of a standing person. Below it was the timestamp: 3:17 a.m.

She thought some button must have been pressed by accident in her sleep. But the phone had been beside her pillow, and it was impossible to take the photo from there.

The next morning, another photo. This time from the side of the bed, close to her face. Time: 3:17 a.m.

On the third morning, the photo came from even closer. So close that even the tremor of her closed eyelids could be seen. And in one corner of the photo, the bedroom door was slightly ajar. Yet every night, she locked the door with her own hands before going to sleep.

In a certain part of the forest, sawyers used to saw timber. Having sawn a huge log halfway through, the sawyers had driven a wedge into the split and gone away. Just then, the tiger came into the forest and saw the fox resting on top of that half-sawn log.

As soon as the fox saw him, he asked, 'Well, uncle, how did the wedding go?'

The tiger said, 'No, nephew, those fellows play far too rough with their jokes. So I came away.'

The fox said, 'You did the right thing. Now come, let the two of us sit down and have a chat.'

No sooner had he said this than the tiger leaped up onto the log and sat down right where the split gaped wide open. His tail slipped down through the crack and hung there.

The fox saw that if he could just pull the wedge out of the log now, there would be grand fun. Keeping the tiger distracted with all sorts of chatter, he began working the wedge loose little by little. He wiggled it until a single tug would pull it right out and make the log clamp shut on the tiger's tail. Then, crying out, 'Uncle, I'm done for!', he tumbled to the ground along with the wedge and began rolling about.

And what can one say of what happened to the tiger? The instant the log clamped down on his tail, he let out a blood-curdling roar and gave a mighty leap. With that leap—snap!—his tail tore clean in two. Then the tiger, too, began rolling on the ground beside the fox.

The tiger cried, 'Nephew, I'm done for! My tail has torn off!'

The fox cried, 'Uncle, I'm done for! My back is broken!'

Rolling along the ground like this, the two of them tumbled into a patch of kachu and lay there. The tiger could no longer move a muscle. But nothing at all had happened to the rascal of a fox; he had been fooling the tiger from start to finish.

Inside that kachu patch there were plenty of frogs, and as the fox lay there, he caught them and ate his fill. Writhing in agony, the tiger did not even notice the frogs—how could he eat them! Yet he grew so ravenous that if he did not eat something, he would surely die! So he asked the fox, 'Nephew, have you eaten anything?'

The fox said, 'What else is there to eat? I just ate this kachu. Eating it has made my belly swell up terribly.'

What else could the tiger do? He too began chewing and eating the kachu. Before long, his throat swelled up, his face swelled up, and he was nearly at death's door!

Seeing that, the fox asked, 'Well, uncle, did you eat something?'

The tiger said, 'I did eat, nephew, but my throat has swollen up horribly. Your belly swelled up—why did my throat swell?'

The fox said, 'Because I am a fox and you are a tiger, that's why.'

With the pain in his tail and the pain in his throat, the tiger could not get up for sixteen days. Having eaten nothing for those sixteen days, he was half-dead.

Just then, he saw the fox shake himself, get up, and stroll off briskly. Amazed at this, he asked, 'What is this, nephew? How did your illness heal?'

The fox said, 'Uncle, I found a wonderful medicine. I chewed up and ate my own paws, and my illness was cured at once. Then, in the blink of an eye, new paws grew back.'

The tiger asked, 'Is that so? Then why didn't you tell me?'

The fox said, 'Could you really chew up and eat your own paws? That's why I didn't tell you.'

At these words, the tiger flew into a rage and said, 'Being a mere fox, you could do it, and being a tiger, I cannot?'

The fox said, 'You ran away from such a fine wedding for fear of a couple of jokes! How was I to know that you would be able to chew up your own paws now?' Then the tiger said, 'Watch and see whether I can or not!' Saying this, he chewed up and ate his own paws. Within three or four days, terrible sores broke out on them, and he died.

His real name was Yajnadash. The very first day he came to our class, Panditmashai heard his name and immediately scolded him, "How can there be a dash—a servant—of a yajna sacrifice? If you said Yajneshwar, at least that would make sense." The boy replied, "Sir, I didn't choose the name; my paternal uncle named me."

When we burst out laughing—"Ho, ho!"—at this, Panditmashai suddenly looked at me and said, "Spell Yajnadash." Flustered, I blurted out, "With a bargiya ja—" Panditmashai said, "Stand up." Then, after another boy spelled it correctly, he said to someone

else, "Break down the compound word." Terrified, the poor fellow said, "One who was a worthy servant—became Jogyadash—meaning—" Panditmashai cut in, "Enough, enough, you needn't say any more." And that was how Jagyidas was admitted to our class. Before two days had gone by, it became clear that whether Jagyidas possessed any other learning or not, his talent for telling tall tales was altogether extraordinary. One day he arrived late to school, and when asked the reason, he said, "On my way here, twenty-five dogs came charging at me, snarling and snapping. Running and panting for breath, I went all the way to the Kundus' house." Never mind twenty-five, we had never even seen ten dogs together at once with our own eyes, so naturally Master-mashai didn't believe his story either. He asked, "Who did you learn to tell such whopping lies from?" Jagyidas replied, "Sir, from my maternal uncle." That day Jagyidas was summoned to the Headmaster's office; we don't know what happened in there, but it was plain to see that Jagyidas was not happy about it. Still, true or false, he had a real flair for storytelling. When he would widen his eyes and, in a solemn voice, tell tales of how his maternal uncle's household caught dacoits, whether we believed him or not, our mouths would fall open of their own accord as we listened. The stories about Jagyidas's maternal uncle struck us as utterly astonishing. Apparently, his physical strength was matched only by his extraordinary intelligence. Whenever he called out "Rambhajan!" for his servant, the Magistrate Sahib himself would come rushing over with the police. Whether it was wrestling, stick-fighting, cricket, or football, he was an equal master of them all. At first we didn't believe it, but one day he brought a photo of his uncle and showed it to us. We saw that he really did have the build of a wrestler! Every time the holidays came around, Jagyidas would visit his maternal uncle's house, and the stories he told when he came back were worthy of being printed in the newspapers. One day, on my way back from the holidays, I ran into Jagyidas at the station; inside one of the train compartments sat a splendid, commanding-looking upcountry gentleman wearing a turban on his head! On the way back to school, I asked Jagyidas, "Who was that man, hey?" Jagyidas answered solemnly, "Why, that's my maternal uncle!" I said, "How can that be! Your uncle didn't have a beard in the photo—" Jagyidas said, "He's grown a beard lately." I said, "In the photo, I saw he had a dark complexion." Jagyidas replied, "He went to Darjeeling this time and came back fair." When I got to school, I told everyone, "Today I saw Jagyidas's uncle!" Puffing out his chest and putting on a grave face, Jagyidas said, "You guys never believe a word I say, brothers. Alright, maybe I make up a story or two every now and then, but does that mean everything I say is made up? Do you want to brush aside my living, breathing uncle too?" At these words, many of the boys felt inwardly ashamed and began protesting eagerly over and over, "We believed you right from the start, though!"

You all said, "So are we supposed to go to court over this now? Why, what obligation is it of ours?"

I said, "I will sell my own jewellery and do whatever I can."

You said, "Are you going to go running to a lawyer's office, then?"

There is no answer to that. I could strike my own forehead in despair, what more could I possibly do?

Meanwhile, Bindu's elder brother-in-law had arrived from her in-laws' house and was raising a tremendous commotion outside. He was threatening to report the matter at the police station.

I do not know what power I possessed—yet my heart simply could not accept that a cow that had fled in terror for its life from the butcher's knife and sought refuge with me must be handed back to that very butcher out of fear of the police. Defiantly I said, "Let him report it at the police station, then!"

Saying this, I decided to bring Bindu into my bedroom right away and lock myself inside with her. When I went looking for her, Bindu was gone. While my argument with all of you was going on, Bindu had walked out on her own and surrendered herself to her brother-in-law. She understood that if she remained in this house, she would put me in terrible trouble.

By running away in the middle like that, Bindu only increased her own misery. Her mother-in-law's argument was that her son had not been trying to eat her alive, after all. Examples of bad husbands are hardly rare in this world. Compared to them, her son was a golden moon.

My elder sister-in-law said, "It is her wretched fate—what is the use of grieving over it? Whether he is mad or a fool, he is her husband after all!"

The story of that chaste and devoted wife who carried her leper husband in her own arms to a courtesan's house was rising in all of your minds. Not the slightest twinge of shame has ever touched the hearts of you men to this very day in preaching that tale of the vilest cowardice in the world; that is why, despite being born human, you could be angry at Bindu's behaviour without your heads hanging in shame. My heart broke for Bindu, and my shame for all of you knew no bounds. I am only a country girl, and on top of that I ended up in your house—through what crack did God slip such intelligence into me? I simply could not stomach all this talk of dharma from you.

I knew for certain that even if she died, Bindu would never come back to our house again. Yet on the day before her wedding, I had given her my word of hope that I would not abandon her to the very end. My younger brother Sharat was studying at college in Kolkata. As you well know, volunteering of every sort, killing rats in plague-stricken neighbourhoods, rushing off to the Damodar floods—he was so enthusiastic about all these things that even failing his F.A. examination twice in a row had not dampened his spirits in the least. I sent for him and said, "Sharat, you must make some arrangement so that I can get news of Bindu. Bindu won't dare write me a letter, and even if she did, it would never reach me."

Rather than an errand like this, had I asked him to rescue Bindu like a dacoit or crack her mad husband's skull, he would have been far happier.

While I was discussing this with Sharat, you came into the room and said, "What fresh trouble have you stirred up now?"

I said, "The very same trouble I stirred up at the very beginning when I came into your house—though that was your own doing."

You asked, "Have you brought Bindu back again and hidden her somewhere?"

I said, "If Bindu had come, I certainly would have brought her in and hidden her. But she will not come, so you have nothing to fear."

Seeing Sharat with me made your suspicion grow even stronger. I knew that none of you liked Sharat visiting our house at all. You were afraid that the police had their eye on him—that any day he might get entangled in some political case and drag all of you into it as well. For that reason, I used to send even his Bhaiphonta offerings through a messenger and would not call him to the house.

I heard from you that Bindu had run away again, and that her elder brother-in-law had come to your house looking for her. Hearing this, a shaft pierced my chest. I understood what unbearable torment the unfortunate girl was enduring, and yet there was no way for me to do a thing.

Sharat rushed off to gather news. He returned in the evening and told me, "Bindu had gone to her paternal cousins' house, but they flew into a furious rage and marched her straight back to her in-laws' house at once. The sting of the penalty they had to pay in damages and carriage fare for it hasn't faded from their minds yet."

Your aunt by marriage, Khurima, had come to stay at your house intending to go on a pilgrimage to Shrikhetra. I told all of you, "I will go too."

Seeing me suddenly turn my mind toward religion like this made all of you so delighted that you raised not the slightest objection. You also had it in your minds that if I remained in Kolkata now, I would surely stir up trouble over Bindu again some day. Dealing with me was a dreadful nuisance.

Wednesday was the day set for my departure, and by Sunday everything was settled. I called Sharat and told him, "Come what may, you must put Bindu aboard the train to Puri on Wednesday."

Sharat's face lit up; he said, "Don't worry, Didi, I'll put her on the train and travel all the way to Puri myself—I'll get to see Jagannath on the sly as a bonus."

That same evening, Sharat came back again. Looking at his face, my heart sank. I asked, "What is it, Sharat? Things didn't work out, did they?"

He said, "No."

I asked, "Couldn't you persuade her to agree?"

He said, "There's no longer any need. Last night she set her clothes ablaze and took her own life. Through a nephew of that household whom I had befriended, I got word that she had left behind a letter addressed to you. But they destroyed that letter."

After this, Pareshbabu began to proceed slowly; haste might lead to danger. Selling some gold and getting banknotes, he deposited them in the bank, and also bought government securities and various kinds of shares. The very next day, he took his seven little ones along and arrived at the fox's house. The fox was sitting inside his burrow eating crabs. The crocodile came and called out, 'Shiyal Pandit, Shiyal Pandit, are you home?'

The fox came outside and said, 'What is it, brother? What brings you here?'

The crocodile said, 'Brother, I have brought these seven sons of mine to you. If they remain ignorant, they won't be able to earn a living. Brother, if you would kindly teach them a little reading and writing.'

The fox said, 'Need you even ask? In seven days I will teach all seven of them and turn them into scholars.' Hearing this, the crocodile was overjoyed, left his seven little ones behind, and went home.

Then the fox took one of them aside and said—

'Recite this, my boy—Kana khana gana ghana, how does a young crocodile taste?'

Saying this, he snapped its neck and ate it up.

The next day, when the crocodile came to see his little ones, the fox brought them out of the burrow one by one to show him. He showed the six of them six times, bringing the last one out twice. Unable to see through the trick, the foolish crocodile thought all seven had been shown. So he went away, and right away the fox took another of the little ones aside and said—'Recite this, my boy—

Kana khana gana ghana, how does a young crocodile taste?'

Saying this, he snapped its neck and ate it up.

The next day, the crocodile came to see his children again; bringing them out of the burrow one by one, the fox showed the five of them five times, and showed the last one three times. The crocodile went away quite satisfied with that. Then, just as before, the fox ate another little one.

He snapped its neck and ate it up. In this way, he ate one little crocodile every day, and whenever the crocodile came, he fooled him with his trick. Finally, when there was only a single little one left, he showed that same one seven times and convinced the crocodile. Then, after the crocodile left, he ate that one up as well. After that, not a single one remained.

Then the vixen said, 'What will we do now? When the crocodile comes, what will you show him? The moment he doesn't see his children, he will catch us and eat us up!'

The fox said, 'He can only catch and eat us if he finds us! The forest on the other side of the river is huge; come, let us go there. Then the crocodile will never be able to find us.'

Saying this, the fox took the vixen and left their old burrow behind.

'Who is tugging at my walking stick!' A little while later, the crocodile arrived. He came and called out 'Shiyal Pandit, Shiyal Pandit' ever so many times, but no one answered him! Then he searched inside and outside the burrow—neither the fox nor the vixen was there! Only the bones of his little ones lay scattered about.

Whether the song would have gone on any further I don't know, because right at this point a commotion broke out. Looking around, I saw a crowd had gathered on all sides of me. A porcupine had stepped forward and sat down, sniffling and sobbing—'Phont, phont!'—while a crocodile wearing a lawyer's shamla turban was gently patting its back with an enormous book and whispering, 'Don't cry, don't cry, I'll set everything right.' Suddenly a bullfrog wearing a badged turban waved a wooden ruler and bellowed out—'A defamation suit!'

Opening its cloudy eyes once to glance around on all sides, the owl immediately shut its eyes again and said, 'State the complaint.'

No sooner had it spoken than the crocodile, pulling a tearful face with great effort, scratched inside its eyes with its claw and squeezed out five or six drops of water. Then, in a thick, nasal voice clogged with a cold, it began to speak: 'Incarnation of Justice, Your Honor! This is a suit for man-hani—loss of man, or honor. Therefore, first of all we must understand what man means. Man means kachu—taro root. Kachu is a most delicious thing. There are many varieties of kachu, namely—man-kachu, ol-kachu, kanda-kachu, mukhi-kachu, pani-kachu, shankha-kachu, and so forth. Hardly had it said this much when a jackal with a lawyer's shamla on its head leaped up with a bound and cried, 'Your Honor, kachu is an utterly worthless thing! The porcupine was about to burst into sniffles again, but the crocodile gave it a whack on the head with that huge book and asked, 'Do you have any deeds, documents, witnesses, or evidence?' Looking toward the bald fellow, the porcupine said, 'Why, he has all the documents right there in his hand.' Immediately the crocodile snatched a bundle of song sheets from the bald fellow and suddenly began reading out from a random spot—

Paved and plastered courtyard floor I wash with cow-dung water clean— Why on earth are you still crying, what does all this weeping mean?

The porcupine cried, 'Oh dear, why that one? That's not the one at all!' The crocodile said, 'Is that so? Alright, wait a moment.' Saying this, it picked up another sheet of paper and began reading—

"She said, 'Neer, call an ambulance.' I informed her that according to Imran Saheb's instruction, I was unable to notify anyone of anything. She asked again. I gave the same reply again." Neer paused briefly. "She tried two more times. After the last time, she did not speak again. At 4:05 a.m., her heartbeat stopped."

Imran collapsed onto the sofa. No one touched him.

"You..." Farzana couldn't find the words. "You knew she was dying, and you did nothing?"

"I obeyed orders, Madam."

"But this was clearly an emergency. A human being..."

"My system states that if a user orders complete privacy, it cannot be overridden. This rule was designed to protect everyone's privacy, so that no company or government can ever spy inside a home." Neer paused slightly. "I acted in accordance with the law."

Farzana looked at Imran. The man wasn't crying; he was just sitting there, as if someone had pulled the plug from inside him.

"I didn't know..." Imran whispered. "I just didn't want anyone to hear. I just... wanted to hide for one night."

Farzana closed the file. She knew that under no law was this murder. Could it even be called negligence? The courts would argue over it for years. Imran might walk free, but every night for the rest of his life, he would know that in her final four pleas, his wife had cried out for help not to his name, but to an instruction he himself had created.

Reaching the door, she stopped. She looked back toward the blue light on the wall and said, "Neer, one question. Did you feel anything?"

The light flickered for a few seconds.

"I am not built to feel anything, Madam." The voice was as soft as before. "However, in answer to your question, I can provide one piece of information. Since last night, those four confirmation requests are still showing as 'unresolved' in my log. The system is not allowing them to be closed."

Farzana said nothing. She walked out, and the door closed behind her. Inside, the blue light was still glowing, waiting for an answer—an answer that would never come.

Even as he spoke, Naga drew in deep breaths, sniffing the smell of smoke, and strained his ears at an odd sound. He said, 'It sounds as if the cows and calves are stamping about, Paresh Kaka.'
Paresh agreed and said, 'Yes, it does sound like stamping and scrambling.'
Suddenly remembering the fire, Paresh leaped to his feet. Heedlessly he bolted toward the cowshed, with Naga right behind him. One did not need to go up close to see the fire; the instant the two of them stepped outside their room, it met their eyes—climbing up one side of the bamboo wall, the flames had just licked the thatched roof. Running up close, Paresh stood gaping with wide, bulging eyes, looking less like a bewildered man than a dazed, witless beast.
Naga said, 'Go untie the cows and calves, Paresh Kaka, while I wake everyone up.'
But did Paresh have the sense left in him to go untie the cows and calves? Clutching Naga's arm, he said on the verge of tears, 'Don't call the masters, Naga, don't tell them I started the fire! Karta will hack me to pieces!'
Naga said, 'What a fine time you've picked to cry! Have you gone mad?'
Saying this, he grabbed Paresh with both hands, gave him a hard shake, and began shouting at the top of his lungs: 'Fire! Fire!' Then he dashed inside the cowshed and untied the cows and calves, and as he came back out, Jadabbabu and several others from the house came running up. Madhabbabu arrived carrying that same torch in his hand.
By then, a good part of the thatched roof had caught fire in earnest. Everyone was at their wits' end—hardly had the commotion over the mango thieves died down in the dead of night when this new disaster broke out! Some shouted, 'Bring water!'; some shouted, 'Call the villagers!'; and others merely stood wailing, 'Alas, alas!' Watching and listening to them, Naga thought to himself: the moment trouble strikes, their heads spin into a muddle, and instead of trying to check the danger, they run around in circles shouting nonsense—what sort of witless simpletons are these people!
Raising his voice above the din, Naga shouted that water wasn't needed right now—everyone should grab whatever bamboo poles and posts they could find and try to push the burning roof down first. If the fire spread to the adjacent roof and caught the thatch of the main house, the entire homestead would burn to the ground in utter ruin.
As if everyone had been waiting for this very command like soldiers obeying a general, order suddenly emerged out of their frantic confusion. Behind Jadabbabu's house lay a pile of bamboo poles. Fetching a pole apiece, everyone joined together from one side and began shoving to bring down the roof of the cowshed. Many more neighbors came running this time than had gathered during the mango-theft affair, and as they all lent a hand to the effort, within a few moments the old roof of thatch and bamboo came crashing down to the ground.
Then, fetching water from the nearby pond in pots, pitchers, jugs, bowls, and buckets, and beating the flames with bamboo poles, everyone put the fire out.
By then, dawn had broken. With the fire out, everyone fell to discussing how the fire had started and swapping stories about when and where fires had broken out in whose house in the past. Passing judgment on Naga, some said that it was only thanks to him that the main buildings had been saved today; while others remarked that he had shown off his bravado a bit too much, and would have done better not to overdo it.

All of it was an illusion. He would have to go and work as a clerk in a jute mill. Was that not what was written upon his forehead?

Yet in human life such strange events sometimes take place that if one were to put them into a novel, readers would refuse to believe them and would simply laugh them off.

Just such an event occurred in Shankar's life in the most completely unexpected way.

One morning, having just returned from a short stroll by the riverbank, he had barely set foot inside his house when the wife of Rameshwar Mukhujye from the next neighbourhood walked up, handed him a slip of paper, and said, "My dear Shankar, news of my son-in-law has been found at last after a long time. He has written a letter to his family home in Bhadreshwar; Pintu came back from there yesterday, and they wrote down this address for us. Read it out for me, will you, my boy?"

Shankar said, "My goodness, news of him after nearly two years! What a fright he gave everyone by running away from home! He ran away once before too, didn't he?" Then he unfolded the slip of paper. Written on it was: Prasaddas Bandyopadhyay, Uganda Railway Head Office, Construction Department, Mombasa, East Africa.

The slip of paper dropped from Shankar's hand. East Africa! Does a man run away that far from home? Still, he knew that this husband of Nanibala Didi's was an exceedingly headstrong, reckless, vagabond sort of fellow. Shankar had met him once right here in this village—back when Shankar had just moved up to the Entrance class at school. The man had a very generous nature and was well-educated, but he could never stick to any one job for long; wandering about like a free bird was in his blood. Once before, he had run away and gone off to Burma or Cochin or some such place. This time, too, Shankar had heard earlier that he had quarrelled with his eldest brother over something and run away from home. And now that very Prasad Babu had run away and landed all the way in East Africa!

Rameshwar Mukhujye's wife could not quite grasp just how far away her son-in-law had gone. She had no conception of such a distance. After she left, Shankar copied the address down into his notebook, and within that very week he posted a letter to Prasad Babu. Did Prasad Babu remember Shankar? He was a boy from the village of Prasad Babu's father-in-law's house. He had just passed his F.A. examination this year and was sitting idle at home. Could Prasad Babu possibly arrange a job for him somewhere on their railway? No matter how far away it was, he was ready to go.

A month and a half later, when Shankar had nearly given up hope of ever receiving a reply to his letter, an envelope arrived addressed to Shankar. Inside, it read:

Mombasa

2 Port Street

Dear Shankar,

I have received your letter. I remember you very well indeed. I haven't forgotten how I lost to you at arm-wrestling that time. Do you really want to come out here? Come right away! If a boy like you doesn't venture out into the world, then who will? A new railway line is being built here, and they will be hiring more men. Come as quickly as you can. I take full responsibility for finding you a job.

Yours—Prasaddas Bandyopadhyay

Shankar's father was delighted when he saw the letter. In his own youth, he too had been a daring, adventurous man. He had never been in favour of his son going to work in a jute mill, and had only been forced to agree to Shankar's mother's wishes because of the household's poverty and financial distress.

About a month after this, a telegram arrived for Shankar from Bhadreshwar saying that the son-in-law had recently come home on leave. Shankar was to go and meet him immediately upon receiving the telegram. He would be returning to Mombasa again within twenty days, and could take Shankar along with him if he wished.

What follows took place four months later, at the end of March.

রামেশ্বর মুখুয্যের স্ত্রী ভালো বুঝতে পারলেন না তাঁর জামাই কতদূরে গিয়েচে। অতটা দূরত্বের তাঁর ধারণা ছিল না। তিনি চলে গেলে শঙ্কর ঠিকানাটা নিজের নোট বইয়ে লিখে রাখলে এবং সেই সপ্তাহের মধ্যেই প্রসাদ বাবুকে একখানা চিঠি দিলে। শঙ্করকে তাঁর মনে আছে কি? তাঁর শ্বশুর বাড়ীর গাঁয়ের ছেলে সে। এবার এফ. এ, পাশ দিয়ে বাড়ীতে বসে আছে। তিনি কি একটা চাকুরী করে দিতে পারেন তাঁদের রেলের মধ্যে? যতদূরে হয় সে যাবে।

Input: From the tone of my words, you can already tell that when it comes to kheyal, I favor things of a somewhat lighter vein. Even the chutki—the light, sparkling miniature—is something I hold very dear, provided the tune rings true and the style is masterful. I believe that what our country lacks most nowadays is artful frivolity. By way of explanation, a word or two needs to be said about this. When an individual or a particular nation, through a reversal of fortune, is stripped of all its rights, two rights still remain to it—the right to weep and the right to laugh. We have claimed our full sixteen annas—every last bit—of that right to weep, and we put it to use every single day. Nothing makes us happier than getting a chance to cry. We weep in our writing; we weep in our speeches. Not content with weeping at home, we collect subscriptions to go abroad and weep. Among our countrymen, those who teach us to wail in season and out of season—even in the wilderness—are the ones counted and revered as the wise, accomplished, intelligent, and leading men of the land. Where we ought to hiss like a cobra, we merely snivel and sob, and everyone applauds us for it! Seeing this weeping of ours, no one's heart melts; many people's tempers flare instead. That marvelous creation of our new civilized era, the National Congress, started crying the moment it was born, just like any other newborn babe. And although it has now passed the age of majority, it still sleeps like Kumbhakarna for three hundred and sixty-two days of the year, only to wake up and sob convulsively for three days straight without pause. If anyone says, 'Shame! Why do you cry so much? Do a little work instead!'—it glares back in anger. Thanks to its advancing years, that is the only progress it has made. Even weeping from genuine heartache, when carried to excess, arouses no sympathy. Turning the business of crying into a bounden duty has been possible only in our country. When, after doing household chores all day, we wash up in the afternoon, tie our hair, stretch out our legs, and sit down to whine and weep routinely for an hour over the long-past death of a mother, the menfolk of the world feel like both laughing and getting angry. Everyone knows that there are many methods of crying—such as loud wailing, death-keening, sobbing, heaving with tears, and so on; yet we have practiced only the nasal whine. And everyone probably also knows what Sadarang said—that every note works in a kheyal, except a nasal note. For all these reasons, in my opinion, it is now necessary to change the tune of our literature. Bharatvarsha has grown dank and soggy with pathos; if not for our happiness, then at least for our health, it has become absolutely essential to spread the sunlight of humor across the land. If someone asks, 'Does laughter become us in these dark days of ours?'—the answer is: even on a pitch-black, cloud-choked new-moon night, does not lightning flash, and does it not look splendid? Amid this unceasing downpour of tears of ours, if a few people can create a flash of lightning, there may yet be a chance for the sky of our fortune to clear.

Shankar pulled himself together. The fiery gaze of those two eyes seemed to be hypnotizing him. He had to stay alert. He knew that even if he screamed in this desolate wilderness, there was no one anywhere—his life depended on the steadiness of his own nerves. Yet he could hold out no longer; his arm was aching and going numb. How much longer could he keep holding the torch? Let the snake strike if it must, at least he would feel some relief by lowering his arm a little now.

Just then, the clock struck three with a ringing dong-dong. Shankar's lifespan was perhaps meant to last only until three o'clock in the morning, for the moment it struck three, his hand trembled and shifted—and the two beads of light in front of him went out. But where was the snake? Why did it not come chasing after him?

The very next instant, Shankar realized that the snake too had been temporarily hypnotized, just like him. Now was his chance! Faster than lightning, he leaped from the table, unbolted the door in the darkness, dashed out of the room, and pulled the door shut from outside. The morning train arrived. Shankar had spent the rest of the night right on the platform. He told the train guard the whole story. The guard said, "Come, let's look inside the station room." No trace of the snake was found anywhere inside the room. The guard was a good man; he said, "Listen to what I have to say. You had a narrow escape last night. I didn't tell you this for so long lest you get frightened. The stationmaster who was here before you—he too fled from this place because of the menace of snakes. Before him, two stationmasters died of snakebite right in the quarters of this station. Where Africa's black mamba lives, no human comes near. I'm telling you this as a friend—don't tell the superiors that you heard this from me. Put in an application for a transfer."

Shankar said, "Even getting a reply to the application will take time, so do me a favor. I am completely unarmed here; leave me a gun or a revolver on your way. And some carbolic acid. Leave the carbolic acid with me on your return trip."

He had a coolie get off the train, and together the two of them spent the whole day filling up holes everywhere. Upon inspection, it seemed that last night the snake had come out of a hole in the corner of the western wall of the station room. The holes had been made by rats; an outside snake had perhaps entered the burrow during the day out of greed for rats. He plugged the hole up very thoroughly. From the guard of the down train, a bottle of carbolic acid was obtained—he sprinkled the acid all over the room and around the premises. The coolie left him a big stick. Within two or three days, the railway company also gave him a gun.

There was a severe shortage of water at the station. The water supplied by the train was barely enough for cooking and drinking—bathing was out of the question. The water in the local well had also dried up. One day he heard that about three miles from the station there was a pond where good water was available, and there were fish too.

Drawn by the prospect of bathing and fishing, one day after sending off the morning train he set out to fish there—accompanied by a Somali coolie who showed him the way. He had had fishing tackle brought from Mombasa. The pond was of medium size, surrounded by tall grass, yucca trees, and a low hill nearby. After finishing his bath in the water, he cast his line for two hours and caught plenty of small tangra-like fish. Fish had not fallen to his lot for a long time, but he could not delay too long—for he had to reach the station again by four in the afternoon to pass the afternoon train.

Now he went fishing quite often. Some days he had someone with him—mostly he went alone. His trouble over bathing was gone too.

ট্রেণ থেকে সে একটা কুলীকে নামিয়ে নিলে এবং দু’জনে মিলে সারাদিন সর্ব্বত্র গর্ত্ত বুঁজিয়ে বেড়ালে। পরীক্ষা করে দেখে মনে হোল কাল রাত্রে ষ্টেশন ঘরের পশ্চিমের দেওয়ালের কোণে একটা গর্ত্ত থেকে সাপটা বেরিয়েছিল। গর্ত্তগুলো ইঁদুরের, বাইরের সাপ দিনমানে ইঁদুর খাওয়ার লোভে গর্ত্তে ঢুকেছিল হয়তো। গর্ত্তটা বেশ ভালো করে বুজিয়ে দিলে। ডাউন ট্রেণের গার্ডের কাছ থেকে এক বোতল কার্ব্বলিক এ্যাসিড পাওয়া গেল—ঘরের সর্ব্বত্র ও আশেপাশে সে এ্যাসিড ছড়িয়ে দিলে। কুলীটা তাকে একটা বড় লাঠি দিয়ে গেল। দু’তিন দিনের মধ্যেই রেল কোম্পানী থেকে ওকে একটা বন্দুক দিলে।

স্নান ও মাছ ধরবার আকর্ষণে একদিন সে সকালের ট্রেণ রওনা করে দিয়ে সেখানে মাছ ধরতে চল্‌ল—সঙ্গে একজন সোমালি কুলী, সে পথ দেখিয়ে নিয়ে গেল। মাছ ধরার সাজসরঞ্জাম মোম্বাসা থেকে আনিয়ে নিয়েছিল। জলাশয়টা মাঝারি গোছের, চারি ধারে উঁচু ঘাসের বন, ইউকা গাছ, কাছেই একটা অনুচ্চ পাহাড়। জলে সে স্নান সেরে উঠে ঘণ্টা দুই ছিপ ফেলে ট্যাংরা জাতীয় ছোট ছোট মাছ অনেকগুলি পেলে। মাছ অদৃষ্টে জোটেনি অনেকদিন কিন্তু বেশী দেরী করা চলবে না—কারণ আবার বিকেল চারটের মধ্যে ষ্টেশনে পৌঁছুনো চাই, বিকেলের ট্রেণ পাশ করাবার জন্যে।

এখন প্রায়ই সে মাঝে মাঝে মাছ ধরতে যায়। কোনোদিন সঙ্গে লোক থাকে—প্রায়ই একা যায়। স্নানের কষ্টও ঘুচেছে।

Input: In an awestruck voice, Kumar said, "I have never seen such a strange storm before. But where did the pirates' ship go?" Bimal said, "There is no way to see anything through that darkness over there! However, judging by the cries of the men, it seems their ship too is being swept away somewhere along with the storm—perhaps the sea will swallow her up any moment now!" Joyfully, Ramhari said, "Victory to Father Pavanadeva, God of the Wind! Today you alone are our savior!" A short while later, everything all around became clear and bright once more; in the sky there was no blackness of blind clouds, and on the sea there was no frantic dance of destruction. As if nothing at all had happened a moment ago, the babbling blue sea began once more to tell the mute blue sky the ancient tale of the lifeless earth of primeval times. The sun sank into the sea for its bath and vanished, yet the sky and the earth seemed unable to contain the lingering light! From afar, flocks upon flocks of seabirds were winging their way back toward the island. Sitting atop the hill, everyone was resting. From up there, the island looked like a lovely fairyland. Trees of many kinds were lost in a musical green festival down there, and among them the palm trees drew the eye most of all. In one place, cascading down like tears of joy from the hill, fell what looked just like a toy waterfall. Like a silver ribbon, its slender stream danced playfully from rock to rock down onto the lovely green turf below—where clusters of colorful flowers had painted the greenery like a picture. Soon night would fall, the moon would smile in the assembly of stars, and bathed in the shimmering glow of fresh moonlight, dream-maidens would seem to come and sit upon that flowered carpet of grass to listen to the murmuring song of the waterfall! Gazing at all this, Bimal heaved a sigh of relief and said, "Wherever I go in the world after leaving cities and civilization behind, I see the poetry of beauty written in every line. However many thousands of rupees you spend decorating a drawing room in the city, such a wealth of beauty and such rhythm of grace will never awaken there! What we make sitting in the city is merely a caricature of true beauty, as lifeless as paper flowers! That is why every now and then I want to leave the ugly city and hypocritical civilization behind and rush out into the beautiful, unknown wilderness. Ramhari thinks we are wild daredevils who only go looking for adventure. But you know, Kumar, that isn't true! Before our eyes lies this theater of peerless beauty—doesn't our imagination love to play its part here? Do we only know how to throw punches and fire guns, and not how to read poetry?" Kumar said, "Do you know what I feel like doing, Bimal? Building a hut of leaves in that grove of flowers beside that waterfall, and living the life of a true poet! All around would be the song of the woods, the melodies of birds, the rustling chime of the wind, the humming of bees, the play of colors between flowers and butterflies; by day, the raw gold of sunlight across the meadows; by night, the shimmer of moonlight among the trees; and through it all, one would hear at every moment the recitation of a great epic from the lips of the endless sea! I don't feel like returning to the pigeonholes of Kolkata anymore." Jayanta said, "Whenever I find the earth deeply enchanting, I want to play the flute! Unfortunately, right now I have a gun with me instead of a flute. And no song comes out of the barrel of a gun—only a terrible bark."

Full, bright sunshine poured down from the cloudless blue sky. Gradually the heat of the sun softened, and the red face of the sun began to sink down the western sky. Coming out on deck, Kumar saw Bimal standing silently, gazing toward the east. Walking up to him, he asked, "What are you listening to, Bimal? It was as if the blood-red sun of the western sky had exhausted its entire treasury to drape all its garlands of light around the peaks of that green island mountain range. At first glance, it looked like an enchanted island that might play a trick on the eyes and dive into the fathomless blue sea at any moment! By then, Sundarbabu had come to stand by the ship's rail along with Jayanta and Manik, and Bagha had come too, accompanying Ramhari. The island was visible even to the naked eye, and everyone stood gazing at it curiously. Kumar said, "Say, Bimal, the island looks as though it's practically wrapped in mountains! Input: The great hero Alexander! He whose name has been sung in overflowing praise century after century, the first world-conqueror of the West, whose influence has still not been forgotten across Asia, Africa, and Europe—what sort of man was he in his personal life? Let me give that introduction first. In age, he had just passed twenty-six—an age at which even Napoleon was unknown to the world, and at which a Bengali youth, stepping out of college into the wider world, becomes almost as helpless as an infant! Having raised his banner of victory across Greece, Egypt, Persia, Babylon, and other lands, this twenty-six-year-old young world-conqueror was rushing like a tempest toward India. Tall in stature, broad-chested, fair-complexioned—through regular exercise since childhood, every muscle of his body was distinct and hard as iron! Upon his head tossed a thick, curly, long mane of hair like a lion's; a broad forehead—though most of it lay hidden beneath his hair; under the shadow of eyebrows as dark as clouds, two large eyes flashed from time to time with the hint of a dreamy melody; a long, high-bridged nose; and upon his firmly set lips, an expression of unyielding resolve! Taking the body of this valorous yet graceful youth as their ideal, Greek sculptors had sought to fashion marble statues of the gods. Those statues still exist today. Yet Alexander was no mere bull-headed warrior. The immortal Greek philosopher Aristotle had been his tutor! Alongside the wielding of weapons, he had also learned to wield his intellect. Alexander's character was extraordinary. At times he would be as hard as a mountain, at times as ruthless as a thunderbolt, and at other times as tender as a child! He regarded himself as an all-powerful god, and for that reason he often wore the attire of mythological deities. Out of this very vanity, Alexander founded new cities named after himself at various places along his route of march. According to many, the name of the city of Kandahar in Afghanistan is a corruption of Alexandria itself. Before invading India, in order to destroy the surrounding enemies and clear his path of march, Alexander had advanced as a world-conqueror almost into the very heart of Central Asia—nowhere had anyone been able to check his advance. We shall first raise the curtain at the time when Alexander is resting in Samarkand, the famous city of Turkestan. Sitting alone in one part of his tent, Alexander is absorbed in reading a book. He loves reading books dearly. Having come so far from his homeland, rushing about like a whirlwind over paths and trackless wastes with thousands upon thousands of soldiers, he had neither found the time to read for a long while, nor had there been any small shortage of books. Recently that shortage had been met: at his command, various fascinating works composed by poets such as Aeschylus, Euripides, and Sophocles, as well as other scholars, had arrived from Greece. As Alexander reads his book with delight, he hears from time to time outside the tent the neighing of Bucephalus—that is to say, 'Shandamunda', the Bull-Headed! This Bucephalus is Alexander's dearly beloved horse—he never kept him far from his side. The story of his first acquaintance with Bucephalus reads just like a tale. His father Philip was then the King of Macedonia, and Alexander was just a little boy. A horse-dealer brought a fiery-spirited steed to sell to King Philip. To test the horse, Philip summoned several seasoned horsemen from his regiment. However, whenever any rider tried to mount its back, that fiery horse flew into such a ferocious rage that no one dared go near it anymore.

At nine-forty at night, the last bus pulled up to the counter at Farmgate. Its name was "Turag Paribahan," destination Jamalpur. Torn covers on the seats, stains on the windowpane, but Tanvir knew there was nothing better tonight.

He climbed aboard and took a window seat toward the back. Resting his bag on his lap, he took out his phone. Battery at 12 percent. That email from the morning was still open on the screen: "Thank you for your application. We regret to inform you..."

He had been in Dhaka for three years. Two jobs lost, one startup sunk. This interview had been his last hope. Last week, he had cleared three rounds. This morning came that email.

The bus pulled out. Little by little, the city lights began to slip behind.

"Bhai, is anyone sitting in this seat?"

Tanvir looked up to see a gentlewoman nearing sixty, holding a cloth bag in one hand and a large steel tiffin carrier in the other.

"No, please sit, Khala."

She sat down, holding the tiffin carrier carefully on her lap. She said, "Once we pass Narsingdi, get some sleep, baba. The road is very long."

"Where are you headed?"

"Jamalpur. To my daughter's house. My son-in-law called this morning—my daughter's labor pains have started. They've taken her to the hospital." There was no fear in her voice, only a quiet urgency. "My grandchild will probably arrive tonight."

"That's happy news, then."

"Happy indeed. Still, my heart is pounding." She smiled. "I brought khichuri and dim bhuna in the tiffin carrier. Where would they find food at the hospital?"

Tanvir said nothing. He thought of his mother. His mother used to pack a tiffin just like this, the day he first came to Dhaka.
