Before leaving, Bindu threw her arms around me and said, "Didi, have all of you truly abandoned me then?"

I said, "No, Bindi, no matter what state you may find yourself in, I will never abandon you to the very end."

Three days passed. A tenant from your estate had given you a sheep for the table; saving it from the fire of your stomach, I had given it a place to live in one corner of our ground-floor coal room. First thing every morning, I would go down myself and feed it grain; having relied on your servants for a day or two, I saw that they were far more inclined towards eating it than feeding it.

That morning, I walked into that room and saw Bindu sitting huddled in a corner. The moment she saw me, she clutched my feet, collapsed to the floor, and began to weep silently.

Bindu's husband was mad.

"Are you telling the truth, Bindi?"

"Could I tell you such a terrible lie, Didi? He is mad. My father-in-law did not approve of this marriage—but he fears my mother-in-law like Yama himself. Before the wedding took place, he went away to Kashi. My mother-in-law stubbornly insisted on getting her son married."

I sank down right onto that heap of coal. A woman shows no mercy to another woman. She says, "She is nothing more than a woman, after all. Even if the boy is mad, he is still a man."

At first glance, one could not tell that Bindu's husband was mad, but on certain days he would grow so violently deranged that he had to be kept locked up in his room. On the night of the wedding he was calm, but after the strain of staying awake all night and all the commotion, from the second day onwards his mind went completely unhinged. At midday, Bindu had sat down to eat her rice off a brass plate when suddenly her husband snatched the plate, rice and all, and flung it out into the courtyard. Somehow the notion had suddenly seized him that Bindu was Rani Rashmoni herself; the servant must surely have stolen her plate of gold and given the Rani his own brass plate to eat rice from. That was why he was furious. Bindu nearly died of terror. On the third night, when her mother-in-law told her to go and sleep in her husband's room, Bindu's heart froze within her. Her mother-in-law had a ferocious temper and lost all sense when angry. She was mad too, and all the more dangerous because she was not completely so. Bindu was forced to enter the room. Her husband was quiet that night. Even so, Bindu's body turned stiff as wood with terror. Late at night, once her husband had fallen asleep, she managed through great resourcefulness to slip away and flee—there is no need to write out the details of it.

My whole body burned with disgust and rage. I said, "A marriage based on such deceit is no marriage at all. Bindu, you stay right here with me just as you were, and let me see who dares take you away."

All of you said, "Bindu is lying."

I said, "She has never told a lie."

You asked, "How do you know?"

I said, "I know for certain."

You tried to frighten me: "If Bindu's in-laws file a police case, we will be in serious trouble."

I said, "Won't the court listen to the fact that they tricked her into marrying a madman?"

Shankar had struck up a close friendship with a Madrasi clerk named Tirumal Appa. Tirumal was a young man who knew English quite well and had a heart full of enthusiasm. He too had run away from home, drawn by the lure of adventure. Sitting beside Shankar since dusk that evening, he had been talking non-stop about his homeland, about his mother and father, and about his little sister. He loved his little sister dearly. Ever since leaving home, it was she whom Tirumal
By the light of the bonfire, Shankar was reading the 'Kenya Morning News'... missed the most. He planned to visit home once at the end of September. Wouldn't the Sahib grant him two months' leave?

Gradually the night grew late. Every now and then the fire died down, and the coolies threw more brushwood onto it. Many of the men got up and went off to sleep. The waning moon of the dark fortnight rose slowly over the distant horizon—casting a play of light and shadow across the entire plain, along with the long, trailing shadows of wild trees.

To Shankar, the beauty of this silent night in a far-off foreign land felt wonderfully strange. Leaning back against a post of the coolies' shed, he gazed steadily at the chiaroscuro of light and darkness across the vast, uninhabited grassland before him, lost in a hundred thoughts. Beyond that baobab tree stretched uncharted territory all the way to Cape Town—and in between lay how many mountains, forests, the prehistoric city of Zimbari, the vast and terrifying Kalahari Desert, the land of diamonds, the land of gold mines!

Once, a great gold-prospecting explorer had been walking along when he tripped over a stone and fell. Picking up the rock he had stumbled over and examining it closely, he saw that it was veined with gold—and right on that spot, a great gold mine was discovered. How many stories like that Shankar had read back home in Bengal!

This was that very Africa—that mysterious continent, the land of gold, the land of diamonds! How many unknown tribes, unknown landscapes, and unknown beasts lay hidden within its boundless tropical forests, who had ever kept count of them?

While pondering all these things, at some point Shankar fell asleep. Suddenly a noise startled him awake. He sat up with a start. The moon had climbed high into the sky, and the dazzling white moonlight was as bright as day. The bonfire had died out completely. All around the ashes of the fire, the coolies lay curled up asleep. Not a sound came from any direction.

Suddenly Shankar's eyes fell on the spot beside him—Tirumal Appa had been sitting right here chatting with him. Where was he? He must have gone inside his tent to sleep, then.

Shankar himself was just getting ready to rise and go to bed when, not far off in the western corner of the plain, the terrifying roar of a lion thundered out. The dim moonlight of the night seemed to shudder at the sound. The coolies scrambled up in panic. Gun in hand, the engineer Sahib stepped out of his tent. It was the first time in his life that Shankar had heard a lion's roar—and in the late-night moonlight across that trackless sea of grass, what an indescribable feeling that roar awakened in his heart! It was not fear, but a mysterious, complex emotion. There was an old Masai coolie in the camp. He said, "The lion has killed a man. Unless it has killed a man, it never roars like that."

From inside the tent, Tirumal's tent-mate suddenly came running out to report that Tirumal's bed was empty. He was nowhere inside the tent.

Everyone was stunned at the news. Shankar went inside the tent himself to check and saw that indeed no one was there. Immediately the coolies lit lanterns, armed themselves with stout sticks, and set out. Every single tent was searched, and everyone shouted out his name at the top of their lungs—but no answer came from Tirumal.

Chand Majhi wanted a maduli too? But a maduli cost three rupees and ten annas. Chand Majhi would have to pay that himself. If a maduli was taken on credit, the maduli wouldn't work at all!

Jadabbabu laughed and said, 'Why should you die, Chand? Give Chand a maduli too, Thakur-mashai.'
Then Chakrabarti Mashai went into the worship room to prepare the madulis, while Chand Majhi took the dust of Jadabbabu's feet on his head and kept repeating over and over that he was not a man, but a god—when suddenly, from out of nowhere, a few animals came charging with a loud clatter of hooves. Jadabbabu turned his head and saw Chakrabarti Mashai's four-legged cow and calf along with a two-legged cowherd. Let loose from the cowshed to go out to the pasture, both the cow and the calf were evidently in high spirits—leaping on all four legs as they galloped along. Chand Majhi, however, did not get a chance to turn his head and look; his whole body suddenly seemed to turn stiff as wood, his eyes rolled up toward his forehead, and trembling all over, he swayed this way and that two or three times before toppling down from the veranda.
Chand had still not regained consciousness. Doctor Ajay had come and examined him, and there was very little hope of Chand surviving. There was nothing more to be done, so leaving Chand behind at Chakrabarti Mashai's house, Jadabbabu had come away. Banka was staying there to nurse his father.
Madhabbabu's wife exclaimed, 'Oh my goodness! Then the fortune-teller was right after all!'
Madhabbabu said, 'He probably had blood pressure, and getting a sudden shock—'
Jadabbabu said, 'Who knows? One moment Doctor Ajay says blood pressure, the next moment he says a weak heart—it's all guesswork.' The morning was already far advanced, though in the cool breeze off the river the heat of the sun could hardly be felt. It was time to cast off the boat now. But in place of Chand and Banka, at least one boatman was needed. Jadabbabu looked toward Naga. Meanwhile, Haru Majhi had gone home, eaten his meal of rice, and come back; now it was Naga's turn to go. Yet despite the urgent pangs in his belly, he had been listening absorbedly to everyone talking on the other boat.
'Naga, listen!'
'What is it, Karta?'
'You need to come with us to Karamtala, Naga.'
'Let's go, Karta.'
But Naga couldn't very well go without eating something first! That problem was solved easily enough. Khoka's mother set luchi, alur dom, and sweets before him, and filling his belly with the very food he had refused a little while ago, Naga took up the oar and sat down.

চাঁদ মাঝি সাগ্রহে বলল, ‘আমারেও একটা মাদুলি দেন ঠাকুরমশায়।’
চাঁদ মাঝিরও মাদুলি চাই? কিন্তু মাদুলির খরচ যে তিন টাকা দশ আনা। সেটা তো দিতে হবে চাঁদ মাঝিকে। ধারে মাদুলি নিলে মাদুলির কোন কাজ তো হবে না!
শুনে চাঁদ মাঝি মুষড়ে গেল। —‘তবে থাক্‌ গিয়া ঠাকুরমশায়! মরণ যদি অদেষ্টে থাকে মরুম, করুম কি!’
যাদববাবু হেসে বললেন, ‘মরবি ক্যান্‌ রে চাঁদ? চাঁদেরে একটা মাদুলি দ্যান ঠাকুরমশায়।’
তারপর চক্রবর্তী মশায় তো গেলেন পূজার ঘরে মাদুলি প্রস্তুত করতে আর চাঁদ মাঝি যাদববাবুর পায়ের ধূলা মাথায় নিয়ে বার বার বলতে লাগল, তিনি মানুষ নন, দেবতা-হঠাৎ কোথা থেকে দড়বড় শব্দে ছুটে এল কয়েকটা জানোয়ার। যাদববাবু মুখ ফিরিয়ে দেখলেন, চক্রবর্তী মশায়ের চারপেয়ে গাই ও বাছুর এবং একটি দু’পেয়ে রাখাল। মাঠে যাবার জন্য গোয়াল থেকে ছাড়া পেয়ে গাই ও বাছুর দু’জনেরই বোধহয় খুব স্ফূর্তি হয়েছিল-চারপায়ে লাফাতে লাফাতে ছুটছে। চাঁদ মাঝি কিন্তু মুখ ফিরিয়ে দেখবার সুযোগ পেল না, সমস্ত শরীরটা হঠাৎ যেন তার কাঠ হয়ে গেল, চোখ কপালে তুলে কাঁপতে কাঁপতে দু’চারবার এদিক্‌ ওদিক্‌ টলে সে দাওয়া থেকে নিচে পড়ে গেল।
এখনো চাঁদের জ্ঞান হয় নি। অজয় ডাক্তার এসে দেখে গেছে, চাঁদের বাঁচবার আশা খুব কম। করবার আর কিছুই নেই, চক্রবর্তী মশায়ের বাড়িতেই চাঁদকে রেখে যাদববাবু চলে এসেছেন। বাঁকা বাপের শুশ্রূষা করছে।
মাধববাবুর স্ত্রী বললেন, ‘ও মা! গণক তো তবে ঠিক বলেছে!’
মাধববাবু বললেন, ‘ব্লাডপ্রেসার ছিল বোধ হয়, হঠাৎ শক খেয়ে—।
যাদববাবু বললেন, ‘কেডা জানে? —অজয় ডাক্তার একবার কয় ব্লাডপ্রেসার, একবার কয় উইক হার্ট—সব আন্দাজী কথা।’ বেলা কম হয় নি, নদীর ঠাণ্ডা বাতাসেও রোদের তেজ টের পাওয়া যায় না। এবার নৌকা ছাড়া দরকার। কিন্তু চাঁদ আর বাঁকার বদলে অন্ততঃ একজন মাঝি তো চাই। যাদববাবু নাগার দিকে তাকালেন। ইতিমধ্যে হারু মাঝি বাড়ি গিয়ে ভাত খেয়ে এসেছে, এবার নাগার যাওয়ার কথা। কিন্তু পেটের ব্যাকুল তাগিদ সত্ত্বেও সে মশগুল হয়ে ও নৌকার সকলের কথা শুনছিল।
‘নাগা শোন!’
‘কি কন কর্তা?’
‘আমাগো লগে তর করমতলা যাওন লাগে নাগা।’
‘চলেন কর্তা।’
কিন্তু যাওয়ার আগে কিছু না খেলে তো চলবে না নাগার! এ সমস্যার মীমাংসা খুব সহজেই হয়ে গেল। খোকার মা লুচি, আলুর দম আর মিষ্টি তার সামনে ধরে দিলেন, খানিকটা আগে যে খাবার সে প্রত্যাখ্যান করেছিল এখন সেই খাবারে পেট ভরিয়ে নাগা বৈঠা নিয়ে বসল।
